corpus.group: Inside and Limbo (Playdead): trial and death, checkpoint spacing, chases, procedural animation, audio (Martin Stig Andersen), no UI, mobile ports

dossier.games: Limbo (Playdead, 2010; Xbox 360 first, then PS3/PC/Vita/iOS 2013-07-03/Switch) and INSIDE (Playdead; development commenced 2010 per Playdead's own slides; Xbox One 2016-06-29, Steam 2016-07-07, PS4 2016-08-23, iOS/Apple TV 2017-12-15, Switch 2018-06-28, macOS 2020-06-23). Both are 2D/2.5D side-view puzzle-platformers built on "trial and death", silent protagonists, zero HUD and zero tutorial text, with audio by Martin Stig Andersen (INSIDE with Søs Gunver Ryberg, Andreas Frostholm and audio programmer Jakob Schmid).
dossier.why_relevant: WOLF//OVERRIDE is a Godot side-view sci-fi horror game with a painterly 2.5D look, hold-to-move plus one USE button, a death model and a mobile target. Playdead's two games are the closest shipped reference for: (1) a side-view camera that "typically points inwards to the screen and only scrolls" with heavy fog/silhouette layering; (2) instant, penalty-free death and respawn that is engineered so audio and streaming never break ("illusion of no time passing"); (3) a per-surface, context-sensitive footstep/breath/cloth system that is the best-documented "real feel" pipeline for a single character (exact speed thresholds and a beat-matching algorithm are published); (4) rooms chunked as ~100 m / 1-3 min puzzle sub-scenes with walk-through continuity and no loading screens; (5) two shipped iOS ports where Playdead documented what touch tweaks they tried, kept and rejected (swipe-toward-object grab, rejected auto-complete); (6) a 2-button, no-UI control vocabulary. Limbo's design talk also gives the decision rules for "learning by dying" that WOLF//OVERRIDE's drop-evidence-on-death model should respect. The main non-overlap: Playdead has no companion, no inventory, and INSIDE's camera/level-design talk (Konsoll 2017) is video-only and could not be transcribed here.

dossier.companion: Not applicable as a companion system: neither Limbo nor INSIDE has an AI partner; the boy is alone, and the engineer-only fallback question never arises. What does transfer is how Playdead makes non-player bodies feel alive and intentional, which is exactly WOLF's problem. (1) The Huddle (INSIDE's late-game blob) is explicitly framed as a group with its own motives: Grøntved's inspiration was crowd-surfing, where "the many individuals share a common goal, but they act slightly differently from one another... Some will gently support the surfer, others will try to keep the surfer fixed in one spot and finally some will downright attempt to tear down the surfer" and the Huddle is "a group of individuals strung together - a group that shares a common goal; that of the player." Its motion is "a network of impulses" where "every impulse is just a vote" from independent logic states (RunState, StumbleState, GetupState, ClimbState, SwimState, GrabState, BalanceAnim, ArmControl, level scripts), and the team "had to tweak for feel by observing the expression of the total system"; result: "there is an unmistakable perceived depth to the motion of the huddle, perhaps because it is so difficult to predict." That is a usable architecture for WOLF: independent intent systems (follow, scout, refuse, protect) voting into one body, with the designer tuning the sum rather than scripting each beat. (2) The Huddle's core is 26 physics bodies with sphere colliders, an adjacency graph of springs with deformable target lengths, and 2 spine bones "driven by logic and animation"; when it falls, the spine is reconfigured vertically instead of rotated ("Could rotate to stand, but looks a bit silly"), and target edge lengths are blended over a short time to hide the pop. (3) Arms grab via an "Aim Point" plus an "Arm Manager" that creates grab positions; "At any point we want at least 2-3 arms holding on to a box"; visual feedback gates simulation: "Boxes can not be lifted until a lifting arm actually touches them." (4) Legs: only 2 pairs of run cycles (high/low) blended by hip-to-ground ray distance, animation speed driven by actual physics velocity "so the feet will not slide", legs half a cycle apart walking and about a quarter cycle apart galloping, deliberate wrong speed to make a leg slide on hard turns, and "Whenever a leg plants, it sends a wave of impulses up the body." Madsen's moral: "to be sure we were on the right track we needed those arms and legs added early... hand drawn stick arms! It does not take much to completely change the perception." (5) The Danish animation talk lists the boy's layer stack (loops, blending, interruptions, simulation/collision/reaction, layers for 'breathe' and 'look around', overrides, idle, themes 'run / sneak / panic / balance', and a slide of 'rejected attempts'), i.e. look-at and breathing are additive layers over locomotion. (6) For crowds (albinos, NPCs) Playdead published the "Starfish Rig": 6 bones total (root, head, 4 extremities from elbow/knee outward), driven by a normal IK rig in the DCC tool, with an inserted vertex above the knee that "pops out creating an illusion of a knee" - useful if WOLF ever needs cheap background figures. (7) In INSIDE the boy mind-controls other bodies via helmets; the game treats those bodies as temporary extensions, not partners (Wikipedia plot summary; no design talk located). UNVERIFIED: any Playdead statement about why they rejected companions.
dossier.level_and_camera: Camera: INSIDE is a 2.5D sidescroller whose camera, per the GDC 2016 rendering talk, "typically points inwards to the screen and only scrolls"; the team exploits this (screen-space reflection rays get sDir.x *= 0 so they never leave the screen). Depth is sold almost entirely by fog and silhouettes: "Many of the initial scenes in the game were literally just fog + silhouettes"; "Simple linear fog!" with one trick: "We clamp the fog to a max-value to enable bright objects to 'bleed through'" (headlights, spotlights), plus a separate glare pass for atmospheric scattering and two separate glow passes because a combined one "interfered too much." Local fog volumes are editor boxes, additive ("we add the light caught by fog in the room, we do not add fog locally"). Underwater, "we also add depth of field to things behind the gameplay plane." Water volumes use a camera-stuck displacement edge spanning "6-12 meters from the camera near clip plane" because "you hardly notice the parallax or depth after a certain point." Shadow decals are "Anchored to boy's feet... giving a very OOT blob shadow look." Level structure (Unite 2016): the whole game is one master scene referencing 250 sub-scenes organised Area > Puzzle > {Gameplay, Environment, Backdrop}; "Each Puzzle span around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay"; Gameplay scenes are mutable and marked dirty when activated, Environment/Backdrop are immutable; a manually authored Potential Visible Set per part of the game, scene bounds vs view frustum, a build-time voxel grid, and "boundscullers" (bounds + facing planes with AND/OR) subdivide scenes; goals were "Game can be completed from start to end without loading screens", "No visual artifacts caused by streaming in content", 60 fps on consoles. Chase/dog sequences: the Unite slides name sub-scenes "Game Start", "River with dog", "Lake", "Fields", "Chicken gun"; the speedrun community splits INSIDE into 11 segments (Forest; Barn & Pig; City; Lineup & Helmet; Search & Dogs; Submersible; Mine; Clock & Breathe & Under; Puzzles; Office; Huddle), which is a reasonable map of its pacing beats. No primary source on chase tuning (dog speed, catch distance) was found; UNVERIFIED. Limbo puzzle rules (Carlsen, GDC Europe 2010 as reported by Game Developer): "think of the player as your worst enemy, and then create the most devious puzzle possible. But then from there, try to work with the player as your friend"; complex problems from "simple and very few elements"; "It's very important that the correct solution is fairly easy to execute" and wrong solutions must be obviously wrong; teach by placement, e.g. forcing the player next to a pullable object with a visual arm cue; use positioning to keep the player from fixating on the wrong element; puzzles that were "far too complex" or that let wrong approaches feel viable were thrown out ("We had to throw out a lot of work all the time"). Playtesting: "several hundred people" brought in, ~150 one-time "tissue testers" who played without guidance while developers "sat behind them, and we didn't ask any questions"; they measured only whether puzzles were solvable, not enjoyment. Limbo checkpoints: Hardcore Gaming 101 says deaths "never set you back more than roughly twenty seconds"; the game has a hidden-egg alternate route through "the last third of the game which is much faster and much more difficult." Limbo's first-playthrough length is 3-4 hours (HG101) / 2-5 hours (Wikipedia); INSIDE any% speedruns are just under 60 minutes, so a normal playthrough is a few hours.
dossier.death_and_saves: Model: "trial and death" (Playdead's own term). Carlsen: "You could call it a learning-by-dying game"; "You don't ever really get penalized for dying, it's just how the game plays"; deaths should "look entertaining" and teach ("it's important that you also treat him nicely"). Gruesome death imagery is used to steer players away from unworkable solutions (Wikipedia, citing Playdead). Checkpoints are unlimited, almost instantaneous, usually placing the boy just before the trap (Wikipedia/HG101: at most ~20 s lost). Limbo rewards low-death play only with an optional achievement for finishing "with five or fewer deaths" and a speedrun community that runs "Hard Route" (eggs route) in 35:15 vs 39:23 normal. INSIDE engineering of the respawn (Wwise Tour 2016): "When main character dies, scenes are reloaded. Audio should retain state and continue during load. When reload is complete, audio should switch to new state instantly. We call this a scene change." Event chain: Boy death (death event) -> Fade out start (prepare_spawn_[savepoint]) -> Fade out complete (pause Wwise updates) -> Unload scenes (scene stop events) -> Load scenes (scene and global start events) -> Fade in start (post spawn_[savepoint], resume Wwise updates) -> Fade in complete. "Wwise commands accumulated during load. All commands are executed at once when scene change is complete. Creates the illusion of no time passing during scene change." This needed a 2 MB command queue and a 1024-sample audio buffer (512 glitched). Streaming side (Unite 2016): "Only reload 'dirty' Gameplay scenes at respawn"; "Cleanup when the player dies or loads a chapter" is where unused native assets are destroyed; a "pre-warm" game state runs before gameplay. Andersen's GDC 2016 talk description promises "strategies for integrating death-respawn sequences into the broader sound structure to preserve overall coherence." A quote attributed to Andersen in a 2019 'Death in Design' interview ("Even if you die and respawn, the music will continue playing underneath") appeared only in a search snippet; UNVERIFIED. INSIDE has a chapter/checkpoint Load menu used for orb hunting (guides refer to "the seventh checkpoint"; exact checkpoint count UNVERIFIED). Speedrun data: INSIDE "All Deaths" 1:03:21 vs Any% 59:58, i.e. seeing every death costs only ~3.5 minutes, which is a derived hint that each death-respawn loop is a few seconds. Relevance to the planned drop-evidence-on-death model: Playdead never attaches a resource cost to death; their whole tuning loop (silent testers, 70% of ideas cut) assumes death is free and frequent. If WOLF//OVERRIDE charges unsecured evidence on death, the Carlsen rules still apply: the fatal thing must be legible before it kills, the correct solution must be easy to execute, and the respawn must be sub-second with audio continuity, or the drop reads as punishment rather than tension.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Not applicable in the strict sense: neither game has an inventory, a HUD, or a tool. Carried state is physical and contextual (boxes, the jet crate, a raft, a lever) and persists only as world state within the current gameplay sub-scene; on respawn, "dirty" gameplay scenes reload so dragged objects return to their checkpoint positions (Unite 2016). Collectibles: Limbo hides eggs (HG101: "Ten hidden eggs throughout the game"; speedrun categories list "9 Eggs" and Xbox-360-exclusive 20/21-egg runs, so the count varies by platform; treat as approximate) and finding all unlocks a faster, harder alternate route; INSIDE hides glowing orbs that must all be deactivated in a playthrough for the secret ending (Wikipedia; guides say 14, count UNVERIFIED here). These collectibles persist across deaths and are tracked by checkpoint/chapter in the Load menu, which is the closest analogue to a "secured evidence" state. iOS note: INSIDE's Shipping on iOS slides list "pulling secrets" among the interactions re-tuned for swipe.
dossier.action_and_impact: Controls: Limbo is "directional input + two buttons (jump and grab)" (Carlsen). INSIDE keeps the same vocabulary. Impact and weight are produced by the audio-state pipeline rather than by camera shake: the boy has an "Effect State" (animation, ground, material, ladder, velocity, landing impact, water state, wetness) written each frame by an "Effect Analyzer" from animation, physics velocity and collider metadata; it is double-buffered so sounds fire on state changes (example: previous frame landImpact 70 with isLanding false, current isLanding true -> "Set land impact parameter to 70, Play land sound", impact "based on velocity in the direction of surface normal"). Landing also restarts breathing: "soft impact: normal exhale, hard impact: grunt". Jump holds breath: "if currently inhaling, stop afterwards; if currently exhaling, do a quick inhale, then stop." Footstep events are "matrix" events keyed by movement speed: idle < 0.07, sneak < 0.37, walk < 0.70, jog < 0.92, run < 1.30, sprint >= 1.30 (engine units/s), and transitions pick context sounds ("from 'run' to 'stop' yields 'brake'", idle->jog plays 'takeoff_mf', sneak->jog plays 'walk'). "Engagement actions" (not engaged / engaged passive / engaged active) switch to a work-grunt sound set when pushing or pulling. Wetness is a parameter that "Is set high when in water or on a wet surface. When dry, approaches 0 over time" and adds a wet layer on top of footsteps. Cloth sounds are generated from geometry: "Tracking a single elbow was enough." Limbo's boy: one coder worked "full-time for 3 years" on him; "He can look forward in time half a second to see what's out there" to pre-place hands, and could catch moving objects in rotating rooms. Limbo audio also marks survival: a "stinger-like sound, triggered when the boy survives" the rotating rooms, and sounds are foregrounded for approaching hazards "before visual revelation, then silenced them as players passed." The Huddle shows physical feedback loops ("Force Feedback from Legs": every leg plant sends impulses up the body; overstretched arms pull the box toward the arm). iOS interaction tuning (Shipping on iOS): "Swipe towards object to grab: left, down... (very useful underwater... especially while drowning)" but only "on things that blocks movement"; they "Started with jetcrate and spread to the rest of the game. Other examples: pulling lever, opening window, pulling out raft, pulling secrets"; they "Tried auto-complete, ends up waiting for triggered animation to end. loses feeling of interaction :(" so they kept the swipe and chose the "Short as possible animation while still prioritising the feeling of interaction" - "Very painful change, since we really liked the weight of the controller input" - hardest where timing mattered ("Sentry gun in city, Sentry gun in sewers"). Hit-stop, screen shake and flash: no Playdead source documents using them; the VFX talk is literally titled "Turn it Down 90%" (Control Conference 2016), consistent with restraint. Shockwave sequence exists (Wwise demo "Shockwave Demo"; Wikipedia "shock wave atrium") but tuning numbers are UNVERIFIED.
dossier.presentation_ui_art: No HUD, no tutorial text, no in-game menus (Carlsen: "should never have any tutorial text"; "we didn't want to have any in-game menus or anything"). Limbo: monochrome with film grain and focused lighting, likened to film noir/German Expressionism; graphics existed before the studio ("The first thing we had was the graphics... The gameplay was the big concern" - Patti); the spider began as a "killer red box" placeholder; ~70% of conceived content was discarded. INSIDE renders in Unity with a light-prepass ("Legacy deferred") pipeline and Playdead's own temporal reprojection AA (open-sourced, MIT). Art is "uncompromisingly simplistic" and leans on: linear fog with a clamp so bright lights bleed through; volumetric light volumes sampled with blue noise (naive sampling needed ~128 samples and 3.2 ms; blue noise lets them "get away with much fewer samples"); TPDF/blue-noise dithering after every pass to kill banding ("Spectacularly easy to add. Potentially make your game look at lot better"); bloom downsample with 9 taps instead of 13 (~0.1 ms saved); custom light entities instead of SSAO - multiplicative "AO decals" (one per bone on characters: "I see 16 characters and I count 16 bones each" ~256 decals), sphere AO for large occluders (submarine), box AO for puzzle crates, and soft projected "shadow decals" (on a draggable box, under the boy's feet, under a platform); local screen-space reflections for puddles; layered water (fog, refraction, reflection); fire flipbook of 3x3 sprites chosen "column sequentially, row randomly" because random alone had "an 11% chance of hitting the same one twice, which looks like a pop"; rain and dust as vertex-shader animation because particles cost too much CPU/overdraw. Characters have "a fake ambient color, that's always there, so we can see it in the dark", a depth-edge rim light "like the boy and all the other NPCs. It helps them fit together", and the boy has a toon ramp (the Huddle uses a smootherstep contrast instead). The Huddle shader fades in bruises, burns and blood from 9 of the 26 rigidbodies as the player abuses it - a cheap "the world remembers what you did" visual. Visual QA: a tool took screenshots "every 5 meters from a playthrough" at "around 1300 locations" and diffed them against reference images to keep platform parity. On iOS they fitted a polynomial brightness curve to "Get it BRIGHT enough" for outdoor screens, and reviewers still called the iPhone image "so dark that I can't tell whether there is something to interact with" (iMore).
dossier.audio: Limbo (Andersen): no conventional score; the brief was "not like a video game"; he kept the "notional silence" rather than add an orchestral spooky score, vocal emotes or narration. Method: "turn a naturalistic soundscape into abstraction by making your sound effects play as 'music'"; every sound ran through "old wire-recorders and tape-recorders" so "they came to echo a distant past"; sounds were not normalised but stored "at the level that I imagine is the maximum they will play back in the game" to preserve dynamics; footsteps use separate toe and heel contacts, and a passive mix that gradually attenuates repeated steps on the same material and restores them on a new surface, with total variation of "approximately 15 decibels"; state-based mixing moves "from a soft dreamscape to brutal realism"; HG101 counts "only six tracks" of music. His GDC 2011 slides frame the game as soundscape/acousmatic composition (reviewers could not agree whether Limbo had music at all), with worked examples: a HOTEL sign turned into "harmonized noise (melodic phrase)", insect transport as "frozen buzzing of insects", rotating rooms interpolating a foundry recording with an orchestral recording and a bowed cymbal, and a drone "activated" by filtering it through a circular saw's swoosh; on the gravity jump the engine pulse filters the soundscape's fundamental note. INSIDE (Andersen, Ryberg, Frostholm, Schmid; Unity + Wwise + modified Wwise-Unity plugin + PlayMaker; "5-year collaboration"): see action_and_impact for the animation-event matrix and Effect State. Voice: a C# "Voice Sequencer" using Wwise end-of-event callbacks alternates inhale/exhale; sound choice via switches Action / Emotion (relaxed, frantic, relieved...) / Intensity; "Voice intensity = lowpass filtered exhaustion" generated by boy movement; intensity can be clamped, with clamps "interpolated in space" ("Useful for indicating proximity to danger") or over time (reactions that relax); each breath fires a callback that "controls additive breathing animation, affecting boy pose"; "Recorded breath sounds have varying durations. Continuous sequencing results in natural, uneven breathing pattern"; when running, breathing switches to rhythmic mode: "1 breath for every 2 steps", aligned gradually by DJ-style beat matching (frequency from footstep events, phase compensation; code published as "Beatmatching Code - steal it!"). Voice direction is done with trigger boxes, state machines and scripts: "The director (Martin) instructs the actor (voice sequencer) how to emote." Room/material: Kill Screen interview - sounds were routed through a real human skull with audio transducers ("speakers without membranes") and contact mics for a bone-conduction, inside-your-head quality; a sword swallower wore a contact mic for stomach sounds and a heartbeat used in the lineup puzzle; "everything has a musical quality to it. So even with footsteps or whatever material, I regard them as musical"; influence "John Carpenter films... the simplicity"; "Only in 1 out of 10 experiments does something interesting happen." Music-driven gameplay: named Wwise User Cues in music segments callback into Unity and the game can read music play position (GDC 2016 "A Game That Listens": without feedback "the game resembles a dancer unable to hear and respond to the sound playing"). Performance: virtual voices, 1024-sample buffer, 2 MB command queue, Wwise pinned to CPU core 5 with Unity workers on cores 2-4, PCM for music and Vorbis quality 10 for everything else, glitches found only by recording console output over S/PDIF and reading spectrograms. Procedural audio: Playdead's INSIDE is sample-based with procedural selection and sequencing, not synthesis; Schmid's 2019 talk notes real-time synthesis as a direction for 140/Cocoon-era work.
dossier.mobile_and_input: Limbo iOS (2013-07-03; App Store today $3.99, 141.6 MB, iOS 13+, PlayStation/Xbox/MFi controllers): "An invisible d-pad on the left side of the screen is used to move left and right and climb ladders and ropes"; "To jump, you swipe up... the boy retains his momentum"; "Holding down your thumb on the right side of the screen makes him interact with objects and switches." Game Informer's main complaint: "the fickleness of the invisible d-pad. Sometimes the boy would just stop moving mid-jog and I would have to reset my thumb", making timing puzzles "notably harder"; verdict "the inferior choice... but it's far from unplayable." Playdead skipped Vita's touchpad because it "didn't suit Limbo at all." INSIDE iOS/tvOS (2017-12-15; Digital Dragons 2018 talk by Mikkel Gjøl): "Same gameplay, levels, rendering-pipeline... Slightly tweaked gameplay to make touch-controls work better." Memory forced the business model: INSIDE needs "~900MB (worst case)" but 1 GB devices allow "~600MB", 2 GB devices "~1200MB", and the App Store cannot filter by RAM, so they "made initial part of game a free trial" with an in-app unlock and a fallback "sorry" scene. Port facts: Unity 5.0 -> 5.6 (64-bit, Metal 2), custom renderer multithreading removed, first proof-of-concept ran "around 30fps", "very, very few script- / game-bugs"; they pre-load and pre-warm every shader variant collected from playthroughs to avoid first-draw hitches; tiled-GPU render-pass work saved ~0.67 ms avg (4.8%); thermal: an iPhone X "can run at 60fps with no framedrops but gets too hot for puny human comfort" (~40°C), so they target human comfort rather than device spec; a runtime overlay shows CPU frequency scale and GPU glass time; Apple TV 4K's fan throttles less. Touch design: "all touches/fingers are treated equally and a state-machine is tracking their individual behavior from touch-start to touch-end. Their states will all be combined. If one finger moves right and another left, the boy will stand still"; "Robust: Hold device with a thumb ON-SCREEN"; swipe-toward-object grab (see action_and_impact); the developer note on the App Store: "You swipe left and right to move (like a virtual stick) but to jump you swipe up, and to interact with objects you tap/hold." Store today: free to start, $9.99 unlock (iMore reported $6.99 at launch), 739 MB, iOS 13+, controllers supported; iMore: requires 2 GB RAM devices (iPhone 6s / iPad Air 2 / Apple TV 4th gen or newer). Reviewer friction: press-and-hold-near-object to interact was called unintuitive (iMore), "Covering up any element of the screen with your thumb does a disservice to Inside's immaculate visual language" (AppUnwrapper), the water creature and the flaming-box throw "took more tries than I would have liked", and iMore recommends Apple TV with a controller as the main device. Switch port: no verified Digital Foundry figures (host blocked); UNVERIFIED.

steal: Death as a 'scene change', not a reload: fade out, freeze audio updates, reload only the dirty gameplay room, replay accumulated audio commands on fade-in so room tone, music and WOLF's vocal state continue with 'the illusion of no time passing'. In Godot: keep the audio bus/room-tone players outside the reloaded scene and queue AudioStreamPlayer changes until the fade-in.

Footstep matrix events keyed by movement speed with context transitions (idle->jog 'takeoff', run->stop 'brake', sneak->jog 'walk'), plus a wetness parameter that decays over time, and a per-surface layer; this is the published blueprint for 'footsteps per surface' and already matches hold-to-move.

Breathing as a sequencer: alternate inhale/exhale samples of varying length (uneven = natural), Intensity = low-pass-filtered exhaustion, Emotion switch sets (relaxed/frantic/relieved), hold breath on jump, exhale or grunt on landing by impact, and beat-match breath to footsteps at 1 breath per 2 steps when running (Schmid's MatchFreqAndPhase is free to use). Drive a small additive chest/shoulder animation from each breath callback.

Voice direction by trigger boxes: clamp WOLF's or the engineer's vocal intensity by location ('Useful for indicating proximity to danger') and let it relax over time after events, instead of scripting barks.

Double-buffered character Effect State written by an analyzer and read by audio/VFX renderers; bugs split cleanly into 'state wrong' vs 'sound wrong'. Fire impact kit (shake, hit-stop, flash, sound) off state changes such as landImpact, not off scattered signals.

Room chunking: one puzzle per ~100 m / 1-3 min, with immutable Environment and Backdrop layers and a mutable Gameplay layer; for 1.5-2 screen rooms with walk-through doorways this maps to one Gameplay scene per room and a shared backdrop, and lets death reload only the room.

Fog and silhouettes as the depth system: cheap linear fog clamped to a max so emissive lights and the sentry's beam bleed through, plus one bright-light glare pass; this is what the painterly 2.5D look needs more than parallax count.

Grounding tricks that read on a phone: a soft shadow decal under the character's feet, multiplicative AO decals per limb, a constant fake ambient so WOLF and the engineer never vanish in the dark, and a depth-edge rim light that makes separate characters 'fit together'.

Carlsen's puzzle rules for the coolant-relay/copy-station/sentry rooms: few elements, correct solution easy to execute, wrong solutions obviously wrong before they kill, teach by placement (stand the player next to the thing to USE), and misdirect by positioning rather than by text.
Playtest like Playdead: fresh 'tissue testers', no questions, watch only whether they solve the room; cut what is not tight (Limbo cut ~70%).

Make deaths legible and short: Limbo loses at most ~20 s; INSIDE's full death tour costs only ~3.5 min over a 60-min run. If dropping unsecured evidence on death is kept, keep the respawn itself near-instant and continuous.

Touch: multi-finger state machine where all touches combine (opposite swipes cancel), rest-thumb-on-screen is allowed, and 'swipe toward the object' triggers USE on things that block movement; choose the shortest USE animation that still feels like an interaction and reject auto-complete.
Ship a 'free first room' trial on mobile if memory or device filtering is a problem, with a graceful 'sorry' scene on unsupported devices.

Playthrough-based QA: record an input playthrough (Playdead's 'Kalle'), replay it nightly, screenshot every 5 m and diff against references; even a lightweight version catches rendering regressions between desktop and phone.

Companion motion as a vote network: let WOLF's follow/scout/lead/refuse behaviours each emit desired impulses or targets and tune the summed expression; add visible limbs/feedback early because 'it does not take much to completely change the perception'.

World-remembers shader: fade in damage, soot or grime masks from gameplay events (Huddle bruises/burns/blood from 9 rigidbodies) as a cheap visual memory of how the engineer treated WOLF or the station.
Blue-noise/TPDF dithering on every low-precision write to kill banding in dark painterly gradients; Playdead calls it 'spectacularly easy to add'.
avoid: Do not import Playdead's 'death is free' assumption wholesale: their trial-and-death tuning (gruesome deaths as hints, unlimited instant retries, silent testers) works because nothing is lost; attaching an evidence penalty without the same legibility rules will read as punishment.

Do not rely on an invisible touch d-pad for precision timing: Game Informer's Limbo iOS complaint was the boy stopping mid-jog until the thumb was reset, and INSIDE reviewers still flagged press-and-hold interaction as unintuitive and thumbs covering the art.
Do not auto-complete interactions on touch to make them easier: Playdead tried it and rejected it because 'ends up waiting for triggered animation to end, loses feeling of interaction'.

Do not add tutorial text, menus or HUD as a shortcut for teaching; Playdead shipped none and designed placement to teach instead. If WOLF//OVERRIDE needs an evidence CASE UI, keep it diegetic or pause-only.

Do not assume the phone can run the desktop frame budget: INSIDE's first iOS build ran ~30 fps and the iPhone X could hit 60 fps only by overheating; profile on a cool device over long runs and expect thermal and frequency scaling.
Do not use a single combined glow pass for fog haze and tight lights; Playdead found they 'interfered too much' and split them.
Do not use white noise or Bayer patterns for stochastic effects (fog, SSR, dithering); Bayer causes moiré, white noise is heavy; blue noise was their answer.
Do not sync a long heavy score to death-respawn; Limbo's and INSIDE's sound continues under respawn and is sparse (six tracks in Limbo), so 'room tone first, music rarely' is the model.

Do not plan on reproducing Playdead's resources: one coder spent three years on Limbo's boy, the Huddle took most of the studio across years, and INSIDE's audio was a five-year two-person collaboration; copy the architectures (effect state, sequencer, scene change), not the scope.
Do not expect Digital Foundry-grade Switch numbers from this dossier: those sources could not be fetched and are marked UNVERIFIED.

corrections.claim: mobile_and_input: "the developer note on the App Store: 'You swipe left and right to move (like a virtual stick) but to jump you swipe up, and to interact with objects you tap/hold.'"
corrections.problem: Misattributed. On the App Store page (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/playdeads-inside/id1201642309) this sentence is in a customer review, not a Playdead note. The reviewer had used a SteelSeries Nimbus controller and wrote just before it: "without that the controls would've been frustrating". The wording is also slightly off: the original says "to jump you have to swipe up".
corrections.correction: Attribute it to an App Store user review, as player opinion. For Playdead's own description of the touch controls, use Gjøl's Digital Dragons 2018 slides: "all touches/fingers are treated equally...", "Hold device with a thumb ON-SCREEN" and "Swipe _towards_ object to grab".

corrections.claim: level_and_camera: Carlsen's rule that complex problems should come from "simple and very few elements"
corrections.problem: Not in the cited Game Developer report of Carlsen's talk, and not in Engadget either. The closest wording is Arnt Jensen in the 'Hanging in Limbo' interview (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/hanging-in-limbo): "I insisted on having very few elements and no inventory". That line is about the whole game having no inventory, not a rule for building puzzles.
corrections.correction: Attribute "very few elements" to Jensen and quote it with its context ("very few elements and no inventory"). This also matters for WOLF//OVERRIDE's inventory: Limbo's director rejected an inventory on purpose ("It's great to put mechanisms in, instead of all this inventory crap").

corrections.claim: presentation_ui_art / action_and_impact: Carlsen: "should never have any tutorial text"; Limbo is "directional input + two buttons (jump and grab)" (Carlsen)
corrections.problem: Misattributed and presented as a quote when it is not one. The report says these were rules set by the director (Jensen) at the start of the project. The words are the reporter's: "the game should only use directional control and two buttons (jump and grab), and should never have any tutorial text." The exact phrase "directional input + two buttons" does not appear anywhere.
corrections.correction: Write: per Game Developer's report of Carlsen's GDC Europe 2010 talk, the director set the rules that Limbo uses only directional control and two buttons (jump and grab) and has no tutorial text. Carlsen's direct quote on this is "we didn't want to have any in-game menus or anything."

corrections.claim: level_and_camera: Carlsen: "think of the player as your worst enemy, and then create the most devious puzzle possible. But then from there, try to work with the player as your friend"; death_and_saves: deaths should "look entertaining"
corrections.problem: Both are the reporter's paraphrase, not quotes from Carlsen. The article reads: "First, he says, think of the player as your worst enemy..." and "make the player learn from their deaths, and make them look entertaining". Carlsen's verified direct quotes are "You could call it a learning-by-dying game", "It's important that you also treat him nicely", "You don't ever really get penalized for dying, it's just how the game plays", "It's very important that the correct solution is fairly easy to execute" and "we had to throw out a lot of work all the time".
corrections.correction: Mark these two as paraphrase from Game Developer's report (no quotation marks attributed to Carlsen), or quote them as the reporter's text.

corrections.claim: level_and_camera / death_and_saves: HG101 says deaths "never set you back more than roughly twenty seconds"; "Wikipedia/HG101: at most ~20 s lost"
corrections.problem: Misquoted, and Wikipedia does not support the number. HG101 (https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/limbo/) actually says checkpoints prevent "even the most irritating of deaths from setting you back more than twenty-ish seconds of progress." That is a reviewer's estimate, not a measurement. Wikipedia only says the player restarts "at the last encountered checkpoint, with no limits" and that reviewers found checkpoints "plentiful". It gives no seconds figure.
corrections.correction: Quote HG101 exactly ("twenty-ish seconds of progress"), label it a reviewer estimate, and cite only HG101 for it. Wikipedia supports "unlimited checkpoint restarts" only.

corrections.claim: presentation_ui_art: volumetric light "naive sampling needed ~128 samples and 3.2 ms"
corrections.problem: Two separate slides are merged into one figure. In the GDC 2016 rendering deck, slide 25 says naive brute-force sampling needs a "prohibitively large number of samples (around 128 required in this scene)". Slide 26 then says "Down to 3.2ms which is still quite slow… severe stepping artefacts", which is the cost after cutting the sample count (later slides compare 32 and 3 samples). So 3.2 ms is not the cost of the naive 128-sample version.
corrections.correction: Write: naive sampling needed ~128 samples; reducing the samples brought it down to 3.2 ms but left severe stepping artefacts; blue-noise sampling then let them "get away with much fewer samples" (about 5% slower per sample than Interleaved Gradient Noise).

corrections.claim: action_and_impact: Limbo's boy: one coder worked "full-time for 3 years" on him
corrections.problem: Stitched quote. In 'Hanging in Limbo', Jensen says "It was an ongoing thing for three years" and Patti says "That was one guy full time on it. Only the boy... A coder, full time. And an animator, not full time." The phrase "full-time for 3 years" does not appear. The "half a second" quote is accurate: "He can look forward in time half a second to see what's out there...".
corrections.correction: Quote the two speakers separately and keep the detail that an animator also worked on the boy part-time.

corrections.claim: mobile_and_input: Playdead skipped Vita's touchpad because it "didn't suit Limbo at all."
corrections.problem: Misquoted. Wikipedia quotes Dino Patti: they "didn't feel it would suit Limbo at all", and says they wanted to give Vita players the "original experience".
corrections.correction: Use: Patti said they "didn't feel it would suit Limbo at all" (as quoted in Wikipedia: Limbo).

corrections.claim: audio: Limbo footsteps use a passive mix that "gradually attenuates repeated steps on the same material and restores them on a new surface, with total variation of 'approximately 15 decibels'"
corrections.problem: Partly misquoted and incomplete. Andersen (Designing Sound 2011) describes two strategies. First, footsteps "start attenuating gradually after the boy has been moving continuously for a shorter period of time, and regain in amplitude when he's standing still". Second, footsteps on the same ground material attenuate "until he steps onto a new material whereby the amplitude gets a small boost." The quoted wording is "about 15dB in total, without taking distance based attenuation and active mixing into account", not "approximately 15 decibels". (The toe/heel split checks out against Wikipedia.)
corrections.correction: List both strategies (attenuation during continuous movement with recovery when idle, plus the per-material fatigue with a boost on a new surface) and quote "about 15dB in total" accurately. This is directly usable for WOLF//OVERRIDE's per-surface footsteps.

corrections.claim: action_and_impact: swipe-to-grab works "only on things that blocks movement"; they "Started with jetcrate and spread to the rest of the game. Other examples: pulling lever, opening window, pulling out raft, pulling secrets"
corrections.problem: Two slides are conflated. Slide 95 ('Make it easier to play on touch') covers swipe-toward-object grab and the note that it works only on "things that blocks movement". Slides 96-97 ('Make it feel better') are a separate change: shortening interaction animations so they match the swipe, after auto-complete was rejected. The jetcrate, lever, window, raft and secrets examples belong to that second change, not to swipe-to-grab.
corrections.correction: Describe them as two separate iOS changes: (1) swipe-toward-object grab, limited to objects that block movement; (2) interaction animations shortened to match the swipe, which started with the jetcrate, spread to levers, windows, the raft and secrets, and replaced the rejected auto-complete.

corrections.claim: numbers: landing-impact rule "hard impact -> grunt, soft -> normal exhale" (source given as the AES 2016 slides); 1 breath per 2 steps (source given as the Wwise 2016 slides)
corrections.problem: Minor source mix-up. 'landImpact 70' and "Set land impact parameter to 70" are in the AES deck, but the line "soft impact: normal exhale, hard impact: grunt" appears only in the Wwise Tour 2016 deck. The AES deck says only "On land: restart breathing with exhale". The 1-breath-per-2-steps and phase 0.0/0.5 material is in both decks, so that citation is fine.
corrections.correction: Cite the Wwise Tour 2016 deck for the soft/hard landing breath rule and the AES 2016 deck for the landImpact 70 example.

corrections.claim: death_and_saves: INSIDE "All Deaths" 1:03:21 vs Any% 59:58 means "seeing every death costs only ~3.5 minutes", hinting each death-respawn loop is a few seconds
corrections.problem: Both times are correct (speedrun.com API: 3801 s and 3598 s), but the inference is overstated. The two categories have different rules and routes. All Deaths requires about 20 specific death types, each with its own setup, and its rules do not mention major skips, so route differences may absorb or hide the cost of dying. Note also that Any% No Major Skips is slower (4089 s) than All Deaths, so the gap is not a clean measure of respawn time.
corrections.correction: Keep the times, drop or soften the per-death inference, and label respawn duration UNVERIFIED unless it is timed from footage.

corpus.group: Little Nightmares and Little Nightmares II (Tarsier): scale, hiding, chases, the AI companion Six in II, camera, audio (Tobias Lilja), checkpoints

dossier.games: Little Nightmares (Tarsier Studios / Bandai Namco, 28 Apr 2017; PS4, Xbox One, PC; Switch 18 May 2018; Stadia 1 Jun 2020; iOS/Android via Playdigious 12 Dec 2023; Enhanced Edition 10 Oct 2025) and Little Nightmares II (Tarsier / Bandai Namco, 11 Feb 2021; PS4, Xbox One, Switch, PC, Stadia; Enhanced Edition PS5/XSX 25 Aug 2021, Switch 2 29 May 2026). Both Unreal Engine 4, side-view 2.5D "dollhouse" rooms, child-scale protagonist, no dialogue, no HUD. LN1 began as a 2012 tech demo called "dollhouse" and a 2013 prototype called Hunger; LN2 adds Mono as the sole playable character and makes Six an uncontrollable AI companion.
dossier.why_relevant: Closest shipped reference for almost every WOLF//OVERRIDE decision: side-view rooms with real depth (and the depth-judgement failures that come with it), an uncontrollable companion the player can only call to (Six in LN2), a hide-and-seek rather than stealth-combat model, chase set pieces, generous near-instant checkpointing, and an audio director (Tobias Lilja) who has described on the record exactly how footsteps, enemy breathing, a "listening state" mix and stem-crossfaded enemy music communicate state in a game with no HUD. Tarsier's stated rejections (co-op, a whistle-to-herd mechanic, calling it "stealth" or "combat") map directly onto WOLF's engineer-only + independent-companion rules.

dossier.companion:
LN1 has no companion (Six is alone; Nomes are skittish NPCs you can hug, 13 in total). LN2 is the reference.

Why Six is AI, in Tarsier's words. Lead producer Lucas Roussel (Xbox Wire): "It was decided early on to have a solo game and move to a new main character for Little Nightmares II." "Adding Six as an AI companion offered several opportunities: It allowed for a more complex level design and longer puzzles that would rely on players ability to understand Six and work with her." "By removing players ability to control Six, we're also bringing interesting situation where players are never fully in charge of Six' destiny." Co-op was considered and dropped at the start of pre-production: "quickly, we discarded this option since our story was a much better fit for a single player experience" (GamingBolt). Narrative designer Dave Mervik (Escapist): "I was really keen to go full new character and let people wonder what happened to Six, but people are in love with that character." Compromise: Six becomes a companion to a new sole playable character (Mono).

What Six actually does (reviews + wiki, consistent across sources): follows Mono most of the game; Mono can call to her (the only time he uses his voice, Push Square) and hold her hand; she "places herself where she needs to be - under a ledge to give you a hand up, carrying objects so you can keep your hands free, and hiding when enemies appear" (PlayStation LifeStyle); "carrying important items if you need more than one" and giving "pointers to puzzles" (Dread Central); she boosts Mono to ledges and takes complementary split tasks in two-person puzzles (Push Square). Fandom wiki: Six initially refuses Mono's help, tries to escape alone, fails to reach an attic handle, then accepts him; later "gives Mono a helping hand for the first time" across a bridge. The game's achievement "In The Palm Of My Hand - Hold tight and we'll be just fine" (13.8% Steam unlock) rewards hand-holding. Story-wise she is unreliable by design (she lets go of Mono at the end), which is the payoff of "never fully in charge of Six' destiny".

How it reads to players: "unlike games such as The Last Guardian, you'll never feel like you're fighting the underlying code" (Push Square); "It's not an escort mission and you never have to worry about Six falling behind or getting in the way" (PS LifeStyle); "she operates just fine on her own so you don't need to babysit her" (Dread Central). Negative: "Sometimes I felt as though her behavior was a little wonky, or would take too long to take a cue/get into position" (Shacknews). Claims that a "dedicated team" built the companion AI appeared only in search summaries and could not be verified in any fetched source: UNVERIFIED.

Design takeaways for WOLF: Tarsier keeps the companion simple and reliable (boost, carry, hide, split tasks) and puts the drama in the story's withdrawal of help, not in flaky moment-to-moment AI. The one player-facing verb (call) plus one contact verb (hand-hold) is enough.
dossier.level_and_camera:
Origin of the view. Mervik (PS Blog 2016): "the first seeds of Little Nightmares were sown in 2012 with a tech demo called 'dollhouse'" - "a cylindrical building as its focal point" where you could "pan, rotate, and zoom in to a bunch of individual, interconnected rooms". Push Square hands-on: development began in 2013 "initially as 'a single room'"; the camera has "subtle camera motion mimicking water movement" (The Maw is a ship). Tarsier describe LN1 as "hide and seek" and refused the word "stealth" to avoid implying "an empowered character" (Wikipedia, citing dev interviews).

Rooms are fully 3D, side-on, cross-section "dollhouse" rooms with a shallow walkable Z. Lilja: "The camera in the game doesn't always allow for you to see the enemy in a room, so the breathing helps to indicate their presence" - the camera deliberately frames less than the room contains, and audio covers the gap.

Known failure: depth judgement. Push Square LN1 review: "The perspective is also a problem, playing out from a cross-section viewpoint but incorporating 3D depth into the scene" - "you'll inevitably misjudge your position and perish." Push Square LN2 review: "The small Z-axis means it's really easy to get slightly the wrong angle when jumping" and fall "through a hole in the floorboards". No fetched source gives the camera's pixel/percentage settings.

LN2 changes (Roussel, Xbox Wire): "We also reworked the camera to offer more top views and in-depth character traversals." "The game features a combination of outdoor and indoors areas which allowed the team play much more with different lighting setups." Design rule: "All enemies and locations should have a purpose, a motivation and a history." "root both environments and characters in a nightmarish logic with a child perspective."

Structure: LN1 = 5 chapters (The Prison, The Lair, The Kitchen, The Guest Area, The Lady's Quarters; Steam achievement names), each one enemy's domain (Janitor, Chefs, Guests, Lady). LN2 = 5 chapters (Wilderness, School, Hospital, Pale City, Signal Tower; Steam achievements Foraged/Schooled/Hospitalised/Paled/Signal interruption), each with a signature enemy (Hunter, Teacher/Bullies, Doctor/Patients/Living Hands, Thin Man/Viewers, Monster Six). Mervik's spatial brief for new locations: "A forest is generally a nice place, but with this it can't just be a normal forest. It has to feel claustrophobic as hell." Scale is read through props: Six "barely a third of their height" of adults (Fandom), tall furniture, chairs and tables as platforms; Mervik (PS Blog 2017) describes Six as "stark colour, small frame, and clean, simple shapes" against a world that is "not only outsized, but also more organic in shape, and presented in a totally different colour palette." Hiding uses room furniture and gaps too small for adults; Nomes model it: "squeezing into narrow gaps where other larger entities cannot fit into" (Fandom). A removed mechanic: "a whistling mechanic used to herd enemies" (Push Square hands-on).
dossier.death_and_saves:
Model: instant death, automatic checkpoints, immediate retry, no manual save, no penalty beyond replay. Deaths are frequent and often informative: "Instant death occurs repeatedly, especially during chase sequences"; players "die the first time before you work out what you need to do"; "one of this game's major improvements is that checkpointing is automatic and very generous"; "Load times are much shorter now than in the past too" (Push Square LN2). "you respawn basically right where you left off or very close to it" (PS LifeStyle). "restarts are rapid" but "we generally found that we had to replay each scene at least twice, because there was some kind of unpredictable trap waiting" (Push Square LN2). Combat misses are lethal: "if you miss it's instant death, and so you'll be forced to repeat skirmishes over and over until you get the timing down."

Tarsier on tech: Roussel: "An efficient streaming system allows quicker loading times when players die in any of the many deadly traps sets in the universe." On PS5: "When dying, players will experience a nearly immediate respawn which is a notable improvement."

Nothing is lost on death (no inventory, no collectible loss; collectibles persist and are per-chapter via Chapter Select, though Fandom notes one Nome area is unreachable if a chapter is started from Chapter Select). The games market death as content: LN1 had a "Nine Deaths of Six" trailer (Fandom). Steam data suggests a no-death/skill tier exists: LN1 "Hard to the Core" is the rarest achievement at 1.6% of players (its exact condition is UNVERIFIED from fetched sources; the flavour text is "What's different about you? Why are you so brave?"); "Elusive" 23.2%. In LN2, "Evasive prey - Not today!" sits at 16.6%.

Length: LN1 "three to four hours" (Push Square); LN2 "6 or 7 hours" (PS LifeStyle), "seven hour campaign" / "twice the length of its predecessor" (Push Square), "literally twice as long" (Shacknews). Mervik on LN1: "We never really wanted to make a long game. The idea always was to make something that got in and got out"; on LN2 he refused to commit to a length because it might make the team "cut out good stuff or add bad stuff."
dossier.inventory_and_evidence:
No inventory in either game. LN1: Six carries only a lighter (Wikipedia), plus context items held in hand (keys, meat, a sausage bridge) that are dropped when you climb or grab. LN2: Mono gets a flashlight in the Hospital that "is just bright enough to stun them [Patients] for brief amounts of time" (PS Blog) and can carry one long object as tool/weapon; Six carries a second item when a puzzle needs two ("carrying important items if you need more than one", Dread Central). Evidence-like content is purely environmental: the chef's skin-scratching animation and side-by-side toilets that Mervik cites as "not saying too much"; Mervik: all characters and locations "have huge histories that the team tries to convey through art, audio, and contextual puzzles"; "You want to give people glimpses of different parts of the Little Nightmares universe."

Collectibles stand in for an evidence system: LN1 13 Nomes to hug + 10 statues to break (both grant masks in the Enhanced Edition); LN2 12 hats (13 counting the Bully head) and 18 Glitching Remains; collecting all 18 unlocks a secret ending ("No More Remains", 5.3% Steam unlock). Collectibles are mostly in side rooms reached by dragging boxes, crawling vents or climbing stacked cages - i.e. optional spatial detours, not pickups on the critical path. Nomes you hug reappear in the LN1 ending, a cheap persistent-memory payoff worth copying for WOLF's "remembers how you treated him".
dossier.action_and_impact:
LN1 has no attack. LN2 adds a deliberately bad melee. Roussel: "We decided to make it quite hard for the character to carry and hit. This design choice was mainly to avoid the player feeling too empowered towards environments and enemies." "You remain a small child struggling in a world not meant for kids." Mervik refuses the word: "Combat makes you think you'll be wading in like Kratos and dispatching enemy after enemy, whereas this is more improvisation" - "giving the player a little more ability to try something else to give themselves a few more seconds to get away rather than changing the whole complexion of the game." Mechanically: "When attacking, there's a bit of a wind up, which means players will need to time their swings" (Shacknews); "slow overhead swing" (PS LifeStyle); "slow, brutal, and terrifying" (Dread Central); critics: "clumsy and slow", "every hit must be a precisely timed strike", and a miss "goes through the enemy without registering a hit" then kills you (Push Square). Weapons only work on small enemies (Bullies, Living Hands); large Residents are never fightable.

Impact and feel: heavy, weighty movement with long holds is the signature ("controls, which are purposefully slow and heavy, keep your fingers on the triggers a lot", Push Square LN2; "feel heavy and lean a little too prominently on uncomfortably long trigger holds", Push Square LN1). Haptics on chase: "the controller pulsates in unison with your pounding heartbeat" (Push Square LN1). Door interaction is analog: "doors can be pushed fast or slow, which the audio also needs to adapt to" (Lilja). Chases are scripted corridor sprints with a hard end beat (Six "jumps to another balcony beyond the Guests' reach"; the Flesh Wall chase in the Signal Tower). Sound as alarm: "if an enemy screams, it's because they are alerted to your presence and ... most likely chasing you" (Lilja). No fetched source gives hit-stop or shake numbers.
dossier.presentation_ui_art:
No HUD at all: "There's no graphical user interface at all in Little Nightmares (like the exclamation marks over the enemies in Metal Gear Solid), so there was a lot of weight on animation and audio to communicate to the player what the enemies are up to" (Lilja). No dialogue: "the complete lack of it" is "integral to creating and maintaining that total sense of detachment and isolation"; "If the monstrous residents of The Maw could talk, and if Six could understand them, she is instantly less out-of-place" (Mervik, PS Blog 2017). Publisher design principle (PS Blog 2021): "to help you feel the same level of confusion and struggle that a child feels, the game explains very little."

Art rules: protagonist = "stark colour, small frame, and clean, simple shapes"; world = "outsized", "more organic in shape", "a totally different colour palette" (Mervik). Enemies are built visuals-first: "The visual concepts of the enemy characters always came first" (Lilja). Tone: "We knew we didn't want to go down that well-trodden path of gore and violence and jump scares" (Mervik, PCGamesN); Tarsier calls it "suspenseful" not horror. CEO Ola Holmdahl positions the budget: "It isn't a triple-A $200m project" and "focus on one thing and we want to polish it up to world-class standards." LN2 lighting: mixed outdoor/indoor rooms to vary lighting (Roussel). Enhanced Edition on PS5/XSX: Beauty mode 4K/30, Performance 60 fps with dynamic resolution, volumetric shadows, ray-traced reflections, 3D audio (Vandal citing Bandai Namco). Menus: LN2's main menu shows the Pale City shore rather than the protagonist (Fandom). Steam reception: 93% positive from 15,962 reviews; Metacritic 83 (PC).
dossier.audio:
Audio director Tobias Lilja (joined Tarsier 2011 for LittleBigPlanet Vita; team of three: Lilja "long sounds", Christian Vasselbring "short sounds"/foley/implementation, Christian Bjorklund support). All quotes from The Sound Architect interview unless noted.

Footsteps and scale: "Just the simple fact that Six is barefoot adds a lot to the feeling of being small and vulnerable, and we tried to emphasize that contrast by mixing quite distinct footstep sounds with heavy background ambient sounds - especially in the first part of the game." Mervik: "the light slap of her bare feet fighting to be heard amidst the heavy, industrial machinery of The Maw, can speak volumes about the scale of the task." Late-game confidence was conveyed "through the music", not new player sounds.

Room tone as information: "Each sound should have a clear function and when possible also give vital information or clues about what was going on in a scene. An example would be really creaky floors that attract enemy attention." Inspired by Bresson's A Man Escaped (off-screen guard sounds): "Doing this kind of thing in a game requires a lot of work since it radically affects gameplay. All disciplines need to be in sync about it." Ambiences are loudest early: "really loud and prominent ambiences. It's most prominent during the early parts of the game"; wet rooms have "dripping water everywhere"; some ambiences are near-musical ("a loud hum from a ventilation shaft with a distinct tone").

Enemy state via breathing: "the breathing helps to indicate their presence" when the camera hides the enemy; "If the heavy breathing suddenly stops, he has probably heard something and might be listening for you." Side effect: players wrongly assumed enemies smell Six - "sounds can also be unintentionally misleading." Sounds loud enough to pass through walls (Chef coughs) became "sonic identifiers". Janitor footsteps mixed with rattling keys.

Adaptive music: "each enemy has their own music track that adapts to their state"; enemies idle at jobs, then "If they notice Six they will go into a pursuit state and chase her. This is where the music intensifies." Hidden-but-heard = "listening" state: "all background sounds and music are quickly pulled down to a minimum to give full focus to the sounds coming from the enemy and from Six, including her heartbeats." With several enemies "the system looks for the currently most aggressive one in the room." Implementation: stems, "we simply crossfade to a different stem mix depending on the state of the enemy. Due to technical limitations there is no tempo syncing going on, the stems just keep looping" - a technique carried over from LittleBigPlanet. "If the music intensifies you know you're in trouble."

Sources and palette: Maw hull "as a kind of instrument"; metal sheets, springs, spring reverb driven by an ebow (used for Six's electric-shock and Janitor stingers), fog horn as in-world musical element leading to trombone/tuba cues; music box, celesta, electric piano and pitch-shifted self-sung nursery phrases for the eating motif, which "morphs" by the final scene; the Lady's hum (Anna Moberg) doubled as motif and ambience. Door creaks: office/kitchen cupboards pasted into "continuous creaking that lasted up to 30 secs", modulated by door speed. Libraries used freely for impacts. Regret: "we didn't do more thorough research about the audio API's of the different platforms ... early on" - recommends middleware for multi-platform consistency. LN2 (gamemusic.net): synth plus organic sources, "possessed music box" nursery-rhyme motifs (Main Theme, Togetherness), chase tracks (Claustrophobia, Bottom Feeders, Shopping Spasm) vs isolating ambient tracks (Playtime, A Little Warmth); reviewers: "music in the game is very limited, instead focusing on sound effects. A jittery noise off-screen will have you running for cover" (PS LifeStyle); "The game is also quiet when it needs to be" (Shacknews). Haptics: LN1 heartbeat pulse in the controller during chases (Push Square).
dossier.mobile_and_input:
Console/PC input: analog stick move, hold-to-run, hold-to-grab/hang (release = fall), jump, crouch, LN2 adds call-Six and swing. The hold model is the series' most criticised ergonomic: "you must hold down the button all the while otherwise you'll lose your grip"; "Hand cramp is a real issue" (Push Square LN2); "uncomfortably long trigger holds" (Push Square LN1); "the controls are sometimes wonky and you don't always go exactly where you think you're going" (Dread Central). Tarsier defend it as intentional weight.

Mobile: LN1 was ported by Playdigious (announced for 12 Dec 2023 per Wikipedia; the Bandai Namco EU page text reads 12 Nov 2023 - date discrepancy, treat the Wikipedia date as the shipped one). Official announcement: three control modes - "Controller Mode offers users the possibility of playing with MFi controllers", "Standard Mode lets you play with the various controls appearing on the screen", "Immersive Mode offers greater immersion in the game's atmosphere" (an on-screen-button-free scheme). Also "Revamped interface", Game Center achievements, mobile cloud save. Mobile price reported as $8.99 after launch discount in a search summary only (UNVERIFIED; TouchArcade returned 403). LN2 has no mobile version. The spin-off Very Little Nightmares (2019, Alike Studio) is a touch-native tap-to-move isometric game: not fetched, UNVERIFIED beyond its existence on speedrun.com. Implication: Tarsier's hold-heavy scheme needed a separate "immersive" touch layer; WOLF's hold-to-move plus single USE is already closer to the mobile-friendly end.
