steal: Lilja's enemy-state audio machine: one looping stem set per enemy, crossfaded by state (idle job -> alerted -> pursuit), no tempo sync needed. In Godot this is N AudioStreamPlayers on one timeline with volume tweens; pick the 'most aggressive enemy in the room' when several exist. Maps directly to WOLF's purge sentry and future room threats.

The 'listening state' duck: when the engineer makes noise but stays hidden, drop room tone and music to near-silence so only the enemy's sounds and the engineer's breathing/heartbeat remain. This is the single best hiding-tension trick in the series and costs one bus snapshot.

Breathing as a readable sensor: give each threat an audible idle breath/hum that STOPS when it is listening. Lilja warns players will over-read it (they thought enemies smelled Six), so pair the stop with one visible tell.

Surface-specific protagonist footsteps mixed deliberately against loud ambient beds in early rooms to sell smallness; keep player sounds constant and convey growing confidence through music and animation instead (Lilja).

Sounds that carry through walls as 'sonic identifiers' for an off-camera threat (Chef cough, Janitor keys). WOLF's next rooms are 1.5-2 screens wide, so the camera will hide threats; let the audio tell the player which threat and roughly where.

Door/valve interaction with analog speed and continuous creak audio modulated by that speed (Lilja's 30-second creak loops). Fits the USE tap-or-hold input: hold = slow/quiet, tap = fast/loud, and loud attracts attention.

Roussel's companion contract: the player can call the companion and hold its hand, but never drive it; the companion boosts, carries the second item, hides when the enemy appears, and takes the complementary half of two-person puzzles. Reviewers praised it precisely because it was reliable and never an escort. WOLF's refusals should be rare, legible story beats, not AI jank.

Keep the companion's betrayal/refusal as the story's point ('players are never fully in charge of Six' destiny'). WOLF deciding not to help should be framed with the same intent, and the engineer-only fallback is what makes it safe.
Persistent memory payoff for cheap: every Nome you hugged reappears in the ending. WOLF can replay small kindnesses or cruelties back in a late room without new systems.

Checkpoint model: automatic, generous, near-instant respawn, death as information. Critics forgave frequent instant deaths because retries were rapid. For the planned 'death drops unsecured evidence' rule, keep the retry just as fast so the cost is the evidence, not the wait.

No-HUD, no-dialogue communication budget: Tarsier put all state on animation and audio. WOLF already has no dialogue tree; resist adding alert icons; add animation tells (enemy stops working, turns head) instead.

Room-as-enemy-domain structure: each chapter is one antagonist's workplace with props at their scale; the antagonist is 'busy minding their own business' until alerted. One threat per wide room, doing a job, is the right scale for 1.5-2 screen rooms.

Chase set pieces end with a hard spatial beat the pursuer physically cannot pass (balcony out of reach, gap too small). Define the 'too small for them' gap as a readable visual grammar in WOLF's painterly rooms.
Mervik's content rule: get in and get out, no padding to hit a playtime; LN1 was 3-4 hours and sold 2M+.

Mobile: ship a third 'immersive' touch scheme with no on-screen buttons alongside standard on-screen controls and MFi/controller support (Playdigious port). WOLF's single USE button makes this viable.
avoid: Shallow-Z depth ambiguity: both games' most repeated criticism is misjudging depth and dying ('you'll inevitably misjudge your position and perish'; 'really easy to get slightly the wrong angle when jumping'). WOLF's one walkable height change per room needs strong ground shadows, contact decals or a locked Z while jumping.

Hold-to-hang and long trigger holds: 'Hand cramp is a real issue', 'uncomfortably long trigger holds'. Keep WOLF's hold-to-move light and never require a sustained hold to avoid death; auto-grab ledges.

Slow, punishing melee as the only action: 'clumsy and slow', miss = instant death. If WOLF's one tool is used against threats, make the miss cost time or evidence, not a death, or keep it non-lethal (stun like Mono's flashlight).

Unpredictable one-shot traps that force 'at least twice' replays per scene. Telegraph traps with audio/animation first; LN2's trial-and-error reputation came from traps that could not be read on first pass.

Companion latency: 'would take too long to take a cue/get into position'. If WOLF is slow to decide, show the decision (head turn, ear flick, whine) within a beat so slowness reads as choice, not lag.

Misleading sound: Lilja's breathing/sniffing was read as scent-tracking. Any WOLF or sentry sound that implies a sense the AI does not have will be believed; audit every tell against the actual detection model.

Deciding audio middleware/platform mixing late: Lilja's stated regret was not researching per-platform audio behaviour early. WOLF is procedural-audio-first on desktop, controller and phone; confirm the Godot bus/filter behaviour on web and mobile now.
Padding to a target length: Mervik explicitly refused; LN2's 'twice as long' was justified by content, and some critics still found it 'leaves less of a lasting impact' (IGN 7/10 via Wikipedia).

Co-op or a playable companion: Tarsier considered and rejected co-op for LN2 because the story needed a single player and an uncontrollable Six. Matches WOLF's engineer-only rule; do not reintroduce a controllable WOLF even as a toggle.
A whistle/herding verb: Tarsier cut 'a whistling mechanic used to herd enemies' from LN1. Keep the engineer's influence on threats indirect (noise, doors, objects) rather than a direct lure button.

corrections.claim: "Why Six is AI, in Tarsier's words. Lead producer Lucas Roussel (Xbox Wire)"; also "Tarsier on tech: Roussel" and "Tarsier's stated rejections (co-op...)"
corrections.problem: Misattributed. Roussel is the publisher's producer, not a Tarsier developer. Xbox Wire says "we reached out to Bandai Namco Entertainment Europe to chat with Little Nightmares II Lead Producer Lucas Roussel". In the GamingBolt interview he says "When Tarsier Studios pitched us the first game". The interview was also translated from Xbox Wire Russia.
corrections.correction: Attribute it as Lucas Roussel, Lead Producer at Bandai Namco Entertainment Europe (publisher), not Tarsier. His quotes are still useful, but they are the publisher's account of the decisions. https://news.xbox.com/en-us/2021/03/12/little-nightmares-2-interview/ ; https://gamingbolt.com/little-nightmares-2-post-launch-interview-dlc-plans-future-ideas-and-more

corrections.claim: On PS5: "When dying, players will experience a nearly immediate respawn which is a notable improvement."
corrections.problem: Wrong platform. In Xbox Wire, Roussel says this about Xbox Series X|S: the SSD gives "incredibly short loading time", and the respawn is "a notable improvement over the original Little Nightmares". PS5 is not mentioned.
corrections.correction: Roussel (Xbox Wire, 12 Mar 2021): on Xbox Series X|S, before the native patch, the SSD gives "a nearly immediate respawn which is a notable improvement over the original Little Nightmares".

corrections.claim: Push Square LN2 review is the source of: "Instant death occurs repeatedly, especially during chase sequences"; "die the first time before you work out what you need to do"; "checkpointing is automatic and very generous"; "Load times are much shorter now"; "The small Z-axis means it's really easy to get slightly the wrong angle when jumping" / floorboards; "Hand cramp is a real issue"; "you must hold down the button all the while otherwise you'll lose your grip"; combat "clumsy and slow", "every hit must be a precisely timed strike", a miss "goes through the enemy without registering a hit"; calling Six is "the only time he uses his voice"
corrections.problem: Misattributed. None of these phrases are in the Push Square LN2 review. All of them are in the PlayStation LifeStyle review by Rebecca Smith (10 Feb 2021). The first one is also misquoted: the real wording is "Instant death is a frequent recurrence and never ceases to be frustrating, especially during chase sequences". The line saying a miss "goes through the enemy ... then kills you (Push Square)" joins a PSLS quote to a Push Square quote.
corrections.correction: Credit these to PSLS (https://www.playstationlifestyle.net/review/843676-little-nightmares-2-review/). Push Square LN2 actually says: "if you miss it's instant death", "restarts are rapid", "replay each scene at least twice", "seven hour campaign", "twice the length of its predecessor", "purposefully slow and heavy", "we experienced a lot of cramping in our hands", "fighting the underlying code", and the boost/split-task description.

corrections.claim: PlayStation LifeStyle quotes: Six "places herself where she needs to be - under a ledge to give you a hand up, carrying objects ... and hiding when enemies appear"; "It's not an escort mission and you never have to worry about Six falling behind"; "you respawn basically right where you left off"; "slow overhead swing"; "music in the game is very limited ... A jittery noise off-screen will have you running for cover"; LN2 "6 or 7 hours" (PS LifeStyle)
corrections.problem: Unsupported. None of these phrases are in the fetched PSLS review at the cited URL. "6 or 7 hours" is from Dread Central ("you'll spend something like 6 or 7 hours as Mono"). PSLS says "approximately double the length of that in Little Nightmares". PSLS does say Six is "an unusually reliable companion", that she "knows what to do anyway", and that calling her "doesn't always work".
corrections.correction: Mark the five PSLS companion, respawn, swing and music quotes UNVERIFIED, or find their real source. Change the LN2 playtime row to cite Dread Central for "6 or 7 hours" (https://www.dreadcentral.com/reviews/481257/little-nightmares-ii-review-big-scares-too-2/).

corrections.claim: Push Square hands-on: the camera has "subtle camera motion mimicking water movement"; development began in 2013 "initially as 'a single room'"
corrections.problem: The quoted wording is invented. The article says "the camera very subtly rocks along with the motion of water" and "originally just a single room". The developer speaking is level designer Matthew Compher, which the dossier never names. The "suspenseful" not horror framing and the cut whistle-herding mechanic are also relayed from Compher.
corrections.correction: Quote it exactly: "the camera very subtly rocks along with the motion of water" and "development kicking off proper in 2013, with a game that was originally just a single room". Attribute both to level designer Matthew Compher via Push Square.

corrections.claim: LN1 began as a 2012 tech demo called "dollhouse" and a 2013 prototype called Hunger
corrections.problem: Conflated. Push Square says development began in 2013 as a single room, with no name given. Wikipedia says the game was first announced as Hunger in May 2014. No fetched source calls the 2013 prototype "Hunger". The 2012 dollhouse demo is verified on PS Blog.
corrections.correction: 2012 'dollhouse' tech demo (PS Blog, Mervik). Full development began in 2013 as a single room (Push Square, Compher). Publicly announced as Hunger in May 2014, renamed Little Nightmares in August 2016 when Bandai Namco signed (Wikipedia).

corrections.claim: Mobile: "the Bandai Namco EU page text reads 12 Nov 2023 - date discrepancy"; "Immersive Mode ... (an on-screen-button-free scheme)"; steal: "ship a third 'immersive' touch scheme with no on-screen buttons"
corrections.problem: Misread date and an unsupported inference. The page shows "11/12/2023" (European day/month order, so 11 December 2023) and says the game is "available today", which matches Wikipedia's 12 December within a day. The page only says Immersive Mode "offers greater immersion in the game's atmosphere". It never says there are no on-screen buttons.
corrections.correction: Mobile launch: 11-12 Dec 2023, with no month discrepancy. Describe Immersive Mode only as the second touchscreen mode, for "greater immersion". Mark the 'no on-screen buttons' detail UNVERIFIED and stop treating it as a design precedent.

corrections.claim: Source: "Little Nightmares II designer wanted to abandon the first game's protagonist - Dave Mervik interview, The Escapist (2020)"; Mervik: all characters and locations "have huge histories that the team tries to convey through art, audio, and contextual puzzles"
corrections.problem: Wrong source metadata, and a paraphrase presented as a quote. The URL resolves to "Little Nightmares II Will Empower Players to 'Improvise' Their Survival" by Samantha Nelson, dated Nov 14, 2019. The 'huge histories' line is the journalist's paraphrase, not Mervik's words. His direct quotes, "go full new character", Kratos/improvisation, the forest line and "cut out good stuff or add bad stuff", are verified.
corrections.correction: Cite it as The Escapist, Samantha Nelson, 14 Nov 2019. Present the 'huge histories' line as the writer's paraphrase of Mervik, not in quote marks as his words.

corrections.claim: GamingBolt (Roussel): "This design choice was mainly to avoid the player feeling too empowered towards environments and enemies."
corrections.problem: Misquoted, and the source is unclear. The text reads "too much empowered", and the quote is from GamingBolt (31 Mar 2021), not Xbox Wire. The same answer also includes "It was critical to keep this oppressive feeling from the first game."
corrections.correction: "This design choice was mainly to avoid the player feeling too much empowered towards environments and enemies. It was critical to keep this oppressive feeling from the first game." Source: GamingBolt, Lucas Roussel (Bandai Namco producer).

corrections.claim: Lilja: "If the heavy breathing suddenly stops, he has probably heard something and might be listening for you" (presented as a shipped enemy-state signal)
corrections.problem: Slightly overstated. Lilja introduces it as an experiment: "We also tried the idea of letting the breathing say something about the state of an enemy." He then says players misread the breathing as smell-tracking. The other Sound Architect claims are verified: the listening-state mix, the most-aggressive-enemy rule, stems crossfaded with no tempo sync, 30-second creaks, the team of three, and the line "no graphical user interface at all".
corrections.correction: Keep the quote, but keep Lilja's framing that this was an idea they tried, and players over-read it. (Note: the Sound Architect page now carries injected spam links, so cite it with care.)

corrections.claim: LN1: "13 Nomes to hug"
corrections.problem: Overstated. The Fandom Nomes page says 13 Nomes count toward the achievement, but the 13th "decided to give Six a sausage". Six eats it rather than hugging it, and it is the only Nome that does not follow her.
corrections.correction: 12 Nomes are hugged and the 13th is eaten. All 13 count toward the 'Little Lost Things' achievement (2.7% on Steam). The ending payoff (hugged Nomes gather on the staircase) is verified.

corrections.claim: Evidence: the chef's skin-scratching animation and side-by-side toilets "that Mervik cites as 'not saying too much'"
corrections.problem: Partly misattributed. In Game Informer's Afterwords, the interviewer raises both examples (the bold question text). Mervik answers that the chef is his scariest thing, and replies to the toilets point: "That's such a perfect example of not saying too much."
corrections.correction: The interviewer raised the side-by-side toilets, and Mervik agreed: "It's always in the details. That's such a perfect example of not saying too much."

corrections.claim: LN2 Steam reviews: "93% positive of 15,962"; LN2 released 11 Feb 2021; Enhanced Edition PS5/XSX 25 Aug 2021
corrections.problem: Minor. The Steam store shows 93% of 15,963 English-language reviews, not all reviews, and lists the PC release as Feb 10, 2021. Wikipedia says the 25 Aug 2021 Enhanced Edition was developed by Supermassive Games and also released on Windows. The Switch 2 date of 29 May 2026 is confirmed by Bandai Namco US.
corrections.correction: 93% of ~15,963 English Steam reviews as of 10 Oct 2026. Steam lists the PC release as 10 Feb 2021 (11 Feb on other platforms). Enhanced Edition by Supermassive Games for PS5, XSX and PC on 25 Aug 2021.

corpus.group: Planet of Lana (Wishfully, 2023): the creature companion Mui, commands vs autonomy, 2.5D presentation, puzzle pacing, death and checkpoints

dossier.games: Planet of Lana (Wishfully, published by Thunderful; Unity; Windows/Xbox 23 May 2023, day-one Game Pass; Switch/PS4/PS5 16 Apr 2024; iOS/Android 9 Dec 2025 via Playdigious, $8.99). Side-scrolling cinematic puzzle-platformer, ~4-6 h, no combat, one playable character (Lana, 11) plus an AI creature companion (Mui, referred to as "she" by the developers). Sequel Planet of Lana II: Children of the Leaf shipped 5 Mar 2026 and is cited only where the devs explain what they changed and why.
dossier.why_relevant: It is the closest shipped analogue to WOLF//OVERRIDE's shape: a 2.5D hand-painted side-view game built in a generic engine by a tiny team, one playable human, one non-playable animal companion that the player commands but does not control, stealth against machines instead of combat, instant death with generous checkpoints, sparse music over heavy room tone, a constructed language instead of dialogue, and a premium mobile port with touch UI. Its directors have explained, on record, why the companion must never be a second player, how the command UI is mapped, what the publisher forced them to throw away (pure 2D, grid movement), what QA forced them to simplify (audio puzzles, robot sound layers), and what the sequel fixed (point-anywhere commands, pace variation, less repetitive biomes). The gaps in Lana (Mui never disagrees, no inventory, no consequence for death) are exactly where WOLF//OVERRIDE's WOLF-memory and evidence-drop ideas can differentiate.

dossier.companion:
MODEL: Mui is a dog in a cat's body, by explicit design. Stjärnljus in the Xbox Wire post: "She may look like a cat, but you can think of Mui's behaviour closer to that of a dog. You can ask her to stay in place, to follow you, and you can also direct her to particular places." Default behaviour is autonomous following ("She will naturally follow you").

COMMAND SET (Xbox pad, from Wishfully's own post): B tap = stay; B hold = follow ("A tap will make Mui stay in one spot, while holding the button down will get her to follow you"); RT hold = bring up a world-space pointer UI moved with the stick that "will also smartly snap to particular points of interest"; A = confirm and "she will dash over there"; Y = contextual Mui action when a prompt pops ("Mui may chew through some rope, push objects down to you"). LT hold = Lana crouch/sneak with auto-hide in tall grass. The pointer is unlocked as a relationship milestone, not at first meeting: in the commentary, "Lana develops this other ability with Mui to waypoint and to actually point her to a specific place on screen." Reviewers found the pointer occasionally imprecise: GamesRadar "slightly finicky to get the cursor to land on the spot I'm aiming for, but generally if you're standing in a good spot in relation to the place you want Mui to go, the button prompt will automatically appear above it." The sequel widened it: "Lana now can point Mui all across the screen, allowing for better collaboration and bigger puzzles" (Stjärnljus, The Game Slayer).

OFF-SCREEN AWARENESS: when separated, "an animated icon dynamically pops up, showing you which direction Mui is located in and what her status is. For example, if she is sitting or moving towards you" (Xbox Wire).

ASYMMETRY DRIVES PUZZLES: Mui fits in tunnels, jumps higher/farther, bites rope/cables, holds buttons down, hypnotises creatures with "white glowing eyes" (later ability); Lana is stronger, moves boxes, "use her broader perspective to provide Mui with instructions" (Windows Central) and is the only swimmer ("Mui is afraid of water, so it's up to you to help them make it across safely" - GamesRadar). Commentary: "gameplay and puzzles are really built around what Lana can do and what Mui can do and what they can do together and separately." The first joint chapter is deliberately a tutorial: "this chapter also serves as kind of like a introduction to what Mui can do... it's also on the simpler side. And as we move on in the game, the difficulty ramps up."

AUTONOMY IS THE POINT, NOT CO-OP: Stjärnljus, commentary: "Can you hand over a second controller to your friend so they can play as Mui? It was a very conscious decision from the get-go and the whole game is based on that you can't do that. That Mui is her own living being and with her own mind... that magic really disappears as soon as another human being takes control over her."

EMOTIONAL LEVERAGE VIA PERIL: the stone-crab puzzle: "this creature is actually only interested in Mui and eating Mui... tell Mui to stop in that little safe spot and Mui's then effectively used as bait." Playtest result: "people have already sort of grown an attachment to Mui and feel a bit bad about using her as bait... that's exactly what we want." Later the roles flip ("Lana can use herself as bait instead this time").

VOICE AS BOND: Lana speaks a constructed language with no subtitles; "it's also very important gameplay-wise for the relationship between Lana and Mui... Lana and Mui is always communicating throughout the game, and that's also why it's so important that Lana got a voice of her own and that Mui answers her." Eriksson (Game Developer): "In the beginning we weren't going to have any dialogue, really. It was just going to be communication through body language... we decided that we needed one more layer of emotional expression for it to work." Body-language idle details carry the affection: RPS notes "every time they have to prepare for a high jump, they do a little butt wiggle"; GamesRadar: "you can pet Mui at any time."

WHAT MUI DOES NOT DO (relevant gap): in no fetched source does Mui refuse, disagree, remember mistreatment, or act on her own route; autonomy is limited to following, idling, reacting, and executing commands. Sequel adds offensive utility ("Mui can now jam robots and machinery") but still frames additions as "any new gameplay mechanics had to strengthen that bond, rather than distract from it" (Eriksson, 99 Percent Lifestyle).
dossier.level_and_camera:
STRUCTURE: 10 chapters (Home/Alone, A New Friend, Secrets in the Dark, The Highlands, The Swamp, The Past, The Ocean/The Turning Tide, The Desert/The Oasis, The End of the Road, Epilogue - IntoIndieGames), strictly linear, left-to-right, no backtracking; biomes announced in advance as "lush green hills... the deep blue expanse of the sea, swamps, old forgotten shipwrecks and finally into the golden sands of the desert lands" (Xbox Wire). Published length "around 4-6 hours" (Thunderful rep on Steam forum); reviewers report five to six.

CAMERA: fixed side view chosen for authorial control: Stjärnljus, "it's much easier to control the camera framing and stage of each scene." Black foreground silhouettes are a deliberate layer that creates "the feeling of looking into a set-piece or theater stage." Shots are composed like film; the commentary repeatedly points to vistas (robot base "far in the distance") used as goal-setting.

2.5D BUILD (Unity): hand-painted textures on 3D rocks/cliffs/ground planes with baked lighting; 2D sprites for grass/trees/leaves; flat-shaded 3D characters; hidden "shadow planes" so 2D trees cast 3D-looking shadows; projected hand-painted images onto 3D planes for depth; "a hand-painted baked lighting solution" rather than a rendering trick; a dynamic wind system across vegetation "to tie the style together and make it feel like a living, breathing world." Stjärnljus on the sequel: "we're not making a full 2D game and we're not making a full 3D game. Everything is made in a certain way, a mix of a lot of sprites and 3D."

WHAT THEY THREW AWAY: the first six months were pure 2D with frame-by-frame animation and grid-based movement inspired by Another World/Oddworld; publisher feedback, "harsh but ultimately made a lot of sense", forced a switch: "The immersion and cinematic feel we wanted to create needed a more dynamic animation system with characters in 3D, and the world also benefited from a more 2.5D look with more 3D elements." Lana's costume was redesigned to "pop more against the backgrounds." Art director Jimmy Chan (Creative Bloq): "We did try to go a little more alien with the art direction in the first game, such as the trees, but it didn't quite work. We need to have [environments] closer to Earth to make it believable."

PACING OF SPACE: devs want "a good frequency of puzzles" but defend "little moments... where you can just sort of take in the nature." Critics split: RPS liked that "when you solved it the game would quickly move on to the next one, which kept the game flowing at a good pace" but called the second act "middle of the road"; Nintendo Life flagged "quite a bit of uneventful running." Sequel response: biome sub-areas that change as you progress "so you don't feel like this repetitiveness" (Chan) and "varying the pace allows the more intense sequences to land with greater impact" while keeping "space for stillness" (Stjärnljus).

MOVEMENT FEEL (warning): RPS: "Lana's movement feels noticeably floaty... When approaching ledges, Lana can't jump up to them if she's too close, meaning I had to move away from the platform to find the sweet spot." Push Square: "animation fidelity over fluidity" causes missed jumps. Stealth uses crouch-to-hide in grass and ledges; machines have varied patrol shapes ("some are airborne and use a spotlight to search, others scuttle across the ground like a spider in specific patterns") and the same enemy type gets new patterns later (GamesRadar).

PUZZLE PIPELINE (Film Stories): a four-person design group brainstorms; lead game designer Dan Faxe sketches; a "prototype phase" in "rudimentary form without any animation" is built in visual scripting by designer Christian Enfors before programmers touch it.
dossier.death_and_saves:
DEATH MODEL: instant and frequent, zero resource cost. Detection by a machine zaps you ("the machines won't hesitate in zapping you if Lana or Mui are spotted" - GamesRadar); creatures "will attack on sight"; falls kill ("chomped by an alien, zapped by a robot, or accidentally yeet yourself off the side of a cliff" - RPS); a boss attack "will kill Lana instantly if she is exposed to it" (IntoIndieGames). Film Stories preview: deaths "far from uncommon". Push Square's sole mechanical complaint: "insta-fail stealth grates."

CHECKPOINTS: automatic and dense. Push Square and Nintendo Life both say "frequent checkpoints"; Family Gaming Database lists "Frequent checkpoints with minimal progress loss" and "Low Pressure - no time-limited tasks". UNVERIFIED (search snippet of a blocked God is a Geek review): the game "saves as soon as one section of a larger puzzle has been completed." No manual save, no lives, no death counter shown; a "Flawless" achievement ("Game completed without dying") sits at 2.4% of Steam players, so almost everyone dies.

QTES: cinematic set pieces use simple QTEs that can be disabled in options (Windows Central: at launch "all that you're really able to do is turn off quick-time events"); speedrun rules confirm "You can turn QTEs off in options" and end timing "when you touch the orb at the final boss (Right Before QTEs)."

CONSEQUENCE: none beyond repeating a few seconds; no evidence, inventory or companion-trust cost. This is a "learn by dying" model identical to Inside/Limbo, which is why critics praised it as relaxing ("you can't really get stuck" - Steam player) and why WOLF//OVERRIDE's drop-unsecured-evidence rule would be a real departure rather than a copy.

COMPLETION FUNNEL (Steam global achievements, fetched): "Sneaky sisters" 91.9%, "The journey begins" 85.2%, "A new friend" (meet Mui) 72.4%, "In control" (hypnosis) 46.5%, "Point of no return" 37.2%, "Home at last" (finish) 36.8%. So roughly 28% of starters quit before meeting the companion and ~37% finish a 5-hour game.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Not applicable as a system: Planet of Lana has no inventory, no held items, no tool, no HUD resource. Interaction is contextual (Lana pushes/pulls/climbs; Mui bites/holds/hypnotises on prompt). The only collectible layer is 10 hidden shrines that unlock achievements and world lore ("clues and collectible shrines to find that paint a wider picture of the world, if you're only willing to look" - GamesRadar); Windows Central found 3 of 10 blind; Steam rates per shrine run from 41.0% (shrine 2) down to 6.9% (shrine 4). Story clues are environmental: "a lot of just background detail as well that sort of gives the players clues to as to what's going on" (Eriksson, commentary), e.g. a woodworking outpost that reveals stone crabs are "work animals". Nothing is lost on death. The lesson for an evidence CASE is negative space: Lana proves a 2.5D companion game can run on zero inventory, so every CASE item in WOLF//OVERRIDE must earn its slot by changing a scene or a WOLF reaction, not by being a collectible.
dossier.action_and_impact: No combat; "action" is stealth, chases, traps and cinematic QTE set pieces. The machines are designed to be dreaded, not fought: "a lot of work went into making the scout robot a very intimidating and scary creature... we really wanted the players to dread those encounters" (Stjärnljus). The one on-screen kill in the demo is a Rube Goldberg trap: "Mui can bite off that rope at the exact right moment. And Lana can use herself as bait instead this time... it's really a turning point in the game where Lana kind of realizes... that they might be able to make a difference." Set pieces alternate with quiet: GamesRadar notes cinematic sequences "ask you to complete simple quick-time events or navigate through a location" and some "offer a moment away from the dangers." Enemy readability: dense black silhouettes "immediately pop off the screen against its colourful backgrounds" and "skitter around like actual spiders" (RPS). Impact feel is carried by audio more than screen effects: the audio engine (FMOD) drives real-time parameters for robot flight, jump-height-dependent landings, and a desert chase that "deliberately omits music to let mechanical sound design take precedence" (Laced). Screen shake is listed as absent/optional (Family Gaming DB "No screen shake"). Hit-stop, flashes and damage states: not applicable (one-hit deaths). Robot sound was iterated down, not up: initial flying-robot sound "way more noisy", overwhelming when several appeared; "We had a lot of layers for the flying sound and we just got rid of 80% of them" (Ameglio). Finale beam: "90% of the beam sound was made with Xfer records' Serum synthesizer."
dossier.presentation_ui_art:
ART ORIGIN: one 2017 Photoshop painting of Lana and Mui facing a spider robot "has been our guiding star style-wise since then"; it attracted the composer and the Xbox deal before a game existed. Inspirations stated: Spirited Away, Totoro, Ponyo, Breath of the Wild, Wind Waker, Another World, Limbo, Inside, Oddworld. Stjärnljus distinguishes from Ghibli: "even though Planet of Lana sometimes feels magical... they're grounded in sci-fi."

TOOLS: Unity; Maya LT for characters/environment pieces; Maya for baking lighting in advanced areas; Photoshop + Substance Painter for hand-painted textures; Wacom concept art.

UI: near-zero HUD. Diegetic/contextual prompts only: Y prompt appears above Mui actions, the RT pointer is a world-space cursor that snaps to interactables, the Mui direction/status icon appears only when separated. No subtitles by design (language is meant to be inferred from tone). Accessibility at launch was thin (only QTE toggle; no remap, no UI toggle, no hold-to-toggle; Wishfully promised a post-launch patch - Windows Central); Family Gaming Database now lists 24 features including fully remappable controls, "No Simultaneous Buttons", "Rapid Repeated Pressing Optional", separate audio sliders, "Play Without Hearing", but still "No difficulty settings" and "Menu text contrast doesn't meet visual standards."

PERFORMANCE: Series X|S and PC ran at the target; at launch Xbox One X was 1080p/60 vs intended 1440p-4K/60 and Xbox One/S 720p/60 vs intended 1080p/60 (Windows Central). Nintendo Life: Switch "runs consistently well" (no numbers). Switch package 7.1 GB; Steam 10 GB; iOS 3.1 GB.

NARRATIVE PRESENTATION: constructed language, "more than 100" story drafts (Eriksson), philosophy "You want to keep building a world that creates more questions than answers." Critics' recurring negative: RPS "lack of emotional highs" in the middle and no "extra twist"; Metacritic critic pulls "puzzles could've been more creative" (CD-Action), "simple traversal puzzles" (Finger Guns). Scores: Metacritic PC 80 (38 reviews), XSX 80 (22), PS5 74 (6); Edge 9/10; Steam "Very Positive" 93%.
dossier.audio:
PHILOSOPHY: sparse, cinematic, film-spotted music over a rich natural bed. Stjärnljus: "We wanted to use music fairly sparsely... We didn't want to flood the game with looping music and just to sort of fill out space. When the music does appear, we wanted it to really communicate something and feel like a real cinematic treat." The natural world "the bird life, the animal life, the wind builds the foundation of the atmosphere and then these little splashes of colour and music come in underneath." Furukawa (Laced): music "spotted" like a film, not adaptive; the Novo world is "intentionally quiet"; one desert chase has no music at all; minimalist undulating patterns (cues "Scout Bot", "Planetarium") so "we can perceive finer details and subtle differences"; strings as foundation, winds/brass on top; no specialty players, budget-driven; Hungarian Studio Orchestra, ~90 players (figure from fetched summary; treat as derived); vocalist Siobhan Wilson only at key emotional moments; themes kept simple enough for a beginner pianist.

SOUND DESIGN (Francesco Ameglio, with Andrea Bo and Marco Furlanetto in the last ~1.5 years; Ameglio from pre-production 2019, ~4 years): FMOD. Foley recorded in a custom-built pit at his studio; "Foley was one element that we could keep as extremely realistic" against surreal ambiences; ship metal recorded including squeaky beam slides. Jump/landing: "there's a system that detects the height of the jump. So if it's a very high jump or a jump from something that's high up, it's going to sound different." Room tone per biome with distinct frequency spectra: forests "open and vast", interiors (shipwrecks, alien bases) tonal and music-like. "Listening to the world" system: "if the player stays still (doesn't move at all), they'll start to hear new sounds being introduced into the ambience", which "meant that we had to design double the amount of ambiences for each biome" (no threshold time published). Mui's voice: Ameglio performed it himself ("I tried to sound as cute as possible"), pitch-shifted/morphed; glass-containment effect done live in engine. Scout robots: bees + servo motors + camera zoom + a 1940s-50s letterpress through Glitchmachines Palindrome; flying units cut by 80% of layers after they drowned each other out. Audio puzzles: QA showed "it was very hard for players to understand where the pitch was" when tones were buried under sound design, so tones were simplified to clear resonant pipe-organ notes with reverb done "in FMOD in the audio engine." Footstep-per-surface inventory: not published (UNVERIFIED beyond grass, stone, metal implied). Breathing/effort sounds: not covered in sources.
dossier.mobile_and_input:
PAD MAPPING (verified from Wishfully's Xbox Wire post): stick = move; LT hold = crouch/sneak + auto-hide in grass; B tap = Mui stay, B hold = Mui follow; RT hold + stick = pointer (snaps to points of interest), A = send Mui; Y = contextual Mui action; contextual A/Y prompts for Lana interactions; QTEs (toggleable). Design pattern worth noting: one button carries two companion verbs by tap vs hold, and the "send" verb is a modal pointer rather than a target-cycle. Windows Central criticised that several controls "require you to hold them down, sometimes for long periods of time" with no hold-to-toggle option.

MOBILE: iOS/Android 9 Dec 2025, ported/published by Playdigious, $8.99 ($7.99 launch week), 3.1 GB, iOS 15.6+ and A12 Bionic or later, "iPhone 16 optimization", 12 languages, MFi controllers, cloud save, Game Center achievements; listing promises "Touch controls with exclusive mobile UI." Patch 1.0.5 (27 Jul) fixed "button disappearance during environmental interactions" and added "button visual feedback in menus", which tells you the touch UI uses on-screen contextual buttons that appear/disappear per interaction. Stjärnljus (GI.biz 2026): "It's a really good port. It plays really well." Exact touch gesture for the Mui pointer and for tap-vs-hold stay/follow: UNVERIFIED (no source documents it). Pocket Gamer: "nothing's been stripped or simplified."

PC: keyboard-only play supported, mouse+keyboard, full remap (Family Gaming DB, post-patch). Vibration optional. No simultaneous button presses required anywhere. Steam: 22 languages, controller support, cloud saves.

steal: Tap-vs-hold on one companion button: Lana maps STAY (tap) and FOLLOW (hold) to B. WOLF//OVERRIDE's two choice buttons can carry four companion verbs the same way without adding inputs, and it ports to a single touch button cleanly.

Modal world-space pointer that snaps to points of interest (RT + stick, A to send). Unlock it as a relationship milestone, not at first meeting; Lana gates 'waypointing' behind the bond forming. The sequel then let Lana 'point Mui all across the screen', so design the snap targets for 1.5-2 screen rooms from the start.

Off-screen companion status icon: when separated, Lana shows an animated arrow with WOLF's state ('sitting or moving towards you'). Cheap, HUD-light, and it is the obvious place to surface WOLF's mood/memory state too.

No co-op, ever, and say why in the design doc: 'Mui is her own living being and with her own mind... that magic really disappears as soon as another human being takes control over her.' Your WOLF-refuses rule is the stronger version of the same principle.

Bait puzzles that make players feel something about the companion: a creature 'only interested in Mui', Mui parked in a safe spot as lure, players 'feel a bit bad about using her as bait'; later flip it so the engineer is the bait. For WOLF, make the choice to use him as bait a thing he remembers.

First shared room is an explicit ability tutorial 'on the simpler side', with the chapter finale forcing the two characters to combine everything learned (rope-bite timing + self-as-bait trap). Structure the Service Junction follow-up rooms like that.

Asymmetry that both characters feel: Mui fits in tunnels, jumps higher, bites rope, holds buttons, is scared of water; Lana moves heavy things, swims, 'provides Mui with instructions'. Give WOLF at least one hard inability (something the engineer must always do) so the engineer-only fallback reads as story, not as a safety net.

Dread, not combat: the scout robot was tuned so players 'dread those encounters', patrol patterns vary per encounter of the same enemy type, and the one 'kill' is a trap built from the room. Use that for the purge sentry.

Sparse, spotted music: the directors and Furukawa agreed early to avoid 'looping music... to fill out space' and to let 'the natural sounds of Novo... build the foundation'. Your procedural room tone should be the default state and music the rare event; consider a music-free chase like Lana's desert chase.

Stand-still ambience reward: new ambient layers fade in only when the player is motionless. Costs double ambience authoring but is a perfect fit for a horror corridor where listening should be a verb.

Jump-height-dependent landing sound and realistic foley against stylised ambience ('Foley was one element that we could keep as extremely realistic'). Map this to your weight/footsteps-per-surface plan: realistic feet, stylised room.

Audio puzzle lesson: hide nothing tonal under sound design; QA showed players 'could not identify pitches', fixed with clean pipe-organ tones plus engine reverb. If a coolant-relay or copy-station puzzle has an audio tell, make it the loudest, cleanest thing in the mix.

Black foreground silhouettes as a 'theater stage' framing layer plus hidden 'shadow planes' for 2D props casting 3D-looking shadows; both are cheap in Godot 2D with CanvasModulate/Light2D and sell the 2.5D depth your parallax rooms want.

Prototype puzzles 'without any animation' in visual scripting (GDScript stubs) before any art; a four-person brainstorm -> sketch -> grey-box -> only then programmer time. Match your 'small, playable steps' rule.

Constructed language with no subtitles, adopted only after playtests showed body language alone was 'stifled'. WOLF's barks/servo tones should carry tone of voice, not just confirmation beeps, and the engineer should audibly answer him.

Make the QTEs (and any button-mash) switchable off from day one; Lana shipped with only that toggle and got criticised for everything else missing (no remap, no hold-to-toggle). Ship hold-to-toggle for hold-to-move and USE-hold before anyone asks.

Ten well-hidden shrines with lore payoff drove a 100% speedrun category and reviewers hunting; find rates from 41% to 7% show how far hiding can go. If the evidence CASE has optional items, aim for that spread rather than everything at 30%.
avoid: Companion with no inner life: in no source does Mui refuse, disagree, or remember; the sequel's answer was more abilities (jamming robots), not more agency. Do not let WOLF's memory collapse into 'unlocks'; it must change what he does in a room.

Floaty, animation-first player movement: RPS 'noticeably floaty... can't jump up to [ledges] if she's too close'; Push Square 'animation fidelity over fluidity'. With instant deaths this becomes the main complaint. Keep hold-to-move responsive and never let a blend tree delay USE.

Insta-fail stealth with zero consequence: 'insta-fail stealth grates' (Push Square) and 2.4% Flawless rate show everyone dies a lot and nothing changes. Your evidence-drop death model is the fix; do not also copy Lana's silent respawn.

Uneventful walking as pacing: Nintendo Life's 'quite a bit of uneventful running' and RPS's 'mediocre middle act'. If a 1.5-2 screen room has a height change and a doorway but no decision, it is filler; put a WOLF route or a choice in it.

Pointer imprecision: GamesRadar found the cursor 'slightly finicky to get... on the spot I'm aiming for'. Snap targets must be generous and the fallback must be a prompt that auto-appears when the engineer stands in the right spot.

Launching with one accessibility toggle and promising the rest later (Windows Central), and shipping last-gen below target resolution: decide remap, hold-to-toggle, UI-scale and screen-shake-off before the first public build, and treat phone frame rate as a ship gate.
Hold-only inputs for long durations with no toggle: Windows Central called them 'exhausting for many players'. Hold-to-move is fine; a long USE-hold needs a toggle or progress-safe release.
Over-layered machine audio: the flying robots were 'way more noisy' and unreadable with several on screen until 80% of layers were cut. Build the purge sentry sound to survive three sentries at once.

Alien-for-its-own-sake environments: the art director admits going 'a little more alien... such as the trees' in game one 'didn't quite work'. Keep the station grounded and readable; let WOLF and the machines carry the strangeness.

Pure-2D/grid-based movement for a cinematic look: Wishfully spent six months on it and were told it killed immersion. Your 2.5D rooms with free movement are already on the right side of that decision; do not regress to tile stepping for the height changes.

Hiding the companion's personality in cutscenes only; Lana earned attachment through constant small idle business (pre-jump butt wiggle, petting at any time, voice responses). If WOLF only emotes at choice points he will read as a lock-and-key.

Puzzles that read as the genre checklist ('moving boxes, climbing ropes, switching buttons', 'nothing particularly innovative' - RPS; 'puzzles could've been more creative' - CD-Action). Every puzzle in a WOLF room should be unsolvable without deciding something about WOLF or the evidence, not just about geometry.

corrections.claim: Audio/action sections: a 'desert chase' that 'deliberately omits music to let mechanical sound design take precedence' (Laced); 'one desert chase has no music at all'.
corrections.problem: Wrong setting. Laced Records quotes Furukawa: 'One scene I really love is when Lana runs through the beach with the giant robot collector legs, and you get to hear these huge machines up-close', and says he 'strongly urged to not have music so that the sound design could take centre-stage.' It is a beach scene, not a desert one. The phrase 'deliberately omits music to let mechanical sound design take precedence' is a paraphrase shown as a quote.
corrections.correction: Say: the beach run past the giant robot 'collector legs' has no music, at Furukawa's own urging ('so that the sound design could take centre-stage'). Source: https://www.lacedrecords.co/blogs/blog/takeshi-furukawa-bet-big-on-bold-melodies-for-planet-of-lana

corrections.claim: 'What the publisher forced them to throw away (pure 2D, grid movement)'; 'publisher feedback ... forced a switch'; 'the first six months were pure 2D'.
corrections.problem: Misattributed and overstated. The Game Developer Q&A says: 'after working for half a year as a studio, we scrapped having the world and characters in 2D only as well as the grid system after early feedback from publishers that were harsh but ultimately made a lot of sense to us.' That was feedback from several publishers during pitching, long before Thunderful signed in roughly 2020-21. Nobody forced it; the studio chose it. The half year is counted from forming the studio, not from the start of the project, which goes back to the 2017 painting.
corrections.correction: Say: after about half a year as a studio, Wishfully dropped pure 2D and grid movement following 'early feedback from publishers that were harsh but ultimately made a lot of sense to us' during pitching. Source: https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/exploring-the-art-and-animation-behind-hand-painted-odyssey-i-planet-of-lana-i-

corrections.claim: Steam funnel: 'Point of no return' 37.2%; 'roughly 28% of starters quit before meeting the companion and ~37% finish'.
corrections.problem: One value is wrong and the base is mislabelled. At fetch time 'Point of no return' was 37.4%; 37.2% belongs to 'Back together!'. Steam global percentages are shares of all owners, including people who never launched the game, not of 'starters'. Measured against the first achievement ('Sneaky sisters', 91.9%), about 21% of starters stop before 'A new friend' (72.4%), not 28%. Likewise 36.8% finishing is a share of owners. Measured against starters it is about 40%. 'Flawless' is 2.4% of owners, which is about 6.5% of finishers.
corrections.correction: Point of no return = 37.4% (Back together! = 37.2%). Say: 27.6% of Steam owners, or about 21% of players who started, never unlocked 'A new friend'; 36.8% of owners (about 40% of starters) finished; about 6.5% of finishers finished without dying. Source: https://steamcommunity.com/stats/1608230/achievements

corrections.claim: Orchestra: 'Hungarian Studio Orchestra, ~90 players' (cited to Laced Records, marked derived).
corrections.problem: Unsupported. The Laced article names the Hungarian Studio Orchestra but gives no player count. The '~90' figure is not in the cited source.
corrections.correction: Drop the 90 or mark it UNVERIFIED. Keep only 'Hungarian Studio Orchestra'.

corrections.claim: Stjärnljus: 'We wanted to use music fairly sparsely... We didn't want to flood the game with looping music...'; the Steal list attributes 'looping music... to fill out space' and 'the natural sounds of Novo... build the foundation' to 'the directors and Furukawa'.
corrections.problem: Not in the Laced interview, which has no Stjärnljus quote about sparse music. It presumably comes from the developer commentary video, but its captions could not be pulled in this pass (YouTube HTTP 429). The Steal wording 'the natural sounds of Novo... build the foundation' does not match the audio section's own wording ('the bird life, the animal life, the wind builds the foundation'). The two can't both be verbatim.
corrections.correction: Cite the quote to the commentary video with a timestamp, or mark it UNVERIFIED. Use one consistent wording and don't credit it jointly to Furukawa. From Laced, Furukawa can be cited for 'spotting' the game with Klas Eriksson 'as would be done in the case of films' and for 'the world of Novo would be very quiet'.

corrections.claim: Family Gaming Database 'now lists 24 features including fully remappable controls'; quoted features 'Frequent checkpoints with minimal progress loss', 'No difficulty settings'.
corrections.problem: Partly unsupported. There are 24 features, but none of them is remapping. The control entries are Multiple Buttons & Single Stick, Keyboard Alone, Mouse and Keys, Inputs Documented, Rapid Repeated Pressing Optional, No Simultaneous Buttons, Vibration Optional, and Adjust Mouse/Stick/Touch Sensitivity. The checkpoint feature is called 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints', defined as losing 'less than 5 minutes'. 'No difficulty settings' paraphrases 'We haven't documented any accessibility features for Difficulty'. 'No Screen Shake' means 'No screen shake effect or it is included but it can be disabled'.
corrections.correction: Remove 'fully remappable controls' from the FGDB claim and use the real labels: 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints' (under 5 minutes lost) and 'No Screen Shake' (absent or can be disabled). If you need remapping, source it from patch notes. Source: https://www.familygamingdatabase.com/accessibility/Planet+of+Lana

corrections.claim: Mobile: '$8.99 ($7.99 launch week)'; listing promises 'Touch controls with exclusive mobile UI'; 'Exact touch gesture for the Mui pointer and for tap-vs-hold stay/follow: UNVERIFIED (no source documents it)'.
corrections.problem: The launch price is wrong and the listing quote is not verbatim. Pocket Gamer (9 Dec 2025) reports a '10% launch discount through December 16th', which makes about $8.09, not $7.99. The App Store text reads 'Revamped interface – exclusive mobile UI with complete touch control'. The claim that no source documents the touch scheme is too strong. The App Store version history (1.0.4) mentions an 'immersive mode', a 'tap' icon that disappears when crouching, and 'Mui's "Go to" action doesn't cancel when you switch back to Lana's control'. So mobile has a mode where you switch control to Mui and a 'Go to' action.
corrections.correction: Price: $8.99 with a 10% launch discount until 16 Dec 2025. Quote the listing exactly. Add the 1.0.4 notes (immersive mode, 'tap' icon, switching control between Lana and Mui, Mui 'Go to') as partial evidence of the touch scheme; exact gestures are still UNVERIFIED. Sources: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/planet-of-lana/id6739130049 and https://www.pocketgamer.com/planet-of-lana/official-launch-android-ios

corrections.claim: Sequel scale: 'about twice the size of the first one' (Jimmy Chan), given as a direct quote.

corrections.correction: Present it as reported speech: per Creative Bloq, Chan estimated 'at a rough count' that the sequel is about twice the size. Chan's own words are about the sub-areas within each biome and 'You don't feel like this repetitiveness'.

corrections.claim: Studio founding: 'Wishfully founded August 2018'.
corrections.problem: Slightly misattributed. GamesIndustry.biz also says Wishfully was formed only after the couple's savings (about EUR 20,000) had run out.

corpus.group: Stray (BlueTwelve, 2022): the robot companion B-12, an inventory of collected items and memories, interaction prompts, movement feel, sound

dossier.games: Stray (BlueTwelve Studio, published by Annapurna Interactive). Released 19 July 2022 on PS4, PS5 and Windows; Xbox 10 Aug 2023; macOS 5 Dec 2023; Nintendo Switch 19 Nov 2024; Switch 2 28 May 2026. Unreal Engine 4, third-person, 12 chapters (Inside The Wall, Dead City, The Flat, The Slums, Rooftops, The Slums Part 2, Dead End, The Sewers, Antvillage, Midtown, Jail, Control Room). Started 2015 as "HK Project" by two ex-Ubisoft Montpellier artists (Viv and Koola); five developers by end of 2017. Won Best Independent Game and Best Debut Indie Game (The Game Awards 2022), Best Debut (GDC Awards 2023), PlayStation Game of the Year (Golden Joysticks 2022). NOTE: no GDC Vault talk or formal postmortem by BlueTwelve was found; the founders avoid interviews, so producer Swann Martin-Raget and the audio team are the primary developer voices. Web search budget ran out late in the run, so a few secondary checks (controls layout, DF article URL) were done by direct fetch only.
dossier.why_relevant: Stray is the closest shipped analogue to WOLF//OVERRIDE's core premise: a silent, single playable animal-scale protagonist paired with an independent machine companion who has his own arc, carries the inventory, translates the world, and ultimately makes a choice the player does not control. It was made by a very small team in a widely available engine, shipped with no HUD, diegetic prompts, a deliberately tiny inventory, lore-as-collectibles (27 memories) that double as the companion's memory, exactly two kinds of death (Zurk swarm, Sentinel detection) with very short checkpoints, one time-limited tool (the Defluxor) bolted onto the companion rather than the player, and an audio pipeline built with no middleware on the engine's own audio system with foley recorded per surface (28 surfaces). Several of the producer's documented "tried and rejected" decisions (fail-able jumps, human NPCs, cat-as-first-person audio) map directly onto decisions WOLF//OVERRIDE is about to make about room width, footsteps per surface, WOLF's routes, and a death model.

dossier.companion: B-12 is a small flying drone the cat finds in Chapter 3 (The Flat): after placing four batteries into computer slots, a hidden room opens, the cat takes a unit from a box on a shelf and places it on a lit spot on the computer wall, and a cutscene introduces B-12 (story trophy "Not Alone"). The name is "a nod to the studio's name, BlueTwelve" (VGC). The design rationale is purely gap-filling, in producer Swann Martin-Raget's words: "The initial inspiration was really having a set of abilities that naturally complete the cat's natural skills. Cats are not really good when interacting with technology" (Inverse) and "With B12 you can also give a set of skills that are complementary to the cat's natural skills" (VGC). Documented abilities (PlayStation.com official intro, Wikipedia, Powerpyx): translates the robot alphabet and robot speech; "can be called upon to help interact with anything electronic (computers, doors, etc.)"; "contains the inventory for quest items" (pick-ups via Square, "like prompted"); "Call him at any time to remind you of your current objective"; "provides torchlight in the many dark areas"; scans objects to recover Memories; and, in Chapter 7, Doc modifies his UV weapon so "B-12 [can] use his weapon instead" (the Defluxor) for a limited period. B-12 also "will get more powerful over time" (Dexerto, quoting devs). Narrative role: "B-12 is a character on his own and has his own story as well" (Martin-Raget, Screen Rant). The companion starts with corrupted memory, recovers it through the 27 memories, is revealed to be a human scientist who uploaded their consciousness, and at the climax sacrifices himself to override the city network and open the city to sunlight (Wikipedia plot). Kotaku's critique is useful as a warning: they call it "a human consciousness trapped in a machine" whose ending is "a completely meaningless ignoble sacrifice" that leaves "what was his purpose? To release a cat... back outside, for what?" unanswered, and argue the ending "prioritizes B-12's story over the game's central premise." Reception summary (Wikipedia): B-12 drew "mixed feedback, with some finding it emotionally compelling while others felt it overshadowed protagonist agency." Also relevant: B-12's dialogue exists because the cat cannot speak; the producer said integrated dialogue was important for "developing a bit of the lore, and the background to characters" (VGC). B-12 does not refuse, disagree, or remember how the cat treated him; there is no relationship meter or divergence in his help (no source describes one, and the trophy list has no such states). Audio identity: "That involved a lot of synthesis, and random foley including a camera mechanism" (Yann van der Cruyssen, A Sound Effect), distinct from the chopped-human-voice robots.
dossier.level_and_camera: Third-person 3D with a camera the producer admitted was a struggle: "designing a game with a quadrupedal character wasn't easy, and there were plenty of technical challenges in regards to camera and animation" (Martin-Raget, Dexerto). Critics "noted occasional camera issues during exploration sequences" and "occasionally awkward controls and camera angles" (Wikipedia reception). Level inspiration is Kowloon Walled City; the team called its "organic construction" "the perfect playground for a cat" because of varied paths and perspectives (Wikipedia, Screen Rant via DualShockers). Structure: 12 chapters alternating linear corridors (Inside The Wall, Dead City, Dead End, Sewers, Jail) with two open hubs (The Slums, Midtown) that each hold 7 of the 27 memories plus most side collectibles; Chapter 4 alone has 8 sheet music, 4 energy drinks and the basketball/paper-bag/TV gags. Traversal is prompt-gated: "You can only jump when a button prompt appears on a nearby ledge, box or pipe, with a successful landing guaranteed" (search-returned review summary). Jumps can be chained by holding the jump button and rotating the camera to string leaps. The designers rejected fail-able platforming: "when you see people playing it... they keep missing the jumps. They keep having close calls," so they "remove[d] the possibility of failure" because "jumping around very easily is something that really fits with the fantasy" (Martin-Raget, Screen Rant). Feedback for an aimed jump is animated, not UI: "when holding the jump button, the Cat wiggles its butt when aiming at a location you can jump to" (Quest for UX). The jump prompt is on by default on a first playthrough and can be disabled in settings once learned. Wayfinding is layered environmental signposting: "string lights and lanterns pointing to the next area," "red & yellow ribbons on ventilation boxes," and "very big and obvious arrow signs" (Quest for UX). Verticality is the main spatial idea: "3D platformer mechanics with enhanced verticality due to the cat's jumping ability" (VGC). A noted failure: the game "abuses its control by refusing to let you jump on barrels and boxes merely because they aren't part of the essential path" (review summary via search). Chapter 1 is a wordless corridor tutorial with three other cats, scratch points (interact with Triangle, then L2+R2), ledge jumps, and a scripted fall (story trophy "Missed Jump").
dossier.death_and_saves: Death is rare and cheap by design. Pre-release, Martin-Raget: "the cat can actually die during two sequences. It's a very short checkpoint, so you spawn back very close" (Screen Rant); the shipped game has Zurk chases in Chapters 2, 7 and 8 and Sentinel stealth in Chapters 10-11, so treat "two" as the design intent rather than the final count. Lives are infinite, not nine (VGC), and the nine-lives joke became the Bronze trophy "No More Lives: Die 9 times" (Powerpyx trophy guide). Death sources: Zurks (mutated bacteria that "swarm and devour") and Sentinels (security drones with visible sight lines) (Wikipedia). Zurk mechanics: "they jump on you and you need to press Circle to get them off" (Powerpyx ch.2); the first chase is "very tight unlike later Zurk chases" and "one of the hardest things to do in the game"; "Reload Last Checkpoint" from the pause menu restarts from the chase start with unlimited retries. In the Sewers, Zurks emerge from pods when approached; avoid by "sticking to the side the pods aren't on" or by killing them with the L1 light (which forfeits the "Pacifist" trophy). Sentinel detection is graduated: "their vision will turn yellow, followed by red" and you "can restart checkpoint and still earn the trophy after" (Powerpyx ch.10), i.e. checkpoint reload is not penalised for the no-detection trophy "Sneakitty". Saves: automatic checkpoints plus Chapter Select; "None of the Collectibles are missable" and all can be gathered after the story via Chapter Select (Powerpyx). The only missable trophy is "I am Speed" (finish in under 2 hours). Chase sequences exist for pacing: they give "variety and surprise to the progression" (Martin-Raget, Screen Rant). Nothing is lost on death: no inventory, memory or progress is dropped, which is the clearest contrast with WOLF//OVERRIDE's planned unsecured-evidence model.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: The inventory lives in the companion, not the player: "Pressing Square like prompted will allow B-12 to pick up and store items for you" (Powerpyx ch.3), and the official PlayStation intro says B-12 "contains the inventory for quest items." It is deliberately tiny: a "small menu for picking up items... there are only a few items in the game, so this really fits the need" (Quest for UX). Evidence/lore is a separate track: 27 Memories, of which 5 are story-automatic (The Flat #1, Rooftops #11, Antvillage #17, Midtown #19, Control Room #27 per Push Square; Inverse counts 3 cutscene-granted). In-world "Memories are indicated by glowing blue squares surrounding the object" and B-12 scans the object (postcard, robot bodies, graffiti, mannequins, signs) to recover it (Push Square). Per-chapter counts: Flat 1, Slums 7, Rooftops 3, Dead End 3, Sewers 2, Antvillage 2, Midtown 7, Jail 1, Control Room 1. Collecting all gives the "I Remember!" trophy (Silver per Powerpyx trophy guide; Gold per the collectibles guide, inconsistent across the same site) and an in-game reward. Each memory reveals the Walled City's history and B-12's own origins, so the collectible register is literally the companion's memory. Other registers: 6 Badges (stickers on the side of the cat's harness/backpack, first in Chapter 4), 12 Scratch Points (one per chapter needed), 10 Nuzzles (5 needed), 8 Sheet Music (Chapter 4, delivered to Morusque), 4 Energy Drinks (Chapter 4, vending machines). Memory and collectible progress is tracked per chapter in Chapter Select. Nothing in the inventory is ever at risk; there are no "secure" points because nothing can be lost.
dossier.action_and_impact: Stray has no player weapon; its one tool is attached to the companion. In Chapter 7 Doc modifies his UV weapon so B-12 can carry it (the Defluxor): hold L1 "for short periods of time" and "Watch the bar to the left of B-12 when you're using it because if you use it for too long then it will short out and you won't be able to use it until B-12 recharges" (Powerpyx ch.7). The bar is diegetic, drawn next to the companion, not on a HUD. Wikipedia: "For limited periods, players can attach a Defluxor to B-12 to destroy Zurks before it overheats." Chases ask only for running and reading spawn direction: "keep running the whole time and go in the direction the Zurk aren't"; Zurks "appear either directly behind you or from one of the two directions" (Powerpyx ch.8). Being latched is a mash-Circle escape, not instant death. Physical feedback on PS5 (PlayStation Blog, DualSense feature): players "feel impact when the cat's paws knock down objects like glass bottles"; adaptive triggers give "satisfying amount of pressure to push down on as the cat scratches surfaces"; meows "emit from both game and controller speaker simultaneously"; players "feel the cat purr through the controller when sleeping." Scratching is itself a two-trigger input (L2 and R2 alternately). Cat behaviours are the "action": knocking paint cans off ledges to break a window, scratching a door so "your robo-pal [opens] it to investigate further," hiding in cardboard boxes, nuzzling robot legs (Inverse preview). No hit-stop, screen shake or damage numbers are documented; Stray's impact vocabulary is haptics, audio and animation.
dossier.presentation_ui_art: Unreal Engine 4, third person. Art direction came from a constraint: the team "started doing some tests with human NPCs, but realized that to have the level of visual quality and fidelity they wanted for the whole game would be extremely time-consuming and very hard to do with a small team"; switching to robots left them "utterly inspired by the contrast between the cats being small, alive, and cute, and the machines being a bit more cold and angular" (Martin-Raget, Inverse). Animation is keyframe/reference-based, not mocap: the team preferred "the freedom that making our own animation was giving us" (Inverse); animator Miko used Oscar the Sphynx cat roaming the office as reference because muscle movement reads better on a hairless cat; "Animating a quadruped is already quite challenging but the subtleties of a cat's movements are incredibly precise and hard to convey properly" (Martin-Raget, PlayStation Blog). Miko and cat programmer Rémi Bismuth iterated every transition to balance looks and responsiveness. UI is fully diegetic: the game has "no HUD (UI stuck on the screen)"; interaction prompts appear on "a screen on the coat the cat wears" with "a small beep-sound accompanying it," chosen because "you don't always have visibility on the Cat" (Quest for UX); the Defluxor charge bar sits beside B-12; badges are stickers on the harness. Jump prompts are the only floating UI and are toggleable. Technical delivery (Digital Foundry as reported by Pure Xbox and Kotaku; Eurogamer article itself unfetched): PS5 3840x2160 at 60 fps dipping to ~1890p, PS4/Pro 1080p30, Series X 4K60, Series S 1080p60, Xbox One X "rarely hits 60FPS" and drops to ~1080p; PC stutter is UE4 shader compilation; load/save stutters up to ~120 ms on PS4/PC (secondary Russian report, UNVERIFIED). Steam Deck ran at 720p medium with irregular frame rates (ElAnalistaDeBits via WCCFTech). Steam lists 16 languages with full audio.
dossier.audio: Composer and sound designer Yann van der Cruyssen with sound designer/mixer Raphaël Monnin, working with no middleware: "We didn't use any middleware... We adapted our design choices to the Unreal audio engine workflow and built custom tools on top of it for some specific needs." Foley per surface: "we recorded nearly all the foley: footsteps, jumps, and lands on different surfaces (we have 28 in total) such as concrete, dirt, carpet, water, wood, tile, plastic, metal, etc." (Monnin), plus "scratches on different surfaces (wall, tree, carpet, metal, etc.)." Vocals: meows from recorded cats and libraries "modified (in terms of pitch, length, EQ, etc.) to make them more consistent," "sorted into several categories (probably about fifteen) such as: grumpy, engaging, discreet, etc."; the most-heard meows came from a cat that visits French developer Eric Chahi's garden "every day at the same time." Perspective decision: "It has also been discussed whether the cat should feel 'first person'... or just as one tiny element among others; we preferred the second option most of the time." Robots: started as "modem-like" Pure Data patches, then "recorded voices (including mine and my parents') that I cut into many small chunks" run through a synthesis chain, with per-character pitch envelopes; some robot sounds recycle unused voice takes. B-12: "a lot of synthesis, and random foley including a camera mechanism." Zurks: "a mix of physical modeling, suction cup manipulations, and various additional layers." Sentinels: "electrical-sounding hums and glitches have been recorded with unusual devices." Room tone: ambiences recorded in Japan, Korea and France during the 2020 lockdown with "all the human components" manually removed; instead of stereo loops, "dedicated objects... scan the surrounding level at start and then either spawn or continuously play several independent localized sound sources," including "moving bursts of debris." Music: "Rather than a fixed linear planning, the music is a mix of several 'playlists' that use conditions, timers, and priorities to adapt to the player's style," with tunes tied to actions or "randomly faded in after a certain period of silence." Shipping lesson: about three months before release they found "starting an audio file at an arbitrary point was not 'simply' possible on some platforms," costing "a month revising every system." Retro palette per Field & Foley show notes: linear predictive coding, 56k modem textures, Korg MS-10, Roland SH-01A. The game won Best Sound Design for an Indie Game (per Field & Foley notes; awarding body not stated there, UNVERIFIED).
dossier.mobile_and_input: Mobile: not applicable in the official sense. Annapurna's official page lists Steam, Mac, PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch only; an iTunes Search API query for "stray annapurna" returned zero Annapurna/BlueTwelve apps on 2026-10-10, so a search-engine snippet claiming an official $29.99 iOS version is UNVERIFIED and contradicted by the store. Handheld data points: Steam Deck 720p medium with irregular frame rates (ElAnalistaDeBits via WCCFTech), Switch and Switch 2 ports exist (Switch 2 on 28 May 2026). Input vocabulary (PS layout, from Powerpyx chapter guides and the trophy guide): Triangle = interact/USE; L2+R2 alternated = scratch (adaptive-trigger resistance on PS5); Circle = meow (also the mash input to throw off latched Zurks); Square = tell B-12 to pick up/store an item; L1 = Defluxor light in short bursts; jump = hold the jump button with a prompt visible, chain by holding and rotating the camera; "Meow 100 times" and "Jump 500 times" trophies confirm meow and jump are first-class buttons. A "dedicated meow button" is called out on the official PlayStation page. UX affordances: jump prompt toggle in settings, no HUD, diegetic harness-screen prompt with beep, objective reminder by calling B-12 at any time. Steam page lists Remote Play on TV; explicit controller-support and Steam Deck verification flags were not present in the fetched page text.
