steal: Make the companion the explanation for why the player can do things they otherwise could not (translate, hack, carry): Martin-Raget's 'set of abilities that naturally complete the cat's natural skills' is exactly WOLF's job, and it justifies engineer-only fallbacks being slower or dirtier rather than impossible.

Put the tool on the companion, not the player, and make its budget diegetic: Stray's Defluxor is a hold-L1 burst with a charge bar drawn beside B-12 that shorts out and recharges. For WOLF//OVERRIDE's one tool, draw the budget on WOLF's body or the engineer's wrist, not in a corner HUD.

Diegetic USE prompt with a beep: the prompt appears on the cat's harness screen with 'a small beep-sound' because 'you don't always have visibility on the Cat.' In a 2.5D painterly room, a small lit panel on the engineer's suit or on WOLF plus a short click solves readability at tighter zoom and on phones.

Prompt-gated, guaranteed traversal for height changes: Stray only lets you jump where a prompt shows, every jump lands, and you can chain by holding. For the one walkable height change per room, a hold-USE 'climb/drop' with guaranteed success and a pre-animation tell (the butt-wiggle equivalent: a weight shift or hand on the rail) fits hold-to-move plus one USE.
Make the jump prompt a first-playthrough default that can be turned off in settings; Stray does this and it respects both new and returning players.

Footsteps per surface at scale: 28 recorded surfaces for steps, jumps and lands, plus scratch variants per material. Budget your procedural footstep system by surface list first (grating, plate steel, concrete, puddle, cable bundle, rubber mat) and vary jump/land separately from walk.

Room tone as localized emitters rather than a stereo loop: scan the room at start and spawn several independent positioned sources plus 'moving bursts of debris.' For wider 1.5-2 screen rooms this is what keeps the left and right ends sounding different.
Music as conditional playlists with timers and priorities and random fade-ins 'after a certain period of silence,' instead of one linear cue per room.
Treat the player as 'one tiny element among others' in the mix rather than first-person; it sold the cat's smallness and would sell the engineer's vulnerability in a hostile facility.

Give the companion a distinct synthesis voice (B-12 = synthesis plus camera-mechanism foley) that is different in method from the facility's machines (chopped human voice), so the ear knows friend from facility.
Graduated detection (blue, yellow, red) for the purge sentry, and let checkpoint reload remain legitimate for any no-detection reward.
Keep deaths few and checkpoints 'very short' so you 'spawn back very close'; Stray's chase sections are explicitly pacing devices ('variety and surprise'), not skill gates.

Lore-as-memory: making the collectibles literally the companion's recovered memories bound B-12's arc to exploration. For WOLF, evidence the engineer secures could also be what WOLF remembers about the engineer.

Observational animation from a real reference (a hairless Sphynx so muscle movement reads) and a dedicated animator-programmer pair iterating transitions. For WOLF, film a real dog on stairs and thresholds.

Audit platform audio behaviour early: 'starting an audio file at an arbitrary point was not simply possible on some platforms' cost a month three months before ship. Test seeking/offset playback of procedural buffers in Godot web and mobile exports now, not at release.
Put progress in Chapter Select with per-chapter counts and make nothing missable; it is why Stray's 100% is a 67-minute run and why players replay.
avoid: A companion ending that overrides the protagonist's story: Kotaku called B-12's upload 'a completely meaningless ignoble sacrifice' and reception noted he 'overshadowed protagonist agency.' WOLF's choices must change the engineer's path, not replace it; the engineer-only fallback rule already guards this.
A companion with no memory of the player: B-12 never refuses or remembers; WOLF's whole premise is that he does, so do not borrow Stray's always-helpful tone wholesale.

Prompt-gated traversal that forbids plausible surfaces: reviewers called out Stray 'refusing to let you jump on barrels and boxes merely because they aren't part of the essential path.' If a crate looks climbable in a painterly room, make it climbable or make it visibly not.

Camera-as-afterthought: the producer admitted 'plenty of technical challenges in regards to camera' and critics still flagged camera angles. Lock the 2.5D camera rules (tighter zoom, parallax bounds, doorway transitions) before building wider rooms.
Floating jump/USE prompts as the only readability tool at phone scale; Stray leaned on a harness screen plus beep for a reason.

Inventory you cannot lose: Stray's inventory is a 'small menu' with no stakes, which fits a cosy cat game but not a death model that drops unsecured evidence. Do not inherit its menu-only presentation; show the case physically.

Tool with an unexplained budget: Stray's guide warns 'if you use it for too long then it will short out' but no number is surfaced; give WOLF's tool a legible pips-or-bar budget and a sound for the last 20%.

Shipping a tight first chase: the Chapter 2 Zurk pursuit is 'one of the hardest things to do in the game' and 'very tight unlike later Zurk chases'; do not make the Service Junction purge sentry your hardest beat.

Relying on a single haptics/platform trick for impact (DualSense purr, trigger resistance): WOLF//OVERRIDE targets desktop, controller and touch, so impact must be carried by the shake/hit-stop/flash/audio kit, with haptics as a bonus.
Stereo ambience loops in wide rooms; Stray replaced them with positioned emitters.

UE4-style load/save stutter at checkpoints: Stray's save hitches (reported up to ~120 ms, UNVERIFIED) were the main tech complaint. Secure-point saves in the death model must not hitch; write asynchronously.
Claiming a mobile version when there is none: Stray has no official iOS/Android build despite search snippets saying otherwise; verify platform claims from the publisher's own page.

corrections.claim: Reception summary (Wikipedia): B-12 drew "mixed feedback, with some finding it emotionally compelling while others felt it overshadowed protagonist agency." Also used in 'avoid': reception noted he 'overshadowed protagonist agency.'
corrections.problem: Fabricated quote. I pulled the article's raw wikitext (en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stray_(video_game)&action=raw) and searched it. The phrases 'mixed feedback', 'overshadow' and 'agency' do not appear in it. The closest Wikipedia line is the opposite: 'several reviewers felt strongly about the protagonist and B-12.'
corrections.correction: Remove the quote. The 'B-12 upstages the protagonist' critique can only be sourced to Kotaku's ending piece (https://kotaku.com/stray-ending-explained-b12-bluetwelve-cat-annapurna-1849366887). Attribute it to Kotaku as one critic's opinion, not as a reception consensus.

corrections.claim: Critics "noted occasional camera issues during exploration sequences" (Wikipedia reception).
corrections.problem: Not in Wikipedia. The only matching text is 'though some noted occasionally awkward controls and camera angles.' The first quote seems to be a paraphrase written as a quotation.
corrections.correction: Keep only the verbatim line: 'some noted occasionally awkward controls and camera angles' (Wikipedia, citing WP, IGN and GamesRadar reviews).

corrections.claim: The designers rejected fail-able platforming: "...they keep missing the jumps. They keep having close calls," so they "remove[d] the possibility of failure" (Martin-Raget, Screen Rant).
corrections.problem: The first two fragments are real. 'remove[d] the possibility of failure' is not in the interview: the words 'failure' and 'remove' do not appear anywhere in it. The design decision is real, but this quote is invented.
corrections.correction: Use the real wording from https://screenrant.com/swann-martin-raget-interview-stray/: 'they keep missing the jumps. They keep having close calls and keep having this wonky feeling that you're not really fluent in this space... It's just going to be very smooth, very easy, and very fluid. Shifting the challenge from judging distances to just looking and jumping around very easily is something that really fits with the fantasy.'

corrections.claim: Kotaku calls the ending "a completely meaningless ignoble sacrifice" and argues it "prioritizes B-12's story over the game's central premise."
corrections.problem: Neither phrase appears verbatim in the Kotaku article. 'meaningless' and 'ignoble sacrifice' appear separately, and the 'prioritizes...' sentence is a paraphrase. 'a human consciousness trapped in a machine' and the 'what was his purpose?' passage are real.
corrections.correction: Quote only the real lines: 'he's a human consciousness trapped in a machine' and 'He obviously uploads his consciousness to the computer, so there's no sacrifice anyway, but beyond that, what was his purpose? To release a cat, a creature that has no interest in anything other than itself, back outside, for what?' Mark the 'prioritizes B-12's story' point as a paraphrase.

corrections.claim: Verticality: "3D platformer mechanics with enhanced verticality due to the cat's jumping ability" (VGC).
corrections.problem: Reworded quote. VGC actually says: 'it's your typical 3D platformer, there's obviously a bit more verticality than you would usually see in the genre, due to the cat's jumping ability.' This is the article's narration, not a developer quote.
corrections.correction: Replace it with the verbatim VGC line and attribute it to the VGC preview writer (https://www.videogameschronicle.com/features/stray-preview-interview/).

corrections.claim: Wikipedia: "For limited periods, players can attach a Defluxor to B-12 to destroy Zurks before it overheats."
corrections.problem: Paraphrase presented as a quote. The wikitext reads: 'For a portion of the game, the player can attach a Defluxor to B-12 to destroy the Zurks, though it can only be used for a limited time before B-12 overheats and requires a brief period to cool down.'
corrections.correction: Use the exact Wikipedia sentence, or drop the quotation marks.

corrections.claim: "I Remember!" is Silver per the Powerpyx trophy guide and Gold per the collectibles guide (inconsistent across the same site).
corrections.problem: The trophy guide lists 'I Remember!' as Gold, and so does the collectibles guide. There is no inconsistency.

corrections.claim: No official mobile version: an iTunes Search API query returned zero Annapurna/BlueTwelve apps, so a snippet about an official $29.99 iOS version is contradicted by the store.

The iTunes Search API also returns zero results for the Mac version, yet a direct lookup of id 6451498949 returns 'Stray | Annapurna Interactive | 29.99 | mac-software' (release 2023-12-01). corrections.claim: No GDC talk or formal postmortem by BlueTwelve was found; the founders avoid interviews, so producer Swann Martin-Raget and the audio team are the primary developer voices. The '28 people and two cats' interview is cited only for its title.
corrections.problem: Overstated. The Unreal Engine interview (first ran 24 Aug 2022; repost teaser at https://padandpixel.com/?p=4918) states: 'We chatted with studio creative and design director Viv and Stray producer Swann Martin-Raget.' So a founder did give at least one interview. Also, a search snippet of the UE page body describes the team as '20 talented people and two full-time cats', which conflicts with the 28 in the title.

corrections.claim: Sentinels: "electrical-sounding hums and glitches have been recorded with unusual devices." B-12: 'a lot of synthesis, and random foley including a camera mechanism.'

corpus.group: The Last Guardian and Ico (genDESIGN / Team Ico): companion autonomy, trust, look-at and procedural animation, the hand-holding mechanic, failure states

dossier.games: The Last Guardian (genDESIGN + SIE Japan Studio, director Fumito Ueda; PS4, released December 2016; in development from 2007, announced E3 2009 as a PS3 title, moved to PS4 in 2012) and Ico (Team Ico / SCE Japan Studio, director Fumito Ueda, producer Kenji Kaido; PS2, 2001; development began 1998 on PS1, switched to PS2 after about two years, roughly four years total, core team of two programmers, four artists and one designer plus Ueda and Kaido, about twenty people near completion). Shadow of the Colossus is referenced only where the sources tie it to the companion lineage.
dossier.why_relevant: WOLF//OVERRIDE's core promise is a companion who chooses, refuses and remembers. These two games are the canonical reference points for exactly that, from both ends: Ico is a companion whose safety IS the failure state and whose bond is tactile (hand-holding changes how you move); The Last Guardian is a companion that was "given its own desires" (Ueda, 2016), is never directly controlled, communicates mood through diegetic cues (eye colour, ear twitches, pawing at ledges), and whose obedience grows across the game. Both were built by a studio that explicitly says it subtracts everything that does not serve the relationship (no HUD, no dialogue you can understand, one enemy type), which is close to the W//O rulebook (hold-to-move, one USE, two choice buttons). Equally important, both carry documented failure lessons: TLG's camera and command latency produced the most consistent review complaints, and Ueda himself said the subtractive approach on Ico "may have gone too far". Caveat on method: the session's WebSearch budget ran out partway through, so a handful of desirable primary pages (Eurogamer/Digital Foundry article, The Guardian interview, GDC Vault listing, speedrun.com, StrategyWiki, Team Ico wiki) could not be fetched and are marked UNVERIFIED or cited through fetched relays.

dossier.companion:
ICO / YORDA. Design premise: Ueda's 1997 pitch was "boy meets girl" with the two holding hands; he made a 3-minute Lightwave pilot movie (Feb-Jun 1997) before the team existed (Wikipedia, Team Ico wiki via search; GDC 2004 notes at auriea.org). At GDC 2004 Ueda explained the language barrier as an AI-expression decision, not just a story one: "The main character never understands what Yorda speaks. We set up the language barrier because we felt we would not be able to express Yorda's AI naturally" (auriea.org notes). Also: "There's something very moving about two people holding hands. That connection feels very real." Mechanics: Yorda does not auto-follow; Ico can "tell Yorda to follow Ico, or to wait at a particular spot" and can "take Yorda's hand and pull her along at a faster pace" (Eurogamer review via Wikipedia). Destructoid's 2018 analysis: "she'll cling to your hand if you ask her to, but as soon as you let go, she wanders off to investigate some interesting-looking rocks" and "Holding hands also changes the physical feel of your movement, so there is a tactile difference to buddying up." Yorda doubles as a soft hint system: "Yorda will sometimes take sudden and extreme interest in a particular area and glide over to examine it" after the player changes the room state (Destructoid). Ueda's production drawings show the mechanical scaffolding: "arm range-of-motion and limit information for the IK setup required for holding Yorda's hand", "different hand and arm gestures to call Yorda from various positions and from different distances and heights", and "poses for pulling Yorda over ever-increasing heights, as well as heights she can climb herself" (Game Anim, 21 Nov 2016). Tried and rejected: enemies were originally humanoid, but "Increased detail in textures and in quality of animation made the attacks on Yorda seem far too brutal", so they became shadow creatures (GDC 2004 notes). Ueda had the fingertips re-animated because he was unhappy with hand animation quality (Intelligent Artifice GDC 2004 report). At GDC 2004 Ueda "noted that the team may have gone too far with this subtractive design process" (GlitterBerri citing 1UP's GDC coverage). Ueda in 2009: "there's a significant relationship between the main character controlled by the player, and then the AI character -- Yorda for Ico" and "the interactive nature of the game allows you to build an emotional relationship with the character without telling it in a linear narrative" (Game Developer Q&A, 8 Oct 2009).

THE LAST GUARDIAN / TRICO. Stance: "The player is never able to control Trico directly. The player must learn to read Trico and respond to him accordingly" and "It is not the boy's pet, but his companion" (Ueda via Siliconera, 25 Jun 2015). "It's not a pet game, but there is a live animal in the game" (Game Informer, 27 Sep 2010). Arc: "initially they have a very unfriendly relationship, and as the story progresses...they'll naturally find a bond"; "Emotional attachment is a key to progression"; "it's not like Trico will not listen to the boy every single time... Maybe it will, maybe it won't" (Ueda, TGS 2010 via Game Developer). Autonomy as theme: "It doesn't always do what you ask it to do. That's one of the themes of The Last Guardian"; on frustration risk: "It would be a lie to stay that I have no worries. But another game where you can completely control a creature wouldn't be enjoyable for me" (Edge May 2016 via Kill Screen). The tuning target, four months before launch: "there are two extremes - if you can fully control a character, what's the point? It becomes a pet. But at the opposite end if you can't control it at all it becomes a nuisance, a barrier to progression" (The Guardian 5 Jul 2016 via PSU). AI scale: "The amount of code is very large compared to AI in conventional games. We've given this creature its own desires, so depending on what action it wants to take, that affects everything" (Ueda via IBTimes hands-on, 26 May 2016). CEDEC 2017 (Famitsu report): per-frame order is AI -> animation -> procedural animation -> physics -> fur -> rendering; the AI is "very simple": decide the object of interest (興味対象の決定) -> move to it -> decide the action; every object carries a dynamic "interest level"; the stated goal was to make users feel Trico "has a heart"; action choice is spatial (enough room: eat the barrel; cramped: use feet; impossible: cry for help). The animation director's own verdict, in a 2021 interview: "I think Trico's AI was not as technically elaborate as to allow for it to have its own will. Instead, we expressed its will with animations, staging, and so forth" (Tanaka, Yufei Zheng appendix). Mood readout is diegetic: eye colour ("a pink tinge denotes wariness and anger", IBTimes; guides list pink = enraged/scared, whitish-blue/white = entranced or interested, black/dark = normal and commandable; PlayStation LifeStyle vs KeenGamer disagree on the exact shade names, so treat the palette as UNVERIFIED beyond pink and the "entranced" state). Touch: a mesh-based collision system lets a rub in the right place produce ear twitches; stroking long enough makes Trico "settle on the ground and close its eyes, with a purring vibration of the Dualshock 4" (PlayStation Blog). Refusal with a reason: in the E3 2016 demo Trico stands "timidly pawing at the edge of the drop, refusing to jump. It is, after all, part cat" (IBTimes). Leading: "Sometimes it will lead you to where you should be going, or offer a hint by doing something repeatedly" (PlayStation Blog). Command latency is designed in: "Commands may take a moment", Trico "needs time to finish investigating areas first" (PlayStation LifeStyle); "Trico gets distracted and doesn't always do what you'd like it to do on first asking" (PlayStation Blog). Commands are gated by the bond: early game you cannot command at all; after a narrator line marks the bond, R1 basics unlock, and R1+button verbs (jump, attack, direction) are discovered through play, not tutorials (PlayStation LifeStyle). Reception split: GamesRadar "the greatest AI companion in games" vs Game Revolution noting Trico sometimes did tasks "without player input, making the act of controlling Trico at times ineffective and unnecessary" (Wikipedia). Ueda's own cat was the primary reference; "imagining cat-like movements" because cats "like high places more than dogs", tigers for scale (genDESIGN interview04).
dossier.level_and_camera:
Ico: a single castle, no HUD at all, one enemy type, gameplay reduced to "escaping the castle" (Wikipedia, GDC 2004 reports). Ueda's production drawings include "a top-down diagram illustrating camera behaviour relative to the player's position" and rope traversal with rotation in 45-degree steps (Game Anim). Yorda cannot climb what Ico climbs; drawings specify "heights she can climb herself" vs heights Ico must pull her over, which is the level-design grammar: every vertical step is a companion decision. Save benches are placed in the world as stone couches (Eurogamer via Wikipedia).

The Last Guardian: the single biggest spatial decision was scale. Ueda: "If we make the levels by fitting Trico's large body size, it become easy to move Trico, but it looks quite loose when the boy goes around... Therefore, we tried to make the levels fitted for the boy as much as we could. It was a difficult part" (Gigazine, 15 Jan 2017). The cost of that choice shows in reviews: IGN (7/10) said it was "rare to even have to think about the camera in a third-person game in 2016"; Polygon said it felt "like a PlayStation 2 game"; multiple reviewers blamed "cramped level design" for the camera (Wikipedia). Trico's procedural layer compensates: foot targets are chosen "at the moment the foot is raised", there is obstacle avoidance, "ceiling-height detection to make Trico duck", and the look-at has wall-collision avoidance so the head never clips through geometry (Famitsu, Game Anim). Trico wandering is a level-discovery tool: "new areas can be discovered by letting Trico wander independently" (IGN preview via Wikipedia). Narrator hints are tied to idle time in a room (see numbers). Workflow lesson from the 2010 reboot: "We decided to do the R&D first, lock the core elements, and then progress with the production of the game"; Trico had to be "flexible and adjustable to any sort of level design" (Ueda, TGS 2010). L1 snaps the camera to Trico, which Colquhoun reads as "a clear visual indicator of how far away Trico is, and if there is something blocking Trico" (Game Developer, 24 Jan 2017). For a 2D side-view game, the camera-fight problem largely disappears, but the scale problem transfers directly: a WOLF that is big enough to read as a wolf will make engineer-scale corridors feel either loose or cramped; TLG chose the engineer's scale and paid for it in companion pathing.
dossier.death_and_saves:
Ico: the companion is the fail state. Shadow creatures "attempt to drag Yorda into black vortexes if Ico leaves her for any length of time"; if she is fully engulfed the game ends and the player "must then restart from a save point"; Ico can also die by falling from height (G4TV/Eurogamer via Wikipedia). Saves are diegetic: "Save points in the game are represented by stone benches that Ico and Yorda rest on as the player saves the game" (Eurogamer via Wikipedia). The shadows' AI targets this: they "try to divert your attention away from Yorda so that other shadow monsters can sneak in and steal her" (Destructoid). Exact seconds for the vortex timer were not found in any fetched source: UNVERIFIED.

The Last Guardian: the companion is the rescue, not the fail state. During capture sequences "most controls are disabled, but L1, which aims the camera at Trico, and R1, which calls Trico to you, still work"; this acts as "a safety net for the player, ensuring that Trico will arrive in an emergency, without giving the beast a sixth sense for danger" and makes "the player and the boy reflexively call to Trico for help" (Colquhoun, Game Developer). Trico's own distress feeds back as chores: feeding barrels, pulling out spears after fights, petting until the eyes return to normal (Wikipedia, PlayStation LifeStyle). Checkpoint/respawn specifics for the boy (what is lost, where you reload) were not in any fetched source: UNVERIFIED. Hints are a soft anti-stuck mechanism rather than a death: roughly 5 minutes idle per hint, 95 total (PowerPyx).
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Largely not applicable; both games are deliberately inventory-free. Ico: no HUD, no health display (Wikipedia). Ico carries a single melee weapon that is upgraded over the game; the specific weapons were not in the fetched extracts, so treat as UNVERIFIED in this dossier. The Last Guardian: one tool only, the mirror shield; the boy "wields a reflective mirror that summons lightning from Trico's tail to break certain objects" (Wikipedia); holding circle "illuminates" it and projects "an ornate crosshair", and Trico fires wherever it points (IBTimes). Barrels are the only consumable and are a companion resource, not a player resource: Trico "predicts the arc of the throw so aims at where the barrel will be in the future" (Game Anim), and barrels have the highest interest level so they can be used to redirect Trico (Famitsu; genDESIGN interview01: "With the barrel, you can make Trico totally occupied by it"). Collectible layer: 95 narrator hints form the only collection-style content and are missable with no chapter select (PowerPyx). The transferable idea for W//O's evidence CASE: the one tool is also the companion's attack trigger, so "tool use" and "companion trust" are the same verb.
dossier.action_and_impact: Ico: one enemy type (shadow creatures), stick combat, no damage readout for Ico; enemies "try to avoid you or wait for an opportunity to creep up on you" and "divert your attention away from Yorda" (Destructoid). Bats in Ueda's drawings react to sound and attack within 5 metres and have deliberately "weak flapping motions" (Game Anim). The Last Guardian: the boy cannot fight; armoured guards carry him off and Trico fights them (Wikipedia). Impact is sold through the companion's mass: "Grass gets crushed underfoot as Trico walks", Trico's animations produce "screen shake effects", and resting on Trico gives "a purring vibration of the Dualshock 4" (PlayStation Blog). Ueda on weight: "If there were no motions of muscles, or reactions when it jumps and lands on the ground, you can't feel its weightiness"; "All physical actions have motion curves, and they have to be connected smoothly" (Gigazine). The animators were told "to emphasize the expression of weight and eliminate popping between animation transitions" (genDESIGN interview04). Contact between boy and Trico uses centre-of-gravity referencing with "motion transitions that would let them dynamically move their feet so as not to fall down" (Ueda, genDESIGN interview04). The ranged attack is a joint act: boy aims the mirror, Trico fires red lightning from its tail (IBTimes). The Projection Trico installation shows the AI's reactivity surface: Trico "becomes agitated when sensing camera flashes and reacts to loud sounds", a stained-glass eye makes it "startled" and "growl at you", a barrel makes it "totally occupied" (genDESIGN interview01).
dossier.presentation_ui_art:
Ico: "subtracting design"; "removing any form of interface elements, keeping the gameplay focused only on escaping the castle, and having a single enemy type" (Wikipedia, GDC 2004). Script-level evidence: of 115 subtitle cards in the game files, 77 are unused, about 70% of written dialogue cut (GlitterBerri). Ueda: "Whether it was the girl's animation or the details of the map, I didn't hold back on removing and subtracting elements as needed. If something felt unfinished or lacking, then I'd remove it" (via Wikipedia). Animation was key-framed, not motion-captured (NYT via Wikipedia); Ueda re-did the fingertips (Intelligent Artifice). His stated animation philosophy: "when you look at a single animated frame, it might not even be drawn that well, but when it's put together and animated smoothly, it looks cool" (Game Anim).

The Last Guardian: "we did not use motion capture in The Last Guardian. It was all done by hard-working animators using keyframe animation" (Tanaka, genDESIGN interview04). Look-at is the named key tech: rotating neck-then-head made Trico "look robotic, almost like a toy snake"; the fix was the "lion dance" (獅子舞) method that "first fixed the head position and rotation followed by the neck", pivoting near the nose tip, inspired by how real animals hold the head still while the body moves (genDESIGN interview04, Famitsu, Yufei Zheng). Limit stated by Tanaka: "with procedural animation it's quite difficult to produce a natural gaze or powerful pose", so hand-key and procedural are blended. Feathers: the "fin method" treats "each feather as strips and processes them individually"; wind strength changes feather stiffness, strong wind makes feathers stand on end, wind is wave-based spatial (Game Anim, Famitsu). Visual language: "delicate watercolour style", fur-like feathers that "drift and flail in the wind" (PlayStation Blog). Ueda's generalisable rule: natural movement "is an outcome of removing unnatural parts over and over again" (Gigazine). The only UI-like layer is in-world: eye colour as mood, a narrator who speaks only after long idle time (first Team Ico game with voice-over, PlayStation Blog June 2016 via Wikipedia), a shield glow as crosshair. Ueda started from Trico's character design, not story or world (Gigazine).
dossier.audio: Ico: the language barrier is load-bearing; Yorda's speech is deliberately untranslatable to the player so the AI's limits are hidden behind a story rule (auriea.org GDC 2004 notes). Calling Yorda is a voiced-and-gestured call on a button, with "different hand and arm gestures to call Yorda from various positions and from different distances and heights" (Game Anim). No further Ico audio specifics were found in fetched sources. The Last Guardian: the call scales with distance: "cupping of his hands for a longer and louder shout when calling to a faraway Trico" (PlayStation Blog). Haptics double as audio: the DualShock purr when Trico settles (PlayStation Blog). Narration is the hint channel, first in the series, spoken by the adult boy as recollection and used for "gameplay hints and other context" (PlayStation Blog June 2016 via Wikipedia); hints fire after roughly 5 minutes stuck, and sitting to meditate (L3/R3) appears to speed them (PowerPyx). Trico reacts to loud sounds and flashes (genDESIGN interview01). Procedural or per-surface footstep audio details were not found: UNVERIFIED.
dossier.mobile_and_input: Neither game shipped on phones; both are PlayStation-only, so touch is not applicable. Input vocabulary (useful because it is tiny): Ico uses R1 to hold Yorda's hand and to call her, triangle to jump, and rope rotation in 45-degree steps (Eurogamer via Wikipedia; Game Anim). The Last Guardian: R1 tap = call; R1 + left stick = point a direction; R1 + triangle = jump; R1 + square = attack/swipe; R1 + cross = scold; R1 + circle = praise; hold circle on Trico = pet (calms pink eyes); hold circle = raise mirror; L1 = camera to Trico; L3/R3 = sit and meditate (PlayStation LifeStyle; KeenGamer; IBTimes; PowerPyx). Commands are locked until the bond narration, then revealed by play (PlayStation LifeStyle). Ueda promised in 2010 "a simpler control scheme" so non-gamers would play (Game Informer 2010). Mapping to W//O's scheme: Ico's "R1 = hold hand" is one held button that changes movement feel; TLG's "R1 = call, R1+X/O = scold/praise" is a tap-vs-modifier pattern that collapses neatly onto one USE plus two choice buttons (USE tap = call, USE hold = contact/pet, choice A/B = praise/scold when WOLF is the context). Performance note from Digital Foundry (via relays, original unfetched): base PS4 "often dips to 20 FPS", PS4 Pro 1900p mode compromises frame rate, PS4 Pro 1080p is the stable mode (Press Start, Gamereactor).

steal: Give WOLF a three-step mind, not a planner: pick an object of interest from per-object interest levels, walk to it, then choose an action by the space available (Famitsu CEDEC 2017). This is cheap in GDScript and is exactly what let Trico read as alive.

Spend the budget on expression, not cognition. Tanaka: Trico's AI 'was not as technically elaborate as to allow for it to have its own will. Instead, we expressed its will with animations, staging'. For a 2D painterly wolf: a 'thinking' idle, a head-turn before refusal, a pawing-at-the-edge loop before a drop, a repeated gesture when leading.

Implement look-at head-first: fix the head on the target, let the neck/body catch up (the 'lion dance' method). In 2D this is a two-bone chain: head sprite rotates to target immediately, neck/shoulder tweens behind it, and the head never clips the room collider.

Make refusal legible and physical before it is verbal: Trico pawing at a ledge told the player 'no, and here is why'. Each WOLF refusal should have a body-language tell that precedes any choice prompt.

Gate commands behind the bond, then let the player discover verbs through play. TLG has zero Trico commands until the narrator marks the first bond; W//O can mirror this: USE-tap does nothing to WOLF until he decides you are worth answering.

Tap-vs-modifier mapping: R1 tap = call, R1 + face button = praise/scold/jump. On W//O's one-USE-plus-two-choices scheme: USE tap = call, USE hold on WOLF = contact (pet/lean), choice A/B = praise/scold when WOLF is in range. Keep the call working even when everything else is disabled (grab/capture sequences), as TLG does with R1/L1.

Keep the call alive as the panic button and the trust meter at once: in TLG calling while captured both summons help and reframes the camera to show how far away and how blocked the companion is. W//O can play a distance-scaled call animation (cupped hands = far) and let the room's parallax layers reveal WOLF's position.

Companion-as-hint: Yorda 'glides over' to the thing that changed; Trico 'offers a hint by doing something repeatedly'. Let WOLF nose at the correct relay/station after a room-state change instead of adding UI hints, and keep a slow idle narrator-style nudge (TLG: ~5 min) as the engineer-only fallback.

Diegetic mood readout instead of a trust bar: eye colour in TLG, held-hand feel in Ico. For WOLF: optic colour/brightness, ear and tail pose, and a different walk cadence when he is on your side vs. tolerating you.

Make contact change movement feel. Ico's hand-hold slows and sways you; TLG's petting ends in a controller purr. If the engineer can lean on or hold WOLF, change acceleration and add a low haptic/rumble-like audio bed for the duration.

Design the rooms for the engineer's scale and solve WOLF's size with pathing rules (ceiling check, foot targets chosen on lift-off, non-walkable avoidance), not by widening everything; TLG chose this on purpose and documented the cost.

Sell weight with contact, not just shake: centre-of-gravity-referenced foot shuffles when the engineer climbs on, 'reactions when it jumps and lands', smooth motion curves. The existing impact kit (shake, hit-stop, flash) should get a 'WOLF landing' profile that is heavier than any player hit.

Subtract until the relationship is all that is left (no HUD, one tool, few verbs) but keep Ueda's own caveat that Ico went too far; keep the CASE inventory as the one exception because it serves the story.

Lock the companion tech before building rooms: the 2010 TLG reboot put R&D first so Trico was 'flexible and adjustable to any sort of level design'. For W//O: finish WOLF's route/lead/scout behaviours on a test room before widening the three live rooms.
avoid: Do not let autonomy read as latency. The most repeated TLG complaint is Trico 'casually ignoring your shouts' with no visible reason; the balance Ueda described (pet vs nuisance) was still being tuned four months before launch. Every WOLF non-response needs a tell within a second: head turn, ear flick, or a look at the thing he is busy with.

Do not make the companion's job redundant to the player's input. Game Revolution: Trico sometimes acted 'without player input, making the act of controlling Trico at times ineffective and unnecessary'. If WOLF is going to do it anyway, do not also ask the engineer to press for it; if the press matters, show the difference.

Do not build rooms at the companion's scale (loose) or cram the companion into player-scale rooms without pathing tech (camera and collision fights). TLG's camera criticism (IGN: 'rare to even have to think about the camera') came from cramped geometry plus a huge body; W//O's 1.5-2 screen rooms with one height change need WOLF-sized clearances planned on the layout, not patched later.

Do not make the companion the game-over screen without warning. Ico's Yorda-engulfed fail state works because the shadows telegraph and the save bench is diegetic; W//O's rule is engineer-only progress, so WOLF must never be the only way to avoid death.

Do not hide the AI's limits behind narrative unless the narrative is also the design. Ico's language barrier was chosen specifically because they 'would not be able to express Yorda's AI naturally'; W//O's WOLF can talk, so a refusal must be motivated by memory or situation, not by vagueness.
Do not fake trust with a visible meter. Both games refused a bar; trust was read from behaviour. A numeric 'WOLF trust' HUD would undo the memory-gating premise.

Do not over-animate the companion with mocap-style realism in a painterly 2D game; both games used keyframe animation with a few strong procedural layers (foot placement, look-at, wind). Pick two or three procedural systems and hand-key the rest.

Do not rely on the ~5-minute idle hint alone as the stuck-player fallback; TLG hints are missable and slow, which reviewers tolerated only because the companion also led. W//O already has hold-to-move and USE on the critical path, so keep an engineer-only progression path visible in the room itself.

Do not ship a platform where the companion's simulation drops the frame rate (TLG dips to ~20 fps on base PS4); on phone, WOLF's behaviour tick and parallax layers should be profiled before adding feather-style per-strand effects.

Do not let the subtraction philosophy delete the player's agency to be unkind; TLG's scold command exists so that praise means something. WOLF's memory of treatment needs both verbs available and both remembered.

corrections.claim: Trico command set: 'R1 + cross = scold; R1 + circle = praise' (numbers entry marked 'verified', source PlayStation LifeStyle), with L1 camera and L3/R3 meditate listed in the same set
corrections.problem: Wrong per the cited source. PlayStation LifeStyle (https://www.playstationlifestyle.net/2017/01/19/psls-help-desk-how-to-control-trico-the-last-guardian/) says 'Cross and circle apparently scold and praise Trico respectively, but I never found these necessary at any point during my playthrough'. It puts no R1 modifier on them, hedges with 'apparently', and says they were never needed. The page does not mention L1 or L3/R3 at all; those come from Colquhoun and PowerPyx. The 'verified' label overstates this. The steal/avoid line 'TLG's scold command exists so that praise means something' rests on this mapping.
corrections.correction: List scold and praise as Cross and Circle (no R1 modifier stated), marked 'apparently' in PSLS, which also says they were never necessary. Cite L1 to Colquhoun (Game Developer) and L3/R3 to PowerPyx. Downgrade the command-set confidence to 'derived', and drop or soften the 'scold exists so praise means something' design rationale, because no source states it.

corrections.claim: Command latency quotes: 'Commands may take a moment', Trico 'needs time to finish investigating areas first' (PlayStation LifeStyle)
corrections.problem: Misquoted: these exact words do not appear in the source. The source says: 'Again, this may take a moment, but Trico will eventually come.' and 'More often than not he just needs to finish sniffing around a bit before moving on to the next area.'
corrections.correction: Use the exact source wording, or present it as a paraphrase without quotation marks.

corrections.claim: 'We've given this creature its own desires...' is attributed to 'Ueda via IBTimes hands-on, 26 May 2016'. The 'pawing at the edge of the drop, refusing to jump. It is, after all, part cat' and 'pink tinge' lines are attributed to IBTimes.
corrections.problem: Misattributed. The IBTimes article by Ben Skipper relays Edge magazine's cover story (issue 294), which contained Edge's hands-on and Edge's interview with Ueda. IBTimes did not play the game or interview Ueda itself. The quote is genuine, but the outlet chain is wrong.
corrections.correction: Attribute it as 'Ueda to Edge (issue 294 cover story), relayed by IBTimes UK, 26 May 2016'. The hands-on descriptions (pawing at the drop, pink eyes, the mirror crosshair) also come from Edge's preview.

corrections.claim: Ueda quotes 'It doesn't always do what you ask it to do...' and 'It would be a lie to stay that I have no worries...' are dated 'Edge May 2016 via Kill Screen'
corrections.problem: Kill Screen (https://www.killscreen.com/dont-worry-last-guardian-still-coming-2016/, published 27 May 2016) gives no Edge issue number or month. 'May 2016' is the date of the relay, not a verified issue date. ('stay' is the source's own typo and is quoted correctly.)
corrections.correction: Cite as 'Edge issue 294 cover interview (issue number per IBTimes UK), relayed by Kill Screen 27 May 2016'. Mark the issue's cover month as UNVERIFIED.

corrections.claim: The pet/nuisance quote (The Guardian, 5 Jul 2016) is described as 'the tuning target, four months before launch' and 'still being tuned four months before launch'
corrections.problem: The arithmetic is wrong. The game released 6 December 2016 (Wikipedia), about five months after 5 July. At the time of the interview, PSU said launch was set for October 2016, which was three months away.
corrections.correction: Say 'about five months before the December 2016 release (when launch was still planned for October)'. The Guardian original remains unfetched, cited via PSU.

corrections.claim: Ico development span: 'about 4 years, started 1998 on PS1, moved to PS2 after ~2 years' (source: Intelligent Artifice GDC 2004 report, marked verified)
corrections.problem: Source misattributed. The Intelligent Artifice report only says the game 'was under development for 4 years'. It does not give 1998, PS1 or the two-year switch. Those details are on Wikipedia (Ico), which states 1998, a move to PS2 after two years, and about four years in total.
corrections.correction: Cite Wikipedia (Ico) for 1998, PS1, PS2 and the ~2-year switch. Cite Intelligent Artifice only for the '4 years' figure.

corrections.claim: Ico pilot movie: '3-minute Lightwave movie (Feb-Jun 1997) before the team existed' (Wikipedia, Team Ico wiki, auriea.org GDC notes)
corrections.problem: The dates are unsupported. The auriea.org notes contain neither '1997' nor any length for the pilot. Wikipedia says Ueda conceived the concept in 1997 and made a Lightwave animation 'with the help of an assistant', but gives no February to June dates. 'Before the team existed' overstates it, since an assistant helped.
corrections.correction: Write 'Concept in 1997; Ueda and an assistant made a ~3-minute Lightwave pilot (Wikipedia)'. Mark the Feb-Jun 1997 dates UNVERIFIED (Team Ico wiki not fetched).

corrections.claim: Tanaka quote presented as 'The animation director's own verdict, in a 2021 interview' and the source as an 'email interview... (Dec 2021)'
corrections.problem: Overstated and missing context. The page does not say the interview was by email or give its date; 15 Dec 2021 is only the blog post date. Tanaka prefaces the line with 'While I was not in charge of Trico's AI, my personal opinion is...', which hedges it. He adds: 'With Trico, we emphasized simplicity of AI to allow for easier controls by artists.'
corrections.correction: Present it as Tanaka's personal opinion, given while he says he was not in charge of the AI. Include the 'simplicity of AI ... easier controls by artists' line, which supports the 'spend on expression' steal better. Drop 'email' and give 'Dec 2021' as the blog post date.

corrections.claim: 'Polygon said it felt "like a PlayStation 2 game"' (via Wikipedia)
corrections.problem: Wikipedia paraphrases this and Kollar's wording is stronger. According to a search snippet (polygon.com could not be fetched, so this is UNVERIFIED), the review says: 'at its weakest, it's not just "like a PlayStation 2 game," but like a particularly rough, unpolished' experience. Wikipedia's text is a paraphrase: 'elements that made the game feel like a PlayStation 2 game rather than something on modern hardware.' Polygon scored it 7.5/10.
corrections.correction: Attribute the wording to Wikipedia's paraphrase, or quote Kollar's sentence marked UNVERIFIED (from a search snippet). Add the 7.5/10 score next to IGN's 7/10.

corrections.claim: 'Touch: a mesh-based collision system lets a rub in the right place produce ear twitches' (cited with the PlayStation Blog purr line)
corrections.problem: Unsupported by the cited source. The PlayStation Blog article (22 Nov 2016) does not contain 'ear', 'twitch', 'mesh' or 'collision'. The genDESIGN interview01 also does not mention them. Only the stroke-until-settle-and-purr line is confirmed.
corrections.correction: Keep only the PlayStation Blog line ('stroke Trico to the point where it starts to settle on the ground and close its eyes, with a purring vibration of the Dualshock 4'). Mark the ear-twitch and mesh-collision detail UNVERIFIED until a source is fetched.

corrections.claim: 'Trico's animations produce "screen shake effects"' (PlayStation Blog)
corrections.problem: Slightly generalised. The source ties screen shake specifically to Trico's leaps: 'its sometimes less than majestic leaps are often accompanied with screen shake effects to dramatically convey a sense of weight'.
corrections.correction: Say screen shake accompanies Trico's leaps and landings to convey weight. That fits the proposed 'WOLF landing' shake profile even better.

corrections.claim: Projection Trico: a 'stained-glass eye makes it "startled" and "growl at you"'; Trico 'reacts to loud sounds' (genDESIGN interview01)
corrections.problem: Minor wording issue. The source says 'the eye symbol' (Tanaka), not 'stained-glass eye'. The loud-sound reaction is described specifically: at TGS 'Trico howled at the main stage whenever it heard loud sounds from it'. The flash line is Ueda's, and the barrel and eye lines are Tanaka's.
corrections.correction: Use 'eye symbol' and 'howled at loud sounds from the neighbouring stage', and attribute each line to the right speaker.

corrections.claim: Avoid list: 'TLG hints are missable and slow' (as a stuck-player fallback); 'missable with no chapter select' (PowerPyx)
corrections.problem: Overstated as a design point. PowerPyx calls the hints missable only for the 'All Talked Out' trophy count, and notes 'Your progress carries over into New Game+'. Missing a hint for the trophy does not mean the help is unavailable to a stuck player. PowerPyx also notes that meditating with L3/R3 'repeats the last hint automatically'.
corrections.correction: Say the hints are slow (about 5 minutes for the first, about 5 more for the next, per PowerPyx). Note that meditating can surface and repeat hints, and that 'missable' refers only to trophy collection.

corpus.group: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons and A Plague Tale: Innocence and Requiem: sibling or companion bonds through mechanics, AI companion behaviour, stealth, death and checkpoints

dossier.games: Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons (Starbreeze Studios, dir. Josef Fares, Unreal Engine 3, Xbox 360 7 Aug 2013, PS3/PC 3 Sep 2013; UE5 remake by Avantgarden, 28 Feb 2024). A Plague Tale: Innocence (Asobo Studio / Focus Home Interactive, custom Zouna engine, 14 May 2019; PS5/Series/Switch 6 Jul 2021). A Plague Tale: Requiem (Asobo / Focus Entertainment, next-gen only, 17/18 Oct 2022). Note: WebSearch budget for this session ran out partway through; everything below rests on pages that were actually fetched, and gaps are marked UNVERIFIED. Several primary pages (Giant Bomb Fares interview, GameSpot rats piece, Unreal Engine remake interview, Epic remake piece, Eurogamer/DF, IGN, HowLongToBeat, speedrun.com) returned 403/404 or are blocked and were NOT used.
dossier.why_relevant: All three games are single-player companion games where the bond is built by mechanics rather than dialogue trees, which is exactly WOLF//OVERRIDE's problem: one playable engineer, one independent robotic wolf. Brothers proves a bond can live in the input itself (one hand per brother, "you connect with your left hand to the bigger brother and right hand to the little brother", Fares) and that removing the companion's input channel is the most powerful grief beat in the medium (the "phantom thumb stick", Markle). A Plague Tale is the direct model for an independent companion: Asobo cut Hugo's order-giving abilities because "What we had was being experienced too much like a robot... So we had to give Hugo back more freedom" (Dedeine), gave him only stay/follow, made him panic and shout when left alone too long, and in Requiem deliberately "limits how many rats Hugo could control" and invents "narrative reasons for Hugo not to be with Amicia" so the companion's power never removes tension (Choteau). Asobo's shift from Innocence ("quite narrow, with only one way to approach a situation") to Requiem's "much wider open areas" while struggling to "keep the narrative rhythm" mirrors the decided move to 1.5-2 screen rooms. Their death model (instant death in Innocence, forgiving return-to-stealth in Requiem, door-checkpoints) gives a measured before/after for the planned evidence-drop death rule.

dossier.companion:
BROTHERS: the companion is not an AI at all; the bond is the control split. Fares: "controlling with two sticks and how it was going to end. That was actually the first thing I came up with." Each brother = one stick to move + the matching trigger to interact (Wikipedia, Game Developer). Abilities are asymmetric and complementary: "Naiee is small and nimble, while the older Naia is stronger and braver" (McCamant); the younger cannot swim and "must cling to his brother's back as he swims for the both of them". Fares refused co-op ("I would rather cut my hands than do that") because the point is that one person's two hands are the two people; puzzle tuning used the shoe-tying analogy: doing a two-handed task alone feels natural, doing it with someone else "is going to feel a bit weird" (Shacknews). The ending beat: after the elder dies, his stick goes dead, producing a "phantom thumb stick" (Markle), then the final water crossing is only completable by pressing the dead brother's input; Fares says "pushing the button for the other brother was actually something that came up later" in development. (Markle's essay assigns the younger brother to the left thumb; Fares and the game's documentation say left = big brother; trust Fares.) The 2024 remake keeps single-player controls but adds a local two-player option (Wikipedia; Steam listing of original remains single-player, controller required). 

PLAGUE TALE INNOCENCE: Hugo (age 5) is an autonomous follower with exactly two orders. Dedeine: "Hugo will never be a backpack. He has its own behavior, his own feelings." / "Any moment you can ask him to stay somewhere, or to follow you." Failure feedback is diegetic and audible: "If you ask Hugo to stay somewhere, and he stays too long, or if you're out of his sight for too long, he will panic, he will shout, he will call for Amicia, and that will probably attract guards." Hugo can be sent through small gaps to open restricted areas (Wikipedia). Asobo TRIED and CUT a richer command set: "We wanted to push the basic abilities and [wanted them] to go much further. We had to cut this [in order to] be honest and sincere with our characters, because it was damaging their relationship too much"; "'Do this, go here, grab that.' It was not natural." Absence is a designed feeling: "The moments where you have to send him off on his own you really feel his presence missing" (Wccftech). Design priority order: "The siblings were in before the rats." Dedeine on depth: "It's not the type of game to have really deep collaborative mechanics so I think where we landed is just right for us." Other companions (Lucas, Melie, Arthur, Rodric) rotate in with one ability each: UNVERIFIED specifics (fandom wiki paywalled, 402).

PLAGUE TALE REQUIEM: Hugo gains Echo ("reveals the locations of enemies through walls") and rat control (Wikipedia). Choteau's balancing rules: the team "limits how many rats Hugo could control" and creates "narrative reasons for Hugo not to be with Amicia"; early sections pair Amicia with Lucas "without Hugo's rat powers, forcing vulnerability"; the team "updates its level and combat design based on whether or not the player has access to those rat powers" (Game Developer). Power is double-edged: "it can become dangerous if he loses control" (EDGE via Wccftech); "his power is much greater, his potential for murder and destruction is much higher and it can be very dangerous to play with fire" (Xbox Wire); over-use "can completely change part of the current chapter" (ActuGaming). Adult companions (Sophia, Arnaud) were written as mirrors of futures Amicia could follow or avoid (ActuGaming). Reviews: companions assist with two-person puzzles such as winches (Shacknews). Sophia's prism and Arnaud's combat roles: UNVERIFIED from fetched sources.
dossier.level_and_camera:
BROTHERS: fixed-angle third-person "overlooking the two brothers" (Wikipedia). Fares: "the most insane part was the camera"; rule: "the camera would always try to put the right brother on the right side, but if you're close it doesn't do that anymore" (Game Informer). Fares attributed new-player success to the camera always keeping both brothers on screen (Shacknews). Puzzles are "quite soft and not too hard" and the team changed the mechanic constantly: "it was important to change the experience all the time, to come up with something new" (Game Informer). 

INNOCENCE: linear by choice: "We chose to make a linear narrative experience to concentrate on what we wanted to tell" (Choteau, DualShockers), though "sometimes the player will be able to choose how to play and this can be 'rewarded'". Light is the spatial grammar: "the only way to stay safe is to use the lights", but staying in light "is not always a good idea when someone is looking for you" (Choteau); "these two little siblings as these little candles in the middle of darkness" (Dedeine). Rats are a 4-LOD crowd (LOD0-1 up to 200 individually drawn animated rats, LOD2 1,258, LOD3 3,500 instanced without tails; Torok, 80.lv), up to 5,000 on screen (Wikipedia). 

REQUIEM: Choteau: "Innocence was quite narrow, with only one way to approach a situation, and we wanted to address that. We've created much wider open areas where you can play as you want" (LevelUp); "the majority of situations have been designed to allow the player to be free in the way they approach the events, from stealth to combat" (WellPlayed); "most sequences can be approached in a low-key or warlike way, and you can even find an alternative that mixes the two options" (Xbox Wire). Cost of opening up, in Choteau's words: "on a beaucoup de mal a garder ce rythme narratif qui fait, pour nous, l'ADN de A Plague Tale, en ouvrant plus le gameplay et les espaces" (we struggled to keep the narrative rhythm that is the DNA of A Plague Tale while opening up gameplay and spaces). Rats now climb and work across floors: "They are now able to climb and are much more efficient at catching their prey by taking advantage of the environment"; "they can overcome obstacles, climb several floors"; "we've been able to push the horizon much farther" and build "locations that evolve dynamically according to the story and events". Laura Mas Maury's GDC 2023 talk is explicitly about "breaking linearity or creating opportunities for the player in a narrative driven game" with case studies "from action sequences to narrative driven areas" by a 70-person team; her Blocktober 2023 thread shows WIP blockouts next to finals and stresses integrating "art and gameplay elements so as not to damage the environments' identities" (80.lv). Talk content itself: UNVERIFIED (members-only video not viewed). Camera in Plague Tale is standard over-the-shoulder third person; nothing developer-stated about it was found.
dossier.death_and_saves:
BROTHERS: no inventory, no combat health; fail states are environmental (falls, hazards) with near-instant restarts: exact respawn distance and checkpoint spacing UNVERIFIED (no fetched source gives numbers). The only death that matters is scripted and mechanical: the elder brother dies, and the player "no longer need[s] to use the second stick" (Markle); the final crossing requires the dead brother's input. Fares: "you're alone and you have to go through those obstacles yourself." 

INNOCENCE: stealth failure is lethal: "Players must use stealth to avoid instant-death encounters" (Wikipedia). Rats are a timed death, not instant: "As soon as you enter, the rats start to climb on the characters, and you have very little time to react. If you go into the light they will jump off" (Dedeine). Difficulty was deliberately low-to-mid, then spiked: "When I was playing the last level I died like ten times... suddenly I needed to pay attention" (Dedeine). Checkpoints are per-encounter autosaves; exact rules UNVERIFIED. 

REQUIEM: softened on purpose. "Unlike the first game, Amicia will not die after being hit once by enemies. She can also return to stealth after discovery and counter attacks" (Wikipedia); "Getting spotted doesn't mean you've got to reload a checkpoint anymore" (Push Square). "Well-timed counter attack will give her an opening to flee" and on death "you back to the start of the checkpoint" (Shacknews). Critics still flagged "concerns included combat safety and checkpoint systems" (Wikipedia reception summary). A fetched search summary of reviews described checkpoints as "usually involves reaching a door" (door-open animation = safe): source page not fetched, UNVERIFIED. Nothing is lost on death in any of the three games; no loot or evidence drop exists, so WOLF//OVERRIDE's drop-on-death rule has no precedent here and must be tested on its own.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence:
BROTHERS: not applicable; no inventory, no collectibles that gate progress (achievements for optional interactions exist: UNVERIFIED detail). 

INNOCENCE: a small, legible toolkit. Sling with crafted alchemy ammo: "fire-starting sulfur stones that ignite braziers, stink bombs that attract rats, or fire suppressants to extinguish torches" (Wikipedia). Dedeine on how the same tools solve three threat types: "Sometimes you need to avoid the rats, sometimes you need to create a path with the lights through the rats... sometimes you will use the rats against the humans." Workbench upgrades: "improve the sling in many ways, the range of the sling, the power of the sling, and lastly the stealthiness" plus "Equipment in general to make her less noticeable to the humans" and "sometimes even Hugo's gear" (GamingBolt). 

REQUIEM: adds knife, crossbow and tar mixture (Wikipedia). Progression is behaviour-tracked rather than point-spent, "borrowed from The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, tracking player behavior to reward abilities organically" (Game Developer): skills "related to prudence, opportunism or combat depending on his/her play style" (Choteau, WellPlayed). Evidence/collectibles: Innocence has collectible curiosities and Requiem has souvenirs/feathers (common knowledge, UNVERIFIED from fetched pages). Relevance: WOLF's memory of treatment is the WOLF//OVERRIDE equivalent of Requiem's silent behaviour tracking.
dossier.action_and_impact:
BROTHERS: almost no combat; the few boss/chase moments are two-handed coordination puzzles. Fares: "Every puzzle and challenge needed to be quite soft and not too hard" and puzzles were "designed to be more comfortable when controlling two rather than one". Team had no formal designer ("We didn't have a game designer") and was half first-timers. 

INNOCENCE: Amicia's sling is a distraction and stun tool first, kill tool second; direct confrontation is death. Asobo pulled combat back for character reasons: "At one point, the sequence in the village had much more combat in it, but we slowed it down because it was not right for Amicia to be as soon ready to kill people" (Dedeine). They also tried "fantastical elements" and dropped them: "it wasn't feeling right, it was like betraying our characters"; "we have cut every aspect of the game that was not serving the story" (Choteau); a full chapter was cut. 

REQUIEM: "She can be much more aggressive. Amicia unfortunately had to get used to dealing death and is no longer taken by surprise" (Choteau, EDGE via Wccftech); "she can now attack in close combat, counter attacks and even, later, use a crossbow" and the violence "will have a huge impact on her evolution, her psyche, her identity" (Xbox Wire). Rats avoid light better so stray rats now hurt: "In Innocence, casting a light sent the bulk of the hoard away, and individual little rats caught in the open weren't a threat to the player" (Choteau); Requiem removes that safety margin. Rats "evolve following Hugo's illness". Combat still "remains dangerous, Amicia cannot survive direct confrontation" (Game Developer summary); Push Square: she "can counter enemy attacks and potentially stab them to death if she has a knife". Impact feedback numbers (hit-stop, shake): not published by either studio.
dossier.presentation_ui_art:
BROTHERS: no readable dialogue; "a fictional language based on Lebanese Arabic" (Wikipedia), "unsubtitled glossolalia" with meaning carried by animation and gesture (McCamant). Fairy-tale Scandinavian folklore look; the brothers' silhouettes and sizes read as their abilities. UI is minimal: no HUD, no prompts beyond trigger-to-interact; the remake moved to UE5 (Wikipedia). 

INNOCENCE: painterly medieval Aquitaine, 1349; light-vs-dark is both art direction and the rule set. Rendering specifics (Torok, 80.lv): deferred with 6 G-buffer targets, cascaded shadow maps for the sun plus depth cubemaps for point lights, compute-shader SSAO and bloom, a "minimal" post stack, then colour grading, tonemapping, UI. Torok's verdict on the rat tech: "it looks like it's mostly brute force." Hugo's state is shown through animation and voice (hand-holding, shouting) rather than icons (Dedeine). 

REQUIEM: journey "south, towards the Mediterranean and its burst of light and colors" (Focus In Focus series); Hugo's Echo is a wall-hack vision mode; Asobo "created a mocap studio... and hired actors" because "we weren't technically at the level we wanted" for faces (ActuGaming). Series X 1440p/30, Series S 900p/30, 40 fps on 120 Hz displays, later 60 fps performance mode at 1080p (DF via Pure Xbox and search summary; the 1080p figure is UNVERIFIED). Won visual and narrative awards at the Pegases and five TGA 2022 nominations (Wikipedia).
dossier.audio:
BROTHERS: score by Gustaf Grefberg (Wikipedia); invented language means the voice track carries emotion, never information, so the game never needs subtitles: a direct precedent for WOLF speaking in machine sound rather than text. 

INNOCENCE: Olivier Deriviere score (Wikipedia). Companion audio is a mechanic: Hugo "will panic, he will shout, he will call for Amicia, and that will probably attract guards" (Dedeine), so the companion's voice is a stealth risk the player manages by keeping him close. Rats as sound mass: 5,000 agents with "too many animations, too many AI at the same time" (Dedeine on why Switch could not run it). 

REQUIEM: won sound design at the Pegases (Wikipedia); "chases with hundreds of thousands of rats" are built as audiovisual set pieces (Choteau). No developer-published numbers on footsteps per surface, room tone or mix buses were found; UNVERIFIED beyond these points.
dossier.mobile_and_input:
BROTHERS: controller-only by design. Steam: "Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons requires a controller to play." Fares: "This game is designed for controllers" and mouse/keyboard is "ruining the experience even more" (Game Informer). Input surface: two sticks + two triggers; the trigger is a single context-sensitive USE per brother (talk, grab ledge, pull). Fares' test result: the scheme helped inexperienced players more than FPS controls (Shacknews). The remake adds optional two-player split (Wikipedia). Mobile: no official phone release found; a one-stick-per-character scheme on touch would be the WOLF//OVERRIDE equivalent of two choice buttons, but it is UNVERIFIED whether any touch port exists. 

PLAGUE TALE: standard twin-stick third-person; companion control is two verbs (stay/follow) on one button, crafting on a radial, Hugo's Echo on one button. No phone version (Innocence had a cloud Switch version; UNVERIFIED detail). Takeaway for a hold-to-move, one-USE, two-choice phone game: both franchises prove a companion needs at most two explicit commands; everything else should be autonomous.
