steal: Give WOLF exactly two explicit commands (stay / come), mapped to the two choice buttons, and make everything else autonomous. Asobo cut 'Do this, go here, grab that' because it made Hugo feel 'too much like a robot'; two verbs is the proven ceiling for a companion that must feel alive.

Make WOLF's refusal and absence loud and diegetic, never a HUD icon: Hugo 'will panic, he will shout, he will call for Amicia, and that will probably attract guards'. For WOLF: a left-behind or mistreated wolf should emit servo whines, bark-bursts or scanner pings that the purge sentry can hear, so the player feels his state through the horror systems.

Engineer the moments WOLF is NOT there as deliberately as the moments he is. Dedeine: 'The moments where you have to send him off on his own you really feel his presence missing.' Pair each wider room with a short engineer-only stretch (WOLF scouting ahead) so his return lands.

Cap the companion's power and justify the cap in fiction. Requiem 'limits how many rats Hugo could control' and writes 'narrative reasons for Hugo not to be with Amicia'. Give WOLF a battery/heat budget per room (a number the player can see on his body, not a bar) so he cannot trivialise the sentry.

Design every essential objective twice, once with WOLF and once without, exactly as Asobo 'updates its level and combat design based on whether or not the player has access to those rat powers'. This is the engineer-only fallback rule stated as a level-design checklist.

Track treatment silently, Morrowind-style, and let it surface as behaviour: Requiem awards prudence/opportunism/combat skills by watching what the player does, not by menus. WOLF's memory should be computed from counted acts (times left behind, times ordered into danger, times helped up) and expressed as willingness, lead distance and refusal odds.

Use the Brothers trick once: a scripted beat where WOLF's input channel goes dead (a choice button does nothing, or the hold-to-move drags). The 'phantom thumb stick' is the single most quoted mechanic in companion design; one use is a gut punch, two is a gimmick.

Opening rooms up: Innocence was 'quite narrow, with only one way to approach a situation'; Requiem built 'much wider open areas' but then 'struggled to keep the narrative rhythm'. For 1.5-2 screen rooms, give each one exactly two readable approaches (lit route vs dark route; engineer route vs WOLF route) and one scripted beat that fires regardless, so rhythm survives.

Keep light as a two-edged rule: 'the only way to stay safe is to use the lights' but light 'is not always a good idea when someone is looking for you'. The coolant-relay and purge-sentry rooms already have this shape; make every room's safety resource also its exposure.

Make the death model readable before it is punishing: Innocence rats give 'very little time to react' but a clear escape (step into light, they 'jump off'). Dropping unsecured evidence on death should show the CASE items physically spill at the body so the player understands recovery in one look.

Soften detection the way Requiem did: 'Getting spotted doesn't mean you've got to reload a checkpoint anymore'; allow re-entering stealth after a break so a wider room is not a one-mistake reload loop. Reviewers still dinged Requiem's checkpoint placement, so put the safe point AT the doorway, since 'reaching a door' is where players expect it.

Let the camera do the companion telling: Fares' rule 'always try to put the right brother on the right side' and keep both on screen. In a side-view 2.5D room, bias the camera framing to keep WOLF in frame when he leads, and let him leave frame only when he chooses to (refusal/scouting), so an empty frame itself reads as a decision.

Say less with words. Brothers' invented language and Hugo's hand-holding carry the bond through animation and voice. WOLF should speak in synth phrasing plus posture (ears, head tilt, lean-away when refusing), with the two choice buttons as the only text.
avoid: Do not build a command menu for WOLF. Asobo tried a richer order set and cut it because 'it was damaging their relationship too much'; a robotic wolf is especially at risk of reading as a remote-control drone.
Do not let WOLF become a 'backpack' or a key. Dedeine: 'Hugo will never be a backpack.' If WOLF is only ever the thing you fetch to open doors, the memory system has nothing to remember.

Do not give WOLF a safety power that removes the horror. Requiem had to make stray rats dangerous again because in Innocence 'casting a light sent the bulk of the hoard away'; any WOLF ability that fully neutralises the sentry needs a cost, a cap, or a narrative absence.

Do not open rooms without a scripted spine. Choteau's own words: opening the spaces made it 'very hard to keep the narrative rhythm'. Wider rooms with one height change are fine; wider rooms with three optional detours and no beat are a pacing hole.

Do not rely on one-hit death with sparse checkpoints in a wider room. Innocence's 'instant-death encounters' worked in corridors; Requiem dropped it the moment arenas widened, and even then 'checkpoint systems' drew criticism. Pair the evidence-drop rule with doorway safe points, not with reloads.
Do not ship the Brothers dead-stick beat as a repeatable mechanic or a puzzle gate; its power is that it happens once and is never explained.

Do not add co-op to 'fix' the companion. Fares: 'I would rather cut my hands than do that'; the whole premise of WOLF//OVERRIDE (one engineer, one wolf who chooses) collapses if a second player becomes the wolf.

Do not add fantastical gadgets that betray the characters. Asobo 'attempted fantastical elements' and removed them because 'it was like betraying our characters', and 'cut every aspect of the game that was not serving the story'. Keep the one tool in the CASE grounded in the engineer's job.

Do not escalate the engineer into a fighter without consequences. Asobo slowed the village sequence because it 'was not right for Amicia to be as soon ready to kill people', and in Requiem violence changes 'her psyche, her identity'. If the engineer can break machines, WOLF should remember the ones that did not need breaking.
Do not rely on text prompts or HUD to communicate WOLF's state; Brothers and Plague Tale both show the bond through animation and sound, and a phone-sized screen has no room for a mood meter.

Do not chase crowd-scale spectacle as the horror engine. Asobo needed 40-70 people, a custom engine and next-gen-only hardware for 300,000 rats; WOLF//OVERRIDE's fear should come from one sentry, light, sound and a wolf who may not come back.

corrections.claim: Choteau's balancing rules: the team "limits how many rats Hugo could control" and creates "narrative reasons for Hugo not to be with Amicia"; the team "updates its level and combat design based on whether or not the player has access to those rat powers" (Game Developer). Repeated in the steal list as Requiem/Asobo quotes.
corrections.problem: Misattributed. None of these are Choteau quotes. They are Bryant Francis's own narration in the Game Developer article: "Asobo was able to maintain that tension with two easy tools: limiting how many rats Hugo could control (he's not a full rat archwizard or something, he's literally a child), and creating narrative reasons for Hugo not to be with Amicia." The level-design line is also Francis paraphrasing, and the wording was changed ("limits" for "limiting"). https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/making-the-rat-tastic-sequel-a-plague-tale-requiem
corrections.correction: Credit these to Game Developer (Bryant Francis, 18 Oct 2022) summarizing Asobo's approach, not to Choteau. Quote exactly "limiting how many rats Hugo could control" and "creating narrative reasons for Hugo not to be with Amicia". Treat the level-design point as Francis's paraphrase, without quotation marks.

corrections.claim: Rats avoid light better: "In Innocence, casting a light sent the bulk of the hoard away, and individual little rats caught in the open weren't a threat to the player" (Choteau).
corrections.problem: Misattributed. This sentence is Bryant Francis's narration in Game Developer. It is not a Choteau quote and it does not appear in the EDGE/Wccftech relay. Also, the article says nothing about Requiem's rats avoiding light better; that is the dossier's own reading.
corrections.correction: Attribute it to Game Developer (Francis): "In Innocence, casting a light sent the bulk of the hoard away, and individual little rats caught in the open weren't a threat to the player." Do not present it as developer testimony.

corrections.claim: Rats are a timed death: "As soon as you enter, the rats start to climb on the characters, and you have very little time to react. If you go into the light they will jump off" (Dedeine). The steal list repeats it as rats give "very little time to react".
corrections.problem: Misquoted, and the meaning shifts. GamingBolt (Dedeine, 8 Aug 2018) reads: "If you go into the light they will jump off and then you can recover. There is a little time to react, I would say." "A little time" is a grace window. "Very little time" implies close to none.
corrections.correction: Quote: "If you go into the light they will jump off and then you can recover. There is a little time to react, I would say." (https://gamingbolt.com/a-plague-tale-innocence-interview-gameplay-features-progression-mechanics-xbox-one-x-and-ps4-pro-enhancements). The design lesson becomes 'give a short, recoverable grace window', not 'almost no time'.

corrections.claim: Design priority order: "The siblings were in before the rats." (Dedeine, PlayStation LifeStyle)
corrections.problem: Not a verbatim quote. The source says: "At the very root of the experience, even before the rats, [the main focus] was the relationship between Hugo and Amicia."
corrections.correction: Use the actual wording: "At the very root of the experience, even before the rats, [the main focus] was the relationship between Hugo and Amicia" (Dedeine, PSLS, 16 Apr 2019).

corrections.claim: Requiem opened its spaces but "struggled to keep the narrative rhythm". The avoid list quotes Choteau as saying opening the spaces made it "very hard to keep the narrative rhythm" and treats the problem as unsolved, a 'pacing hole'.
corrections.problem: Overstated, and partly misquoted. "Very hard to keep the narrative rhythm" is not in the source; it is a loose translation presented as a quote. The dossier also leaves out the sentence that follows, in which Choteau says they solved it: "Cela a été beaucoup de recherche et de travail pour y arriver mais je pense qu'on a réussi a trouver un bon compromis." The answer was to a question about linear progression with a single ending.
corrections.correction: Quote the French as given, and add the next sentence: it took a lot of research and work, "but I think we managed to find a good compromise" (ActuGaming, 8 Sep 2022). Frame it as a solvable tension that Asobo says it balanced, not as a warning that opening up breaks pacing.

corrections.claim: Critics still flagged "concerns included combat safety and checkpoint systems" (Wikipedia reception summary). The steal and avoid lists repeat that "checkpoint systems" drew criticism.
corrections.problem: Unsupported as cited. That phrase does not appear on the Requiem Wikipedia page, and its Reception section lists no checkpoint criticism. Partial support exists elsewhere: Shacknews (Sam Chandler, 7/10) criticises checkpoint resets after unexpected detection, and Push Square names "instant-fail stealth sections" as its main drawback.
corrections.correction: Drop the Wikipedia quote. Cite Shacknews (https://www.shacknews.com/article/132688/a-plague-tale-requiem-review-score): if other foes are around after a counter, "there's a good chance she'll die, sending you back to the start of the checkpoint". Cite Push Square for the remaining "instant-fail stealth sections", which it calls "fairly few and far between".

corrections.claim: Avoid list: Innocence's instant-death encounters worked in corridors, and "Requiem dropped it the moment arenas widened".
corrections.problem: Overstated. Requiem kept instant-fail sections. Push Square says "instant-fail stealth sections" remain, though "fairly few and far between". Wikipedia says only that Amicia "will not die after being hit once" and can "return to stealth after she was discovered". No source ties the change to wider arenas.
corrections.correction: Say: Requiem made most encounters survivable after detection (multiple hits, counters, return to stealth) but kept a few instant-fail stealth sections, which reviewers disliked. No developer source links the softening to room width.

corrections.claim: Source list: 'Why Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is not meant for co-op (Fares interview, Shacknews...)', kind 'developer interview (primary)'. The dossier cites it as independent support next to Game Informer.
corrections.problem: Misclassified. Shacknews did not interview Fares. The article relays the Game Informer Afterwords interview ("Fares told Game Informer"), so it is not an independent primary source and adds no corroboration.
corrections.correction: Reclassify Shacknews as a secondary relay of the Game Informer Afterwords interview (27 Sep 2013), and cite Game Informer as the primary source for "I would rather cut my hands than do that", the shoe-tying analogy and the camera/new-player point.

corrections.claim: Fares: puzzles were "designed to be more comfortable when controlling two rather than one" (action_and_impact section).
corrections.problem: Unsupported as a Fares quote. It is not in the Game Informer interview or the Shacknews relay. Shacknews only paraphrases that the rope and log sequences were tuned to the scheme. Fares's actual words are the shoe analogy: "When you tie your shoe by yourself you feel comfortable. If you do it with someone else, it's going to feel a bit weird."
corrections.correction: Remove the quotation marks or replace them with the verified shoe-tying quote and its rope/log examples ("A good example, for instance, is with the rope sequence or when you carry a log").

corrections.claim: Rats "can overcome obstacles, climb several floors" (Requiem developer quote).
corrections.problem: Unverified. The phrase is not in the EDGE relay on Wccftech, the KeenGamer/GamesRadar relay, WellPlayed or Game Developer. The verified lines are Choteau via EDGE: "They are now able to climb and are much more efficient at catching their prey by taking advantage of the environment", and Francis's narration in Game Developer that rats "operate on multiple floors at the same time".
corrections.correction: Mark "overcome obstacles, climb several floors" UNVERIFIED, or replace it with the verified EDGE quote and the Game Developer narration.

corrections.claim: Push Square: she "can counter enemy attacks and potentially stab them to death if she has a knife".
corrections.problem: Misquoted. The review says she can "counter enemy attacks — even stabbing them to death if she has a knife in her inventory".
corrections.correction: Use the exact wording from Push Square (Liam Croft, 17 Oct 2022, 8/10).

corrections.claim: Combat still "remains dangerous, Amicia cannot survive direct confrontation" (Game Developer summary).
corrections.problem: Shown in quotation marks but not verbatim. Game Developer says: "Combat is still quick and dangerous—Amicia is not ready to go toe-to-toe with murderous assholes." Shacknews also shows she can survive some direct encounters by countering.
corrections.correction: Quote "Combat is still quick and dangerous" exactly, or paraphrase without quotation marks. 'Cannot survive direct confrontation' overstates the source.

corrections.claim: Innocence rat LOD budget: "LOD0-1: up to 200 individually drawn animated rats; LOD2: 1,258; LOD3: 3,500 instanced without tails".
corrections.problem: Ambiguous enough to understate the figure. Torok's frame analysis lists LOD0 = 200 and LOD1 = 200 as separate tiers, so up to about 400 full-detail rats in that capture. LOD2 has the tail curled against the body, and only LOD3 drops the tail and uses instancing. These are counts from one captured frame, not engine limits.
corrections.correction: State: in Torok's captured frame, LOD0 200, LOD1 200, LOD2 1,258 (tail curled), LOD3 3,500 (instanced, no tail), about 5,158 in total. These are per-frame observations, not published budgets (80.lv, 24 Jun 2019).

corrections.claim: Dedeine: "Sometimes you need to avoid the rats, sometimes you need to create a path with the lights through the rats... sometimes you will use the rats against the humans."
corrections.problem: Only partly verified. GamingBolt has "But sometimes you will use the rats against the humans" and "Sometimes players will use the absence of lights, basically the shadow to hide from the other humans, but it will expose you to the rats." The first two clauses were not found verbatim.
corrections.correction: Quote only the verified sentences, or mark the first two clauses UNVERIFIED.

corrections.claim: Adult companions (Sophia, Arnaud) were written as mirrors of futures Amicia could follow or avoid (ActuGaming).
corrections.problem: Slightly overstated. Choteau speaks about the new mostly adult companions in general and does not name Sophia or Arnaud. His words: "pour montrer à Amicia des trajectoires à suivre ou justement, des trajectoires à ne pas suivre".
corrections.correction: Say: Choteau said the new, mostly adult companions show Amicia futures to follow or avoid. The names Sophia and Arnaud are not in that interview.

corrections.claim: Audio section: rats as sound mass, "5,000 agents with 'too many animations, too many AI at the same time' (Dedeine on why Switch could not run it)".
corrections.problem: Conflates two sources. The Destructoid piece (5 Jul 2017) quotes Dedeine saying "there's too many rats, too many animations, too many AI at the same time" but gives no rat count, and it is about rendering and CPU on Switch, not sound. The 5,000 figure comes from Wikipedia and Game Developer.
corrections.correction: Cite the two facts separately and do not present the Switch quote as evidence about audio.

corpus.group: BioShock Infinite (Elizabeth), Titanfall 2 (BT-7274) and Half-Life 2 (Alyx and Dog): companion AI design talks, how companions stay useful without stealing agency, robot companion characterisation

dossier.games: BioShock Infinite (Irrational Games, 2013) - Elizabeth; Titanfall 2 (Respawn Entertainment, 2016) - BT-7274; Half-Life 2 / Episode One / Episode Two (Valve, 2004-2007) - Alyx Vance and Dog.
dossier.why_relevant:
All three are the canonical case studies for a companion who is useful, has a will of its own, and never steals the player's agency: Elizabeth is the "you-centered" helper who hands you resources and is never escorted; BT is a robot partner whose personality is expressed through protocols, literal-mindedness and non-cutscene dialogue choices; Alyx and Dog are Valve's playtest-driven lessons on follow-vs-lead, nagging, hint pacing and scripted set-pieces for a robot buddy with no real combat AI. WOLF//OVERRIDE's WOLF (independent, can refuse, remembers treatment, engineer-only fallback always exists) sits exactly in the gap these teams explored: every one of them found that the companion must STATE goals then step aside, must be seen helping (spotlight, throw, catch prompt), and must cheat invisibly (teleport, scripted marks) rather than block the player.

NOTE ON SOURCING: the two GDC 2014 Elizabeth talks and the GDC 2018 Titanfall "Action Blocks" talk were fetched only as GDC Vault session pages (members-only video); their contents are reported through fetched contemporaneous write-ups (GamesBeat, Game*Spark, Inside Games). Edge magazine's BT interview and the 1UP Episode One preview were NOT fetched; they are reported via Wikipedia and marked derived. Valve Developer Wiki (npc_dog/npc_alyx) and the BioShock/Titanfall fandom wikis were blocked (bot challenge) and are not cited. The session's web-search budget ran out after ~15 searches; everything below comes from fetched pages.

dossier.companion:
ELIZABETH (BioShock Infinite). Design brief per the GDC 2014 session page: she had to be "both leader and the follower, both dynamic and scripted, both the entertainer and the entertained" (https://gdcvault.com/play/1020831/...). Levine's rule: "a very you-centered AI" - the player is never obliged to protect her; she tosses ammo, points out enemies and brings in tears, and "impacts gameplay all the time" (https://gamingbolt.com/?p=35700). Levine said people wanted to cut her "a million times"; during level reviews he'd ask "where's Liz right now?" and get "she's back in the closet over there... Nobody knew how to manage her." Fix: a multi-disciplinary "Liz Squad" led by AI programmer John Abercrombie with Levine on writing/direction, plus artists, animators and mocap (Eurogamer 2012 via gameranx). Abercrombie's talk, per the fetched JP write-ups: (1) A SILENT Elizabeth was tried and rejected - with no voice the game had to steer the camera at her when she wanted to show something, which testers found pushy; verdict was "remove her or give her dialogue." (2) Positioning used a soccer-defender rule: keep her ON SCREEN, between Booker and his destination, so she can interact with things without the player turning around; "goal-side" pathing by Tim Austin only arrived in the final year of a ~4.5-year project (GamesBeat). (3) When she called out a sniper and players couldn't find where she was pointing, they added an icon "spotlight on the challenge, much like a dramatic entrance would require a spotlight in the theater" (Abercrombie, GamesBeat). (4) "Booker, catch!": the first version had her fetch supplies via a short animation, which re-created the silent-Elizabeth camera-stealing problem; the shipped version is a BUTTON CONFIRM (X) that briefly redirects the camera to her for the catch and then restores the player's previous view direction - reframing a reload as "perceived heroic assistance"; a colleague reported surviving at critical health/ammo only because she delivered, turning her from "following AI" to "helping hero" (Game*Spark). (5) "Combat Mode": because she is invulnerable, strolling through firefights broke her humanity, so her demeanour switches in danger with an emotional recovery period after. (6) "Smart objects" scatter the world so she notices, approaches and touches things (flowers, benches, rocks to skip); Levine: she could do "dozens" of things at the beach (NBC). (7) Cheating: if she falls too far behind she is quietly teleported to the player's side; Abercrombie: players "will only know what they see on the screen and hear from the speakers" (GamesBeat). Lockpicking was originally a one-time event and became a recurring mechanic; hand-keyed animation replaced mocap for in-game expressions (Wikipedia).

BT-7274 (Titanfall 2). Protocols as the game states them (widely quoted; exact wording UNVERIFIED here because wiki pages were blocked): Protocol 1 Link to Pilot, Protocol 2 Uphold the Mission, Protocol 3 Protect the Pilot. Writing: early scripts "deemed too 'bossy', and writers took five months to rework them"; the team avoided Optimus Prime/WALL-E comparisons and aimed for "a lovable partner and a 20-foot-tall war machine" (Edge via Wikipedia, derived). McCandlish: "the Titan, because he's an android, he's not trying to be funny, but it's fun to find those ways for the character to come out" (TheSixthAxis). Humour is literal-mindedness: BT quotes a "64% chance of success" for throwing Cooper across a chasm (PS Blog; Game Informer reports "60 percent") then dryly lists outcomes of a miss - "lacerations, broken limbs, decapitation, spinal injuries" (Game Informer). Dialogue: at set moments a prompt lets the player pick a reply with up/down on the d-pad, usually "direct or snarky"; Game Director Steve Fukuda: "these dialogue options don't change the outcome of the game, they give you a fun way to banter with BT by choosing the tone that best reflects your own personality" (Destructoid via SegmentNext). Wikipedia: options were added so players could "bond with the Titan without using any cutscene." Design: "a large emotive eye, so players would know where the titan is looking" and small arms for natural interaction (Wikipedia). Art-book detail: BT is right-handed while Cooper pilots him and switches to left-handed when Cooper is ejected (GamingTrend). Critique worth noting: Bullet Points argues all BT's kindnesses are "the result of computer protocol" and his thumbs-up is undercut when identical janitor robots do it too - i.e. a gesture meant to read as personal must be unique to the companion.

ALYX AND DOG (Half-Life 2 series). Alyx's AI was described as "personality code" rather than "AI code," and she was "explicitly programmed to avoid performing too many mechanical or repetitive actions, such as repeating lines of dialogue" (1UP preview via Wikipedia, derived). Valve's Episode One commentary is the richest primary material: Matt T. Wood: "we originally designed Alyx to nag the player pretty frequently... after about three minutes of this, the one thing it definitely did was make the player hate Alyx." Chet Faliszek: "playtests showed it was much more satisfying for players when Alyx stated a goal and then stepped aside until that goal was accomplished" - hint lines were cut, then partially restored as player-REQUESTED help on +use. Bill Van Buren: trying to express urgency through Alyx's acting "proved to be unsustainable... if the player didn't choose to advance, Alyx eventually ran out of lines or animations and was forced into her very non-urgent idle states" - so she trusts the player's pace. Wood: an early map had "Alyx led the player through the whole thing"; after "the high level decision to have Alyx follow the player" the leading content became irrelevant. Doug Wood: follow speed looks best "faster than the player's normal speed, but slower than the player's sprint speed." Robin Walker: Alyx running backwards while shooting was "realistic but boring"; last-minute crouch-and-aim "didn't change combat effectiveness but made her much more fun to watch." Jim Dose's Response Rules let writers trigger lines by situation (warn of danger, call for help when mobbed, ask for light). Erik Wolpaw: "If you don't like Alyx, you won't have fun with Episode One... Alyx being likeable was one of our most crucial goals"; under red light she looked sneering, blue fixed it. Keith Huggins: brief recovery after the stalker-pod attack so the player sees she is affected, "not... a bullet-spitting robot." Episode Two, Marc Laidlaw: "she is careful not to steal the player's fun by doing it all herself. She doesn't actually solve the puzzle, although she sometimes thinks she has." John Guthrie: the vortigaunt's shock attack lets "the player finish them off" - allies soften, players kill. Richard Lord: in the car "Alyx fires more slowly, taking more time to aim" so she isn't a turret. DOG: designed after "classic movie robots" like Robby the Robot, almost unchanged from first sketch; he "lacks actual combat artificial intelligence - all battle scenes are scripted"; with no enemies he fetches and throws small objects; threatened, he flees (Combine OverWiki citing Raising the Bar). Bill Fletcher: "Players love Dog, so we made sure he was first thing you see" in Episode One; Van Buren: the van-toss across the gorge started as a joke in a design cabal meeting, then solved three problems at once - crossing an impassable gap, letting Dog "plausibly get left behind," and an intimate Alyx/Dog beat. Yahn Bernier: a BUG made Dog's head shake after "You did do the math, right?"; testers laughed, so they animated it on purpose. Danika Wright: Dog's personality comes from "shifting bodyweight and broad hand gestures" and "expressive spinal motions" because he has no face; the race-with-Dog mechanic "was born out of testing the level over and over."
dossier.level_and_camera: Elizabeth: her positioning is a camera problem solved as a level problem - the soccer rule keeps her inside the player's forward view cone between Booker and the goal, so levels are reviewed with "where's Liz right now?" as a standing question; interest points ("smart objects") are authored into each space so she always has something to do. Camera is otherwise never taken from the player except the brief, button-confirmed catch redirect. Titanfall 2: levels were built from "action blocks" - one-week prototype vignettes, "over 100" made, each required to "revolve around the relationship between a Pilot and their Titan" (Hardcore Gamer); the campaign's internal "211" rhythm was two pilot-combat parts, one pilot movement/puzzle part, one Titan-combat part per level (Wikipedia). BT's physical size makes him the gate: the throw across the abyss (PS Blog) and pilot-only interiors give a built-in reason to split the pair and reunite. Half-Life 2: Valve's "gates" - obstacles only the companion can remove - hold the player in earshot for critical dialogue (crashed gunship moved only by Dog, "a lot of care ensuring Dog hit marks without trampling player," Van Buren). Dog's rubble lift is "one of few instances we take control of player's view," used to point at the Citadel (Fletcher). Alyx's ledge traversal uses "a combination of AI and scripted animations... what matters most is how it looks to player" (Walker). Areas were rebuilt repeatedly to keep the player in a space while Alyx talks; the final solution had Alyx climb out while the player finds another route, and Matt Scott admits "we're not especially happy with this crutch."
dossier.death_and_saves: Elizabeth cannot die and cannot be targeted; Levine's stated reason was that she must never be an escort burden (GamingBolt). The invulnerability is masked by Combat Mode acting rather than by HP. Alyx can be downed in some scripted fights but is effectively unkillable in general play; Combine OverWiki claims it takes "five simultaneous Overwatch Sniper Rifle shots to kill her" (UNVERIFIED wiki number). Her Episode Two injury was authored as a story beat (Hunters cause it, giving them "a powerful introductory moment," Joe Han) and healing was started in preceding maps so she is "healthy enough to run at regular speed" when gameplay resumes (Q!). BT: two "deaths" - a memory-core transfer to a new chassis and the final sacrifice (Bullet Points) - the companion's body is disposable, the core persists. None of these games tie companion state to the player's death/save loop; not applicable beyond: companions are reset by checkpoint like everything else.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Elizabeth is the inventory assistant: she scavenges and tosses ammo, health, salts and money, picks locks (a one-off that became a recurring mechanic) and opens tears to pull in cover, turrets or weapons - Levine calls tears "essentially like a summoning spell" that gives options "without overcomplicating" the toolkit (GamingBolt). The key UX rule is that receiving an item costs a deliberate button press plus a sub-second camera nod, so the player always perceives the gift. Titanfall 2: BT is the loadout - he can take any Titan loadout found in the world (Hardcore Gamer); the player has no classic inventory. Half-Life 2: Alyx hacks consoles and doors as a scripted key; Dog's "inventory" is physics objects he fetches and throws. No exact numbers (cooldowns, pick counts) were obtainable from fetched sources - UNVERIFIED.
dossier.action_and_impact: Elizabeth's combat contribution is deliberately indirect (call-outs with a spotlight icon, supply throws, tears) so she never kills for the player; the "Booker, catch!" camera nod is the impact beat for a resource gift. BT: the player is inside BT for Titan combat and outside him for pilot sections; the throw is BT's signature physical interaction, pre-announced with a probability line so the joke lands before the stunt. Alyx: Valve kept her lethal but readable - combat animations with "convincing physical contact with enemies," chosen by a system that "monitors positions and fires animations when correctly aligned" (Walker); a shotgun was given to her because "their ponderous handling makes great animations"; the flashlight-directs-Alyx's-fire sequence was originally weaponless but testers disliked having no gun, so weapons returned (Steve Bond). Dog has no combat AI; every fight he is in is scripted so it always looks spectacular and never competes with the player.
dossier.presentation_ui_art: Elizabeth: faces were made "slightly less realistic, emotionally expressive with large eyes" rather than photoreal; period dress needed heavy cloth work; "Combat Mode" expressions swap so she doesn't look cheerful in gunfire; Disney-Tangled-like scripted animations were cut to avoid comparison (Wikipedia). UI: an icon spotlight on the thing she is pointing at; an X prompt for catches. BT: one big emotive eye so "players would know where the titan is looking"; handedness flips when Cooper disembarks; dialogue choice UI is a two-option d-pad prompt (up/down). Alyx: Episode One raised facial shape targets "by about 50%" and added specular/rim lighting to skin, jacket and teeth (Ken Birdwell, Jason Mitchell); lighting colour changed her read (red = sneering). Dog: a faceless robot read entirely through body weight, hand gestures and spine; Phong + environment-mapped scrapyard shader with "rusty bolts to damaged metal flaps" (Derrick Birum).
dossier.audio: Elizabeth: silent companion rejected - voice is what lets her direct attention without hijacking the camera; barks like sniper call-outs are paired with a visual spotlight. BT: Glenn Steinbaum's flat delivery is the comedy engine - jokes come from literal, probabilistic phrasing, not from BT trying to be funny (McCandlish). Alyx: Response Rules system lets writers attach lines to situations (danger, mobbed, asks for light); urgency lines were cut when playtesters hated nagging after ~3 minutes; lines are rotated to avoid repeats. Dog: no speech; a bug-born head shake became a canonical reaction. Footsteps/room tone specifics: not covered by fetched sources - not applicable.
dossier.mobile_and_input: All three are console/PC games; none shipped touch input - not applicable. Transferable input facts: Elizabeth's gift requires one confirm press (X) with camera auto-nod; BT's dialogue uses only up/down on the d-pad with two choices and a short window; Alyx's optional hints are requested with +use. These map directly onto WOLF//OVERRIDE's one USE button and two choice buttons.

steal: State-then-step-aside (Faliszek): WOLF says the goal once, then shuts up until it is done; optional hints only when the engineer presses USE on WOLF. Never nag on a timer - Valve measured hate at ~3 minutes.

Follow, don't lead, by default (Wood/Van Buren); make WOLF's leading explicitly 'his own route' moments (scouting ahead, going through a wolf-sized gap) rather than pulling the engineer along - and keep the engineer-only fallback visible when he leads or refuses.

Follow speed tuned between walk and run (Doug Wood): give WOLF a follow gait faster than the engineer's walk and slower than any dash so he never lags or overtakes; teleport him silently when out of view and beyond a distance threshold (Abercrombie's cheat).

Keep WOLF on screen, goal-side (soccer rule): in a side-view room, bias WOLF to the lane between the engineer and the next doorway/objective so his reactions and look-ats are seen without the camera moving.

Make help a visible, confirmed beat (Booker, catch!): when WOLF brings evidence or a tool, show a prompt, require one USE tap, and give a short camera nudge/hit-stop toward WOLF so the player credits him; log it in the CASE as 'retrieved by WOLF'.
Spotlight what the companion points at (Abercrombie): when WOLF alerts (sentry, trap, hidden panel), draw an icon on the object, not just a bark.
Companions soften, players finish (Guthrie, Laidlaw): WOLF can stagger or distract the purge sentry and can 'think he solved' a puzzle, but the final input stays with the engineer.

Dialogue choice as tone, not branch (Fukuda): WOLF//OVERRIDE's two choice buttons can be 'direct' vs 'warm/snarky' replies that change WOLF's memory and relationship state without forking essential progress - still cheap, still meaningful to the companion.

Protocol-driven robot voice (BT): write WOLF's refusals and disagreements as literal, probabilistic, rule-citing lines ('Protocol: protect the engineer. Entering coolant relay: 31% survivable. Declining.'); the humour and the character come from literal-mindedness, not from trying to be funny.
One big readable eye / body-language acting (BT, Dog): make WOLF's gaze direction and spine/weight shifts the main expression channel; use lighting colour deliberately (Valve: red read as sneering).
Combat Mode demeanour swap (Abercrombie): WOLF switches posture, idle set and bark set when danger is active, with a recovery window after, so being unkillable or absent never reads as indifference.

Companion-only gates (Van Buren): one obstacle per room that only WOLF can clear (lift a tank, hold a door) to hold the engineer in a dialogue beat - but always with the engineer-only alternative route, which AGENT.md already requires.
Harvest accidents (Bernier): when a physics or animation bug makes WOLF look like he reacted on purpose and testers laugh, keep it and script it.

Build from action blocks (Respawn): prototype WOLF-and-engineer vignettes as one-week blocks (WOLF scouts a vent, WOLF carries the case across a drop, WOLF refuses a door) and wrap rooms around the ones that work.
avoid: Silent companion who points by stealing the camera - Irrational tested it and testers called it pushy; if WOLF cannot talk, he must signal with icons/light/sound, never by moving the view.

Urgency acting that depends on the player moving - Alyx 'ran out of lines or animations' and fell into calm idles, undermining the tension; do not author WOLF stress states that decay into neutral if the engineer dawdles.
Leading the whole route - Valve cut it after testers found it annoying and it made Alyx 'omniscient'; WOLF leading should be rare, opt-in and short.
Long companion-driven pauses without payoff - the Alyx console 'get her bearings' beat was 'a long pause in the action without a lot of payoff' and was scrapped.
Companion as turret - in the car Alyx 'fires more slowly, taking more time to aim'; a WOLF that instantly neutralises every threat makes the engineer a spectator.
Making help an uninterruptible animation - the first 'catch' prototype pulled attention like the silent-Elizabeth camera lock; confirm with a press instead.
Generic gestures that other NPCs also perform (Bullet Points on BT's thumbs-up vs janitor bots): WOLF's signature behaviours must be unique to WOLF or the bond reads as protocol.
Bossy robot scripts - Respawn spent five months stripping bossiness; refusals and disagreements must be phrased as WOLF's judgement, not orders to the player.
Weaponless companion-reliant sections - Valve's flashlight-only zombie sequence lost its 'no gun' version because testers disliked having no agency; an engineer-only path must never require WOLF.
Leaving the companion in a closet - Levine's 'where's Liz right now?'; review every room with 'where is WOLF, what is he doing, can the engineer see it?'

Escort fragility - all three games made the companion unkillable or scripted-only in combat; a WOLF who can be lost to ordinary enemies turns him from partner into burden (reserve WOLF harm for authored story beats, as Valve did with Alyx's Hunter injury).

corrections.claim: Danika Wright: Dog's personality comes from "shifting bodyweight and broad hand gestures" and "expressive spinal motions" because he has no face (used again in presentation_ui_art and in the steal item 'One big readable eye / body-language acting (BT, Dog)').
corrections.problem: Misattributed subject. In the Episode Two commentary (EP2-Comment037, Danika Wright) this passage is about the VORTIGAUNT, not Dog: "Turning the vortigaunt into an expressive character was a challenge for animators, given that he doesn't have what you'd call a traditional face. To bring out his personality, the animators concentrated on shifting bodyweight and broad hand gestures... we concentrated his performances on expressive spinal motions." Her only Dog node (EP2-Comment172) is the race to the base. Source: https://combineoverwiki.net/wiki/Developer_commentary/Half-Life_2:_Episode_Two
corrections.correction: Attribute the bodyweight, hand-gesture and spine technique to Valve's Vortigaunt animation in Episode Two. The lesson for a faceless companion still holds, but the example is not Dog. Keep Danika Wright's verified Dog quote: "Racing Dog to the base was not a preconceived plan. It was born out of testing the level over and over."

corrections.claim: Alyx "is effectively unkillable in general play"; avoid list: "all three games made the companion unkillable or scripted-only in combat".
corrections.problem: Contradicted by the dossier's own cited source. Combine OverWiki says Alyx's health regenerates quickly but "It is still possible for her to die during combat, however, and at several points, the player is required to protect her from taking damage. Her death will result in a black screen fade and failure message, then the game will reload." (https://combineoverwiki.net/wiki/Alyx_Vance). Only Elizabeth is invulnerable, and Dog is scripted.
corrections.correction: Alyx is very durable (fast regeneration; the wiki claims five simultaneous sniper shots, still UNVERIFIED), but she can die, and her death fails the game and reloads. Half-Life 2 and its episodes include sections where you protect her. Rewrite the 'escort fragility' item to say that two of the three cases (Elizabeth, Dog) remove companion death, while Valve kept a high-durability, fail-on-death Alyx.

corrections.claim: Levine: Elizabeth "impacts gameplay all the time"; tears are "essentially like a summoning spell" that give options "without overcomplicating" the toolkit (GamingBolt).
corrections.problem: Two misquotes. The article's actual wording is "We want her impacting on what's going on all the time" and "another way you could impact on the world that wouldn't be too complicated – your hands are already full!" Also, the interview dates from July 2011, before release, so it describes design intent and not the shipped game. https://gamingbolt.com/?p=35700
corrections.correction: Quote it exactly: "We want her impacting on what's going on all the time"; "essentially like a summoning spell"; and that it "wouldn't be too complicated – your hands are already full!" Mark it as a 2011 pre-release interview.

corrections.claim: Dog "lacks actual combat artificial intelligence - all battle scenes are scripted"; with no enemies he fetches and throws small objects; threatened, he flees (Combine OverWiki citing Raising the Bar).
corrections.problem: Misattributed source. On the OverWiki Dog page, Raising the Bar is cited only for the first-sketch and Robby the Robot note. The combat-AI, flee and throw lines are uncited wiki trivia about a SPAWNED Dog ("If a spawned Dog is approached by anything threatening, even a common Headcrab, he will flee. If no enemies are present, he will find a nearby small object and throw it at the player"). That describes the behaviour of a Dog entity spawned outside the authored levels, not a documented design statement. https://combineoverwiki.net/wiki/Dog
corrections.correction: Cite it as uncited OverWiki trivia (UNVERIFIED) about the behaviour of a spawned npc_dog. Raising the Bar supports only the claim that Dog went from first sketch to game with few changes and drew on classic movie robots such as Robby the Robot.

corrections.claim: Action blocks: "over 100, each a one-week prototype (McCandlish)", sourced to Hardcore Gamer; each was "required to revolve around the relationship between a Pilot and their Titan".
corrections.problem: Sources are merged. Hardcore Gamer gives "over 100 action blocks" and the Pilot/Titan-relationship rule but does not mention one week or McCandlish. The one-week detail comes from McCandlish in TheSixthAxis ("a series of one week periods where each week, you as a designer would pick something from the wide buffet"). There he also says the blocks "didn't have to be directly related to what existed of the campaign or story at that point, and loosely it could really be anything," and puts the count at "dozens if not hundreds". That softens the 'required' framing.
corrections.correction: Write: "over 100" action blocks (Hardcore Gamer, no developer named), built in one-week cycles (McCandlish, https://www.thesixthaxis.com/?p=272760). Note that McCandlish describes the brief as loose. The Pilot/Titan-relationship constraint comes from Hardcore Gamer's summary, not a quote.

corrections.claim: Steal list: "Valve measured hate at ~3 minutes"; numbers row: "Time before Alyx's urgency nagging made testers hate her: about 3 minutes (verified)".
corrections.problem: Overstated as a measurement. The commentary is an anecdotal observation: "after about three minutes of this, the one thing it definitely did was make the player hate Alyx" (Matt T. Wood, alyxnag). The same node gives the broader finding: "players much preferred to set the pace themselves and... especially disliked virtually any hint of bossiness from Alyx."
corrections.correction: Present it as Valve's playtest observation of "about three minutes" of frequent nagging ("Hurry up!", "Keep moving!"), not a measured threshold. Pair it with the pace-setting and bossiness finding.

corrections.claim: Doug Wood's follow speed: "faster than player walk speed, slower than player sprint speed".
corrections.problem: Mistranslated term. The commentary says "faster than the player's normal speed, but slower than the player's sprint speed" (alyxrunspeed). In Half-Life 2 the 'normal' speed is the default run; walking is a separate, slower key. 'Walk' therefore sets the band too low.
corrections.correction: Use "between the player's normal (default) movement speed and sprint speed". For WOLF: faster than the engineer's standard hold-to-move pace and slower than any burst or dash.

corrections.claim: BioShock Infinite development length: "approximately 4.5 years"; "a ~4.5-year project" (GamesBeat).
corrections.problem: Overstated. GamesBeat says Abercrombie's team developed the companion techniques "slowly over the course of some four and a half years". That is a span for Elizabeth's AI techniques, not a stated length for the whole project. The same article also says Abercrombie "joined the team in 2013", which conflicts with the March 2013 release, so its timeline details are shaky. https://gamesbeat.com/how-soccer-and-theater-helped-irrational-create-bioshock-infinites-elizabeth/
corrections.correction: Write: per GamesBeat's report of the GDC talk, Elizabeth's AI techniques evolved over about 4.5 years, and Tim Austin's goal-side pathing arrived only in the final year of development. Do not present 4.5 years as the project length.

corrections.claim: "Booker, catch!" reframed a reload as "perceived heroic assistance" (Game*Spark); the silent Elizabeth's camera-steering was something "testers found pushy".
corrections.problem: "Perceived heroic assistance" is not in the source. Game*Spark (translated) has Abercrombie say the simple reload turns Elizabeth from "an AI that just follows" into "a hero who helps you". The 'pushy' verdict is Abercrombie's own description ("a very pushy method; you could say it interferes with the player"), not attributed to testers. Also, Game*Spark and Inside Games carry identical text by the same writer, so they are one source, not two corroborating ones. https://www.gamespark.jp/article/2014/04/01/47488.html
corrections.correction: Remove the quotation marks around 'perceived heroic assistance', or replace it with the translated line ('from an AI that only follows to a hero who helps'). Attribute 'pushy' to Abercrombie or the team. Count the two Japanese write-ups as one source. The X-button confirm, the momentary camera turn to her and the return to the prior direction are confirmed by the source.

corrections.claim: BT's throw is his "signature physical interaction"; "BT's physical size makes him the gate: the throw across the abyss".
corrections.problem: The throw is presented as an interactive mechanic, which is missing context. Wikipedia's Titanfall 2 development section says action blocks explored a Titan throwing the pilot, but "The concept of Titan throwing pilots was ultimately discarded from the gameplay and became part of a cinematic cutscene." The PS Blog and Game Informer previews describe the scripted moment with a dialogue choice. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanfall_2
corrections.correction: Note that Respawn prototyped the throw as gameplay, cut it, and kept it as a scripted cutscene with a dialogue choice. A lesson worth stealing in its own right: a signature companion stunt can be authored as a one-off beat rather than a systemic mechanic.

corrections.claim: Avoid list: "Leading the whole route - Valve cut it after testers found it annoying and it made Alyx 'omniscient'".
corrections.problem: Misreads the node. In alyxconsole (Matt T. Wood), the console 'get her bearings' beat was added "to make Alyx seem less omniscient" while she led. The leading content became irrelevant after "the high level decision to have Alyx follow the player", which the alyxnag node ties to players preferring to set the pace and disliking bossiness. Omniscience was a side effect they patched, not the stated reason for the cut.
corrections.correction: Write: leading made Alyx seem omniscient, and the console fix to make her 'get her bearings' was a long pause with little payoff. The whole sequence was cut once Valve switched Alyx to follow, because players wanted to set the pace and disliked bossiness.

corrections.claim: Van Buren: the van toss "solved three problems at once - crossing an impassable gap, letting Dog 'plausibly get left behind,' and an intimate Alyx/Dog beat."
corrections.problem: Slightly restructured. The commentary (dog_throw, Episode One) lists the 'key goals' as getting Alyx and the player across the gorge, and Dog playing a key role "while also plausibly getting left behind". The intimate Alyx/Dog view is listed among the outcomes along with "a surprising and visceral entrance to the Citadel". It also notes "making sure the van didn't kill the player took some thought."
corrections.correction: Quote it as: it satisfied 'key goals' (cross the impassable gorge; Dog plays a key role while plausibly getting left behind), and in the end it also gave an intimate view of Alyx and Dog and a visceral Citadel entrance. 'Three problems' is the dossier's own framing.

corrections.claim: Richard Lord: in the car "Alyx fires more slowly, taking more time to aim" so she isn't a turret.
corrections.problem: Drops a qualifier. The full line is "while the vehicle is moving, Alyx fires more slowly, taking more time to aim at high speeds," after "Alyx constantly targeted and fired her gun at everything. This made her feel a bit like a turret."
corrections.correction: Include 'while the vehicle is moving... at high speeds'. The slowdown is tied to movement, not a blanket fire-rate cut.

corrections.claim: Elizabeth faces made "slightly less realistic, emotionally expressive with large eyes" (Wikipedia); the Liz Squad was "led by AI programmer John Abercrombie"; Elizabeth "cannot be targeted".
corrections.problem: Source mix-ups. The 'slightly less realistic... large eyes' line is Abercrombie's, from the Game*Spark write-up. Wikipedia instead says she moved from mocap to hand-keyed animation and a 'more exaggerated look' because playtesters stopped noticing her. Wikipedia says the Liz Squad was 'claimed to be led by either Amanda Jeffrey or John Abercrombie'; Levine (Eurogamer via Gameranx) names Abercrombie. No fetched source says she 'cannot be targeted'; Game*Spark says only that she cannot die in combat for story reasons.
corrections.correction: Attribute the large-eyes line to Abercrombie via Game*Spark. Cite Wikipedia for the switch to hand-keyed animation (playtesters stopped noticing her). Note that Wikipedia is ambiguous about who led the Liz Squad and that Levine credits Abercrombie. Remove 'cannot be targeted' or mark it UNVERIFIED.

corpus.group: Somerville (Jumpship), Another World and Flashback (including the 2023 remake): cinematic 2.5D side-view storytelling, rotoscoped weight, wide rooms and camera, doorway and screen transitions

dossier.games: Another World / Out of This World (Eric Chahi, Delphine Software, 1991; 15th Anniversary 2006, 20th Anniversary 2011-13); Flashback: The Quest for Identity (Paul Cuisset, Delphine Software, Amiga 1992 then Mega Drive/SNES/PC); Flashback (VectorCell/Ubisoft 2013 2.5D remake, directed by Cuisset); Flashback 2 (Microids, 16 Nov 2023, Cuisset as designer; a SEQUEL, not a remake); Flashback Remastered (Microids 2018, 77/100 Metacritic on Switch); Somerville (Jumpship, Unity, 15 Nov 2022 PC/Xbox, 31 Aug 2023 PlayStation; director Chris Olsen, exec producer Dino Patti ex-Playdead). NOTE: the brief says "the 2023 remake"; the 2023 product is Flashback 2 (sequel). I covered Flashback 2 plus the 2013 remake and 2018 remaster so the lesson set is complete.
dossier.why_relevant: All three lineages are side-view cinematic games with a lone human and a non-verbal companion (Lester + Buddy the alien; Somerville's father + the family dog), no HUD or dialogue, death-heavy stealth/chase rooms, and screen-sized rooms stitched into levels. Chahi's "immersion of the player with no exterior elements to the world (score, energy gauge etc.) displayed on the screen" is the design creed WOLF//OVERRIDE's painterly 2.5D look is reaching for. Jumpship explicitly built Somerville's character art on "Eric Chahi/Delphine Software's 'Another World' and 'Flashback'" as "the perfect character reference", then moved to a 3D side-view with a cinematic camera, which is the same move from flat rooms to layered parallax rooms the game is making now. Flashback 2013 and Flashback 2 are the cautionary half: two 2.5D conversions of the same IP by the original designer that scored 40-54 and 30-37 on Metacritic, with reviewers tracing the failure directly to the 2.5D camera, aiming and collision. Somerville's reviews document the exact companion, camera and interaction-point problems WOLF's scouting/leading routes and USE prompts must avoid.

dossier.companion: ANOTHER WORLD (Buddy): the alien is a silent, non-controllable ally who opens the way through the prison break and finale; per Wikipedia "Lester and his alien ally cannot sustain any damage, and the game ends immediately if either of them is struck", so the companion's safety is a hard fail state, not a resource. He speaks "in an unintelligible alien language" with no subtitles; the relationship is shown by action only (he kicks the guard, carries Lester at the end: "the two escape on a dragon-like creature"). Chahi's method for these beats was improvisational: "building a story layer by layer without knowing where it was going" and "listen to what I felt. What do I feel right now?" (Game Developer GDC 2011 report). Buddy proved strong enough to lead the 1994 sequel Heart of the Alien, where "players controlled Buddy rather than Lester" (Wikipedia). FLASHBACK: no companion; Conrad is alone except NPC quest-givers; "not applicable" for companion AI. SOMERVILLE (the dog): the family dog travels with the father for roughly the first two hours; The AU Review describes the behaviour model: it "whimpers when enemies or items of interest are nearby, or barks when he realises he can't catch up with you". Olsen on petting: "I think all game dogs need to be petted, don't they?" (Escapist). The dog is a signalling companion (danger/interest hints, catch-up bark), not a tool or a route-maker. Failure data: Flickering Myth found "even when the dog wandered off, my concern was limited due to the lack of character shading"; PC Games DE logged that "AI companions fail to follow player properly" as a bug. Jumpship's animation tech is the real companion lesson: Olsen's goal "What if we could play a character who wears the emotional baggage you have accumulated playing as them?", built from IK look-at and arm aim ("All the head and partial chest movement is IK driven and separated"), emotional states as "synced layers we surge with suitable curves", and when frightened "more rapid IK head movement and a wider range of randomised look positions" (Tech Anim post). That is a direct spec for a WOLF who remembers treatment: run memory into the look-at rate and randomised look range, not into dialogue.
dossier.level_and_camera: ANOTHER WORLD: fixed single-screen rooms at 320x200, 16 colours (Chahi "spent a week defining the 16 color palette"), flip-screen transitions, no scrolling; rendering is polygon-only for characters, after Chahi "abandoned pure polygon backgrounds" because tiny "pixigons" were infeasible and went to bitmaps. Height changes were avoided outright: level transitions used "a teleporter -- a decision made not primarily for aesthetics, but because it's difficult to create animation and collision for stairs". Camera cuts are used as "cinematic punctuation -- brief sequences only -- give emphasis to a major event". Pacing per room: the beast chase "gives the first level a slow rhythm before creature arrives, and a quick change to a fast and stressful situation". Engine: 68000 asm polygon routine reaching "about 10 displayed polys per 50 frames per second" after a week on Atari ST, final game "approximately 20 frames per second"; a custom interpreted language with "20 instructions and 256 variables". FLASHBACK: "non-scrolling screens, nearly all of which feature multiple levels of altitude" (Wikipedia) navigated "static screen to static screen" (Dreamcast Junkyard); movement is deliberately grounded: "realistic human running speed and jumping ability, and realistic weakness. He dies if he falls from a great height"; seven levels; backdrops hand-drawn. Cuisset: moving to Mega Drive "I had to change the whole interface, and I decided to have a game that would be more action focused". FLASHBACK 2013/2023 (what breaks when you go 2.5D): 2013 moved to "2.5D using Unreal Engine 3" with 360-degree aiming and lower difficulty, Metacritic PC 54 / X360 50 / PS3 40. Flashback 2's 2.5D camera: "the restrictive view means the player cannot aim and shoot successfully", Conrad "constantly gets trapped behind insurmountable objects like steps, small walls, and unassuming rocks", "enemy attacks are impossible to see or dodge", environments "small and basic, providing no sense of exploration" (TheSixthAxis 2/10); Gamereactor: the 2.5D layering "only confuses and irritates as Conrad can never really hide or use the three-dimensional environments in a meaningful way, but mostly just gets stuck in things". Microids' June 2024 patch had to add lock-on, laser aim, aim-assist tuning and "Cameras and HUD revamp in the final zone". SOMERVILLE: Unity, "full 3D movement" in a side-on world (Olsen: "I'm not really interested in platforming, so don't expect too much of that"). Camera is authored per shot: Olsen wanted "strong graphic framing, that confidence to give something relatively still a lot of life", citing John Harris paintings and "the locked-off wide shots in Evangelion"; the game pulls "the camera far away from the action, making you feel like an observer or spy" (TheXboxHub) and zooms "all the way out to not only show how alone the player is, but also show the scale of the incident stretching off in the distance" (VGC). Costs of that choice: "mäßige Kameraführung" (PC Games DE), "the perspective will randomly disappear into a wall and prevent you from seeing where the hell you're going" (Flickering Myth), and players missing "the slightest opening which you need to get through" (TheXboxHub). Olsen's own arc: "as we progressed and my need to get the camera in close, grew - We knew we had to address our characters faces", so faces and "smear frame controls" were added to the rig.
dossier.death_and_saves: ANOTHER WORLD: one-hit death for Lester or Buddy, "the game ends immediately if either of them is struck", but "numerous checkpoints enabling the player to keep restarting at the last point indefinitely"; early versions gave "an alphanumeric code for these checkpoints" to write down. Chahi did not want death to feel like watching himself die: "I didn't want him to look too similar to me -- I was using rotoscoping... So it was too disturbing". Deaths are so cheap that the Amiga any% TAS (17:56.073) "features the use of intentional deaths as part of the optimization strategy". The 20th Anniversary Edition added "three difficulty modes". FLASHBACK: health is the force shield that "absorbs a certain number of shots before needing recharging, acting as Conrad's health" (shield units: exact count UNVERIFIED), plus instant death from falls. Progress via passwords per level; Cuisset stored "the save game" in "the memory on the sound chip" on Mega Drive; the Dreamcast port added "VMU support for on the fly saving". Design loop is memorisation: "memorise where to roll and where to jump in order to survive" (Dreamcast Junkyard). FLASHBACK 2: shipped with instant respawn and had to be patched in June 2024 so that "After a GAME OVER, the player is now spawned at the last savepoint instead of instantly respawning", plus "New and better located savepoints" and a "3-medkits limit"; evidence that free respawn drained tension. SOMERVILLE: no HUD, no health; deaths in chase and stealth rooms restart at a nearby checkpoint; checkpoints are "generous" but chases produce "tiresome repetition of the same beat numerous times" (Flickering Myth), and Game Informer had to "restart checkpoints often" because grabbing "levers and switches is inconsistent". Relevance to the evidence-drop death model: none of these games lose anything on death; their tension comes from spectacle and the respawn distance, which is why Flashback 2 had to move respawns back. WOLF//OVERRIDE's "dying drops unsecured evidence" is a genuine gap in this lineage and should be paired with checkpoints as dense as Another World's, not Flashback's level-end passwords.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: ANOTHER WORLD: no inventory screen and no on-screen text; the only persistent tool is the pistol with "three capabilities: a standard fire mode, the ability to create force fields to block enemy fire, and a powerful charged shot that can break through force fields and some walls"; HUD limited to "an oxygen bar during the swimming sequences". FLASHBACK: a small item inventory (keys for doors, shield recharges, a portable force field, a late-game teleporter) and story delivered through "pre-recorded holocubes" and "lost memories" found in the world (Dreamcast Junkyard, Wikipedia); the holocube is the closest existing analogue to an evidence CASE: a found object that plays back testimony. FLASHBACK 2: 2024 patch made the "Molecular Analyzer" (scanner tool) "automatically triggered when necessary" and let "directional buttons" work "in menus and inventory", i.e. the inventory UI shipped unusable on pad. SOMERVILLE: no inventory; two then three light-reactive powers on the triggers (blue "softens", red "hardens", purple "attracts and repulses" the alien matter), each needing a light source: "connection to generators/lamp posts to function" (AU Review). Evidence lesson: the games closest to WOLF//OVERRIDE carry zero or near-zero items; Flashback's holocube and Another World's single multi-mode gun are the precedents for "one tool" plus found testimony.
dossier.action_and_impact: ANOTHER WORLD: weight comes from rotoscoped polygons; Chahi used a genlock, "a new device for the Amiga at this time, which allowed users to layer video behind the game screen", filming himself (and, per Wikipedia and secondary sources, his brother) to trace. The laser gun was lifted from "the dynamism of Star Wars' battles"; shield-versus-charged-shot gives readable impact without numbers. FLASHBACK: Cuisset kept "24 frames per second, as it was really the most beautiful" after trying lower rates; "We couldn't compromise Conrad's animation, and the number of frames it needed"; a chasing creature ("not exactly a lion") was cut because it needed too many frames. Rotoscoping was "tracing video images onto transparencies". Movement commits: "we don't have a jump button for example", so animation-based movement demands anticipation (CNC). Gamereactor describes the original's "smoothly slow and slightly awkward way of moving" and notes it collapses in Flashback 2 against "25" enemies instead of two. SOMERVILLE: impact is cinematic rather than combat; threats are chase and stealth beats; feel from the animation stack (physics props, IK, "smear frame controls"). Jank reports: characters "blink out of existence for a moment", protagonist "stuck in geometry while trying to solve a puzzle" (Game Informer); clipping "through or get snagged on objects" (Flickering Myth); animation clipping on collision (PC Games DE). Lesson for the impact kit: commit animations and low enemy counts (two, not twenty-five) are what make rotoscoped weight work; crowd-scale combat breaks it.
dossier.presentation_ui_art: ANOTHER WORLD: zero HUD outside the swim oxygen bar, zero text, alien speech unintelligible; Chahi's rule was "immersion of the player with no exterior elements to the world (score, energy gauge etc.) displayed on the screen" and he treated montage and "dramatic structure" as the real product, not spectacle. The intro "validated the use of polygons and the interpreted language". Publishers wanted it to "become point and click" and he refused because "the effort to do this would have been too huge". FLASHBACK: hand-drawn backdrops with rotoscoped sprites; cinematics between levels; passwords and holocube playback as the only UI. SOMERVILLE: "not a single line of dialogue spoken" (GamesRadar via Pure Xbox); minimalist characters built for "readable silhouettes" with "negative space" and "costume accents for joints to bring out readable body dynamics"; "wonderfully minimalist art style is still capable of cinematic scale" (VGC). The painterly, wide, locked-off framing is Olsen's cinematography background made playable. Failure to note: the camera choices that make the stills beautiful are the same ones that hid doorways and interaction points from reviewers.
dossier.audio: ANOTHER WORLD: sparse music used as punctuation, alien dialogue as unintelligible speech (no subtitles); the soundtrack credit to Jean-François Freitas appears only in search snippets here (UNVERIFIED). FLASHBACK: not covered in fetched sources beyond the Mega Drive sound-chip memory being reused "to store the save game". SOMERVILLE: nominated for the D.I.C.E. Award for Outstanding Achievement in Audio Design; VGC: "one of the best-sounding games of the year" with headphones, "sporadic music and atmospheric ambience"; Game Informer: "Bizarre sound effects paint strange explosions in the distance and the occasional light, synth orchestration and unassuming piano pieces are expertly used to punctuate scenes". The dog carries audio signalling: whimpers near enemies or items of interest, barks when it cannot catch up (AU Review). Direct fit for WOLF: let the companion's vocalisation be the room-tone layer that changes before the player sees the threat.
dossier.mobile_and_input: ANOTHER WORLD 20th Anniversary: shipped "new intuitive touch controls or a classic D-pad" on mobile, plus three difficulty modes, proving a one-button-plus-direction cinematic platformer ports to touch cleanly. FLASHBACK 1992: stick plus one action button, no dedicated jump ("we don't have a jump button"); Cuisset rebuilt the interface for the Mega Drive pad ("We had to use a new interface, and develop a new way to move the characters"). FLASHBACK 2 (controller): June 2024 patch notes list what shipped broken: "Sprint can be activated with a simple press of the Sprint button", "Crouch is now activated with [Crouch] while Conrad is not moving", "The directional buttons can now be used in menus and inventory", "Manual enemy lock-on button", "Manuel reloading replaced by an overheat system". SOMERVILLE: stick movement, powers on controller triggers ("activated with the controller triggers", VGC); no mobile version; interaction trigger points were "way too finnicky and precise" (Flickering Myth) and ledge grabs "harder than it should be" (Game Informer). Whether Somerville uses hold-to-interact is UNVERIFIED from fetched sources. For phone touch, Another World's 20th Anniversary touch scheme is the only shipped precedent in this set.

steal: Chahi's no-HUD creed: keep every status element diegetic; the only exception he allowed was a context bar (oxygen) that appears solely during the sequence that needs it. For WOLF//OVERRIDE, show evidence security state on the CASE object itself, not a corner widget.
Cinematic punctuation, not cutscenes: Chahi used 'brief sequences only' to mark major events. Use 1-3 second locked-off cuts for the door blast, tank drop and exit bolt, then return control.
Room rhythm from the beast chase: a slow, empty first beat then a sudden fast beat in the same room. Design each 1.5-2 screen room with one slow half and one stressed half.
Dog-style companion signalling: let WOLF whimper/growl when threats or evidence are near and bark or stop when the engineer outruns him; it is audio-first hinting that costs no UI.

Jumpship's emotional-layer rig: drive WOLF's look-at rate and randomised look range from his memory of how he was treated (calm = slow wide looks; distrust = rapid, narrow, away-from-player looks). Head and chest IK separate from the walk cycle so no new animation states are needed.
Readable silhouettes with negative space and joint accents, so WOLF and the engineer read at the widest painterly zoom and still work when the camera comes close.

Flashback's committed, no-jump-button movement and 24 fps rotoscoped weight: keep the engineer slow-ish and committed, and keep enemy counts tiny (two sentries, never a crowd) so the weight stays legible.
Holocubes as found testimony: evidence items that play back a short audio/visual record when USE is held, giving the CASE a reason to exist.
Another World's checkpoint density: instant, indefinite restarts at the last checkpoint with one-hit deaths. Pair it with the evidence-drop rule so dying stays scary without long replays.

Teleporter-over-stairs honesty: Chahi skipped stairs because of animation and collision cost. Budget the one walkable height change per room as a ramp or ledge with a dedicated mount animation, not a stair set.
Flashback 2's post-hoc fixes as a pre-flight checklist: lock-on or no aiming at all, better-placed savepoints, no instant respawn, pad-navigable menus, tutorials for every new verb.
Somerville's wide pull-back shot to show scale and isolation, used once or twice per act, with the player kept in control during the pull-back.
avoid: Letting the authored camera hide the exit: Somerville reviewers missed 'the slightest opening' and had the camera 'disappear into a wall'. Any walk-through doorway in a parallax room needs a lit, silhouette-visible threshold at the chosen zoom.

2.5D collision clutter: Flashback 2's Conrad 'constantly gets trapped behind insurmountable objects like steps, small walls, and unassuming rocks'. Keep walkable depth to one lane; foreground parallax must never collide.
Aiming or dodging across depth in a side view: both 2.5D Flashbacks failed on it ('cannot aim and shoot successfully', 'impossible to see or dodge'). Keep combat to one USE verb with on-rail targets.
Instant respawn with no cost: Flashback 2 had to patch in spawn-at-savepoint and a medkit cap because free respawn removed tension.
Finicky interaction trigger volumes: Somerville's were 'way too finnicky and precise' and lever grabs 'inconsistent'. USE prompts on phone need generous volumes and a visible hold progress.

Companion that drifts or fails to follow with no feedback: Somerville's dog 'wandered off' without the player caring, and PC Games DE logged companions failing to follow. WOLF's refusal or lag must be a readable choice, never a pathing bug.
Repetitive chase failure loops: Somerville's chases forced 'tiresome repetition of the same beat'. Vary the restart (shorter run-up, WOLF already positioned) after two deaths.
Lowering difficulty and adding XP/skill trees to a cinematic platformer: the 2013 remake did both and scored 40-54.
Growing enemy counts to feel modern: Gamereactor pins Flashback 2's collapse on fighting '25' at once with the original's slow movement.

Building silent story beats without 'character shading': reviewers felt nothing for Somerville's dog or family because the characters were blank. Give WOLF visible preferences before asking the player to care about his memory.
Fetch quests with 'distances travelled so short you'll often wonder why the NPC couldn't just go'. Each engineer-only fallback must justify the walk with a new room beat.
Trusting stills: Somerville's praise was for sound and framing while play surfaced jank in geometry, clipping and physics. Validate each room by hands-on play, per AGENT.md, before claiming feel.

corpus.group: Oddworld (Abe's Oddysee, New 'n' Tasty, Soulstorm): stealth side-scrolling, possession, rescuing companions, QuikSave and checkpoints, environmental storytelling, chanting as a verb

dossier.games: Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee (Oddworld Inhabitants, PS1/PC 1997); Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus (1998, referenced for QuikSave and Mudokon moods); Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty! (Just Add Water / Oddworld Inhabitants, 2014 remake); Oddworld: Soulstorm (Oddworld Inhabitants with Frima and Fat Kraken, 2021; Enhanced Edition Nov 30 2021; Switch Nov 18 2022).
dossier.why_relevant: Oddworld is the closest canonical ancestor of WOLF//OVERRIDE's shape: a 2D/2.5D side-view cinematic platformer where a powerless protagonist (Lanning: "the rather pathetic chump that you actually are", "at the bottom of the global corporate food chain") survives an industrial horror facility by stealth, speech and sabotage rather than combat. Its 25-year arc covers exactly the decisions on the table now: flip-screen rooms versus 1.5-2 screen scrolling rooms with a 2.5D camera (New 'n' Tasty, Soulstorm's "2.9D"); checkpoints versus player-placed saves (Lanning admits the 1997 checkpoint system "was such a cluster*** it was maddening" and that QuikSave was the fix); companion characters who follow, obey, misbehave and die (Mudokons, including colour-coded moods and a "sorry" verb); a scavenging inventory bolted onto a stealth game (Soulstorm, widely judged "superfluous"); and a non-combat verb (chanting/possession) that is the game's signature. Both the hits and the documented misses map onto WOLF's companion, the evidence CASE and the death model. Caveat: no GDC Vault postmortem of Abe's Oddysee exists (verified by a GDC Vault keyword search: only a 2007 Burning Man panel and a 2006 Jaffe interview), so primary material is Lanning's PlayStation Blog posts and quoted interviews, not a formal talk.
