dossier.companion: Mudokons are the series' companion system and they are the inverse of WOLF: dependent, command-driven, and the game's score. In Abe's Oddysee the player "hold[s] down the GameSpeak button and press[es] various commands" so Mudokons "follow, stay put, activate mechanisms" (Wikipedia, Oddysee); the Oddworld Library notes Abe can "utter any of a number of set phrases" only while standing still, and "Sligs will respond to certain GameSpeak, but Mudokons will follow orders from Abe". Co-founder Sherry McKenna is cited saying "communication" was central (Wikipedia). Unwinnable calls the system "quite simple, [yet] incredibly effective": "Follow me!" and "Wait!" plus a fart for comedy. Abe's Exoddus (1998) added emotional states that must be read and repaired: Angry (red) is calmed by saying "sorry"; Depressed (blue) "may commit suicide"; Sick needs a healing chant; Blind must be told to "wait" or they walk into hazards; Wired (lime, laughing gas) is "calmed only by being slapped" (Wikipedia, Exoddus). Soulstorm's followers "follow every move Abe makes when they follow him, including jumping and hoisting"; the possession "chi" meter grows "based on how many Mudokons are following him at the time", and Lanning says you can "harness their collective energy" and hand crafted items "to your followers" (PS Blog Feb 2021, June 2020). The documented failure mode is pathing and compliance: Push Square found "hiding in a locker should see your followers doing the same, but every now and then, one or two of them would decide not to bother"; TheSixthAxis calls them "lovable idiots" who "jump gallantly into the meat grinder because they can't think for themselves". The Enhanced Edition shipped "improved Slig and follower AI (more intelligent and responsive)" after "seven additional months of polish" (Oddworld Library, Soulstorm). Possession is the other companion-like mechanic: Abe takes over a Slig, uses "Slig-exclusive GameSpeak", and "Abe remains vulnerable during possession" (Wikipedia, Oddysee); possessed Sligs "do not follow orders" from other Sligs (Oddworld Library). Relevance: WOLF should never be a Mudokon (obedient, countable, disposable). But the readable mood state, the "sorry" repair verb, the idea that the companion's condition changes which commands work, and a power meter that scales with relationship are all directly transferable to a wolf who remembers.
dossier.level_and_camera: 1997: flip-screen rooms with a fixed camera. Unwinnable: a "single-screen platformer, where each screen is like its own mini level"; the fixed view hid secrets ("machinery blocked certain ground sections, requiring players to crouch"). Lanning explicitly chose the "locked camera, the movie-esque tone and vibe" of Prince of Persia, Out of This World and Flashback, and rejected 3D ("it didn't appeal to me at all") (PS Blog 2012). Leaving and re-entering a screen reset its puzzle (Wikipedia, NnT). 2014 remake: continuous scrolling, which the developers said "dramatically changes the gameplay" (Wikipedia, NnT). Stewart Gilray's concrete redesign for the lost screen-reset: a woken sleeping Slig now times out — "Say he walks around for 10 seconds and you haven't moved, he won't have heard anything and will go back to sleep again" (Push Square 2012). The camera adds "subtle camera movements... to showcase more of the environment, while the perspective will actually change as you begin to run faster" (Push Square 2012); the remake moved "from 2D sidescroller to a 2.5D sidescroller" with "a much broader perspective" (GameRevolution). 2021: Soulstorm is marketed as "2.9D environments" of "massive cinematic scale" (PS Blog Feb 2021), with platforms that "twist and turn into the foreground and background" (TheSixthAxis) and a camera "pulling out to show the scale", with "secrets everywhere, with diverging and hidden paths" (Push Square). Scope: "15+ sprawling levels" plus "two bonus levels if you unlock the good ending" (TheSixthAxis); the Library lists 17 main levels from "The Raid on Monsaic" to "Eye of the Storm" plus 10 Toby's Escape and 10 Vykkers Labs levels. Lanning on scope: "Soulstorm's scope and scale are larger than we have tackled before" (PS Blog June 2020). The cost of the bigger, deeper camera shows in reviews: "jumps are still difficult to judge", ledge climbs and monkey bars "frustratingly tricky" (Push Square); a reviewer "fell through the level floor three times in an hour" (TheSixthAxis). Takeaway for 1.5-2 screen rooms: the flip-screen puzzle-reset was load-bearing and had to be replaced by explicit timers once scrolling arrived; and depth-shifting platforms trade readability for spectacle.
dossier.death_and_saves: Abe's Oddysee: unlimited lives, respawn "at the last checkpoint"; some reviewers praised "frequent checkpoints and unlimited lives", others criticised that PC versions lacked mid-level saving, forcing "replaying of levels" (Wikipedia, Oddysee). Lanning's own verdict: "the checkpoint system was such a cluster*** it was maddening", they "completely screwed the save system by release", and "fixed that issue on Abe's Exoddus and even created the 'quick save'" (PS Blog 2012). Exoddus QuikSave lets players "designate their own checkpoints"; Wikipedia says it was absent from Oddysee "due to programming conflicts". New 'n' Tasty keeps both: QuikSave returns and checkpoints were densified so "the most any player would have to redo is a maximum length of three screens" (Wikipedia, NnT, citing a Gilray podcast). Soulstorm dropped QuikSave for checkpoints; "the abundance of checkpoints is warmly received" (TheSixthAxis) and "quite a few checkpoints in each level" are "generally okay" (Push Square), though Destructoid flagged "checkpoint placement" (Wikipedia, Soulstorm). Lanning's Level Select rule: "There are no save points. You must play the entire level all the way through to earn your new Quarma score and badges... if you die, don't worry, you will respawn at the nearest check point" (PS Blog Apr 2021). Death as a tool: speedrunners use the Death Delay Glitch ("By timing your jumps, you can delay Abe's death using a grenade, a UXB or... bees and bats") and SDA lists categories "with Deaths" and "Resets" — 8:57 any% with deaths and large skips, 35:55 no-major-glitch, 1:18:16 100% (Sam 'Samtastic' Locke). Lesson: the series never had a "lose progress on death" model; the pressure came from permanent Mudokon deaths counted at the end, not from Abe's own deaths. WOLF's plan (death drops unsecured evidence, safe points secure it) is a hybrid of Exoddus's player-placed save and Soulstorm's per-level tally.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Oddysee has no inventory; the "evidence" is the Mudokon count, revealed at the end: "at least 50 Mudokons (of the possible 99)" for the good ending, otherwise Abe dies (Wikipedia, Oddysee); Unwinnable: "only if you save at least half does Abe fully triumph". Exoddus scaled this to 150 of 300 ("Killing all 278" also unlocks a "Maximum Casualties" ending, per Wikipedia; the 278/300 discrepancy is in the source). New 'n' Tasty raised the count to "all 299 Mudokon slaves" and imported Exoddus's bottle caps (drop and throw) (Wikipedia and GameRevolution). Soulstorm added a full "Scavenger's Economy": "loot from trash cans, pickpocket, and search through lockers for items to craft into weapons and tools" (PS Blog June 2020); vending machines exchange resources for products you can use or hand to followers (PS Blog Feb 2021). Items include smoke screens, IED stun mines, flamethrowers, antidotes; ingredients like sleech guano, haggut moss, meetlebat venom, moongrass, paramold (Oddworld Library); duct tape binds enemies non-lethally and Moolah buys inventory or opens cash gates (Wikipedia). Per-level badges reward "looting a specific number of interactive items, finding a specific number of secret areas, or apprehending as many enemies as possible" (Wikipedia). Reception of the inventory layer was poor: "rooting around in every bin and locker... gets tiresome pretty quickly, and crafting feels superfluous" (Push Square). Lanning also said a tiered "panic" escalation with "giant Slig Mama robots" was cut, and that "you start out with the game you want to make, but then you deliver the game that you can make" (Dexerto). Relevance: an evidence CASE should stay closer to the Mudokon-count model (few, meaningful, counted at a safe point) than to Soulstorm's bin-rummaging.
dossier.action_and_impact: The series is a cinematic platformer: "Abe commits to his movement whenever he takes a step or jump, and the controls do not permit fine adjustment" (Wikipedia, Oddysee); movement verbs are "walking, running, sneaking, rolling, or hopping" plus hoisting (Oddworld Library). Chanting is the signature verb and is explicitly performative: "a continuous noise Abe makes with a bowed head and palms pressed together"; when a Slig hears it "the lights will reach for the Slig, and Abe will possess it" (Oddworld Library). Possession can only happen in safe areas: chant suppressors (flying orbs) "zap" Abe elsewhere (Wikipedia). Once possessed, a Slig can "shoot enemies" and the player can "destroy the host when finished"; Abe's body stays exposed the whole time. Exoddus extended possession to Glukkons, Paramites, Scrabs and Abe's own fart as "a flying explosive". Soulstorm pushes toward action: "some areas demand 'hard core action'", others "stealth and planning" (PS Blog Feb 2021); "Farts and 'come here' won't cut it, not anymore" (PS Blog Sept 2020); a double jump was added (Push Square). Impact feedback is tied to hardware: "You can feel Abe's heartbeat during suspense filled action sequences" via DualSense haptics (PS Blog Feb 2021). Lethality is scored: Quarma includes "an additional tally that counts the number of enemies killed" and killing Sligs hurts the score (Wikipedia, TheSixthAxis). Documented feel problems: throwables were "extremely hit and miss" and "Abe not being able to jump where I want him to" (TheSixthAxis, Push Square). Lanning's framing of the whole: the player should "think and strategize" rather than use "brute force" (Shacknews summary).
dossier.presentation_ui_art: Oddysee used "pre-rendered 3D graphics" because the team "believed they could create more high-end, artistic visuals with pre-rendered sprites" than real-time 3D of 1997 (Oddworld Library); Lanning wanted film quality through "animations, their sound effects" (PS Blog 2012) and the team drew on "backgrounds in 3D animation and film production" with extensive cutscenes (Wikipedia). UI philosophy: "a bare minimum of heads-up display" (Oddworld Library) — the rescue count is only disclosed at the end. Budget $4M with a $10M GT Interactive marketing spend, "the publisher's largest to date"; working title "Soul Storm"; began January 1995 (Wikipedia). New 'n' Tasty: Unity after a switch from Unigine in December 2012 ("three months to get to the stage they reached before the switch", "eight months to rebuild the entire game"); 1080p60 on PS4; in-engine cutscenes replacing FMV; loading screens that give "information on an upcoming puzzle or enemy" (GameRevolution); 14 staff ("4 environment artists, 2 character artists and animators, 4 programmers and 1 designer") in 16 months versus 35 staff in 1997; budget $5M (Wikipedia, NnT). Soulstorm: Unity, team of 30 with Frima and Fat Kraken; marketed as "2.9D"; Destructoid found menu navigation "testy at times and requires a firm few (button) mashes" (Wikipedia, Soulstorm). Environmental storytelling: RuptureFarms "resembles a colossal oil refinery" run by Glukkon executives (Unwinnable), and Lanning's whole premise is "rendering the journey out of the more powerless beings" (PS Blog 2012). Relevance: painterly 2.5D rooms with near-zero HUD and tips delivered only during loads is a proven fit for horror-stealth pacing.
dossier.audio: Abe's Oddysee: soundtrack by Josh Gabriel, sound design by Ellen Meijers; EGM's 1998 guide named it "Best Voice Acting of 1997" (Wikipedia). GameSpeak is fundamentally an audio mechanic: every command is a spoken line and the chant is "a continuous noise" that enemies hear, so sound is the stealth-and-command interface itself (Oddworld Library). Lanning counted "sound effects" among the things that made it feel like film (PS Blog 2012). New 'n' Tasty: Michael Bross composed most of the music and "does not begin writing a piece of music without first listening to and understanding the original's"; GameSpeak was expanded with "more dialogue variations" (Wikipedia, NnT). Soulstorm: Josh Gabriel returned; Lanning promised "mind-blowing 3D audio" on PS5 and the haptic heartbeat (PS Blog June 2020, Feb 2021); the Enhanced Edition listed "audio balance improvements" (Wikipedia). No source fetched gives footstep-per-surface or room-tone implementation details for any entry (UNVERIFIED beyond the above). Relevance: WOLF's procedural audio can own the "command is sound, sound is danger" loop — anything the engineer says to WOLF should be audible to threats.
dossier.mobile_and_input: Original input is a chord: hold the GameSpeak modifier, then press a command button (Wikipedia, Oddysee); GameSpeak only works while Abe stands still (Oddworld Library), which keeps the command set off the movement verbs. New 'n' Tasty shipped on iOS/Android on December 14, 2017 and Switch on October 27, 2020 (Wikipedia, NnT); its touch control scheme is UNVERIFIED (no fetched source describes it). Soulstorm reached Switch as the "Oddtimized Edition" on November 18, 2022 (Wikipedia); no mobile version is documented. Input complaints across Soulstorm reviews are about commitment and judgement rather than button count: "jumps are still difficult to judge" (Push Square) and menus needing "a firm few (button) mashes" (Destructoid via Wikipedia). Relevance: WOLF's hold-to-move plus one USE and two choice buttons is leaner than Oddworld's 8-command GameSpeak chord; the Oddworld lesson is that a modifier-plus-button chord can survive on controller but any menu-heavy inventory (Soulstorm) becomes a liability.

steal: Hide the tally. Oddysee shows 'a bare minimum of heads-up display' and only reveals the Mudokon count at the end; WOLF's evidence CASE should show what is secured only at safe points, not as a live counter.

A visible, colour-coded companion state that changes which verbs work (Exoddus: red angry needs 'sorry', blue depressed will self-harm, blind must be told to wait). Give WOLF 3-4 readable states (posture, eye light, idle sound) and let the two choice buttons mean different things per state.

'Sorry' as a first-class repair verb. Exoddus made apology a button that fixes a relationship; WOLF remembers treatment, so a cheap apology that only works once per grievance is a strong, honest mechanic.
Command is sound, sound is danger. GameSpeak lines and the chant are audible to enemies; route WOLF's instructions through the procedural audio so calling him in a sentry room is a real choice.

Replace screen-reset with explicit timers. Gilray's fix for scrolling rooms: a disturbed sentry 'walks around for 10 seconds' then sleeps again. Put a visible/audible ~10 s alert decay on the purge sentry rather than resetting on room exit.

Checkpoint spacing by replay cost, not by room: New 'n' Tasty's rule was 'a maximum length of three screens' to redo. Define WOLF's safe-point spacing as 'never more than N seconds of replay' and test it on the route.

Player-placed saves fixed Oddysee's biggest shipped failure (Lanning: checkpoint system 'was such a cluster***'); the evidence model can keep that virtue: let the engineer secure evidence at any safe terminal, not only at scripted checkpoints.
Companion power scales with relationship: Soulstorm's chi meter grows with follower count. Let WOLF's willingness/route options expand with trust rather than with items.
Possession as 'control the enemy, expose yourself'. A WOLF-driven override of a machine or sentry should leave the engineer's body vulnerable in-world, which is both horror and tension for free.
Quarma counts kills as well as rescues. If WOLF//OVERRIDE tracks anything beyond evidence, track the harm the engineer caused, and let WOLF's memory be the readout.
Loading or room-entry tips 'on an upcoming puzzle or enemy' (New 'n' Tasty) instead of tutorials in the HUD.
Hard mode that 'replicates the original game's difficulty' is a cheap way to ship both a strict and a forgiving death model: strict = evidence drops on death, forgiving = evidence auto-secures.
A 'death delay' is a known feature of this genre's speedruns; design the evidence-drop so dying mid-air or mid-animation has one deterministic drop point, or runners will find the exploit.
avoid: Do not make WOLF a Mudokon: obedient followers who mirror 'every move Abe makes' were still called 'lovable idiots' who 'jump gallantly into the meat grinder'; one follower refusing to hide in a locker broke stealth in reviews. WOLF's refusals must be authored decisions with a reason, never pathing failures.

Avoid a scavenging economy bolted onto stealth. Soulstorm's bins, lockers, pickpocketing and vending machines were judged 'tiresome pretty quickly' and crafting 'superfluous'; the CASE should hold evidence plus one tool, nothing to grind.

Avoid depth-shifting '2.9D' platforms that twist into the background; they cost readability ('jumps are still difficult to judge', floor clips 3 times an hour). Keep the one height change per room on a single walkable plane with clear silhouettes.

Do not ship a save system you have not played end to end; Oddysee 'completely screwed the save system by release' and Lanning still calls it maddening 15 years later. Hands-on validation of the death/evidence loop on every route before it is called done.
Avoid hiding essential ground behind foreground machinery without a tell; Oddysee's crouch-to-find secrets worked for optional content, but WOLF's engineer-only fallback paths must be readable.

Avoid an 8-command chord menu on touch. GameSpeak only works while standing still and needs a modifier plus a command; with one USE and two choice buttons, do not grow the verb set past what fits on a phone.
Avoid thresholds that require near-perfection to see the real ending (Soulstorm needs 80% in 12+ levels to even unlock levels 16-17); if evidence gates endings, make the gate legible early.
Avoid throwable or impact systems whose outcome is 'extremely hit and miss'; the impact kit should resolve deterministically or the horror reads as bugs.
Do not count on scale to carry feel: Soulstorm's 'massive cinematic scale' arrived with checkpoint-placement and menu complaints. Wider rooms (1.5-2 screens) are enough; depth is not required.
Do not plan content you cannot ship: Soulstorm cut its tiered 'panic' escalation and Slig Mama robots; Lanning: 'you deliver the game that you can make'.

corrections.claim: Exoddus scaled this to 150 of 300 ('Killing all 278' also unlocks a 'Maximum Casualties' ending, per Wikipedia; the 278/300 discrepancy is in the source). Numbers table: '300 total, 150 for the good ending'.

It says 'Rescuing at least 150 is necessary to get the good ending' and 'If the player kills all 278 Mudokons, the player is awarded with invincibility' (the 'Maximum Casualties' ending). The Oddworld Library Exoddus page gives no Mudokon count either. The source has no 278/300 discrepancy; the 300 figure came from somewhere else.

corrections.problem: Half of this contradicts the cited Wikipedia sentence. That sentence goes on: 'though this doesn't count against a level's overall Quarma rating.' TheSixthAxis's reviewer felt pressure to play as a pacifist. Rework the 'steal' bullet to match: the kill count was a visible tally, not a score penalty.

corpus.group: Alien: Isolation: manual save stations, the alien AI director, audio and lighting craft, motion tracker as diegetic UI, inventory and crafting

dossier.games: Alien: Isolation (Creative Assembly / SEGA, October 2014; first-person survival horror; Amanda Ripley versus a single unscripted xenomorph on Sevastopol station; mobile port by Feral Interactive later). Covered: manual save stations, the two-tier Director/Alien AI and menace gauge, senses and difficulty tuning, audio (dynamic mix, high dynamic range, layered score), lighting and lo-fi presentation, the motion tracker as diegetic UI, crafting and inventory, Working Joes, level-design rules (multiple exits, vents) and features they cut (third-person camera, weapon crafting, acid blood). Research note: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through, so the later facts come from direct fetches of known URLs. A few mechanics I could not re-fetch are marked UNVERIFIED below (locker breath-holding, whether time pauses while crafting, tracker range, the "hostiles nearby" save warning, the Wwise channel-packing detail).
dossier.why_relevant: Alien: Isolation is a well-documented case of a horror game built on one persistent, independent agent whose behaviour comes from systems, not scripts. WOLF//OVERRIDE needs the same craft for WOLF: an independent actor who seems to decide for himself, is readable, and is never a cheat. Its manual save stations show how saving becomes "part of the fabric of the horror" (Hope), which maps directly onto your decided model where safe points secure carried evidence. Its motion tracker is a low-fi diegetic readout with a real cost, a good model for an evidence CASE plus one tool. Its audio team's rules (high dynamic range, silence, a mix that reacts to the threat's distance) fit your procedural audio, room tone and breathing plans. Its level rule of "multiple exits... be it a door or a vent" carries straight into wider 1.5 to 2 screen rooms with one height change and walk-through doorways. One caution: it is first-person and roughly 12 to 18 hours long, and critics said it dragged and that save points were too far apart. Take the tension tools and not the length.

dossier.companion: Alien: Isolation has no companion, so this section borrows from its independent agents. (1) An independent agent made from two layers. In Bray's description, a Director "always knows where the player is" and periodically sends the creature toward the player's area without giving exact coordinates. The alien itself acts only on its own senses. For WOLF: keep a small "pacing" layer that decides when WOLF offers to scout, lead or wait, separate from WOLF's own perception and his memory of how the engineer treated him. The pacing layer may suggest. WOLF's character decides. (2) Readable state tells. Woolley (PC Gamer) says the Working Joes moved from human faces to synthetic ones because "it was too easy to confuse humans and synthetics in stressful situations." The new look let them "inform the player of changes in gameplay, like the colour of their eyes turning red to let you know that they're about to attack." WOLF needs a light or eye-colour tell for help, hesitation and refusal, paired with posture so it does not rely on colour alone (AGENT.md rule). (3) Learning that is not punitive. Thompson (2017, from Bray) says behaviours unlock over the campaign, and "none of these conditions come from events that lead to a players death." WOLF's memory gating should key off how the engineer treated him, never off deaths, so failing does not change his personality. (4) Imperfection that reads as thought. The alien's pathing is deliberately sub-optimal and backtracks to suggest doubt. Let WOLF pause, sniff, glance back and reconsider when scouting, rather than taking the optimal path. (5) Fairness. Thompson reports that designers could mark areas the alien never searches. Švelch found that "simulationist" players felt the AI "played dirty" and suspected a "tether" or teleporting. WOLF should never know something the engineer could not have learned, and the game should show where his information came from (a sniff, a sound, a terminal).
dossier.level_and_camera: Camera: first-person. Creative Assembly prototyped a third-person camera and rejected it: "It felt as though the alien was hunting the character, not you... Third person felt like an Alien game; first person felt like Alien" (Hope, GDC 2015 via Game Developer). In PC Gamer Hope adds: "In third-person it became a game about jockeying the camera and looking after your avatar... If you're hiding behind an object and you want to get a better view of your surroundings, you have to move." For a 2D side view, the lesson is to make the player move to gain information (peek at a doorway, step onto the height change, raise the tool) instead of widening the view for free. Keep the tighter zoom you already decided on. Level rules from designer Catherine Woolley (PC Gamer): "Not trapping the player in a scenario they can't escape from was a must"; "we had to ensure that there were multiple exits from rooms, be it a door or a vent. And, of course, places to hide"; "plenty of routes and corridors off the main path and secondary rooms that added story, gave you a breather, or an alternative way"; vents mattered because "they were ways for the alien to move around too." The station was built from "five distinct archetypes... habitation, science, medical, engineering, and technical," each visually distinct. AI support for level design (Thompson 2020): the front-stage patrol region is limited to a zone around the vent the alien came out of, and the vent sweep has 12 or more designer-selectable configurations per location or campaign phase. Hand-placed "search" points and "spot" (stand and watch) points direct the alien. Adapting to 1.5 to 2 screen rooms: give each room two ways out (a doorway plus a crawl route or upper ledge via its one height change), one hiding spot, and one quiet side alcove. Use the upper or lower height as the "vent" layer the threat, or WOLF, can travel along.
dossier.death_and_saves: Saving: manual save stations only (emergency phone-style terminals), plus an autosave at mission or level starts reported by players in Steam threads. Wikipedia, citing Gamasutra 2015: the player inserts Amanda's access card and there is "a three second pause before the save can be completed, meaning the player can be killed while attempting to save." Design intent (Hope, Game Informer): "a core component of horror is in 'small victories,' small achievements that allow the player to breath again"; "Saving becomes part of the fabric of the horror"; he admits "perhaps some of the save point locations could be seen to be a little challenging, but having said that, has saving ever felt so sweet?" Critics, per Wikipedia, faulted "trial and error progression and frustrating distances between save points." Player data is mixed: one thread says saves were well placed, with mission 7 having "too many" and the mission 6 morgue section too few; another player said they were so frequent they felt neither tension nor relief. Steam players also report that reloading puts the alien back in the vents or "somewhere else," so the AI's state resets on load. A "hostiles nearby" warning at the save station is mentioned by a player but is UNVERIFIED. Death: the alien kills in one hit (Thompson). The Director's behaviour unlocks never depend on player deaths. Direct mapping to your death model: (a) a safe point should take a short, readable, interruptible action (around 1 to 3 seconds of committed animation with sound) that secures the evidence carried in the CASE, so securing feels like a small victory; (b) dying drops only unsecured evidence and should never cost more than one room's worth of progress; (c) place secure points at every room's exit or every 1 to 2 rooms. This avoids the "frustrating distances" complaint while keeping the risk of committing to the save.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Crafting from scavenged components, with blueprints found in the story. Recipes (Gamepressure guide, matched by GameRevolution): Medikit = SCJ Injector, Compound B, Bonding Agent, Scrap x10. Noisemaker = Charge Pack, Sensor, SCJ Injector, Scrap x10. Flashbang = Blasting Cap, Sensor, Bonding Agent, Scrap x10. Smoke Bomb = Ethanol, Sensor, Bonding Agent, Scrap x10. Molotov = Ethanol x2, Blasting Cap, Sensor x2, Compound B x2, Scrap x25. Pipe bomb = Ethanol, Blasting Cap x2, Sensor x2, SCJ Injector x2, Scrap x25. EMP Mine = Charge Pack x3, Sensor x2, SCJ Injector, Bonding Agent x2, Scrap x25. Many items share components, so each crafted item is a trade-off ("There's not much of them so make only the items you really need"). Per-component carry caps exist, but the counts are UNVERIFIED. Whether the world keeps running during crafting is also UNVERIFIED; it is widely reported as real-time, but I could not fetch a source. Rejected: early in development, crafting weapons was explored and dropped: "this game isn't really about pulling the trigger" (Hope, PC Gamer). Acid blood was also cut because "we were starting to make an alien simulator." Ideas came from asking what the team would do if an alien were loose in the studio: "Some people said they would probably pick something up and throw it to distract it." The alien adapts to overused tools: "the more you use an item or device, the less effective it will be" (Hope, PlayStation Blog). Mapping: your CASE plus one tool should follow the same principle. A few distinct, readable states (carried/unsecured versus secured), no stat-heavy loot, and a tool built on an instinctive action (throw, distract, block) rather than a weapon. Show the CASE contents diegetically, for example tags on the case and a readout, rather than a full-screen menu that hides the threat.
dossier.action_and_impact: The player is "underpowered and underprepared" by design (GDC session description). Hope wanted "simple A to B choices—'should I stay or go?'" and "There isn't big gun waiting for you in a locker that will save you." Threat combat facts (Thompson 2020, from game data): the alien treats an armed player as a "threat" and an unarmed one as a "target." After the first flamethrower encounter it varies its response (hissing to hold the player at bay, ambushing from vents, flanking), and within one unit of distance it ignores flamethrower pain and grabs. Attacks need visual confirmation, touch, or several senses firing while the player is in a crawlspace, plus a valid navmesh path. The alien will not attack from a vent except in ambush. Working Joes have about 6x an armed human's health (reactor variants +50%), are slow, and give up once the player reaches a distance threshold from their combat area. Woolley calls them "a middle difficulty... with a slow walking speed being their main weakness." Mapping: your impact kit (shake, hit-stop, flash) suits the door blast and tank drop. Keep the engineer's actions small and instinctive (close, distract, drop, run). Make the threat's reaction to them state-based and varied, not escalating damage numbers. Use a slow, readable mid-tier hazard like the purge sentry as a breather between high-tension beats, as the Joes were.
dossier.presentation_ui_art: Lo-fi sci-fi: a rule of "not creating anything that the film crew could not have created as a prop in 1979" (Wikipedia citing GameFront). UI lead Jon McKellan (PC Gamer): "I'd record UI elements onto old beaten VHS tapes, deliberately magnetise the screen and the cables, and just destroy things whilst playing the recorded footage back on screen." That gave effects "more varied than what any of the previous software-driven tests achieved." He also noted that "Excluding the MU-TH-UR computer interface, no other screen on the Nostromo is interactive... Everything is a readout or a gauge," so they built their own interactive visual language from its "text... style, colour, borders." The film looped on studio screens; McKellan saw it "4 times a day for over 4 years." Fox supplied archive material; Develop reports 3 TB. Lighting: deferred renderer with "hundreds" of dynamic lights per scene (Wikipedia citing Develop 2014). Particles were rendered into a separate G-buffer and lit directly, so steam and smoke catch light volumetrically, with GPU particles numbering "thousands if not up to a million" (Michael Bailey via DSOGaming). Light is gameplay: the flashlight is a beacon the alien reacts to, and human NPC sight takes a "massive" penalty in the dark while Joes take a minor one (Thompson 2020). Low-fi tech is a statement: the motion tracker's "two simple dots" support "the idea that technology isn't the answer" (Hope, GDC via Game Developer). Mapping: give each painterly parallax room one or two motivated light sources plus lit haze or steam layers. Make terminals readouts with a few chunky physical controls. Keep the terminal look confined to Settings, per AGENT.md; elsewhere use diegetic readouts on WOLF and the CASE.
dossier.audio: Audio team (Sam Cooper, Byron Bullock; The Sound Architect, 2014). Approach: "work backwards from the perspective of the player... what it is we hope to make the player feel in any specific moment." The team researched "psychoacoustics and innate or conditioned responses to certain sounds and frequencies." On pacing: "it can be fatiguing to feel tense constantly and the fear loses its impact if it's relentless, so we like to ease up on the tension... They'll never feel completely 'safe.'" Ambiguity was deliberate: sounds carry "subtle and more abstracted elements" that keep the player "second-guessing." Mix (Bullock): "a dynamic system that could react to both the player and Alien," with "lowering the soundtrack before a scare or focusing in on certain sounds." Also: "a very high dynamic range... the odd metal creak, distant ship rumble, the sound of her footsteps"; "We've not been afraid to use quiet and silence"; "any sound can put you on edge, especially when you hear something moving in the vent above you or a blip on your motion tacker [sic]." Interfaces sound "analogue, tactile and real," built from floppy drives, tape machines and original film reels (the "space whale"), reworked with "Double tracking, adding sub harmonics, morphing, time-stretching." Tools: Wwise plus the in-house Cathode/"Cage" visual scripting tool, so sound, VFX, lighting and design could work on one sequence together. Music (Henson and Smith, MCV): composed in "kit form" so the audio department could assemble it, with "almost 200 minutes of music." Hope (PlayStation Blog) says the score adjusts "in real-time." A Wwise detail (three stereo stems packed into a 6-channel file, mixed at runtime by Stealth, Threat and an "Obstructed_Distance_To_Alien" parameter) comes from a search snippet of AudioTechnology's "Listen or Die," which I could not open: UNVERIFIED. The alien listens too. It hears footsteps by speed tier (crouch, walk, run), weapon fire registers faster than movement, and the motion tracker is audible at about 1.5 m. Opening lockers, doors or vents does not alert it (Thompson 2017/2020). Mapping: drive procedural layers from one or two parameters (threat distance with an occlusion term, and WOLF's alert state). Give footsteps per surface a loudness tier the world can react to. Keep room tone quiet enough that a single vent scrape reads.
dossier.mobile_and_input: The original was built for keyboard/mouse and controller. On PS4 the DualShock 4 light bar "flashes in-sync with the motion tracker's ping, increasing in frequency as the Alien approaches" (Hope, PlayStation Blog), so the threat signal also appears on the hardware. Feral Interactive later ported the game to Mac, Linux and mobile; its support FAQ includes "How does the saving system function in Alien: Isolation?", but the answer text was not returned, so touch-control specifics are UNVERIFIED. Kinect/PlayStation Camera microphone detection, where a player's real scream could give them away, appears in a search snippet only: UNVERIFIED. The motion tracker's "focus" input moves depth of field between the tracker and the world, and a loading tip warns "the motion tracker is only accurate in the direction you are facing" (quoted in Švelch 2020). Mapping to hold-to-move, one USE and two choice buttons: (a) put the tool or tracker readout on a hold of USE so raising it is a commitment with a cost (noise or slower movement), not a free HUD; (b) mirror threat proximity on controller rumble or light and on phone haptics as an optional accessibility channel; (c) make save or secure a hold-USE with a visible 1 to 3 second fill that can be cancelled.

steal: Make safe points a small, risky victory: a 1 to 3 second hold-USE secure action with audible beeps and a light that can be interrupted, which locks the CASE's carried evidence. Hope: saving should be "part of the fabric of the horror" and "small victories" let players breathe.

Use two layers of AI for WOLF and for threats: a pacing director that only nudges (send toward the area, back off after a peak) and an agent that acts on its own senses. Back off after a pressure peak, with a cooldown, as the menace gauge did.
Make WOLF's unlocks and memory depend on how he was treated, never on deaths ("none of these conditions come from events that lead to a players death").
Add deliberate doubt to WOLF's scouting: backtracking, pauses, glances and sniffing, like the alien's purposely sub-optimal paths.
Give WOLF and every hazard a readable eye or light state tell that changes before an action, as the Joes' eyes turn red before they attack. Pair it with posture or shape, not colour alone.
Room rule from Woolley: every room gets 2 or more exits (doorway plus a crawl or ledge route on its height change), one hiding place, and one quiet side space. Never trap the player.
Use the second height or crawlspace layer as the threat's 'vent' layer, and play position-tracking sounds along it, as vent movement was voiced at world points.
Treat noise as a tiered resource: footsteps per surface feed a loudness tier (crouch, walk, run) the world can hear. Doors and lockers do not alert threats, so hiding never betrays the player.
Make the tool a low-fi readout with a cost: raising it narrows the view or makes noise, and it is accurate only in the facing direction. Mirror its ping on haptics or light.

Drive procedural audio from one threat-distance-with-occlusion parameter plus WOLF's alert state. Keep a high dynamic range and real silence so a single vent scrape reads, and duck music before a scare.
Build tools from an instinctive verb (throw to distract, block, drop) rather than a weapon, based on the 'alien loose in the studio' exercise. Make a tool lose effect if overused.
Light is gameplay: one or two motivated sources per parallax room, lit steam or haze layers, and darkness that genuinely reduces sight for human-like enemies.
Distress UI and textures through physical processes (tape, CRT capture) for authentic, varied artefacts, and keep a period 'could have been a prop' rule for props and interfaces.
Use a slow, readable mid-threat (the purge sentry) as a breather between peak beats, as the Working Joes were added because constant alien pressure "would be way too stressful."
avoid: Do not space secure points far apart. Critics hit "frustrating distances between save points" and "trial and error progression"; cap loss at about one room's unsecured evidence.
Do not overuse one threat loop. A critic quoted on Wikipedia: "By the 300th time I dived under a table or into a locker, I wasn't scared anymore — I was annoyed." Keep rooms short and vary beats.

Do not give WOLF or the director knowledge the player cannot trace. Players accused the alien of being 'psychic', 'teleporting' or on an 'invisible tether' (Švelch 2020). Show the source of WOLF's information.
Do not market or describe AI as 'learning from you' when it is scripted unlocks. Developer claims and press ('learns from each interaction') diverged from the actual behaviour-tree unlock system.

Do not take a third-person-style camera lesson the wrong way: Creative Assembly found third person became "jockeying the camera and looking after your avatar". In 2D side view, avoid free wide views; make information cost movement.
Do not let simulation features break play. Acid blood was cut because "we were starting to make an alien simulator."
Do not turn the tool into a gun-shaped power fantasy ("There isn't big gun waiting for you in a locker"). Weapon crafting was tried and dropped.

Do not make the threat cheat with teleports except for authored story beats (the alien teleports only twice, for cutscenes). Do not reset ongoing state in a way that feels like a cheat on reload without communicating it.
Do not keep tension relentless. The audio team warns fear "loses its impact if it's relentless." Schedule quiet moments with the engineer and WOLF.
Do not copy the 12 to 18 hour length or its padding; reviewers called it "unnecessarily long, repetitive."

corrections.claim: Manual save has 'a three second pause before the save can be completed' (numbers table: 3 seconds, Wikipedia citing Gamasutra 2015); steal/death advice built on '1 to 3 seconds'.
corrections.problem: Unsupported number. Wikipedia's citation for that sentence is Gary Napper's 'Game Design Deep Dive: The save system of Alien: Isolation' (Game Developer, 11 Feb 2015, https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/game-design-deep-dive-the-save-system-of-i-alien-isolation-i-). I fetched it and it gives no duration. It says you 'put in your access card, wait for the systems in the fictional machine to warm up, and then wait for the three simple lights to blink off -- all the while knowing that you could be killed at any moment.' The 'three seconds' looks like Wikipedia's own reading of 'three lights'.
corrections.correction: Cite the primary source: Napper, the design director, describes a card insert, a warm-up and 'three simple lights' blinking off while the player stays killable. Mark '3 seconds' as UNVERIFIED (Wikipedia only). Present the 1 to 3 s secure-hold as a WOLF//OVERRIDE design choice, not as a measured Alien: Isolation value.

corrections.claim: Saving: manual save stations only, 'plus an autosave at mission or level starts reported by players in Steam threads.'
corrections.problem: The developer contradicts it. Napper's deep dive says: 'We have no "soft saves" or checkpoints in the game. The only way of saving is to locate a terminal in the world.' The dossier also skips this primary source's rejected approach: the team began with 'the usual checkpoints and menu-based saves' and dropped them.
corrections.correction: Either remove the autosave claim or mark it UNVERIFIED and in conflict with the design director's statement. Add Napper's account: checkpoints and menu saves were tried first and rejected in favour of manual terminals.

corrections.claim: Avoid list: 'Do not market or describe AI as "learning from you"... Developer claims and press ("learns from each interaction") diverged from the actual behaviour-tree unlock system.'
corrections.problem: The quote is misattributed and the lesson is unsupported. 'Learns from each interaction' comes from Wikipedia's development section, which says the unlocking behaviours create 'the illusion that the Alien learns from each interaction' (citing an '18 things' feature). It is not a press or marketing claim that clashed with reality. Švelch 2020, the dossier's own source, says 'the pseudo-learning component of the Alien's AI was never criticized' and the 'quasi-learning component was received mostly positively and without much controversy'.
corrections.correction: Drop this avoid item or reverse it: unlocking behaviours that look like learning were accepted by players. What simulationist players found unfair was the alien's apparently 'psychic' knowledge (from the Director), presumed teleporting and being 'tethered' to the player.

corrections.claim: Švelch found that 'simulationist' players felt the AI 'played dirty' and suspected a 'tether' or teleporting.
corrections.problem: Misattributed wording. 'Played dirty' does not appear in Švelch's Game Studies paper. It comes from the Tampere PlayLab summary ('simulationists often felt the AI was unjust and played dirty'). The paper's wording is that simulationists found three things 'unfair': 'psychic' knowledge, presumed teleportation and being 'tethered'.
corrections.correction: Attribute 'played dirty' to the Tampere PlayLab summary, or quote Švelch directly: simulationists found the Alien's 'psychic' knowledge, presumed teleportation and 'tether' unfair.

corrections.claim: 'In Bray's description, a Director "always knows where the player is"...'
corrections.problem: Misquoted and attributed to the wrong person. The words are Tommy Thompson's paraphrase in his 2017 article: 'The director observes the player throughout the game, always knowing your location' and 'while the director always knows where you are, the alien has to figure it out for itself.' The exact string 'always knows where the player is' does not appear.
corrections.correction: Quote Thompson (2017, summarising Andy Bray's nucl.ai 2016 talk): 'the director always knows where you are, the alien has to figure it out for itself'. The Director's job is 'to point the alien in the direction of the player periodically, to give it a hint as to where it should be looking.'

corrections.claim: 'AI support for level design (Thompson 2020): ... Hand-placed "search" points and "spot" (stand and watch) points direct the alien.'
corrections.problem: Wrong source article. The search and spot locations, and the designers' 'specific areas the alien never looks', are in Thompson's 2017 article (The Perfect Organism), not the 2020 data-mining piece.
corrections.correction: Cite Thompson 2017 (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-perfect-organism-the-ai-of-alien-isolation) for the search and spot locations. The vent-region limit and the 'at least 12' vent sweep configurations are correctly from 2020.

corrections.claim: Sales 'by May 2015 (Europe and US)': over 2.1 million, below SEGA's expectations.
corrections.problem: Slightly wrong date. Wikipedia says 'By March, it had sold over 2.1 million copies in Europe and the US'. The supporting GameSpot report is dated 11 May 2015. The figure runs to March 2015 and was reported in May.
corrections.correction: Write: over 2.1 million in Europe and the US by March 2015 (reported by GameSpot on 11 May 2015), below Sega's expectations.

corrections.claim: 'the motion tracker's "two simple dots" support "the idea that technology isn't the answer" (Hope, GDC via Game Developer)'
corrections.problem: Partly misattributed quote. In Parkin's write-up, 'two simple dots on a screen to indicate their position' is Parkin's own narration, outside the quotation marks. Hope's quoted words are only 'supports the idea that technology isn't the answer; it's not a magic bullet.'
corrections.correction: Attribute 'two simple dots' to Parkin's description and quote Hope only for 'supports the idea that technology isn't the answer; it's not a magic bullet.'

corrections.claim: Motion tracker audible to the alien at 'about 1.5 m' (numbers table: verified; audio section: 'the motion tracker is audible at about 1.5 m').
corrections.problem: Overstated precision. Thompson 2017's sentence attaches the distance to the whole list: 'The alien can "sense" player footsteps when walking or running, gunshots, and even the motion tracker when the player is around 1.5 meters away.' Thompson 2020, from game data, gives no metre value: the tracker makes noise only 'within a very short radius', and movement noise radii differ by crouch, walk and run. So 1.5 m is a talk-derived approximation, not a confirmed tracker-only value.
corrections.correction: Change confidence to 'derived'. Quote the full 2017 sentence, and add 2020's data-mined 'very short radius' with no metre value.

corrections.claim: Tools: 'Wwise plus the in-house Cathode/"Cage" visual scripting tool'.
corrections.problem: Not in the cited source. The Sound Architect interview names only 'an in-house tool dubbed Cage'. 'Cathode' does not appear there.
corrections.correction: Write 'Wwise and an in-house visual scripting tool dubbed Cage' (Byron Bullock). Add the Cathode name only with a source that names it.

corrections.claim: PC Gamer: 'In third-person it became a game about jockeying the camera and looking after your avatar... If you're hiding behind an object and you want to get a better view of your surroundings, you have to move.'
corrections.problem: The ellipsis changes the meaning. The cut sentence is 'But in first-person it's you that's being hunted.' The 'you have to move' line describes first person, not third person. The design lesson drawn still holds.
corrections.correction: Quote it with the missing sentence, or make clear that 'you have to move' describes the first-person version: 'But in first-person it's you that's being hunted. If you're hiding behind an object... you have to move.'

corpus.group: Signalis (rose-engine): six-slot inventory, save rooms and item boxes, diegetic and retro UI, horror pacing, documents as evidence, ending design

dossier.games: Signalis (rose-engine: Yuri Stern and Barbara Wittmann, Hamburg; published by Humble Games and PLAYISM; Unity; released 27 October 2022 on PC, PS4, Xbox One and Switch). Version 1.2 "KRÄHE" reached PC on about 25 October 2023 and consoles on 11 October 2024. It is a top-down, third-person survival horror game made from low-poly 3D and 2D sprites, with first-person puzzle screens and anime cutscenes. It started in 2014 as a lower-resolution 2D side-scrolling shooter made as a university prototype.
dossier.why_relevant: Signalis is the best recent example of the exact systems WOLF//OVERRIDE has decided to build: a deliberately tight six-slot inventory, a storage box shared by every save room, a "tool slot" for equipment kept outside general storage, documents that become a permanent readable archive rather than items you carry, death that sends you back to your last manual save, and endings computed silently from how you played, not from explicit choice prompts. That last point fits WOLF's memory of how the engineer treats him. It is also a two-person indie project. Its prototype was a 2D side-scroller before it became top-down, so its lessons about mood come from a project of similar scale. Its post-launch 1.2 patch is a primary record of which inventory rules players pushed back on and what the developers loosened: modules stopped costing slots, an optional +2 slots was added, and players could throw away unwanted heals.

dossier.companion:
Not directly applicable. Elster is the only playable character and there is no gameplay companion. Two transferable ideas still apply.

(1) Relationship and attitude are scored silently from behaviour, not from choice prompts. The ending is chosen by three hidden counters, Leave, Circle (Memory) and Death (Promise), fed by play statistics:
- more than 25 and more than 35 unique NPC conversations: +1 Leave each
- "Healing Time Fraction" above 60% and above 80%: +1 Leave each
- more than 40 unique "No Entry" door checks: +1 Leave
- more than 5 minutes of natural-regeneration time: +1 Death, counted twice
- more than 1900 base damage taken, more than 8 near-death survivals, more than 5 deaths: +1 Death each
- more than 90 and more than 120 kills: +1 Death each
- under 6 hours of play: +2 Circle; over 12 hours: +1 Death
- more than 5 minutes in one late memory segment: +1 Leave
The highest score wins and a tie goes to Memory (signalis.wiki.gg/wiki/Endings, datamined from a Steam guide).

Wittmann: "Endings are determined based on the players' overall playstyle. It was not our intention that players replay the game to try to get another ending" (Vice). This maps directly onto WOLF remembering how the engineer treats him: count the treatment, never show a morality meter.

(2) The emotional core is a remembered relationship (Elster and Ariane). The M/C Journal paper describes one ending where recognition fails ("I'm sorry, but I don't remember") as "the end of memory, character, and game." Losing memory is the worst outcome, which is relevant to WOLF memory gating.
dossier.level_and_camera:
**Camera and views**
- Top-down third-person exploration and combat, built from low-poly 3D models and 2D sprites (presskit, Gaming Boulevard).
- The camera cuts to "highly detailed first-person event & puzzle screens" (presskit features list). Wittmann and Stern's vertical slice showed "how we use perspective shifts and cutscenes to evoke a mysterious feeling" (Gamecity Hamburg interview).
- Destructoid credits the shifts between top-down, first-person and cutscenes with "unsettling tension."
- Hardcore Gamer: the top-down view keeps a good viewing distance.

**Origin as a side-scroller**
- The 2014 prototype was "a 2D side-scroller in a much lower resolution" (presskit history). mxdwn reports it was a side-scrolling shooter, limited by university time constraints, and became top-down after it was well received at showcases.
- No source explains why they left side view. UNVERIFIED.

**Map**
- The map fills in automatically as you explore and marks puzzle locations and door requirements (Inverse).
- The game counts unique "No Entry" door checks, so checking locked doors is tracked behaviour (wiki Endings).

**Level structure**
- Hardcore Gamer: "only about two" save rooms per level or chapter, "and thus only about two item boxes." It names repeated treks through enemy hallways as the main flaw: "feels frightening the first time, but it quickly becomes annoying."
- Some puzzles require "find the right frequency" on the radio. Others need images recalled from earlier (Nintendo Life).
- No source gives room widths, screen counts or pixel dimensions. Not available.
dossier.death_and_saves:
**No checkpoints**
- From the in-game manual: "There is no auto-save or checkpoint system in SIGNALIS! When Elster dies, all progress since your last manual save is lost" (wiki Instruction Manual).
- Saving happens only at stations in save rooms. Each save room has a storage box, and "Items stored in the storage box can be retrieved in every save room" (manual).
- Nintendo Life advises keeping "a couple of save files on the go, just in case."
- Whether saves are unlimited (no ink-ribbon-style cost) is UNVERIFIED; no fetched source mentions a save cost.

**Save-room spacing and design**
- Hardcore Gamer: about 2 save rooms and item boxes per level or chapter.
- Destructoid describes the save room as the moment of decision: standing "over a storage box, counting how many bullets" you expect to need. Resources are "just barely enough," yet the game provides "just enough ammo and tools to skate by" without needing to save-scum.

**How death feeds the ending**
- More than 5 deaths and more than 8 near-death survivals each add to the Death/Promise ending score (wiki Endings).
- Natural health regeneration only happens below 26/100 HP (12/100 on Survival difficulty), and time spent there is also scored.

**Health display**
- Injury warnings appear on screen when health is near fatal (manual).
- Nintendo Life: "The way Elster hunches over when she is injured is your only 'health bar' unless you pause the game."

**Enemies that come back**
- Enemies revive. The manual warns "even finished enemies may recover if Elster loiters too long in one area."
- Only burning prevents it: the Thermite Flare is "Used to incinerate enemies," "preventing them from reviving," with at most 3 carried (wiki). Push Square calls the thermite charges "scarce."
- Inverse: unless "burnt to a crisp with a flare, they will always come back."
dossier.inventory_and_evidence:
**Six slots**
- From the manual: "Elster can only carry 6 item stacks at a time." Key items, weapons, ammo and healing all compete for these slots (Inverse: the limit "puts pressure on the player to balance weaponry, ammo, healing items, and puzzle materials").
- Stern (Vice): "Personally, I think if you're comfortable in a survival horror game, something isn't quite right."
- Also Stern: "We designed much of the game around the number six, but tested the game with various inventory sizes." Testers filled their inventory whatever the size, hoarding weapons and ammo they did not need. He found this funny and said: "Perhaps we should have put a note somewhere that says 'Only take what you need!'"
- Hardcore Gamer: "at least half of your inventory will be used up almost all the time," and some puzzles require assembling six items in one place.

**Stacks**
- Repair Patch: up to 8 per stack. It heals "a small amount of health over time" (wiki).
- Thermite Flare: up to 3.
- The manual says some healing items "can regenerate Elster's health slowly over time when outside the inventory."

**Tool slot and modules**
- Tools (Autoinjector, Disposable Stun Prod, Eidetic Module, Flashlight Module, Receiver, Thermite Flare) "can be equipped and used in the Tool slot" (wiki Tools).
- Built-in LSTR interface modules cost nothing: Repair Logic (combine, repair, inspect), Targeting, Map, Memory/Archive and Diagnostics (wiki Module).
- At launch, the Flashlight and Eidetic modules each cost one of the 6 slots. Nintendo Life complained the camera "costs an inventory slot that is better served by carrying more health packs."

**The 1.2 "KRÄHE" change**
- Patch notes: "Added an option to adjust the inventory capacity: By default, the Flashlight Module and Eidetic Module will no longer take up an inventory slot," plus "an option to extend the inventory size" and "an option to allow using health items while at full health to dispose of them" (GoNintendo patch text).
- Players report three settings, chosen in the main menu only:
  - Classic: the original 6 slots, modules cost slots.
  - Revised (new default): 6 slots plus a temporary bonus slot for each module, shown as 7 or 8.
  - Extended: Revised plus 2 more regular slots, so 8 + 2 (ResetEra, Steam discussion).

**Documents as evidence**
- Read documents never cost slots. "Memories refers to the section in the LSTR menu interface that stores previously read text and images. The player can go back and re-read these texts at any time" (wiki Memories, 126 entries listed).
- Some documents are puzzle keys, for example "Memorandum: Wall Safe Codes," which exists in a normal and a garbled version.
- Eidetic Module: "Allows recording of up to 6 visual memories." These are greyscale screenshots, and the oldest is overwritten when the limit is reached (wiki).
- Receiver: tunes 50 to 250 kHz to pick up text data. Later it also carries image data and fights one enemy type by matching its frequency (wiki Receiver).
- Inverse: "Keeping physical notes could be the difference between an easy path forward or having to make a dangerous trip back." In other words, the game hands some note-taking to the player.
- The wiki lists 80 key items.
dossier.action_and_impact:
**Aiming and shooting**
- Hold a button to ready the weapon; movement slows while aiming. A target box appears around enemies and "shrinks when you have clear line of sight" (manual, as summarised).
- Downed enemies can be finished with a separate input (F) "to save ammo," but may still recover if you linger. Running makes "Elster more noticeable to enemies" (manual).
- Nintendo Life: "Holding one button to aim and another to shoot is good for hit-and-run tactics." Hardcore Gamer: you stand in place while aiming.
- Destructoid: "Lock-on gets a little finicky." Boss fights are the commonly cited weakness; Nintendo Life says they "don't lend themselves to a straight-on fight."

**Weapon damage by difficulty (Casual / Normal / Survival, wiki datamine)**
- Pistol: 40 / 30 / 12
- Revolver: 100 / 50 / 30
- Rifle: 200 / 160 / 80
- SMG: 40x3 on Casual down to 8x3 on Survival
- Flare gun: 70+5 on Casual down to 18+5 on Survival

**Puzzles**
- Destructoid praises the puzzles as tactile: fuses, dials and clicking boxes.
- No source describes hit-stop, screen shake or flash timings. Not available.
dossier.presentation_ui_art:
**Art direction**
- The look is "retro pixel art" combined with "dark sci-fi anime" (Gamecity Hamburg).
- Yuri Stern credits himself with pixel art, 3D modelling, art direction, programming, writing and sound design. Barbara Wittmann did 3D and 2D animation, concept art, game design and writing (presskit).

**Diegetic interface**
- The UI is Elster's own machine interface, the LSTR, built from modules: Map, Memory/Archive, Diagnostics, Targeting and Repair Logic (wiki Module).
- The M/C Journal paper says the screen "self-reflexively pays homage with a slightly convex monitor-like display." It also notes that the player picks up a book "detailing the functions of their avatar, essentially this is the instruction manual for both avatar and player," so the tutorial is a world object.
- Health is shown on the body: Elster hunches when injured (Nintendo Life).

**Mood and influences**
- Stern aimed for a "dream-like quality" drawn from the emotional logic of real dreams rather than conventional narrative structure (Vice).
- Wittmann: the game is in conversation with its inspirations but works without the player recognising them (Vice).
- The Bloody Disgusting interview reportedly has Stern saying the horror "comes mostly from the oppressive systems and mechanics of old-school survival horror," and "I'm more concerned with atmosphere, symbolism, and character than with scaring the players." UNVERIFIED: these quotes come from a search snippet, because the page returned 403.

**Endings**
- There are four normal endings (Leave, Memory, Promise, and an early "False" ending) plus a secret "Artifact" ending that needs radio frequencies and a 20-digit code on a second playthrough (wiki).
- Stern: "If there was a 'true ending,' we wouldn't have made any other endings" (PSU, 9 Jan 2023). Also "We were always aware that a lot of people would grade the endings on a classic good-bad scale" (Vice). He built the early ending for players who, like him, rarely finish games.

**Accessibility (1.2)**
- Added an option to reduce high-frequency flicker and an option to invert the Y axis in first-person scenes.
dossier.audio:
**Credits and awards**
- Composers: 1000 Eyes and Cicada Sirens. Sound design credit goes to Gidon Wolff and also appears in Yuri Stern's role list (presskit).
- Won Best Audio Design and Best Debut at the 2023 German Computer Game Awards (Wikipedia, citing deutscher-computerspielpreis.de).

**How the music reacts**
- Nintendo Life: "Music is subtle, sometimes dropping to a whisper only to roar to life when enemies approach." Also: "the way the music changes when they catch sight of Elster is nerve-wracking." So detection is announced through music, not a UI icon.

**Sound as a mechanic**
- The radio Receiver turns sound into puzzles: frequencies carry codes and images and can be used against one enemy type.

**Not found**
- No fetched source gives specifics on save-room music, footsteps by surface or mix levels. UNVERIFIED and not covered.
dossier.mobile_and_input:
There is no mobile version; Signalis shipped on PC, PS4, Xbox One and Switch. Input lessons that still apply:
- Aiming is a hold, with a separate fire button.
- Finishing a downed enemy is a separate contextual input.
- Running is a stealth cost.
- The inventory opens on a single key (Tab per the manual) and shows health.
- 1.2 improved "interaction angles for hole jumping and ladder climbing interactions." Precise contextual prompts mattered enough to patch, which is relevant to WOLF//OVERRIDE's single USE button on touch.
- Inventory capacity can only be changed from the main menu, not mid-run (ResetEra).
- The game partly relies on players keeping physical notes (Inverse). On a phone that is a burden, which argues for an in-game capture tool like the Eidetic Module.

steal: Design the evidence CASE around one small fixed number, as rose-engine did with six, and say it in the fiction. Signalis calls it 6 'item stacks' and holds that number constant. Stern: 'if you're comfortable in a survival horror game, something isn't quite right.'

Keep the one tool outside the CASE in its own Tool slot from day one. Signalis's modules cost inventory slots at launch, reviewers complained, and the 1.2 default stopped charging slots for them. Start where they ended up.

Keep what you have read separate from what you carry as proof. Signalis archives every read document in a permanent Memory tab you can re-read at any time (126 entries) at zero slot cost. Physical key items still cost slots. For WOLF//OVERRIDE: reading or scanning a log goes into the archive and is never lost; a physical evidence item goes in the CASE and can be dropped on death until secured.

Make every safe point open the same shared stash: 'Items stored in the storage box can be retrieved in every save room.' Securing evidence at any safe point puts it in one shared locker, so the player never has to remember which room holds what.

Turn the safe point into a decision scene: standing 'over a storage box, counting how many bullets' (Destructoid). Show a two-column CASE / SECURED view with the next room's known needs or threats hinted beside it.
Show health on the body. Elster's hunch is 'your only health bar' (Nintendo Life). Use the engineer's posture, breathing and footsteps, and WOLF's look-at, instead of a HUD bar on the main screen.
Let the music react to detection: 'dropping to a whisper only to roar to life when enemies approach.' Use this with procedural room tone so the purge sentry's alert state needs no UI icon.

Score behaviour quietly for WOLF's memory, the way Signalis scores endings from counters (conversations, healing habits, door checks, deaths, kills) with thresholds and a tie-breaker. No visible morality meter, and never call any outcome good, bad or true. Stern: 'If there was a true ending, we wouldn't have made any other endings.'

Make threats that come back unless properly dealt with, plus a scarce tool that settles them for good. Signalis's downed enemies recover if you loiter, unless burned with a Thermite Flare (max 3). For example, a purge sentry reboots unless the engineer pulls its core or WOLF chooses to hold it down. Keep an engineer-only option.
Use a capped in-game capture tool (Eidetic Module: 6 snapshots, oldest overwritten) so phone players never need pen and paper for codes. Inverse notes Signalis players relied on 'physical notes.'

Put a meaningful instruction manual in the world, as Signalis does with an in-world manual item that the M/C Journal calls the manual 'for both avatar and player.' WOLF's or the engineer's service manual can teach USE, choices and securing evidence.

Use short perspective shifts for detailed interactions (Signalis's first-person 'event & puzzle screens'). Within WOLF//OVERRIDE's painterly 2.5D, cut to a close-up of the copy station or relay panel for tactile dials and fuses, which Destructoid calls the puzzle 'highlights.'

Log locked-door checks and show them on the map, like Signalis's auto-filling map that marks door requirements and its tracked 'No Entry' checks. That data can also feed WOLF's hints ("you've tried that bulkhead three times").

Add the 1.2 quality-of-life options from the start: let players drop or use unwanted heals at full health, offer a flicker-reduction toggle, and offer an optional larger-CASE setting chosen at the start (Signalis's Classic, Revised and Extended).
avoid: No autosave and no checkpoints at all. Signalis loses everything since the last manual save, which is too harsh for short phone sessions. WOLF//OVERRIDE's plan (death drops unsecured evidence only; safe points secure it) is the better-bounded version. Keep the loss visible and recoverable, and never roll back room progress.

Spacing save rooms and stashes about two per chapter while puzzles need many items in one place. Hardcore Gamer's main complaint was backtracking: hallways 'frightening the first time' that become 'annoying after repeated treks' and feel like 'padding.' With 1.5-2-screen rooms, put a safe point at least every 2-3 rooms.
Letting tools and modules eat CASE slots. Signalis had to patch this after reviews said the camera 'costs an inventory slot that is better served by carrying more health packs.'

Assuming players will 'only take what you need.' Stern's testers hoarded at every inventory size they tried. Show in the UI what the next area needs, or have WOLF comment, rather than hoping for restraint.
Healing items the player cannot drop. Signalis had to add 'using health items while at full health to dispose of them' in 1.2.

Finicky lock-on and boss fights that don't fit the core verbs ('Lock-on gets a little finicky'; bosses 'don't lend themselves to a straight-on fight'). WOLF//OVERRIDE's hold-to-move and single USE should never have to aim precisely under pressure.

Hidden ending math that players can't read, combined with players who label results good or bad. If WOLF's memory changes outcomes, show WOLF's attitude in the moment through barks, refusals and positioning, so it never feels arbitrary, and avoid a single best outcome.
Expecting players to keep their own notes for codes and frequencies. That fails on phone, so provide in-game capture or let WOLF remember.
Letting lore overload the evidence. Push Square's main con was that the lore 'occasionally becomes excessive.' Each evidence item should change a decision or WOLF's attitude, not only add backstory.
Copying genre conventions wholesale. GamesRadar's verdict (headline only; the review body could not be fetched) was that Signalis 'Adheres too closely to Resident Evil's aging rules.'

corrections.claim: Vice inventory quote: Stern "found this funny" and "He built the early ending for players who, like him, rarely finish games" (inventory_and_evidence, presentation_ui_art).
corrections.problem: Misgenders Yuri Stern. The rose-engine press kit (http://rose-engine.org/press/Presskit_SIGNALIS.html) says "Yuri Stern (they/them) and Barbara Wittmann (she/her)". The quotes themselves are accurate and correctly attributed to Stern in Vice (https://www.vice.com/en/article/signalis-game-rose-engine-interview/). The early-ending point also comes from Vice, not PSU, but the dossier places it right after the PSU citation.
corrections.correction: Use they/them for Stern: "They found this funny" and "Stern built the early ending for players who, like them, don't finish most games". Cite Vice for that point, quoting: "that ending was my way of trying to make sure people like me get to see an ending even if they usually don't finish games."

corrections.claim: Push Square's main con was that the lore "occasionally becomes excessive" (avoid list).
corrections.problem: Misquote. The word "excessive" does not appear in the Push Square review (https://www.pushsquare.com/reviews/ps4/signalis). Its only listed con is "Lore gets a bit heavy at times". The body says "even if some sections can get a little lore-heavy", and it frames that as worth reading: "when a game is designed this tightly, it's well worth listening."
corrections.correction: Push Square's only con: "Lore gets a bit heavy at times" (Sam Brooke, 25 Oct 2022, 8/10). Present it as a mild complaint, not a main flaw.

corrections.claim: Ending scoring: "under 6 hours of play: +2 Circle"; "highest score wins and a tie goes to Memory" (companion section and numbers table).
corrections.problem: Incomplete in a way that changes the design lesson. The wiki (https://signalis.wiki.gg/wiki/Endings) also says "The game starts with 2 points in 'Circle'." So Memory starts 2 points ahead, gets +2 more under 6 hours, and wins every tie, which makes it the built-in default. Also, "Healing Time Fraction" is not a measure of healing habits. The wiki defines it as the share of active play time spent at 80% health or higher, sampled over 11 segments.
corrections.correction: Add: Circle/Memory starts at +2 before any play statistic counts, and ties go to Memory. Healing Time Fraction = the fraction of play spent at 80% or more HP (>60% gives +1 Leave, >80% gives +1 Leave). The memory-time row counts only "the Penrose segment after Nowhere". For WOLF: decide on a deliberate default attitude and a tie-break rule, as Signalis does.

corrections.claim: Steam user reviews when fetched: "96% of 21,634, Overwhelmingly Positive"; published by Humble Games and PLAYISM.
corrections.problem: The 21,634 count is English-language reviews only. The store tooltip reads "96% of the 21,634 user reviews in your language are positive" and the line is labelled "English Reviews" (https://store.steampowered.com/app/1262350/SIGNALIS/). The Steam page now lists the publisher as "Balor Games", not Humble Games. The press kit lists Humble Games ("Publisher worldwide") and PLAYISM ("Sub-Publisher Asia"), which reflects the launch arrangement.
corrections.correction: "96% positive of 21,634 English-language Steam reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive), fetched Oct 2026; the all-language total is higher and was not captured." Publisher at launch: Humble Games worldwide, PLAYISM Asia. The current Steam listing shows Balor Games.

corrections.claim: Level structure: Some puzzles require "find the right frequency" on the radio. Others need images recalled from earlier (Nintendo Life).
corrections.problem: Unsupported quote. The Nintendo Life review (https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/switch-eshop/signalis) contains no "frequency" or "radio" text. It supports only the image-recall half: "Many require you to recall images from earlier in the game, so you'll want to either have a pen and paper handy or use the Switch's screenshot function."
corrections.correction: Drop the "find the right frequency" quote, or source the radio-puzzle claim to the press kit ("puzzle-solving through code-breaking, radio signals") or the wiki Receiver page. Keep the Nintendo Life image-recall quote. It also directly supports the in-game capture tool idea (pen and paper, or the Switch screenshot button).

corrections.claim: Campaign length: "8-9 h (Hardcore Gamer)"; save rooms "about 2" per chapter marked confidence "unverified".
corrections.problem: The reviewer says only "clocking in at eight hours". The "9 hours" on that page comes from an embedded How Long To Beat widget, not the reviewer. The save-room claim is under-rated: the review text is verified as "the game has only about two of them per level/chapter, and thus only about two item boxes" (https://hardcoregamer.com/reviews/review-signalis/429203/).
corrections.correction: Hardcore Gamer: 8 h (reviewer). Mark "about 2 save rooms/item boxes per level/chapter" as verified (reviewer estimate). The same paragraph blames modules "taking up their own slots (even while equipped)" for the backtracking, which supports the Tool-slot recommendation.

corrections.claim: Nintendo Life: bosses "don't lend themselves to a straight-on fight."
corrections.problem: Slightly misattributed subject. The sentence is about the combat mechanics, said in the context of bosses: "The combat mechanics are simple but don't lend themselves to a straight-on fight."
corrections.correction: "The combat mechanics are simple but don't lend themselves to a straight-on fight", followed by "Holding one button to aim and another to shoot is good for hit-and-run tactics but it doesn't meld well with big battles" (Nintendo Life, on boss fights).

corrections.claim: Testers filled their inventory whatever the size, "hoarding weapons and ammo they did not need" (Vice).
corrections.problem: Slightly incomplete. Healing was included too: "testers would still always fill up their inventory to the brim with as much weapons, ammo and healing as they could carry even if they didn't need it. I thought that was very funny."
corrections.correction: Say "weapons, ammo and healing". Quote: "fill up their inventory to the brim ... even if they didn't need it."

corrections.claim: Presskit credits: Stern did pixel art, 3D modelling, art direction, programming, writing and sound design; Wittmann did 3D and 2D animation, concept art, game design and writing.
corrections.problem: Partly inaccurate. The press kit lists Stern as "Game design, programming, art direction, pixel art, concept art, 3d modeling, writing & sound design" and Wittmann as "3D & 2D animation, game design, concept art, add. prop art, add. writing, administration". The dossier drops Stern's game design and concept art and turns Wittmann's "add. writing" into writing.
corrections.correction: Use the press kit wording exactly. Both are credited with game design and concept art. Stern has the main writing credit and Wittmann has "add. writing". Sound design is credited to Stern and to Gidon Wolff (external).

corrections.claim: Development span "2014 to Oct 2022; full time from the 2020 publisher deal", cited to Gamecity Hamburg.
corrections.problem: Mixed sourcing. Gamecity supports only "Once we had signed with a publisher in early 2020 we went into game development full time" and the prototype in a games class. The 2014 start and the "Bachelor thesis" come from the press kit. mxdwn says the side-scroller was "due to time constraints" and was reworked "the summer after showcasing". That is a timeline, not a stated reason for leaving side view, so the dossier's UNVERIFIED flag on the why is correct.
corrections.correction: Cite the press kit for 2014 ("Many iterations and a Bachelor thesis later") and Gamecity for full-time development after signing with Humble Games in early 2020 (the deal came from a gamescom 2019 pitch).

corpus.group: Resident Evil 2 (2019) and Resident Evil 4 (2023): inventory grids and attaché cases, typewriters and autosave split, safe rooms, files, the Ashley companion in RE4

dossier.games: Resident Evil 2 (Capcom, 2019 remake; directed by Kazunori Kadoi; audio director Kentaro Nakashima) and Resident Evil 4 (Capcom, 2023 remake; directed by Yasuhiro Ampo and Kazunori Kadoi). iOS/iPadOS/macOS ports exist for both (RE4 released on Apple platforms 20 December 2023, per the wiki).
dossier.why_relevant: Between them, these two games cover almost everything WOLF//OVERRIDE has decided to build next. RE2 (2019) has a small slot inventory with +2-slot upgrades, a shared item box at safe rooms, typewriter saves that are free on lower difficulties and cost ink ribbons on Hardcore, autosave turned off on the hardest mode, an honest-audio stalker (Mr. X), an impulse response recorded for every room, and room tone used as a weapon. RE4 (2023) has a grid attaché case with item rotation and auto-sort, weapon storage at typewriters, no autosave on Professional, and Ashley, a companion the developers rebuilt specifically so she stays present without getting in the way. Their lessons cover the evidence CASE, the safe points that secure evidence, the death model, wider rooms with sound-driven threats, real room tone and footsteps, and how a companion should share space with the player. WOLF is independent and not an escort, though, so Ashley's fail states are mostly things to avoid.
