steal: Model unsecured evidence on Celeste's strawberry followers. Evidence the engineer picks up trails as 'unsecured': show it with a visible tether, CASE icon or pulse. It becomes secured only at a safe point. Death calls the equivalent of Leader.LoseFollowers() and the item drops. This is the decided model, and Celeste shows it reads clearly without a tutorial.

For essential evidence, use Celeste's seed rule, not Hollow Knight's Geo rule. On death, an essential item returns to where it was found ('the ones collected will move to their original positions'), so it can never be lost for good, which keeps the engineer-only path intact. Only optional evidence should drop at the death spot as a Shade-like cache that a second death can erase.

Mark the drop on the map as Hollow Knight does (Shade 'location marked on the map'). Make recovery a quiet pickup, as Silksong's Cocoon is (you break it and it gives a small refund, '9 Silk'). Do not make it a fight, as the Hollow Knight Shade is. Let WOLF offer a Jiji/Silkeater-style fetch that depends on trust and that he can refuse, while the engineer can always walk back for it.

Make safe points do the Hollow Knight bench bundle: save, set respawn, restore the engineer, secure the CASE contents and commit map data. Copy the quill rule as WOLF's scouting: the rooms he scouts or explores appear on the map only when synced at a safe point. That gives safe points a reason to exist beyond saving.

Fill CASE entries in stages like the Hunter's Journal: a stub appears on first contact, and full notes unlock with more examination, a WOLF scan or a safe-point review. Allow some entries to come from inspection, not use, as Goam's entry comes from inspecting it.

Add Celeste-style forgiveness windows suited to hold-to-move: about 0.1 s ledge grace on the walkable height change, buffering of USE and choice presses for roughly 0.1 s before a station comes into range (Celeste's buffer length is UNVERIFIED), and 4 px corner nudges so doorways and step-ups never catch the engineer's collider.

Use Celeste's frame-rate-independent camera ease, pos += (target-from)*(1-k^dt) with k=0.01, clamp it to room bounds, and add authored CameraAnchor pulls for 1.5-2 screen rooms (for example, ease toward WOLF or a threat when it matters). Push the camera ahead (+48 px style) only during scripted rushes.

Trigger footsteps from animation frames (contact frames 0 and 6), passing a surface index from the floor collider into the sound. Use separate events for steps, landings and wall or handhold contact. Swap to a footstep instead of a landing thud on small drops. Add landing squash scaled by fall speed (up to 1.6/0.4 in Celeste; use a gentler value for a human engineer).

Use short hit-stop and directional shake at authored impacts, as Celeste does: Freeze 0.05 s on dash start, 0.1 s on big launches, directional shake 0.1-0.2 s along the impact direction, with graded rumble. This calibrates the existing impact kit's door blast, tank drop and bolt.

Show strain on the engineer's body, not in a HUD: Celeste's red flash plus light rumble below 20/110 stamina, and hair colour for dash state. For WOLF//OVERRIDE, use breathing audio, a stance change or a tint when the engineer is hurt, carrying something heavy or low on air.

Build WOLF's 'follow then lead' on a replay buffer like Badeline's chaser: record the engineer's positions and sounds for about 4 s and have WOLF replay them at a delay (time-tagged snapshots, 0.02 s tolerance). The path is guaranteed walkable, so WOLF needs no pathfinding for the basic follow.

Locate WOLF by sound as Cornifer is located: when WOLF scouts ahead, an audible cue (claws, servo whine, a short bark) carries across the room, plus a visible trace on the floor, so the player can find him without a HUD arrow.

Build the assist menu as independent toggles, as Celeste does: game speed 50-100% in 10% steps, skip a challenge, invincibility from environmental hazards, and a 'pause to aim/decide' option like Dash Assist. Use the revised wording ('to fit your specific needs'), not the original 'we recommend playing without' line, and never tie assist use to WOLF's memory or trust.
Keep the space physically coherent ('98% pure') and block out rooms first with plain tiles (Team Cherry used 64x64), then playtest spacing before painting the parallax layers.
Present death as learning, as Celeste's postcards do ('The more you die, the more you're learning'), and make 'Save and Quit... resume from the same screen' a promise.
avoid: Do not let a second death permanently delete essential evidence, as Hollow Knight's replaced Shade deletes Geo. Permanent loss is acceptable only for optional material, which keeps the engineer-only fallback intact.

Do not make recovery a fight with a hostile double (the Hollow Knight Shade). WOLF//OVERRIDE has no combat loop, and a mandatory fight on the way back at the death site breaks the non-combat horror pacing. Silksong itself moved to a passive cocoon.

Do not use long corpse runs or toll safe points. Hollow Knight's toll benches (50-150 Geo) and widely spaced benches suit a 50-bench Metroidvania, not three short rooms; keep a safe point within about one room of any hazard.

Do not make knowledge you need cost money or depend on finding a specific NPC, as Hollow Knight does by gating the map behind finding Cornifer and buying a quill. Team Cherry called the map system their hardest problem. Give the engineer a basic map by default and let WOLF's scouting add detail.

Do not use gatekeeping assist language. Celeste's own original text ('We believe that its difficulty is essential... We recommend playing without Assist Mode') was rewritten in v1.3.0.0 after criticism. Avoid the name 'Cheat Mode', which Thorson dropped as 'judgmental'.
Do not make assist or accessibility choices change WOLF's memory, trust or story outcomes; Celeste assist use has 'no judgement or implication' of playing wrong.

Do not copy Celeste's or Hollow Knight's movement constants wholesale. They are tuned for an acrobatic pixel-art platformer (dash 240 px/s, no acceleration in Hollow Knight). A grounded engineer needs slower, weighted values, tuned by hands-on play on the actual route.

Do not make hold-to-USE wasteful when interrupted, as Hollow Knight's Focus wastes Soul on a hit. On touch and in a horror context, keep partial progress or refund it, and show the interruption clearly.
Do not add Steel Soul-style permadeath or Golden Strawberry-style 'any death resets the chapter' rules to the main path. If they exist at all, keep them optional post-game challenges.

Do not claim any feel improvement from these numbers without playing the affected route in a game window (AGENT.md). Headless tests and stills do not validate timing windows, camera ease or footstep cadence.

corrections.claim: Celeste's base resolution 'usually quoted as 320x180' is UNVERIFIED because Celeste.GameWidth/GameHeight are not in the released file (also listed in numbers[] as confidence 'unverified').
corrections.problem: Under-claimed. A primary source the dossier already cites states it outright. Maddy Thorson's 'Celeste & Forgiveness' article (item 8, Wide Wall-Jump Window) says: 'this is a 320x180-resolution game so that's a quarter of a tile'.
corrections.correction: Mark 320x180 as verified and cite https://maddymakesgames.com/articles/celeste_and_forgiveness/index.html. It is the developer's own statement. GameWidth/GameHeight are still absent from Player.cs, but the article settles the value. The same line also gives an 8 px tile (2 px = a quarter of a tile).

corrections.claim: Audio: 'a landing right after a step plays a footstep instead of a landing thud (playFootstepOnLand)'. Steal: 'Swap to a footstep instead of a landing thud on small drops.'
corrections.problem: The code was misread. In Player.cs, playFootstepOnLand is set to 0.5f only in ClimbHop() (line ~3294), the hop over the top of a wall when climbing up. It counts down each frame. On landing, the code plays char_mad_footstep instead of char_mad_land if the timer is above 0, then resets it. A normal step does not set it, and fall height plays no part in it.
corrections.correction: Write: 'For 0.5 s after a climb-hop over a ledge top, a landing plays a footstep instead of a landing sound (playFootstepOnLand = 0.5f in ClimbHop).' For WOLF//OVERRIDE, the transferable rule is that a mantle or step-up onto the walkable height change should end on a footstep, not a thud. A 'small drop' rule is not in the source and would be a new design choice.

corrections.claim: Landing squash 'scales the sprite to X 1.6 / Y 0.4 at maximum fall speed (scaled by Speed.Y/240)'; numbers[]: 'scale X 1.6, Y 0.4 (lerped by fallSpeed/240)'.
corrections.problem: Overstated. The code is squish = Math.Min(Speed.Y / FastMaxFall, 1), and FastMaxFall is 240. Normal MaxFall is 160, so a normal maximum-speed landing gives squish of about 0.67, which is about X 1.4 / Y 0.6. The full 1.6/0.4 only happens at fast-fall speed (holding down).
corrections.correction: Write: 'Squash lerps from 1/1 to 1.6/0.4 by Speed.Y/240 (FastMaxFall). A normal max-fall landing (160 px/s) gives about 1.4/0.6, and the full 1.6/0.4 only comes from a fast-fall.'

corrections.claim: Steal: on death an essential item should return to where it was found, citing Celeste's seed rule ('the ones collected will move to their original positions'). Death section: 'Dying with a follower loses it, because LoseFollowers() sends it back.'
corrections.problem: Misattributed trigger, plus a claim the source does not support. (1) The wiki's seed rule is about touching the ground: 'If you touch the ground before gathering all seeds in a room, the ones collected will move to their original positions'. It is not about death. (2) Player.cs only shows Die() calling Leader.LoseFollowers(). What a strawberry does when it loses its leader is in Strawberry.cs/Follower code, and the NoelFB/Celeste repo does not include them (it holds only Source/Player and Source/PICO-8). The Collectables wiki page also does not describe what happens to followed strawberries on death.
corrections.correction: Quote the seed rule as a ground-touch reset. Present 'a followed strawberry returns to its spawn on death' as common in-game knowledge that the fetched sources do not show (UNVERIFIED from source). The design recommendation (essential evidence returns to its origin) is still sound, but it is WOLF//OVERRIDE's own rule, not a Celeste quote.

corrections.claim: Hollow Knight inventory: 'Maps only update when you rest at a bench.' (shown as a quote from the Map and Quill wiki).
corrections.problem: This is not verbatim. The wiki's wording is: 'After uncharted areas have been explored, resting at a Bench will update the map.' The words 'only update' do not appear on the page.
corrections.correction: Quote the wiki's actual sentence, or paraphrase without quotation marks. The quill requirement is also on the page: maps cannot be updated without the Quill.

corrections.claim: Hollow Knight map prices: 'maps 30-150 Geo'.
corrections.problem: Wrong range. According to the wiki table, Cornifer charges 30-150 Geo and Iselda charges 40-200 Geo. Fog Canyon and Queen's Gardens cost 200 Geo from Iselda.
corrections.correction: Write 'maps 30-200 Geo (Cornifer 30-150, Iselda 40-200; Resting Grounds is sold only by Iselda, 75 Geo)'.

corrections.claim: 'Gibson called the map system the hardest problem'; Avoid: 'Team Cherry called the map system their hardest problem.'
corrections.problem: Overstated. In Game Informer, Gibson said 'The map and the mapping system took a long while to come together' and 'Turns out drawing maps is tough! We threw out a lot of them before we reached the final version.' He did not call it the hardest problem. He also said 'we're pleased with how the system turned out. It's a wonderful balance.' Using it as a warning misses that.
corrections.correction: Write: 'Gibson said the map system "took a long while to come together" and that they "threw out a lot" of map drafts.' Drop 'hardest problem'. If the 'avoid' point is about gating knowledge behind purchases, base it on WOLF//OVERRIDE's own reasoning, not on a quote Team Cherry did not give.

corrections.claim: Focus: 'full vessel 2.923 s; about 1.791 s with Quick Focus'.
corrections.problem: This compares numbers measured differently. In the wiki's timing table, one container is 2.673 s for base (3 x 0.891 s, without the 0.25 s startup) and 1.791 s for Quick Focus (3 x 0.597 s, also without startup). The 2.923 s figure includes the startup. With startup, Quick Focus would be about 2.04 s (derived, not stated on the wiki).
corrections.correction: Write 'full vessel 2.923 s including the 0.25 s startup (2.673 s without it); Quick Focus 0.597 s per mask, 1.791 s per vessel without startup'.

corrections.claim: Original Assist Mode warning text applied to 'v1.3.0.0 and earlier'.
corrections.problem: Off by one version. The wiki says 'The text was tweaked in version 1.3.0.0', so the old text was in versions before 1.3.0.0, not in 1.3.0.0. (The dossier's own 'avoid' list correctly says it was rewritten in v1.3.0.0.) The wiki also gives a less charged reason than 'criticism': the old text 'unintentionally could have sounded gatekeepy'.
corrections.correction: Write 'original text (before v1.3.0.0); changed in 1.3.0.0 after community feedback that it "unintentionally could have sounded gatekeepy"'.

corrections.claim: Rooms: Wikipedia, 'checkpoints between single-screen challenges'.
corrections.problem: This is a paraphrase shown as a quote. Wikipedia's text is: 'divided into multiple single-screen challenges, with checkpoints in between screens.'
corrections.correction: Use the exact wording, or remove the quotation marks.

corrections.claim: Juice: 'DirectionalShake(dir, .1f-.2f) on wall bounces and dashes'; 'Celeste.Freeze(.05f) hit-stop at every dash start'.
corrections.problem: Partly mislabelled. The 0.1 s directional shakes (lines ~1908 and ~1948) are in SuperBounce and the side-bounce routine, which springs and bumpers trigger. They are not wall bounces, and 'wall bounce' is a separate Celeste technique. The 0.2 s shakes are in DashCoroutine and RedDashCoroutine. Freeze(.05f) in DashBegin is skipped when Engine.TimeRate <= 0.25, so it does not happen on every dash.
corrections.correction: Write 'DirectionalShake 0.1 s plus Medium rumble on spring/bounce launches; 0.2 s along DashDir during dashes; Freeze 0.05 s at dash start unless time is heavily slowed; Freeze 0.1 s plus Strong rumble in ExplodeLaunch (bumpers and pufferfish)'.

corrections.claim: Camera eases 'Each second it closes 99% of the remaining gap, regardless of frame rate'.
corrections.problem: Slightly overstated as a universal rule. The code is Math.Pow(0.01f / multiplier, dt), and the multiplier is 8 in StTempleFall, which gives 99.875% per second. In StReflectionFall the camera snaps straight to the target. CameraLockMode can also clamp X after the bounds clamp.
corrections.correction: Add: 'k = 0.01 in normal play; 0.01/8 during temple fall; instant snap during reflection fall; camera locks can further constrain X.'

corrections.claim: Stumble animation 'after falling more than 50 px at maximum speed'.
corrections.problem: Incomplete condition. The code requires highestAirY < Y - 50, Speed.Y >= MaxFall and |Speed.X| >= MaxRun. The player must also be running at full speed sideways.
corrections.correction: Write 'stumble when landing after a drop of more than 50 px at max fall speed while also moving at full run speed horizontally'.

corrections.claim: Destructoid (via Wikipedia) praised the Shade as solving 'appropriate punishment for failing, and a risk-reward system'.
corrections.problem: Narrower than the source. Wikipedia says Destructoid 'praised this feature, as well as the holding down of a button to heal'. The quote covers the Shade and hold-to-heal Focus together.
corrections.correction: Write 'Destructoid praised the Shade and the hold-to-heal Focus together...'. This makes the quote support the dossier's hold-USE recommendation as well.

corrections.claim: 'The Cuphead difficulty debate prompted it' (Assist Mode), with the Vice quotes attributed to Thorson.
corrections.problem: Attribution nuance. In Vice, the Cuphead link is reporter Patrick Klepek's narration ('Assist Mode wasn't always part of Celeste. The release of Cuphead changed things... Thorson was paying close attention'), not a statement from Thorson. The Thorson quotes ('judgmental', 'workshopping the name', 'float around', 'breaks the game... letting go') are verbatim and correctly attributed.
corrections.correction: Write 'According to Vice's Patrick Klepek, the Cuphead difficulty debate influenced Thorson's thinking.' Keep the verified Thorson quotes as they are.

corpus.group: Return of the Obra Dinn, Outer Wilds and Her Story: knowledge and evidence as progression, logbooks and deduction UI, how collected records carry story without exposition

dossier.games: Return of the Obra Dinn (Lucas Pope / 3909, 2018); Outer Wilds (Mobius Digital / Annapurna Interactive, 2019); Her Story (Sam Barlow, 2015). Research note: this session's shared WebSearch budget ran out partway through, so some Outer Wilds developer interviews could not be found and fetched. Outer Wilds is the least primary-sourced of the three. Its Ship Log UI details below are marked UNVERIFIED.
dossier.why_relevant: All three games make knowledge the main way forward, which is what WOLF//OVERRIDE's evidence CASE and its death model (unsecured evidence drops, safe points secure it) are built around. Obra Dinn shows a logbook that lists every slot up front as blank pages, fills them as you discover things, and locks correct answers in batches so they can't be brute-forced. Outer Wilds shows the opposite approach to death: death resets everything except the ship's computer log, so knowledge is the only thing that survives. Her Story shows a story told only through fragmented records found by searching. Its limits ("only the first five clips") control pacing, and the author tuned how easy each record is to find with word-frequency analysis. Together they answer three of WOLF's next decisions. What should survive death (knowledge yes, physical evidence maybe)? How should the CASE be laid out (chronological, chapter-headed, honest about what is still blank)? How do you carry story without exposition (no notes lying about, key words held back, the player puts the order together)? None of the three has a companion like WOLF, so the companion lessons here are inferences, not sourced practice.

dossier.companion: Mostly not applicable. None of the three has an independent companion like WOLF. Obra Dinn's helper is an object, the Memento Mortem watch, and its organiser is the book. Outer Wilds has other Hearthian travellers you locate by their music on the signalscope (Game Developer music feature: Prahlow chose "instruments that matched their personality"), but they don't travel with you. Her Story's only other voice is a chat window that appears at the end. What carries over is an inference for WOLF, not documented practice. (1) WOLF can play the role of the translator or signalscope: another way to perceive records. He can catch a sound the engineer can't, or recall an earlier treatment that recolours a record. He must never be the only holder of the CASE. Essential evidence and its log entries must be readable and securable by the engineer alone. (2) WOLF's memory of how he was treated can show up as his own annotation on CASE entries: agreeing, disagreeing or refusing to comment. The engineer's factual record stays intact either way. (3) Like the Outer Wilds travellers, WOLF can be found by sound (a far-off servo whine or howl) when he scouts ahead, which ties his scouting routes into the audio plan. All three suggestions are design proposals, not something any of these developers said.
dossier.level_and_camera: Obra Dinn is one first-person ship. Pope rendered it at 640x360 "as a stylistic choice" because "character models don't hold up well at a higher resolution" (tig-29), and later moved to 800x450 (tig-37). Every shape is outlined so "shapes and geometry are always clear to see" (Game Developer). Its levels are frozen death scenes (49 flashbacks in 10 disasters, tig-33) set inside the same ship. You walk through a frozen moment and find the next corpse inside it, which chains you back through time. Pope weighed three ways of finding corpses, including "Auto Drop" and "Inception Style", and preferred Auto Drop (tig-25). Outer Wilds is a 3D solar system that changes over a 22-minute loop. Alex Beachum's GDC 2020 talk "The 4D Level Design of 'Outer Wilds'" covers levels that "control the pacing and delivery of narrative information" inside a physics simulation that changes over time (listing only; talk content not fetched). Her Story is a single fixed desktop screen with no level. Lessons for WOLF's 1.5-2 screen side-view rooms: treat each room as an Obra Dinn scene, an event with a chapter heading, and put the next room's lead (a body, a log, a sound) visibly inside the current one. Use a room's height change to hide one record that is readable but not obvious. Keep silhouettes and interactables legible at the tighter zoom, as Pope's outlining rule does.
dossier.death_and_saves: Outer Wilds is the key reference for WOLF's death model. "Whenever the Hatchling dies, the game resets to the beginning; this happens regardless after 22 minutes", and "Nothing is brought back ... with the exception of the data on the spacecraft's computer" (Wikipedia, Gameplay). Death and time cost you position and world state, never knowledge. Obra Dinn has no death. Its counterpart to "securing" is the batch lock: "After entering the third correct fate ... there's a little fanfare reveal and those pages in the book are locked from editing" (Pope, tig-30). Correct work becomes permanent only after it passes a confirmation threshold. Her Story has no fail state. It ends when the player has seen enough clips and a chat window asks whether they are finished (Wikipedia; Mechanics of Magic). Recommendation for WOLF: separate KNOWLEDGE from ITEMS. Anything read, copied into the CASE log or witnessed should persist through death, as in Outer Wilds. Only physical or unsecured evidence objects (a carried data core, an uncopied printout) should drop on death. Securing at a safe point should feel like Obra Dinn's lock: a short stamp, the entry turning from handwriting to type, the page locked. Never let death erase what the player learned. That punishes the curiosity these games reward.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: OBRA DINN BOOK (primary, Pope): it began as a manifest with "three gameplay-critical sections: the crew list, the crew sketch, and the deck map" (tig-27). At PAX Australia players were "confused about the separate pages and navigating between them", and he worried they would think "there's just some manifest page I haven't found yet" (tig-25). He replaced it with The Book, which lists "chapters and every death in the entire game, initially as blank pages. As you find corpses and visit their flashbacks, pages are filled" (tig-30). Its "linear layout also makes explicit the flow of time, something which is totally lost otherwise" (tig-30). The design grew "from the idea of naming the flashbacks with chapter headings" (tig-30). Fates use a fixed grammar, "[Person A] [was shot by] [Person B]" (Subject-Verb-Object), and each death can "have multiple correct fates so hopefully players won't get stuck" (tig-30). Validation works in sets of 3 from anywhere among the 60. His reason: "Cheating one fate is easy but cheating three fates requires just enough work, intent, or both that you'd be better off solving it the right way" (tig-30). Per Wikipedia (secondary) the last six fates validate in pairs. The book's job, in his words, is to "collect and organize the deluge of information ... It establishes the chronology of events, shows details for each death, contains clues for identities" (tig-37). Rule on sources: "there'll be no notes lying about. Everything is presented in the muster roll, environmental structure, black-screen dialog, and frozen flashbacks" (tig-20). Clues come from "job, location, wardrobe, conversation" (tig-20). OUTER WILDS SHIP LOG: the only thing that persists, organised "either by location or in a web of connections" (Wikipedia; the in-game names Map Mode and Rumor Mode come from search snippets). Exact card states, "more to explore" markers and the HUD-mark feature are UNVERIFIED, because the wiki fetch failed. HER STORY DATABASE: 271 clips "lasting from a word or two to a minute" (Quickplay). Search shows "only ... the first five clips associated with a word" so "the more revelatory stuff was saved until later, when players could pick out multiple words" (Barlow, PocketGamer). Player tags are custom, and a "database checker" shows viewed clips from red to green (Wikipedia). Barlow had "the computer calculate how well connected clips were" (Game Developer) and found "words that were over-used, or under-used, or clips that might be too easy or too hard to find" (PocketGamer). Murder clips leave out the words murder, dead, killed and the names involved (Quickplay critique). For WOLF's CASE: show every evidence slot per room as blank pages with chapter headings. Use short fixed-grammar entries. Accept several correct readings. Batch-confirm any deduction. Run a script over the evidence graph to check that each item has at least two discovery routes, at least one of them engineer-only.
dossier.action_and_impact: Mostly not applicable. None of the three is an action game. The one transferable "impact" moment is Obra Dinn's confirmation: "a little fanfare reveal" plus pages locked from editing (tig-30), and a "little stamp" on the first muster-roll page showing the count of correct fates (tig-20 player report). For WOLF, give securing evidence at a safe point one short, coherent reaction from the existing impact kit: a soft stamp sound, a brief flash on the CASE slot, maybe a few frames of hit-stop. Don't use the screen shake meant for blasts. Keep it tied to the real state change, as AGENT.md requires.
dossier.presentation_ui_art: Obra Dinn: 1-bit, dithered, outlined art. Pope reworked the dither so "the dither pattern is not sliding across as you would expect" (Game Developer). Book metrics: "the screen is 800px wide, each page is 310px wide" (tig-37). A direct render of the crew sketch "isn't as legible (saw this at PAX)", so he hand-drew it at about "4-6 characters per day" (tig-26), aiming for woodcut-style shading (tig-27). Wardrobe and "obvious diversity that would show up in a rough sketch" solved crew recognition (tig-24). Near release he admits he "cheaped out" on one transition with "a twitching page-flip kinda thing" (tig-37). Her Story's in-world desktop was "part Apple II, part Windows 3.1 and part Windows 98" (PocketGamer). Footage went through "two dusty old VHS players" (Game Developer) rather than digital filters. Barlow liked "making the computer itself a prop in the game" (Wikipedia citing The Guardian). Outer Wilds: the Ship Log is a diegetic ship computer, as described above; visual specifics UNVERIFIED. For WOLF: draw the CASE as a physical evidence case or clipboard in the painterly 2.5D style, not the Settings terminal look (AGENT.md keeps the terminal look in Settings). Use a two-page spread that fits phone width. Give each entry a recognisable thumbnail with a label and shape, not colour alone. Show empty, found (unsecured) and secured states as distinct shapes and labels.
dossier.audio: Obra Dinn: each memory starts with "black-screen dialog" before the frozen scene (tig-20), so audio comes first and sets up the image. There are 29 speaking roles across nationalities, and accents are clues (tig-33; The Register). The plan to write 49 unique songs gave way to one theme per chapter with two variations (Road to the IGF). He reports all 20 flashback songs done and first-pass sound for all 49 scenes from commercial libraries (tig-33). A fanfare plays on each 3-fate confirmation (tig-30). Outer Wilds: the signalscope picks up each traveller's instrument, so music is how you find people. Prahlow wrote the banjo theme to feel "a little bit off-center" and used flowcharts of motifs to "score the last loop of the game like a third act finale" (Game Developer). Her Story: the audio is the performance itself, run through VHS. For WOLF (procedural audio): play a dialogue or sound-only fragment over black or a dimmed room before a recovered record appears. Give the CASE a distinctive procedural "secured" chime that is never reused elsewhere. Let WOLF's scouting be found by a directional sound motif, the way travellers are found by signalscope.
dossier.mobile_and_input: Her Story shipped on iOS on the same day as Windows. By 10 August 2015, about 40,000 of its first 100,000+ sales were iOS (Wikipedia). It relies on typed free-text search. Obra Dinn's book is mouse-driven, page-flipping and drop-down selection; the details of its console and mobile ports were not verified. Pope designs for players who skip text: "there are people that won't read important text in any situation, and I want the game to work for them" (tig-29). Outer Wilds: not verified for touch. For WOLF's input (hold-to-move, one USE, two choice buttons, Pause): no free-text entry. Any deduction should be selection-based, cycling options with the two choice buttons and confirming with USE, in Obra Dinn's fixed-grammar style. Open the CASE from Pause, or a dedicated short hold, with Back and Pause always working. Turn pages with the choice buttons. Size touch targets for phones and keep a visible focus outline for keyboard and controller, per AGENT.md.

steal: Blank-page CASE: like Obra Dinn's Book (tig-30), show every evidence slot for the current rooms up front as empty pages under a chapter heading per room-event, filled in as found. Players see scope and chronology without exposition and never wonder whether a missing page blocks them.

Knowledge survives death: copy Outer Wilds' rule that only the ship log survives the reset. Read or copied records and witnessed facts persist through death; only carried, unsecured evidence objects drop. Death then costs position and items, never learning.

Batch-locked confirmation: if the CASE ever asks the engineer to conclude something (who sabotaged a relay, what a record means), confirm in batches (Pope: 3 of 60) and lock confirmed pages with a stamp and fanfare. 'Cheating three fates requires just enough work ... that you'd be better off solving it the right way.'
Securing as a ceremony: at a safe point, turn unsecured entries from handwriting to typed print (or similar), lock them, and play one distinct procedural chime. That is a clear, honest state change.
Fixed-grammar entries: write CASE lines in Subject-Verb-Object form ('Relay 3 was shorted by [?]') and accept several correct readings so players don't fail on wording (tig-30).

No notes lying about: following Pope's GDC-demo rule (tig-20), evidence comes only from authored sources the world justifies: copy stations, terminals, room structure, sound fragments, WOLF's memory. No random diary pickups.
Audio-first records: play a recovered fragment as sound over black or a dimmed room before showing the image, like Obra Dinn's 'black-screen dialog'. It's cheap and fits the procedural-audio plan.

Pacing by query limits: borrow Her Story's 'first five clips' quirk. Hide a revelatory record so it only appears when two leads are combined (say, both copy stations in Records Access), so revelations arrive late without locked doors.

Tune discoverability with a script: as Barlow did with word frequencies, have a headless check list every evidence item's discovery routes and flag items with fewer than two routes or no engineer-only route.

Paper-prototype the mystery: Alex Beachum tested whether players could piece the whole mystery together with a paper prototype, then a text adventure, before building it in-engine. Do the same for WOLF's evidence chain before building wider rooms.

Recognisable entries: Pope found that clothing and 'obvious diversity that would show up in a rough sketch' fixed recognition. Give each CASE entry a distinct silhouette or thumbnail plus a label so it reads at phone size.
Honest progress meter: Her Story's red-to-green database checker becomes a per-room count of real evidence found and secured (e.g. 2/4), never padded.
avoid: Don't rely on tutorial popups for the CASE or the death and secure rules. Pope at PAX Aus: 'Nobody read the hints and so most people got stuck' (tig-30). Teach through the first room's placement and one forced secure.

Don't dump the full reference document at the start. Pope's PAX build handed players 'a 50lb manifest' with every deck map and a sea chart, and it confused them (tig-25). Reveal CASE sections as rooms open.
Don't use split navigation that hides pages. Separate manifest pages confused PAX players (tig-25); keep the CASE one linear spread with page numbers.

Don't confirm single answers. A per-item check invites brute force; even with batches of three, a June 2019 commenter said cycling names 'felt that this brute forcing is the intended method' (tig-37 thread, player opinion).
Don't erase learned knowledge on death. It punishes curiosity; Outer Wilds keeps the log precisely so knowledge is never lost.
No free-text input. Her Story's typed search doesn't fit WOLF's hold-to-move, USE and two-choice input or phone play; use selection and cycling only.
Don't make strict wording the gate. Pope added multiple correct fates so players aren't stuck by entering 'something they thought was correct but wasn't flagged as so'.
Don't make WOLF the only route to a record or to the CASE. If WOLF refuses or the relationship is broken, the engineer must still find, read and secure every essential item.
No fake or decorative progress. AGENT.md forbids fake loading or progress; counters and stamps must reflect real saved state.
Don't underestimate scope. Pope estimated 3-6 months and shipped after 4.5 years; scope 'slowly got out of hand' (80.lv). Add evidence one room at a time, playable at each step.
Don't present the UNVERIFIED Outer Wilds Ship Log specifics (card states, 'more to explore' markers, HUD marking) as sourced facts in public docs or credits without fetching a primary source first.

corrections.claim: Pope weighed three ways of finding corpses, including "Auto Drop" and "Inception Style", and preferred Auto Drop (tig-25).
corrections.problem: Misleading. Auto Drop was his initial preference, but tig-25 says he went with the third option, Key Style, which the dossier leaves out. Exact quote: "My strong preference was for Auto Drop, but the end-game and a few flashbacks would really benefit from Inception Style. Key Style lets me combine both of these." In the same post he rejects Inception Style because "returning to the ship often is important to ground the player".
corrections.correction: Pope compared Auto Drop, Inception Style and Key Style (a found corpse works like a key, and you go back to the present ship to open the new flashback). He strongly preferred Auto Drop but adopted Key Style because it combines both. https://dukope.com/devlogs/obra-dinn/tig-25/ (22 Nov 2016)

corrections.claim: Numbers: Obra Dinn fates to deduce in the 2016 GDC demo = 6 (Wikipedia, derived)
corrections.problem: Contradicted by the primary source. On tig-20 a player asked "How many can be deduced in this demo?" and Pope replied "3, so you got them all." Wikipedia's "only six fates" disagrees with the developer.
corrections.correction: 3 deducible fates in the GDC 2016 demo (Pope, tig-20 thread, 13 Apr 2016, https://dukope.com/devlogs/obra-dinn/tig-20/). If the Wikipedia figure is kept at all, mark it as conflicting with the primary source.

corrections.claim: Avoid list: 'even with batches of three, a June 2019 commenter said cycling names "felt that this brute forcing is the intended method" (tig-37 thread, player opinion).'
corrections.problem: Wrong date. The comment is by sherjilozair and is dated 1 August 2019. Pope's own post is from 9 June 2019. The quote itself is accurate.
corrections.correction: A tig-37 thread commenter (sherjilozair, 1 Aug 2019) wrote: "Since the game explicitly tells me that I get to know correct fates in pairs of three, it felt that this brute forcing is the intended method." They also said this made them miss using the hammocks to identify topmen and seamen.

corrections.claim: Numbers: 'Obra Dinn: flashback songs completed (vs 49 originally planned unique songs)' = 20, source tig-33
corrections.problem: Misattributed. tig-33 confirms 20 songs ("Each disaster now has two one-minute songs: A & B"), but it describes the original plan as "write a bunch of tracks in different styles and assign them to the flashbacks". The 49-unique-songs plan comes from the Game Developer Road to the IGF interview, not tig-33.
corrections.correction: Cite both sources. Road to the IGF: "originally planned to write unique songs for all 49 flashbacks ... ended up instead composing a unique theme for each chapter, with two alternating variations". tig-33: 20 songs total (10 disasters x A/B, one minute each).

corrections.claim: Her Story: maximum results shown per search = 5 (first five, chronological), verified via PocketGamer
corrections.problem: 'Chronological' is unsupported. PocketGamer says only "it could only show the first five clips associated with a word", and Wikipedia does not state an order either.
corrections.correction: Write '5 (the first five clips associated with a word)' and drop 'chronological', or mark the ordering UNVERIFIED.

corrections.claim: Pope rendered it at 640x360 "as a stylistic choice" because "character models don't hold up well at a higher resolution" (tig-29).
corrections.problem: The second phrase is presented as a quote but isn't verbatim, and it leaves out his hedge.
corrections.correction: Verbatim: "Right now the game is limited to just 640x360 as a stylistic choice. A little arbitrary but everything so far has been designed against that and some things (mostly character models) don't hold up well at a higher resolution." (tig-29, 18 Apr 2017). He later moved the whole game to 800x450 (tig-37).

corrections.claim: Avoid list: 'Pope estimated 3-6 months and shipped after 4.5 years; scope "slowly got out of hand" (80.lv).'
corrections.problem: Overstated and misattributed. In 80.lv, 'slowly got out of hand' is the interviewer's paraphrase, not Pope's words, and it refers only to the character count, not the project's overall scope. The 3-6 month and 4.5 year figures are correct (tig-00; Game Developer).
corrections.correction: 80.lv (interviewer's paraphrase): "he first made the minimum number of characters required to operate the ship but it slowly got out of hand." Pope himself (Game Developer): first target was 80 people, "the most I could do was 60", and scaling up from the demo "added almost another year".

corrections.claim: Prahlow ... used flowcharts of motifs to "score the last loop of the game like a third act finale" (Game Developer).
corrections.problem: Slightly overstated. The article says Prahlow used flowcharts "to track the narrative", not motifs. The 'third act finale' quote credits his pre-production of the score and "narrative building blocks".
corrections.correction: Prahlow used flowcharts to track the sprawling narrative, and his pre-production of the score and "narrative building blocks" let him "score the last loop of the game like a third act finale".

corpus.group: Unravel Two and Gris: 2.5D art direction, readable characters on painterly backgrounds, colour and light as storytelling, companion tether

dossier.games: Unravel Two (Coldwood Interactive / EA, 9 June 2018; PS4, Xbox One, PC; Switch later; PhyreEngine; local co-op or one player controlling two tethered Yarnys). Gris (Nomada Studio / Devolver Digital, 13 Dec 2018; Switch, PC/Mac, later PS4; Unity; art by Conrad Roset, music by Berlinist). Supporting context: Unravel (2016), the first game, for the yarn-length and real-location art approach. Research limits: the session's web-search budget ran out partway through. YouTube refused the transcript download for Martin Sahlin's GDC talk "Unravel: Using Empathy as a Game Mechanic" (HTTP 429), so I could confirm the talk exists but not what it says. GamesIndustry.biz, The Verge, Eurogamer, Polygon and Wired could not be fetched, so claims from them come only through Wikipedia and are labelled that way.
dossier.why_relevant: Both are side-view 2.5D games where one small figure has to stay readable against lush, painterly or photographic layered backgrounds. That is WOLF//OVERRIDE's main art problem. Unravel Two is the best shipped example of two linked characters controlled by one player: a tether, an anchor that works as a safe spot, merge and split, three-stage hints, and UI markers tinted to the character's colour. That maps onto WOLF scouting and leading while the engineer stays the only playable character. Gris is the reference for colour and light as story progression, for art problems the team logged (readability forced level and camera tweaks; a dress-colour mechanic was dropped because of camera angles; making grey early areas appealing was hard), for an art pipeline built under memory limits, and for music that changes when the player enters a puzzle zone. Neither is horror and neither has a death model like WOLF's, so their no-fail and gentle-tension choices are mostly lessons on what to change, not copy.

dossier.companion: UNRAVEL TWO is a two-character game that one player can run alone. Sahlin calls it "a two-player single-player game" (Gamereactor) and says "That yarn between you kind of becomes your lifeline, so you'll be climbing from each other or swinging from each other" and "The other character is essentially your anchor and so wherever you put them, that's a safe spot for you to return to" (TheSixthAxis). The official text adds "Two Yarnys – always!", and a single player can "create two Yarnys of your own" (Steam). Solo players spend much of the time merged: "you'll often be merging the two Yarnys into one, ending up with a nice irregularly striped hybrid" (TheSixthAxis). The tether limits range: "you can't venture far from one another," which players "quickly learn to use ... to your advantage" by dangling, swinging and wedging the yarn over things (Game Informer). The bond is presented as a craft promise, not a meter: "you're constantly saving each other, helping each other and sometimes messing with each other" (TheSixthAxis). In-world UI markers take each Yarny's colour. Sahlin chooses darker colours "so all the interface things like the markers that show you the lasso range become a bit more subtle" (TheSixthAxis). Measurable sign that solo control of two characters works: the one-player-two-characters Any% record (1631 s) is faster than the two-player Any% record (1834 s) (speedrun.com). GRIS has no AI partner in the sources I fetched. Its developers say gameplay and music are there "to help bridge the gap between Gris and those characters" (Into the Spine). UNVERIFIED: a small creature companion in the later chapters; I could not fetch a source for it. Neither game has a companion with independent will, refusal or memory, which is WOLF's main difference. So take Unravel's anchor, merge and split, and colour-coded cues, and not its always-obedient partner.
dossier.level_and_camera: Unravel Two has 7 main stages and 20 challenge levels, 27 in all (Game Informer: "seven lengthy stages" and "20 challenge levels" that are "much shorter ... often consisting of a single screen"; speedrun.com's level list also has 27 entries: Foreign Shore, Hideaway, Little Frogs, Nightswimming and so on). Environments are "Inspired by real Scandinavian locations" with "natural landscapes and complex urban environments," and the world will "flourish and evolve" as you progress (Steam). Unravel's ground-level macro framing aims to "bring your perspective down to ground level ... so that you can really look closely" (CGMagazine, Unravel 1). My measurement from Steam screenshots (DERIVED): a Yarny is about 100-145 px tall in a 1080p frame (about 9-13% of screen height), on a sharp mid plane with a heavily blurred foreground and background. Gris: the chapters are organised "around different colours," and the team "started working from a full storyboard, just like with an animated feature" (Gamereactor). According to Wikipedia (summarising GamesIndustry.biz; original not fetchable), "readability ... resulted in several level design and camera angle tweaks during development." Also from that summary: a dress that changed colour as colours unlocked "proved impractical due partly to the camera angles," and grey early areas were hard to make appealing until the team drew on Iwagumi-style aquariums. Nomada: "the scenery is very important, and sometimes takes the spotlight over the main character" (Colossal). My measurement from Steam screenshots (DERIVED): Gris is about 90-100 px tall (about 8-9% of 1080) in a traversal shot, and about 25 px (about 2.4%) in a vista shot, where she reads only as a dark silhouette against the brightest area, a moon disc. Steam's level count for GRIS is not published. Speedrun.com splits it into per-chapter segments named Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, Acceptance and End; those are community labels, but Wikipedia says the team consulted a psychologist about the five stages of grief.
dossier.death_and_saves: Gris has no death and no fail state: "free of danger, frustration or death" (Steam); "we knew Gris couldn't die in the game as it didn't fit with the story, and we wanted to encourage casual gamers" (Cuevas, Film Stories/Wireframe); "You can play knowing that you are not going to fail. At the same time, there are some challenges in the game - but they're all optional" (PCGamesInsider). Puzzle tuning, via Wikipedia quoting Mendoza: "If there's a puzzle you can probably finish it at the second or third try. When the puzzle is more complicated, we give the player options." The team says no-death made tension hard: the challenge was to "Implement things like the lack of death and still maintain a sense of urgency or challenge" (The Average Viewer). Unravel Two: there are hazards and chases ("being chased by a bird or escaping a burning forest", Game Informer), with a "three stage hint system to try and nudge you along" (TheSixthAxis) and "Optional hints ensure that anyone can get through the puzzles" (Game Informer). The parked partner is "a safe spot for you to return to" (Sahlin), a spatial safe point rather than a menu save. UNVERIFIED: Unravel Two's checkpoint spacing and death or respawn timing; no fetched source gives numbers. Unravel 1: the yarn runs out with distance travelled and is refilled at spools, and Wikipedia cites a reviewer calling the resulting backtracking "the game's worst aspect." Neither game has evidence loss on death, so WOLF's drop-and-secure model has no direct precedent here.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Not really applicable, as neither game has an inventory. Gris has optional collectibles called Mementos, plus lights collected and returned to statues to restore colour ("Gris can travel to four locations to collect lights and restore colour back to her world at statues," Wikipedia). The useful pattern is that progress items are physically returned to a landmark that visibly changes the world. That is close to WOLF's "secure evidence at a safe point": make securing evidence change the room's light or colour. Speedrun data puts All Mementos at 5696.48 s against 4904.73 s for Any%, roughly 13 extra minutes of optional collection. Unravel Two has no inventory in the fetched sources; its "spark" is the progress object ("the little spark that you're chasing splits into two parts," Sahlin).
dossier.action_and_impact: Gris gives the dress a new ability in each chapter: a "heavy block of stone," "creating pathways made of constellations," "gliding across gaps, swimming underwater and singing to interact with the environment" (Wikipedia). Design rule: "We didn't want to have repetitive mechanics, and we love to add a twist after you have mastered a skill" (Cuevas, Film Stories). Restraint as story: the player starts unable to jump, to reinforce that "something is wrong with this girl" (Wikipedia, via GamesIndustry.biz). Unravel Two deliberately raised character power: "you run a little faster, you jump a little higher and your swing is a little more powerful" so "you're a much more capable character this time around" (Sahlin, TheSixthAxis). Yarn bridges work as launchers: "using yarn bridges to pull down and then launch your Yarny higher" (TheSixthAxis). Unravel's guiding rule: "the simple act of getting from here to there should be fun" (CGMagazine). Neither source gives hit-stop, shake or frame timings: not applicable or UNVERIFIED.
dossier.presentation_ui_art: GRIS colour as structure: "The most important thing in the game are the colours," starting "with black and white"; "One of the mechanics had to be to discover colours, unlocking colours" (Gamereactor). The goal was "a game that evolved visually, not only mechanically" (Cuevas, MCV). Pipeline: "Every frame you see has been hand-drawn digitally - we even briefly thought about doing it on paper and then scanning it but it was too much" (Gamereactor). They tested "different pencil strokes, scanned paper textures, scanned watercolour stains" and "shaders that could help us make it look as close as possible to traditional hand-drawn animation" (Film Stories). "We tried to do the same filters that Photoshop has"; hardware "can't do 20,000 by 20,000-pixel frames"; "we had to work a lot on the memory and how we play with all these frames which are all hand-drawn" (PCGamesInsider). Staffing: "probably 80% of the people in the studio working on the art and animation" (Gamereactor), and "70% of the people involved in Gris are not from the typical video game industry" (Roset, Gamereactor). Asset reuse: "Asset repetition is inevitable, but we didn't want that to kill the organic feel"; the aim was to "feel as one cohesive illustration" (The Average Viewer). UI: "almost no text, only simple control reminders illustrated through universal icons" (Steam). Readability problems led to camera and level changes, and the colour-changing dress was cut (Wikipedia). From screenshots (DERIVED): Gris is a small dark-red or near-black figure, kept at the strongest value contrast, often silhouetted against the lightest area of the painting. UNRAVEL TWO: saturated red and blue yarn characters on photoreal, desaturated, heavily depth-of-field-blurred Scandinavian scenes (DERIVED from Steam screenshots). The story plays as "ghostly images in the background," which Game Informer says made it "hard to connect with." Lasso-range markers take the character's colour (Sahlin).
dossier.audio: Unravel Two (Håkan Dalsfelt, A Sound Effect): the brief was "Realistic, calm and discreet. I imagine that the yarn characters are sneaky creatures"; "I want it to sound like a small yarn character in a big world"; "I want the game to sound more like a nature documentary"; "The goal is that you can leave the game sound on without it being annoying." The rest of the soundscape is "very ambient (including character sounds) and leave room for the music." The hard problem was "a good balance between character sound effects and the rest of the soundscape." Music from levels continues into the lighthouse hub and then fades: "there are many music transitions in this game and I put lots of work into making them perfect so people won't notice." Tools: FMOD Studio ("I think I've used it for 15 years now"), Audacity, a Zoom H2n for field recordings (the Rapids level), and The Recordist and Moon Echo libraries. The music brief was modern music using "traditional Swedish folk music instruments." That article does not cover footsteps per surface, the yarn sound or two-character mixing. Gris (composer Marco Albano, MCV): "when you enter a puzzle zone, the music switches from intense or emotional to more relaxing to let you concentrate." Singing is a traversal and interaction ability. Music is by Berlinist, who were pitched the game early "so they could start thinking on which type of music they wanted to do and how it would evolve throughout the game" (Film Stories). UNVERIFIED: Gris footstep or foley specifics.
dossier.mobile_and_input: Mostly not applicable. Unravel Two is local co-op only (Wikipedia), and Steam lists Remote Play Together. One player can drive both Yarnys by switching and merging; the single-player-two-character speedrun category exists and holds the faster record (1631 s against 1834 s for the two-player Any%). Gris shipped on Switch and PC at launch. Its text-free icon prompts ("universal icons", Steam) suit touch and localisation. UNVERIFIED: Gris's later iOS and Android ports and their touch layout; I fetched no source for them.

steal: Value-first readability: make the engineer and WOLF the strongest light-dark contrast in every frame, and put them against the lightest or calmest patch of the painted backdrop, as Gris silhouettes a 25 px figure against a moon. Check rooms in greyscale before colour.

Give each character a hue the background never uses at full saturation (Unravel Two's saturated red and blue Yarnys on desaturated nature). For example, engineer warm orange and WOLF cyan; at full saturation, those hues appear only on the characters and live interactables.

Depth-of-field parallax: keep the walkable layer sharp, and soften the near-foreground and far-background layers with blur and lower contrast, as Unravel Two does. The painterly richness stays where the player is not looking.

Keep the player character at about 9-13% of screen height in play (Yarny measured at about 100-145 px of 1080; Gris about 90-100 px in traversal). Allow 2-3% vista framing only during non-interactive beats.

Tint WOLF's in-world cues (scout pings, the leash-range ring, 'I can reach that' markers) with WOLF's body colour, as Unravel tints lasso-range markers by Yarny colour, so players can tell WOLF's offers from environment prompts. Per AGENT.md, pair the colour with a shape.

Anchor = safe spot: Sahlin's 'wherever you put them, that's a safe spot for you to return to'. Make safe points physical places, and let WOLF choose to hold one temporarily when trust is high, while the engineer-only fixed safe points always remain.

Solo play over two characters: Unravel's merge, where the two travel as one until a puzzle splits them. WOLF follows by default; scouting and leading are moments when he splits off, shown by an authored action, then returns.

Colour as progression: Gris unlocks colours by chapter. Securing evidence at a safe point could visibly return a light or colour channel to the room, as Gris returns lights to statues, so the state change is real and not decoration.
Teach, then twist: 'add a twist after you have mastered a skill' (Cuevas). Each new room reuses USE-hold or the door blast with one new complication.
Restraint as story: Gris cannot jump at first because 'something is wrong'. Withhold one engineer ability early and return it as a story beat.

Puzzle tuning target: solvable on the 2nd or 3rd try, plus Unravel's three-stage hints. For WOLF this maps well onto WOLF giving escalating hints when he trusts the engineer, with a neutral environmental hint for the engineer-only path.
Make grey industrial rooms beautiful through composition, not colour: Gris solved its drab early areas with Iwagumi-style aquarium layouts (a few strong shapes, lots of negative space).
Storyboard and colour-script every room before building it, as Gris did 'from a full storyboard, just like with an animated feature'.

Adaptive music by zone: Gris drops to calmer music in puzzle zones 'to let you concentrate'. Unravel carries level music into the hub and fades it. In WOLF//OVERRIDE, let room tone thin out at copy stations and puzzles, and swell during sentry or tank beats.

Audio scale brief: 'a small ... character in a big world' and 'more like a nature documentary'. Keep the engineer's footsteps and breath close and quiet, and the facility's room tone large and distant.

Paint at a fixed working resolution and budget layer memory early: Gris's hardware 'can't do 20,000 by 20,000-pixel frames', so reuse painted modules but break repetition so the room still reads as one illustration.
Near-textless prompts: Gris uses 'only simple control reminders illustrated through universal icons'. This helps touch, controller and localisation at once.
avoid: Tiny-character vistas while the player needs precision: Gris frames its heroine at about 2.4% of screen height in vistas, and per Wikipedia readability problems forced level and camera tweaks. Do not zoom out during a sentry or tank sequence.

Systems that recolour the character and fight the camera: Gris's colour-changing dress was cut partly because of camera angles. Keep the engineer and WOLF silhouettes and key colours stable; show state with small accents.
Letting scenery 'take the spotlight over the main character' (Nomada's own words) in rooms with interactables; painterly detail must not compete with stations or doors.

UI markers so subtle they disappear: Sahlin likes dark Yarny colours that make range markers 'more subtle and discrete'. For accessibility on phone screens and dark horror palettes, give WOLF's cues a minimum contrast and a shape.

Resource backtracking: Unravel 1's yarn depletion and refill caused backtracking that a reviewer called 'the game's worst aspect'. Make sure evidence dropped on death can be retrieved on a short, readable route.
Story told only through ghostly background images: Game Informer found Unravel Two's background vignettes 'hard to connect with'. Keep WOLF's reactions and choices foregrounded and authored.

A physical tether that leashes WOLF: Unravel's rope works because the partners have no will of their own. WOLF must be able to stay, refuse or wander, so use a range ring as information, not a constraint on him.

Copying Gris's no-death design: it fits grief, not horror. Nomada admitted keeping 'a sense of urgency' without death was the hard part. WOLF's evidence-drop death model should keep stakes without punishing replays.
Paper-and-scan per-frame pipelines: Nomada rejected them as 'too much' for a small team. Use painted layers plus shaders and texture overlays.
Copying either game's art or music. Use them for principles only and credit them as research sources, not contributors (AGENT.md).

corrections.claim: Readability forcing 'several level design and camera angle tweaks', the colour-changing dress that 'proved impractical due partly to the camera angles', and the Iwagumi-aquarium fix are all from Wikipedia 'summarising GamesIndustry.biz 2019-01-15'. The 'unable to jump... something is wrong with this girl' line and Mendoza's 'second or third try' quote are also labelled 'via GamesIndustry.biz'.
corrections.problem: Misattributed. In the Wikipedia source (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gris&action=raw), the readability, dress and Iwagumi sentences cite ref 'artbehind', which is Andrew Webster, 'The art behind the gorgeous indie game Gris', The Verge, 20 Dec 2018. The jump line cites EGMNOW (Antonio Sanchez, 5 Aug 2019) and Red Bull (James Pickard). The Mendoza quote comes straight after the Red Bull citation. The GamesIndustry.biz article is cited only for the founding story, the 'a mix of Journey and Ori' aim, and accessibility.
corrections.correction: Credit the readability, dress and Iwagumi claims to The Verge (via Wikipedia, original not fetched). Credit the no-jump 'something is wrong with this girl' claim to EGMNOW and Red Bull (via Wikipedia). Credit Mendoza's puzzle quote to Wikipedia, probably from the Red Bull interview (UNVERIFIED in the original). Keep GamesIndustry.biz only for the founding story and the Journey/Ori accessibility aim.

corrections.claim: One-player-two-characters Any% (1631 s) is faster than two-player Any% (1834 s), a 'measurable sign that solo control of two characters works', and one player 'drive[s] both Yarnys by switching and merging' in that category.
corrections.problem: Misleading. The speedrun.com 'Any% 1P2C' rules (https://www.speedrun.com/api/v1/categories/9kvo6ve2) say: 'complete a new game as fast as possible in multiplayer mode as a single player (1 player, 2 controllers).' That is one person holding two controllers in co-op mode, not the game's single-player switch-and-merge mode. The 'Any%' category allows 'up to 2' players and is not strictly two-player. The two records come from different runners and years (the 1P2C runner Lenaaa also holds 2nd in Any% at 1994 s with a partner), so the gap tells you about speedrunning coordination, not design.
corrections.correction: Report the numbers (1834 s for the 2-player Any% WR by SunSugar & prais, 2024-11-30; 1631 s for the Any% 1P2C WR by Lenaaa, 2025-03-04, one person with two controllers in multiplayer mode). Drop the claim that this shows solo two-character control or merge works. Mark solo-mode merge and switch as described only by TheSixthAxis's writer.

corrections.claim: 'In-world UI markers take each Yarny's colour' / 'Lasso-range markers take the character's colour (Sahlin)'.
corrections.problem: Overstated. Sahlin never says the markers are tinted by Yarny colour. His full quote (TheSixthAxis) is: 'I like making it a little bit tricky, so I like to pick the darker colours so all the interface things like the markers that show you the lasso range become a bit more subtle and discrete. That's why I like the greys... like a grey and an orange, maybe?' That implies markers follow the player-chosen yarn colour, but he does not state it. He also presents it as a personal way to make the game harder. Yarn colours are customisable, so 'saturated red and blue' is only the default look.
corrections.correction: Say: 'Sahlin implies the lasso-range markers follow the player-chosen yarn colour; he picks dark colours to make them subtler and the game "a little bit tricky"' (inference, not stated). Note that colours are player-customisable.

corrections.claim: Gris: chapters organised 'around different colours', and the team 'started working from a full storyboard, just like with an animated feature' (Gamereactor), given as the developers' words.
corrections.problem: These are the Gamereactor writer's summary of a video interview, not quotes from Nomada. The page reads: 'In the interview, we also talk about how chapters in the story are based around different colours, about how they ditched a dress-based mechanic, and about how the team started working from a full storyboard, just like with an animated feature.' The only on-page developer line there is Cuevas: "It's almost like making a movie".
corrections.correction: Label both as Gamereactor's paraphrase of a video interview with tech director Adrián Cuevas. Quote Cuevas directly only for 'It's almost like making a movie'. The same paragraph is also a second source for the dropped dress mechanic, though it gives no reason.

corrections.claim: Unravel Two's 'three stage hint system' (TheSixthAxis) and solo players 'often ... merging the two Yarnys into one', listed with Sahlin's statements.
corrections.problem: Minor attribution issue. Both phrases are the TheSixthAxis writer's own narration (byline Stefan L), not quotes from Sahlin. The hint line is part of a description of the main game being 'designed to be a little easier'.
corrections.correction: Credit both to the TheSixthAxis hands-on author, not to Sahlin, and treat them as press description rather than a design statement.

corrections.claim: Gris 'gives the dress a new ability in each chapter'.
corrections.problem: Overstated. Wikipedia says Gris 'can collect these lights to gain new abilities, such as turning into a heavy block of stone and creating pathways made of constellations', and that the final power is singing. It does not say there is one ability per chapter. The Gameplay section ties only the heavy-block ability to the dress.
corrections.correction: Say Gris gains new abilities across the game (heavy stone block via the dress, constellation paths, gliding, swimming, singing), per Wikipedia. Do not claim one per chapter unless a source confirms it.

corrections.claim: UNVERIFIED: a small creature companion in the later chapters; 'GRIS has no AI partner'.
corrections.problem: Partly verifiable. Wikipedia's plot says Gris 'encounters various living beings, some of which help her on her journey', and Into the Spine has Nomada describing 'several characters that act as a supporting cast'. Neither describes a persistent companion.
corrections.correction: Say: helper creatures appear and some help her (Wikipedia; Into the Spine), but no fetched source describes a persistent AI companion. The specific 'small creature companion' stays UNVERIFIED.

corrections.claim: Paper-and-scan per-frame pipelines: Nomada rejected them as 'too much' for a small team. Also, '20,000 x 20,000 px' is the frame size the hardware could not handle, 'why paintings were cut down'.
corrections.problem: Slightly overstated. Cuevas said 'we even briefly thought about doing it on paper and then scanning it but it was too much' (Gamereactor) and gave no team-size reason. The 20,000 px line (PCGamesInsider, Cuevas) is about teaching print artist Roset that games cannot use print-scale frames: 'we needed to work at a certain resolution'. It says nothing about cutting paintings down.
corrections.correction: Quote 'too much' without adding 'for a small team'. Restate the 20,000 px fact as: 'games can't do 20,000 by 20,000-pixel frames; we needed to work at a certain resolution' plus memory work on hand-drawn frames.

corrections.claim: Unravel 1: yarn runs out with distance travelled and 'is refilled at spools'.
corrections.problem: Wording mismatch with the cited source. Wikipedia says walking too far unravels Yarny 'into a slim frame, unable to reach further', and 'This frame can be refilled by interacting with balls of red yarn in the game environment.' The 'worst aspect' reviewer is Peter Paras of Game Revolution.
corrections.correction: Replace 'spools' with 'balls of red yarn placed in the environment' and name Game Revolution's Peter Paras as the 'worst aspect' reviewer.

corpus.group: Mobile ports of side-scrollers (Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares, Oddworld New 'n' Tasty, Alto's Odyssey, Monument Valley): touch control schemes, readability on small screens, performance targets, session length

dossier.games: Limbo (Playdead; iOS port 3 July 2013, Android 11 Feb 2015), Inside (Playdead; iOS 15 Dec 2017, iPhone/iPad/Apple TV), Little Nightmares (Tarsier/Bandai Namco; mobile port by Playdigious, iOS and Android 12 Dec 2023), Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty (Oddworld Inhabitants; iOS, Android and Shield 14 Dec 2017), Alto's Odyssey (Team Alto/Snowman; iOS 21-22 Feb 2018, Android 25 Jul 2018, plus Alto's Adventure 2015 for context), Monument Valley (ustwo games, 2014; GDC Europe 2014 talk by Ken Wong). Project check, read-only: apps/game/project.godot uses a 960x540 viewport, stretch mode canvas_items and the gl_compatibility renderer on desktop and mobile.
dossier.why_relevant: WOLF//OVERRIDE is a 2.5D side-view horror game. It plans phone touch support with hold-to-move, one USE button (tap or hold), two choice buttons and Pause, so it is the same kind of port as Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares and New 'n' Tasty. All four had to fit a controller-designed side-scroller onto a phone. Their reception shows a pattern: atmosphere survives the move to a phone, while precise movement and visible thumbs on the screen cause the problems. Alto's Odyssey and Monument Valley were designed for touch from the start. They show two limits worth copying: dropping mechanics that need more than one touch, and treating every screen as a readable, self-contained composition. Monument Valley also has the best public session-length data in this set: about 90 minutes average to finish across 1,000+ beta testers, 10 levels, and a 50% completion rate.
