dossier.companion: Mostly not applicable: Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares, Alto and Monument Valley have no AI companion. Monument Valley's Totem is a scripted puzzle helper, not covered by fetched sources. New 'n' Tasty is the one relevant case. Abe gives orders to fellow Mudokons through GameSpeak. On mobile, Pocket Gamer's GDC 2016 hands-on says voice commands work by "tapping an icon and then on the sentence you want Abe to say". This replaces the console's direct button-per-phrase mapping with a two-step menu. For WOLF//OVERRIDE, this supports keeping communication with WOLF to the two choice buttons, shown as large labelled targets rather than gestures. The two-step tap works on touch because it is unambiguous, and it does not need a quick reaction. Do not put WOLF's lines, reactions or refusals where the thumbs are, so the player sees what he does even while holding a move.
dossier.level_and_camera: All four side-scroller ports kept their console camera and composition. Game Informer said Inside's "visuals and animation have not been scaled back in any way for mobile". Little Nightmares is 2.5D with authored camera views. The TapTap reviewer found that on a phone the "fixed camera views will sometimes be a detriment", "not allowing you to see far off creatures". On a small screen, a threat at the edge of the frame turns into a few pixels. Monument Valley went the other way: each level is a self-contained frame. Ken Wong (GDC Europe 2014, via Game Developer) said "Every screen is going to be a work of art that you can hang on a wall" and described "little worlds" floating "surrounded by water or air or just gallery space". The team also printed "every screen of the game and pasted them all on a wall" as a colour script (Creative Bloq). Alto uses a 2.5D parallax landscape on a single auto-scroll axis. Harry Nesbitt's stated rule is to simplify a form "until you're left only with its essence", so the player's mind fills in the detail. For WOLF//OVERRIDE's planned 1.5 to 2 screen rooms with a tighter zoom, three implications follow. (1) Any threat must enter readable range, at a few seconds' walk, before it matters, because a fixed or tight camera on a phone hides distant hazards. (2) The one walkable height change per room should be large and clearly silhouetted, not a thin ledge. (3) Each room should read as a composed frame (Monument Valley's wall-of-screens check) and be reviewed at actual phone size, not only on a desktop monitor.
dossier.death_and_saves: Limbo was built on "trial and death". Playdead placed plentiful checkpoints, and Jeppe Carlsen said "death wasn't a penalty in the game" (Wikipedia, Limbo). Inside also "continues from the most recent checkpoint" (Wikipedia). On touch, the danger is that input errors cause deaths. GSMArena reports that Limbo iOS "failed to register your swipe" and "you end up jumping when you don't want to, which also often results in death". Game Informer's Limbo player "would just stop moving mid-jog" and "have to reset my thumb". On mobile, Little Nightmares' "loading times also take a long time to complete, even during checkpoint loads or do-overs" (TapTap, ROG Phone 5), which multiplies the cost of every death. Both Playdead mobile ports, Little Nightmares (Bandai Namco: "mobile cloud save") and Inside (iCloud, per review sources) sync saves across devices. Monument Valley's beta players took about 90 minutes to finish 10 levels (Wikipedia citing beta data). That works out to roughly 9 minutes per level (DERIVED). For WOLF//OVERRIDE's planned rule that dying drops unsecured evidence, a phone adds three risks. Misread touches will cause some deaths. Phone sessions are interrupted. Reloads are slow. Recommendations: (a) put a safe point within roughly 5 to 10 minutes of play (DERIVED from the Monument Valley per-level average, not a sourced target); (b) never treat an app suspend, call or focus loss as a death; pause and persist state instead; (c) respawn within about 1 to 2 seconds with no full scene reload if possible, because slow checkpoint loads drew criticism in the Little Nightmares port; (d) keep dropped evidence in the same room so recovery is a short walk.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence: Not applicable in the sense of direct precedent: none of these six games has an evidence or inventory system documented in fetched sources. Indirect lessons: Monument Valley uses "colors to signify where the player can interact" (Wikipedia, citing Wong), and Alto's Odyssey dropped a grappling hook because "it complicated the one-touch gameplay" (Wikipedia; Engadget). For a CASE inventory on a phone, that means: open the CASE with Pause or a single large button, never a gesture; give every item slot a touch target of at least 44x44 pt on iOS and 48x48 dp on Android; keep the one tool on the existing USE input instead of adding a second action button. The CASE screen pauses play, so it can use larger cards rather than a dense grid.
dossier.action_and_impact: Sources say little about screen shake, hit-stop or flash on mobile; detail there is UNVERIFIED. Two relevant patterns did come up. Limbo's iOS jump keeps momentum: "the boy retains his momentum" when jumping while moving, so mid-air thumb correction is not needed (Game Informer). That reduces the precision touch demands. Monument Valley's team wrote device-specific conversion: they had to "create systems and adjust code and art to convert our creator-friendly levels into device-optimised levels" (Creative Bloq). For WOLF//OVERRIDE's impact kit (shake, hit-stop, flash), keep the effects but give shake and flash a setting with an off option. On a hand-held screen, camera shake moves the image relative to the eye more than on a monitor (designer reasoning, not sourced). Keep timed events (door blast, purge sentry, tank drop) forgiving of a touch delay, because touch is "very imprecise" (Ken Wong quote, UNVERIFIED, search snippet only: the bit-tech source returned 502).
dossier.presentation_ui_art: Ports differ on control visibility. Limbo iOS shows "not ... a single control on screen" and has "no controls screen" (GSMArena). Little Nightmares offers a choice: "Standard Mode lets you play with the various controls appearing on the screen, while Immersive Mode offers greater immersion" (Bandai Namco). A TapTap review says Immersive mode "replaces most of the controls with gestures". New 'n' Tasty added "a new tutorial with pop-up guidance" and "gradual introduction to the starting area" for mobile, plus "resizable and moveable buttons" (Engadget). Engadget also notes that observers found the on-screen controls "busy". The occlusion problem is the critique that recurs most. On Inside, Game Informer wrote that "Covering up any element of the screen with your thumb does a disservice to Inside's immaculate visual language". On Limbo, the art survived "a giant thumb or two in the way". Platform numbers: Apple HIG sets a default hit target of 44x44 pt (minimum 28x28 pt), 17 pt default text (minimum 11 pt) and about 12 pt padding around bezelled controls (about 24 pt without a bezel), and asks for text that can enlarge to at least 200 percent. Android recommends touch targets of at least 48x48 dp. Game Accessibility Guidelines gives 2.4 cm as ideal and 0.96 cm as the minimum on phones. Art direction: Alto relies on minimalism ("an 'impression' of a reality, without the need to rely on details"). Monument Valley requires that "Every level has to look like a piece of graphic design" and uses colour to mark interactive objects. For WOLF//OVERRIDE's 960x540 canvas_items viewport, DERIVED and assuming a landscape phone about 390 pt tall (UNVERIFIED device figure): 1 viewport px is about 0.72 pt. A 44 pt target is then about 61 viewport px, 28 pt about 39 px, and 11 pt text at least about 15 px high. Interactive stations should pair colour with shape or motion, as AGENT.md already requires, and stay readable at that scale. Keep the bottom-left and bottom-right corners free of key art and dialogue, because thumbs rest there.
dossier.audio: Fetched sources give little port-specific audio data. Alto's Adventure's soundtrack is described as "mellow" and "soothing" (TouchArcade, quoted on Wikipedia). Team Alto added Zen Mode after learning that players used the game to relax and "cope with illness or loss" (Engadget, Eli Cymet). A claim that Inside's sound "come[s] through flawlessly" with headphones appeared only in a search snippet of AppUnwrapper (403, UNVERIFIED). Practical inference, not sourced: WOLF//OVERRIDE's procedural audio (room tone, footsteps per surface, breathing) will often play through a single small phone speaker. Check that essential cues (sentry warning, WOLF's refusal, evidence dropped) are clear in mono and at low volume, and pair each with a visual or haptic cue. Test with headphones and with the phone speaker separately.
dossier.mobile_and_input:
Control schemes, in detail:
- **Limbo iOS (2013):** sources disagree. GSMArena says you "slide left or right on the screen to move", "Swiping up makes the character jump and swiping down makes him drop down and grab the ledge", and "press and hold anywhere on the screen" to interact. Game Informer describes "an invisible d-pad on the left side" with swipe-up to jump. Playdead said they were "rethinking the controls and performing extensive optimizations" (press release). The device floor was iPad 2, iPad mini, iPhone 4S and the latest iPod touch. Price was $4.99 at launch and is $3.99 now. The current listing needs iOS 13, is 141.6 MB, and supports PlayStation, Xbox and MFi controllers.
- **Inside iOS (2017):** "an invisible d-pad, sliding your thumb in cardinal directions to move", "Sharp slides upward make him jump", and "tapping and holding the screen" to interact. It works with two thumbs or one. It is a free download to try; the store lists a $9.99 unlock today (launch price reported as $6.99, from UNVERIFIED snippets). It runs on iPhone, iPad and Apple TV, needs iOS 13 or tvOS 11, is 739 MB, and supports controllers.
- **New 'n' Tasty mobile (2017):** "there wasn't a virtual stick in sight" (GDC 2016 hands-on). Slide left or right to move, swipe up to jump, down to roll. Swipe on the side of the screen for "use" and "sneak". Movable and resizable buttons, full controller support, a resolution option and a post-effects toggle. $7.99, no in-app purchases.
- **Little Nightmares mobile (2023):** three modes (Controller/MFi, Standard on-screen buttons, Immersive gestures). On-screen buttons cover move, jump, crouch, interact and light. The TapTap reviewer found Six "slightly harder to accurately control" in narrow passages. Playdigious said at announcement that controls came first; the port was later delayed for polish.
- **Alto's Odyssey:** tap to jump, hold for tricks, hold to wall-ride. "Anything ... that required more than one touch input, didn't really feel right." The grappling hook was cut.
- **Monument Valley:** touch-native design. The team studied "how people interact with the screen, how to maintain their attention and how to curb frustration" and tested with non-gamer ustwo staff.

Performance: Little Nightmares ran "comfortably at low graphics settings and 60FPS, with occasional stutters" on a Snapdragon 888 phone, with long checkpoint loads. No fetched source gives fps targets for Limbo or Inside on iOS (UNVERIFIED).

Session length: Monument Valley beta players averaged 90 minutes for 10 levels, and 50% of players finished. Inside is 2 to 3 hours (App Store), Limbo 2 to 5 hours. Godot note: the project already uses gl_compatibility, and Godot's docs say "Compatibility is usually good enough for 2D".

Mapping to WOLF//OVERRIDE inputs:
- **Hold-to-move:** a floating relative-drag zone on the left half, where the origin is wherever the thumb lands (Inside/Limbo style), plus a small visible ghost ring for feedback. Re-centre the origin when the thumb drifts, to avoid Limbo's "stop moving mid-jog" failure.
- **USE (tap/hold):** a visible 44 pt+ button at bottom right with a hold-progress ring, so the tap/hold difference is never guessed.
- **Choices:** two large labelled buttons that appear only when a choice is live.
- **Pause:** a top-corner button of at least 44 pt.
- **Optional:** an "Immersive" gesture mode later, as Little Nightmares offers, but not as the default.

steal: Move by relative drag that starts wherever the thumb lands on the left half of the screen (Inside's 'invisible d-pad', Limbo's 'slide left or right'). This fits hold-to-move with no fixed stick art over the scene. Add a faint ghost ring at the touch origin, and re-centre the origin when the thumb drifts past a threshold, so the engineer never 'just stop[s] moving mid-jog'.

Treat a hold as interacting, as Inside's 'tapping and holding' and Limbo's 'press and hold anywhere' do. Map it to USE, and show a fill ring on the button so the player can see whether the input counted as a tap or a hold.

Offer selectable control modes as Little Nightmares does (Controller / Standard / Immersive). Ship Standard with visible buttons as the default, add a minimal gesture mode later, and switch to the controller prompt set automatically when a pad connects, since Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares and New 'n' Tasty all support controllers on phones.
Let players move and resize the touch buttons (New 'n' Tasty). This reduces thumb occlusion and helps players with large or small hands.

Make choices a deliberate two-step tap like New 'n' Tasty's GameSpeak ('tapping an icon and then on the sentence'). For WOLF, show the two choice buttons as large labelled cards only while a choice is live, never as gestures.
Teach controls in context. New 'n' Tasty mobile added pop-up guidance and a 'gradual introduction to the starting area'. Limbo's lack of any controls screen is the counterexample.
Use Alto's one-touch rule as a scope filter. Reject any tool or WOLF command that needs two simultaneous touches, as they did with the grappling hook ('it complicated the one-touch gameplay').

Run Monument Valley's 'wall of screens' check: print or screenshot every room at phone size side by side to judge readability and colour consistency. Mark interactive objects with colour plus shape, since MV uses 'colors to signify where the player can interact'.
Playtest with non-gamers, as ustwo did with staff from 'a plethora of different backgrounds'. Watch for players who are stuck or tired, then fix the room, not the tutorial text.

Plan sessions around Monument Valley's measured pace (about 90 minutes over 10 levels, about 9 minutes each). Put a safe point that secures evidence at roughly that interval or shorter, and auto-pause and persist on app suspend.
Expose resolution scale and a post-effects toggle like New 'n' Tasty mobile. Keep the gl_compatibility renderer (Godot: 'Compatibility is usually good enough for 2D').
Sync saves across devices if WOLF ships on iOS: Little Nightmares ('mobile cloud save') and Inside (iCloud, per review sources) both did.
avoid: Gesture-only critical actions with no visible feedback. Limbo iOS swipes 'failed to register' and caused unwanted jumps that 'often results in death'. With dropped evidence at stake, a misread swipe is far more costly in WOLF//OVERRIDE.

Covering the scene with thumbs and buttons. Game Informer called this 'a disservice to Inside's immaculate visual language'. Keep the engineer, WOLF, threats and dialogue out of the bottom-left and bottom-right thumb zones.
Busy on-screen button clusters. Observers called New 'n' Tasty's mobile controls 'busy'. Stay with the planned one move zone, one USE, two contextual choice buttons and Pause.

A fixed or tight camera that hides threats. Little Nightmares on a phone did 'not allow you to see far off creatures'. Make the purge sentry and other threats readable several seconds before contact at the new tighter zoom.
Slow death and checkpoint reloads. Little Nightmares mobile's 'loading times also take a long time ... even during checkpoint loads or do-overs'. Respawn without a full scene reload where possible.

Assuming desktop performance carries over. Little Nightmares needed low settings to hold 60 fps with stutters on a Snapdragon 888. Profile WOLF's parallax layers, procedural audio and impact effects on a real low-to-mid phone before claiming mobile support (per AGENT.md, device tests are their own check).

Touch targets below platform minimums: 44x44 pt on iOS (28 pt absolute minimum), 48x48 dp on Android, and 0.96 cm on phones per Game Accessibility Guidelines. At 960x540 that means USE, choice and Pause buttons of about 61 px or more (derived).
Treating an app suspend, phone call or notification as a death or quit that loses unsecured evidence.
Shipping with no controls explanation, as Limbo iOS did ('no controls screen'). WOLF's tap-versus-hold USE in particular needs to be shown.

corrections.claim: New 'n' Tasty mobile added "a new tutorial with pop-up guidance" and "gradual introduction to the starting area", plus "resizable and moveable buttons" (Engadget).
corrections.problem: Misquoted. None of these three quoted strings appears in the Engadget article (https://www.engadget.com/2017/12/14/oddworld-new-n-tasty-ios-android-shield/, raw HTML checked). They are paraphrases shown inside quotation marks.
corrections.correction: Engadget's actual words are "They've also added a new tutorial complete with pop-ups, and ease you into the game's starting area more gradually than before" and "It also has full external controller support, and you can resize or move buttons." Quote these, or drop the quotation marks.

corrections.claim: Engadget also notes that observers found the on-screen controls "busy" / "Observers called New 'n' Tasty's mobile controls 'busy'."
corrections.problem: Overstated and attributed loosely. This is one outlet, TouchArcade, as reported by Engadget, and the wording is softer. The stated reason is that the PS4 game uses most controller buttons.
corrections.correction: "Touch Arcade notes that the 2.5D puzzle-oriented platformer already uses most of your controller's buttons on PS4, so the mobile game's on-screen touch controls can get a little busy" (Engadget, citing TouchArcade).

corrections.claim: Monument Valley requires that "Every level has to look like a piece of graphic design" (in the art direction section, near Wong's quotes).
corrections.problem: Unsupported quote. It is not in Creative Bloq, the Game Developer GDC Europe 2014 report or the GDC Vault listing, and a web search found no source for it. A similar line on Unity's site is about Monument Valley 3 and comes from John Lau, not Ken Wong.
corrections.correction: Use Ken Wong in Creative Bloq (https://www.creativebloq.com/computer-arts/making-monument-valley-71412213): "each level in the game is a hand-crafted combination of puzzle, graphic design and architecture." Or use Wong via Game Developer: "Every screen is going to be a work of art that you can hang on a wall."

corrections.claim: Inside is 2 to 3 hours (App Store); numbers table: "Inside campaign length per App Store listing: 2-3 hours".
corrections.problem: Misattributed. The App Store listing (https://apps.apple.com/app/playdeads-inside/id1201642309) has no official length. "about 2-3 hours, total" comes from a review shown on the page, not from Playdead's metadata.
corrections.correction: Say "about 2-3 hours, per a review quoted on the App Store page", or cite a dedicated playtime source. Other listing facts check out: 739 MB, iOS 13+/tvOS 11+, controller support, free with a $9.99 full-game unlock.

corrections.claim: Inside syncs saves via iCloud ("Inside (iCloud, per review sources)"; steal list: "Inside (iCloud, per review sources) both did").
corrections.problem: Unsupported. No fetched source mentions iCloud for Inside: not Game Informer's iPhone article, not Wikipedia, not the App Store listing. Only Limbo iOS has a verified iCloud claim, from GSMArena.
corrections.correction: Mark Inside cloud saves as UNVERIFIED. Keep Limbo (GSMArena: "Your progress gets saved automatically and even synced across devices over iCloud") and Little Nightmares (Bandai Namco: "mobile cloud save") as the verified examples.

corrections.claim: Little Nightmares mobile release date: 12 December 2023 (source: Wikipedia).
corrections.problem: The cited source does not support the day. Wikipedia only says "Mobile versions were released in December 2023". The publisher's "available today" announcement was published 2023-12-11T10:19 UTC.
corrections.correction: 11 December 2023, per Bandai Namco EU's "Little Nightmares available today on mobile, on iOS and Android" (https://en.bandainamcoent.eu/little-nightmares/news/little-nightmares-available-today-mobile-ios-and-android). Note that some regional storefronts may show 12 December.

corrections.claim: Alto's Odyssey dropped a grappling hook because "it complicated the one-touch gameplay" (Wikipedia; Engadget).
corrections.problem: Misattributed in part. The Engadget article (2018-02-22) never mentions a grappling hook. Wikipedia's wording is "they complicated", not "it complicated", and the fetched sources show no primary developer quote for it.
corrections.correction: Cite Wikipedia only ("Other mechanics such as a grappling hook were considered, but were axed because they complicated the one-touch gameplay"). For the primary principle, use Harry Nesbitt in The Sweet Setup: "anything that required more than one touch input, didn't really feel right."

corrections.claim: Team Alto added Zen Mode after learning that players used the game to relax and "cope with illness or loss" (Engadget, Eli Cymet).
corrections.problem: Overstated causality. Engadget gives the letters quote and the Zen Mode history (added June 2016) separately. It credits Zen Mode to listening to player feedback in general, not to those letters.
corrections.correction: Say: Zen Mode, a consequence-free mode, was added to Alto's Adventure in June 2016 after player feedback. Separately, Cymet said players wrote that Alto "helped people relax at night and cope with illness or loss of a loved one".

corrections.claim: Monument Valley has "about 90 minutes average to finish across 1,000+ beta testers, 10 levels, and a 50% completion rate"; derived as about 9 minutes per level.
corrections.problem: Two datasets are merged. The 90 minutes and 1,000+ testers come from the December 2013 beta (Wikipedia, citing Polygon). The 50% completion is from ustwo's post-launch infographic covering all users (Gigazine, Jan 2015), not from beta testers. The 9-minute figure also assumes the beta held all 10 shipped levels and that the average covers finishers only; neither is sourced.
corrections.correction: Report them apart: "December 2013 beta: over 1,000 testers, average finish time 90 minutes (Wikipedia/Polygon)" and "post-launch: 50% of users completed the game; 24% bought Forgotten Shores (ustwo infographic via Gigazine)". Keep the 9 minutes per level labelled as a rough DERIVED figure.

corrections.claim: Playdead placed plentiful checkpoints, and Jeppe Carlsen said "death wasn't a penalty in the game" (Wikipedia, Limbo).
corrections.problem: Overstated attribution. Wikipedia says reviewers found the checkpoints plentiful, not that Playdead stated this as a design decision. The Carlsen line is Wikipedia's paraphrase ("Carlsen stated that their goal was to ensure death wasn't a penalty in the game") of Gamasutra's GDC coverage, not a verified direct quote.
corrections.correction: Write: reviewers found the checkpoints plentiful (Wikipedia, citing Eurogamer). Carlsen's stated goal was that death not be a penalty, with entertaining death animations (Wikipedia paraphrasing Gamasutra GDC coverage). Fetch the Gamasutra piece before using quotation marks.

corrections.claim: Little Nightmares on a phone: the TapTap reviewer found that "fixed camera views will sometimes be a detriment", "not allowing you to see far off creatures", framed as a phone or small-screen problem.
corrections.problem: Overstated as phone-specific. The quote is accurate, but the reviewer raises it as a general stealth gripe ("while they on the other hand can detect you quite for afar"). The same review calls the port a 1:1 conversion of the PC/console game, so the camera is not a phone-only issue.
corrections.correction: Present it as a general fixed-camera stealth problem that a small screen may make worse (designer inference). The phone-specific complaints in that review are the stutters at low settings, the long checkpoint and do-over loads, and Six being "slightly harder to accurately control" in narrow passageways.

corrections.claim: Limbo iOS jump keeps momentum, "so mid-air thumb correction is not needed" (Game Informer).
corrections.problem: Inference presented as sourced. Game Informer says only: "If you are already moving, when you swipe up to jump, the boy retains his momentum." It says nothing about mid-air correction.
corrections.correction: Keep the quote, and label "reduces the need for mid-air correction" as designer inference.

corrections.claim: Monument Valley development: 55 weeks, $852,000, 8 people (Gigazine).
corrections.problem: Mostly fine, but the team size is unclear in the cited page: Gigazine's English text says "eight teams based in London". Wikipedia gives 10 months of development and a $1.4 million total cost, which matches $852k plus Forgotten Shores' $549k over 29 weeks.
corrections.correction: Say "55 weeks and $852,000 for the base game; Forgotten Shores 29 weeks and $549,000 (ustwo infographic via Gigazine)". Treat "8 people" as approximate until it is checked against ustwo's original infographic.

corrections.claim: Monument Valley was "tested with non-gamer ustwo staff".
corrections.problem: Slightly overstated. Dan Gray (PocketGamer.biz) says they could "borrow testers from a plethora of different backgrounds, skill sets and ages". That source does not say the testers were non-gamers.
corrections.correction: Quote Gray directly. The non-gamer framing comes from Wong's GDC Europe talk report (Game Developer: "How is this going to appear to 'normal' people?"), not from a description of the testers.

corpus.group: Robot and dog companions across games (Dogmeat in Fallout, the dog in Fable II, D-Dog in Metal Gear Solid V, Trico, B-12, BT): how players bond with non-human companions, barks, idle behaviour, pointing and fetching, refusal

dossier.games: Fallout 1 / Fallout 3 / Fallout 4 (Dogmeat); Fable II (the dog, Lionhead 2008); Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (D-Dog / DD and the Buddy system); The Last Guardian (Trico, genDESIGN / SIE Japan Studio 2016); Stray (B-12, BlueTwelve Studio 2022); Titanfall 2 (BT-7274, Respawn 2016). Also one academic study on player attachment to game characters (Bopp et al., CHI PLAY 2019).
dossier.why_relevant:
WOLF is an independent robotic-wolf companion who helps, disagrees or refuses and remembers how the engineer treated him. These six companions cover the whole design space. Fable II's dog is autonomous with no command button. Dogmeat is a fetch-and-point utility dog that cannot die in FO4. DD is a scout that marks enemies. Trico is a deliberately disobedient creature you must coax. B-12 is a robot sidekick that carries the inventory and holds memories. BT is a robot partner whose bond is built through animation, a large eye and short two-way dialogue moments with no cutscenes. Between them they show what makes players bond with a non-human companion: projection, loyalty, competence, physical care and readable gaze. They also show what makes players resent one: refusal that cannot be read, a bossy objective-giver, a pathing obsession, a companion turned into a robotic command menu.

Research caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out early in this run. The Verge, IGN, Polygon, Eurogamer, Wired, The Guardian and VG247 are blocked to the fetch tool, and Fandom, GameSpot, StrategyWiki and the Unreal Engine interview returned 402/403. So D-Dog's numeric mechanics (bond meter, detection radius, command list) are UNVERIFIED and left out of the numbers list. I found no GDC Vault talk specifically about Trico, the Fable II dog, BT, DD or B-12 that I could fetch, so none is cited. Developer quotes come from interviews and features (PlayStation Blog, Game Developer, Edge via GamesRadar, Game Informer, The Escapist, Destructoid).

dossier.companion:
WHAT MAKES PLAYERS BOND (sourced):
1. Autonomy reads as life. Molyneux on the Fable II dog: "We give you no control over the dog... No control over the dog." He explained that a "Go and attack those enemies" button had made it "some sort of robot dog", and that "the very fact that you don't control him makes him feel real." The dog "feels like something that has a mind and that has an agenda" (Game Developer 2007 / search-summarized GDC 2007 coverage). His GDC 2007 laws were "It must not piss you off" and "The dog must care about you". The dog "will always run ahead of you and respond to your actions", and takes "note of the weapon you're fighting with and who you're attacking" (Engadget). Training was reward and punishment feeding a Black & White-style decision tree: "When you give feedback to your dog, it gets an extra data sample to build the tree" (AIGameDev via GameBanshee).
2. Silence plus competence plus loyalty. Avellone on why Dogmeat is "arguably the most successful NPC companion ever": "One, he doesn't talk, so the players can project a personality on to him. Two, he's effective in combat... and three, he's a dog that stays with you through thick-and-thin." Tim Cain: "Dogmeat's loyalty to the player was set to 100 percent, and he would never leave you for any reason" (The Escapist, 2009). Kill Screen (2015) calls FO4 Dogmeat "Fallout 4's rock. He's stable. Dependable", "perfectly, doggedly mute", and says his presence "lends the impression that a path can be found through the enormity of the game."
3. Ambiguity and refusal as a theme (Trico). Ueda: "it doesn't always do what you ask it to do. That's one of the themes", "The role of the creature is ambiguous", and "another game where you can completely control a creature wouldn't be enjoyable for me" (Kill Screen, citing Edge/IGN). In the 2011 Game Informer demo, "Trico doesn't always follow your orders" and sometimes "simply ignores him" like "a haughty feline". Vases of a liquid "Trico adores" are the incentive, the bond "grows naturally" and obedience improves with it. Ueda wanted it to feel "like the bond you would form with a pet". "Trico is the member of the duo with power" because "The boy is unable to defeat the enemies on his own" (PS Blog 2010). Ueda's success test: "if the player feels the existence of Trico, like it's really there" (PS Blog 2016).
4. A robot partner built from body language first (BT). Fukuda: "It was important that the player felt reassured... you needed someone you could trust, someone reliable and safe." Early scripts "erred towards the bossy" because BT was also "the player's main objective-giver". The fix was short player-to-BT conversations "intended as a way of strengthening their bond with BT without resorting to cutscenes". The trigger was BT asking whether the player was OK after a fall into a pit (Edge/GamesRadar). BT "is primarily a construction of animation, since its voice only came in right at the end". Wikipedia (citing The Verge, not fetchable) says the team gave BT a large eye "so players would know where the titan is looking" and that the script rework took five months.
5. A robot sidekick as the voice and memory of the protagonist (B-12). Martin-Raget: "a lot of iteration on B-12's character like how robotic his personality should be and whether his general tone should be more dramatic or more hopeful" (Destructoid). B-12's memories are found through the game and add story context (Wikipedia).
6. Research: Bopp et al. (2019) surveyed 213 players and found seven distinct forms of attachment. They range "from feeling excited about the characters' gameplay competency, admiring them as role models, to deep concern for characters' well-being". So competence and vulnerability both create a bond, but they are different bonds.

BARKS: Dogmeat "growls at enemies while tracking them or barks at containers, then stomps his front paws while pointing his head toward discoveries". If he cannot reach a container "he points in their direction". He also announces finds unprompted ("Dogmeat found something" / "Dogmeat found an enemy") (fallout.wiki). Per search-summarized coverage, the Fable II dog barks to alert you to enemies and sniffs out treasure (dig spots).
IDLE: FO4 Dogmeat plays with teddy bears out of combat (fallout.wiki). The Fable dog could be seen "pooping in the neighbor's flowers" and "playing with his ball, or burying it" (AIGameDev). Stray's cat sleeps because "nothing is more typical of a cat than just sleep and do nothing" (Destructoid). The Last Guardian's boy "places hands on nearby walls, and reaches to pet Trico without player interaction" (Wikipedia).
POINTING / FETCHING: Dogmeat's fetch and find commands, unprompted finds, and pointing toward unreachable containers. The Fable II dog finds treasure and leads the way to quest objectives (Wikipedia). D-Dog is a recon buddy whose effectiveness depends on the relationship (Wikipedia). His exact marking radius and bond numbers are UNVERIFIED.
REFUSAL: Trico ignores commands when "in a bad mood". FO4 human companions warn once, then refuse to travel at hatred (fallout.wiki). Dogmeat never refuses (no affinity). Quiet in MGSV leaves for story reasons, not as a reaction to how you treated her.
dossier.level_and_camera:
Trico: the levels are built around the creature's body and moods. Gates and glass "eyes that frighten Trico" block its progress. The boy commands Trico "to leap onto ledges or head in a certain direction", and "new areas can be discovered by letting Trico wander independently" (Wikipedia, citing The Verge/IGN). Reviewers blamed "cramped levels" and the camera for frustration (IGN via Wikipedia). Lesson: a big companion in tight rooms plus a fighting camera turns independence into annoyance.
Fable II: the dog scouts. It runs ahead, guesses where you are going and leads toward objectives (Engadget; search-summarized coverage).
Titanfall 2: the campaign was built from "action blocks", short prototypes stitched together. The level formula was "211": "Two parts Pilot combat, one part Pilot mobility and puzzling, one part Titan combat". The companion-dependent share was explicitly budgeted. The BT-throws-the-pilot prototypes were "chopped down, because the team found it difficult to implement into something interactive, into several cutscene sequences" (Edge/GamesRadar). PS Blog: BT offers to throw Jack across an abyss at "a 64% chance of success".
Stray: the team dropped standard platforming after players "consistently miss[ed] jumps", which "didn't feel cat-like". They built a guided movement system that still allows choice (Wikipedia, citing an RPS preview). B-12 "provides torchlight in the many dark areas" (PlayStation.com).
For WOLF//OVERRIDE's 1.5 to 2 screen rooms, each with one height change: give every room a WOLF-only route (vent, upper catwalk in a parallax mid-layer, a gap he can jump) that he chooses to take. Have him wait at the far doorway or the height change and look back. Keep the camera framing both characters when WOLF is scouting ahead, or show an edge-of-screen eye-light pip. Do not let his body block the walk-through doorways.
dossier.death_and_saves:
Fallout 1: Dogmeat could die, and lead designer Chris Taylor "was shocked when I heard of all the work people went through to keep Dogmeat alive to the end" (Escapist). Kotaku (2009) on Fallout 3: if you don't protect him, "his death becomes a sad reminder of the consequences of reckless slaughter". Fallout 4: Dogmeat is essential. When downed he can be revived with a Stimpak (fallout.wiki), and players were told before launch that he can't die (Uproxx headline, cited by Wikipedia, not fetched). Kill Screen notes his "suicidal disregard for his own safety" in combat. Fable II: "The dog cannot be killed, but can become injured and ineffective, requiring healing by the player". In the ending you can choose to bring the dog back (Wikipedia). Titanfall 2: BT's sacrifice is the authored emotional climax, a story event and not a fail state. The Last Guardian: the boy pets Trico "to calm it after a battle" and removes spears thrown at it (Wikipedia).
For WOLF//OVERRIDE's death model (dying drops unsecured evidence, safe points secure it): WOLF should not permanently die from AI error. Use the Fable/FO4 pattern of downed, damaged and less effective until the engineer repairs him at a safe point. Optionally, at high trust, WOLF can stand guard over or point toward the spot where the engineer dropped evidence. The engineer-only fallback is a visible drop marker. Safe points are a natural quiet moment for the Trico-style care beat: hold USE to steady WOLF or clear debris from him.
dossier.inventory_and_evidence:
B-12 holds the quest inventory: "Items in this inventory can be shown to robot inhabitants to progress". He also "stores 'memories' that can be inspected later", and you can "Call him at any time to remind you of your current objective" (PlayStation.com). FO4 Dogmeat fetches items, bites enemies to reveal them, or brings back what is in containers. His base carry weight is 150 lbs, and 25 lbs in Survival unless he wears gear (fallout.wiki). Fallout 3 Dogmeat "will fetch food, ammo and weapons" (Kotaku). The Fable II dog finds buried treasure (dig spots) and hidden quests (search-summarized coverage, Wikipedia). Trico's food barrels and vases are both a fetch quest and a bonding tool: Ueda wants players to know "How does it feel to actually feed Trico?" (PS Blog 2016).
For the evidence CASE: keep the CASE on the engineer, not inside WOLF. B-12 shows that a companion-as-backpack becomes a UI device and weakens independence. Do steal Dogmeat's point-and-wait: WOLF freezes, faces an evidence item, and lights his eye. If the item is unreachable he points in its direction. The engineer must still walk over and USE. WOLF's 'memories' (B-12) fit the existing WOLF memory-gating direction: evidence the engineer shows WOLF can unlock his recollections. Any essential evidence must stay findable without WOLF.
dossier.action_and_impact:
Trico is the muscle: "Trico is able to defeat an enemy with one swipe" and "The boy is unable to defeat the enemies on his own — that's the gameplay element involved" (PS Blog 2010). "The boy doesn't possess combat skills, so you need to work together with Trico" (PS Blog 2016). The Fable II dog attacks downed enemies and adapts to the player's weapon and target (Wikipedia; Engadget). Dogmeat bites enemies to make them detectable, and a perk upgrades him ("Attack Dog" must be unlocked via the perk chart; fallout.wiki). B-12's combat tool (the Defluxor) is time-limited and needs a cooling period (Wikipedia), and the publisher says "B-12's skills are limited so you'll also need to use stealth" (PlayStation.com). D-Dog is described as reconnaissance help (Wikipedia). His specific stun/knife equipment and numbers are UNVERIFIED.
For the impact kit (shake, hit-stop, flash): when WOLF acts (holding a door, hitting a sentry, bracing for the tank drop), give his action its own short hit-stop and a camera nudge toward him, so the player sees his agency. Copy B-12's cooldown: a WOLF assist is strong but limited, so the engineer-only path stays meaningful.
dossier.presentation_ui_art:
Eyes and gaze carry the relationship. For BT, Wikipedia (citing The Verge) says the team designed "a large emotive eye, so players would know where the titan is looking", plus small arms for natural interactions. Trico's eyes "reflect different colors to reflect its current mood" (Kill Screen). Trico's ears "react with a cat-like 'twitch' if they touch ceilings" (Wikipedia). The design was "deliberately unbalanced because looking strange was important" (Ueda via IGN, cited by Wikipedia). It was hand-keyframed, not motion-captured, and the PS3 build "actually had more motion patterns than the PS4 version did" (Cane and Rinse 2019). Ueda: "They can only communicate via gestures, motion, and reactions" (PS Blog 2016). BT was built by animator Shawn Lee Wilson before any voice existed, acting out its walk and gestures in the mocap room (Edge/GamesRadar). Fable II's dog coat tracks morality: grey neutral, golden good, black evil (Wikipedia). Dogmeat's "intelligent, and kind dog eyes" are what Kill Screen singles out. Stray's devs used their cats, Murtaugh and a sphynx named Oscar, as reference (80.lv).
For WOLF in painterly 2.5D: one strong eye light whose position shows gaze (look-at) and whose color or pulse shows mood. Add a reactive ear or antenna flick for secondary motion. Block WOLF's poses before writing his lines. Show trust through posture (distance kept, tail or ear carriage), not a meter.
dossier.audio: Dogmeat: growls while tracking enemies, barks at containers, and has unprompted find barks (fallout.wiki); "occasionally barks when he finds something worthwhile" (Kill Screen). The Fable II dog barks to alert you to enemies (search-summarized GDC coverage). BT's voice "only came in right at the end of the game's development"; its character was set through animation first (Edge/GamesRadar). Stray has a "dedicated 'meow' button" for player-driven expression (PlayStation.com). The devs noticed the office "cats in the office started reacting to what was on our screens" when they heard game sounds (80.lv). For WOLF's procedural audio: separate bark families for "found evidence" (bright, short), "threat" (low growl or servo whine, held while tracking), "refusal" (a clipped negative tone plus a head turn) and "content idle" (soft servo settle). Keep him mostly non-verbal or sparse, since silence is the projection lever Avellone credits. Never play a refusal sound without an animated reason.
dossier.mobile_and_input:
There is a range of control models. At one end is the Fable II dog with zero commands ("There is no 'Go and attack those enemies' button"); you steer it through praise and scolding gestures and your own actions. Next is Trico: no direct control at first ("You can only control the boy", PS Blog 2010), then commands learned over the game. Next is Dogmeat's command set: stay, fetch/find and Enter Doghouse, whispered when crouched or shouted at distance (fallout.wiki). Next is B-12, called with one button ("Call him at any time", PlayStation.com). At the far end is Titanfall 2's occasional short dialogue choices, which a hands-on called "not... as central to the experience as... Mass Effect or a Telltale game" (PS Blog). The exact count of BT reply options is UNVERIFIED (a search snippet of a Stevivor preview says "one of two ways"; I could not fetch the page).
This fits WOLF//OVERRIDE's input set (hold-to-move, one USE, two choice buttons, Pause): use the two choice buttons for BT-style quick replies (two options, no timer pressure, player-paced per AGENT.md). Tap USE on WOLF to ask where to go, a B-12-style objective reminder that WOLF answers by pointing or by refusing. Hold USE on WOLF to steady, pet or repair him, the Trico care beat. Do not add a command wheel. On phone touch, WOLF's pointing must be visible at small scale, which favours eye light and a body-direction freeze over small icons.

steal: Molyneux's two laws as WOLF acceptance tests: WOLF must never annoy (never block a doorway, the camera, the player's line or a USE target) and must visibly care (checks on the engineer after a fall, a blast or a near-death).

Scout ahead and guess the destination (Fable II): in 1.5-2 screen rooms WOLF trots 1-2 body lengths ahead toward the likely exit, stops at the height change or the next doorway, and looks back. Start with the dog's 'run ahead and respond to your actions' rule before any scripted leading.

Point-and-freeze on finds (Dogmeat): WOLF stops, aims his head and eye light at the evidence, does a paw-stomp or servo-tick, and plays a short 'found' bark. For unreachable items he points in their direction. Allow both unprompted finds and asked-for finds.

Gaze you can read (BT's 'large emotive eye so players would know where the titan is looking'; Trico's mood-colored eyes): one eye light that shows look-at direction and mood color. Use it for refusal, attention and fear.

Refusal as readable mood with a motive (Trico 'simply ignores him' when in a bad mood; vases win him over): WOLF's refusals show a cause (fear stimulus, a remembered mistreatment, low trust), a body reaction and a way back (wait, repair, show evidence, apologize via a choice button). The engineer-only path always remains.
Bond-gated reliability (Trico's obedience improves as the bond grows): trust changes how readily and how fast WOLF helps, never whether essential progress is possible.

Quick two-option replies without cutscenes (Titanfall 2): short player-paced exchanges triggered by real events, e.g. WOLF asking whether the engineer is OK after the tank drop. Respawn found exactly that pit moment made room for a player response.
WOLF states odds (BT's '64% chance of success') before risky asks like the door blast. It is characterful, it is information, and it sets up the trust payoff.
Care beats as interaction (Trico: pet to calm after battle, pull out spears, feed): hold USE on WOLF after a blast to steady him or clear debris. WOLF remembers it.

Downed, not dead (FO4 essential Dogmeat revived with a Stimpak; the Fable II dog 'injured and ineffective, requiring healing'): WOLF damage costs his scouting or assist until a safe-point repair. This pairs with the evidence-drop death model.

Cheap secondary motion that sells physical presence (Trico's ear twitch on ceilings; the boy auto-touching walls and Trico): WOLF ear or antenna flick under low pipes, engineer's hand brushing WOLF when adjacent and idle.
Animation before voice (BT animated before its voice existed): block WOLF's idle, point, refuse and follow poses first, then add barks or lines.
Idles that make quiet moments (Dogmeat's teddy bear, the Fable dog burying its ball, Stray's cat sleeping): WOLF sniffs vents, scans, sits near the engineer and settles while the player reads.
Companion memories as story delivery (B-12's recovered memories): tie WOLF memory-gating to evidence the engineer chooses to show him.
Budget WOLF's share of each room explicitly, like Titanfall's '211' ratio, so his routes, assists and refusals are planned per room rather than sprinkled.
avoid: A command-menu dog: Molyneux said an attack button made the Fable dog feel like 'some sort of robot dog'. WOLF is a robot, but a command wheel would erase the independence that is his whole premise.

Unreadable or long refusals in cramped spaces: Trico's independence plus 'cramped levels' and camera trouble drew IGN's 'frustrating' and 'ineffective' criticism. Cap any WOLF stall, always telegraph its cause, and keep the engineer-only route open.

Attention obsession bugs: the Fable II dog at one point 'would just be obsessed with anything that was evil' and followed evil NPCs 'to the ends of the earth'. Give WOLF a leash radius and a target-priority cap.

A bossy objective-giver: BT's early scripts 'erred towards the bossy' because BT doubled as the quest-giver, and the rework took months. Don't let WOLF nag about objectives; let him point, wait or decline.

AI-caused permanent companion death: Fallout 1 players reloaded to keep Dogmeat alive, and FO4 Dogmeat has a 'suicidal disregard for his own safety'. Never let WOLF's pathing or AI choices kill him permanently or cost the player evidence.
A companion as a pure utility backpack: B-12 carries the inventory. Keep the evidence CASE on the engineer so WOLF stays a character with opinions, not a menu.

Making a mechanic interactive when it reads better as a beat: Respawn found BT throwing the pilot 'difficult to implement into something interactive' and turned it into cutscene sequences. Keep any WOLF-carries-engineer moment a short authored beat.
The 'cute pet' or 'really useful ally' default (Ueda wanted neither). WOLF's help must have a cost or an opinion attached.

Floating '+15 liked that' style notifications (Fallout 4's affinity reactions are tied to explicit like/dislike values). In a horror tone, show memory through WOLF's behaviour and posture rather than numbers or toasts. This is a design judgement, not a sourced finding.
Claiming unverified D-Dog numbers (bond meter range, spotting radius): these could not be fetched this run and should not drive tuning.

corrections.claim: Quoted line in the action section: "Trico is the member of the duo with power" because "The boy is unable to defeat the enemies on his own" (PS Blog 2010).
corrections.problem: Unsupported quote. The 24 Sep 2010 PS Blog interview (https://blog.playstation.com/2010/09/24/team-ico-talks-fumito-ueda-on-the-last-guardian-shadow-of-the-colossus/) contains no 'duo' and no 'member of the duo with power'. What Ueda actually says is: "Trico is able to defeat an enemy with one swipe. So in that sense, he functions as a guardian of sorts. But the boy is unable to defeat the enemies on his own — that's the gameplay element involved."
corrections.correction: Remove the 'member of the duo with power' quotation marks, or reword it as the dossier's own paraphrase. Quote 'functions as a guardian of sorts' instead. In the same interview Ueda also says "It's not a pet game", which is worth keeping next to the Game Informer 'bond... with a pet' line.

corrections.claim: Reviewers blamed "cramped levels" and the camera, which drew IGN's 'frustrating' and 'ineffective' criticism. The lesson drawn is that a big companion in tight rooms plus a fighting camera turns independence into annoyance.
corrections.problem: Misattributed and partly inverted. On the Wikipedia page the IGN point (Marty Sliva) is about the camera and 'the cramped nature of certain levels' making sections 'more frustrating'. 'Ineffective' is a different reviewer: Game Revolution's James Kozanitis. His complaint was the opposite: Trico kept traversing and doing tasks 'even without player input', which made controlling Trico 'ineffective and unnecessary'.
corrections.correction: Attribute 'frustrating' and 'cramped' to IGN (Sliva) and 'ineffective and unnecessary' to Game Revolution (Kozanitis). Add the second lesson the GR critique really teaches: too much autonomy can make the player's commands feel pointless. WOLF's independence should leave the engineer's asks meaningful, not just guard against stalls.

corrections.claim: Molyneux quotes are sourced to 'Game Developer 2007 / search-summarized GDC 2007 coverage': no control over the dog, the 'Go and attack those enemies' button that made it 'some sort of robot dog', and 'makes him feel real'.
corrections.problem: Mixed attribution. The Game Developer piece (Jason Dobson, 24 May 2007) quotes a Lionhead video diary, not the GDC talk. It contains 'We give you no control over the dog...', 'You haven't got a dog button' and 'makes him feel real, makes him feel like something that has a mind and that has an agenda'. It does NOT contain 'robot dog' or 'Go and attack those enemies'. Those come from MCV's coverage of Molyneux's GDC 2007 talk 'Innovations in Fable 2' (https://mcvuk.com/?p=150851): "There is no 'Go and attack those enemies' button, because we found that approach made it into some sort of robot dog."
corrections.correction: Cite MCV (8 Mar 2007, GDC 2007) for the robot-dog and attack-button quote. Cite Game Developer (24 May 2007, Lionhead video diary) for the no-control, mind and agenda quotes. Add MCV to the source list.

corrections.claim: Fable II dog scouting: it 'runs ahead, guesses where you are going and leads toward objectives' (Engadget; search-summarized coverage), and it 'finds treasure and leads the way to quest objectives' (Wikipedia).
corrections.problem: Overstated. Engadget only says it 'will always run ahead of you and respond to your actions'; no fetched source says it 'guesses where you are going'. Wikipedia qualifies the leading: 'lead the way to quest objectives (when required, though this is rare; typically the player is led to objectives via a sparkling gold "bread crumb" trail)'.
corrections.correction: Say the dog runs ahead and responds to the player's actions. Objective guidance in Fable II was mainly the gold breadcrumb trail, not the dog; it led only rarely. Mark 'guesses your destination' as UNVERIFIED. This supports WOLF's design: a separate engineer-only guidance cue should carry essential wayfinding.

corrections.claim: Training was reward and punishment feeding a Black & White-style decision tree. Idle examples: the Fable dog could be seen 'pooping in the neighbor's flowers' and 'playing with his ball, or burying it' (AIGameDev via GameBanshee).
corrections.problem: Overstated. The GameBanshee/AIGameDev text is an inference from a talk at the Apply AI Innovations event in London, not GDC: 'Based on Peter's descriptions... it seems a decision tree is still used'. The pooping and ball lines are hypothetical training examples ('if your dog likes pooping in the neighbor's flowers, you could correct that...'), not documented in-game idles.
corrections.correction: Label the decision tree as AIGameDev's inference ('it seems'), not a confirmed mechanic, and name the event as Apply AI Innovations, London 2007. Present pooping and ball-burying as Molyneux's examples of trainable behaviour, not observed idle animations.

corrections.claim: Numbers row: 'Dogmeat has an affinity system: No (no affinity, no perk, no romance)', source fallout.wiki/Affinity.
corrections.problem: Partly wrong and unsupported. The fallout.wiki Dogmeat (Fallout 4) page lists 'Perks: Attack Dog' and says 'Dogmeat is the only companion whose perk Attack Dog must be unlocked via the perk chart'. The Affinity page never states that Dogmeat lacks affinity; it mentions him only in 'Heal Dogmeat' reaction rows for other companions.
corrections.correction: Dogmeat has a companion perk (Attack Dog), unlocked through the player's perk chart rather than through affinity. 'No affinity' is plausible but is not stated on the cited page, so mark it derived or UNVERIFIED.

corrections.claim: Fallout 4 affinity scale: 'max 1000 (idolize)... -1000 hatred (refuses to travel after one warning)'. Passive gain is '40 - 0.033 x affinity' every 10 minutes.
corrections.problem: Max value is wrong, and two conditions are missing. fallout.wiki says 'Raising their affinity to 1000+ (max is 1100) will result in them "idolizing"'. The table labels 1000 'Infatuation'. The warning comes at 'a sufficiently negative value' and refusal after it 'drops further'; the page does not pin refusal to exactly -1000. Passive gain requires that 'at least 1 XP has been earned' in the ten-minute period.
corrections.correction: Max affinity is 1100, and idolize is reached at 1000. Refusal follows a single warning once affinity drops further; this is permanent. Passive gain of 40 - 0.033 x affinity is awarded per ten minutes of following, only if at least 1 XP was earned.

corrections.claim: The exact count of BT reply options is UNVERIFIED (a search snippet of a Stevivor preview says 'one of two ways').
corrections.problem: Understated. The dossier's own fetched source, the PS Blog preview (Massongill, 11 Aug 2016, https://blog.playstation.com/?p=179974), says the branching moments 'presented Jack with two response choices, mapped to the DualShock 4's directional pad'. The example reply was "What about the other 36%?!"
corrections.correction: Verified from the demo: two response choices per moment, on the d-pad. That matches WOLF//OVERRIDE's two choice buttons directly. Cite the PS Blog, not the Stevivor snippet.

corrections.claim: D-Dog is a recon buddy whose effectiveness depends on the relationship (Wikipedia); 'D-Dog is described as reconnaissance help (Wikipedia)'.
corrections.problem: Partly unsupported by the cited source. The MGSV Wikipedia article describes D-Dog only as 'a wolf pup raised to assist Snake in the field', and separately says 'The companions' abilities and their effectiveness depends on the player's relationship with them.' It does not call D-Dog recon or a scout, or say he marks enemies.
corrections.correction: Keep the relationship-dependent effectiveness, which is supported. Mark D-Dog's scouting and enemy-marking role UNVERIFIED for this run, like the other D-Dog mechanics. (Kill Screen 2015 only says D-Dog 'can be directed to rip out enemy throats'.)

corrections.claim: Trico 'was hand-keyframed, not motion-captured, and the PS3 build "actually had more motion patterns than the PS4 version did"' (Cane and Rinse 2019). Trico ignores commands when 'in a bad mood'.
corrections.problem: Minor misattribution and overstatement. The Cane and Rinse interview supports only the motion-patterns quote. The keyframe claim comes from Wikipedia: 'programmed key frame animations instead of more common motion capture techniques'. 'In a bad mood' was Ueda joking during a demo ('"It seems like he's in a bad mood today," Ueda jokes'), not a described mood mechanic. Trico then complied after a few more calls.
corrections.correction: Cite Wikipedia (its ref 18) for keyframe rather than mocap. Present 'bad mood' as Ueda's joke in the 2011 Game Informer demo. The documented design intent is that 'The occasional lack of cooperation is intentional' and that obedience improves as the bond 'grows naturally'.

syn.dimension: COMPANION DESIGN: autonomy vs usefulness, trust and memory, refusal, barks and idle behaviour, look-at, leading and scouting, non-human bonding, helping without dependency. CORPUS NOTE: the corpus I received was cut off partway through the Stray dossier's companion field ("B-12 is a small flying drone the cat finds in Chapter 3 (The Flat): a..."). Any later dossiers did not arrive. So for Stray I could use only its games/why_relevant/sources fields: B-12 carries the inventory, translates the world, the 27 memories double as his memory, the Defluxor is mounted on him, and he makes a choice the player does not control. Inside/Limbo have no companion; their evidence transfers only as architecture for bodies that feel alive. Where a dossier correction applies, I used the corrected version. I read the current repo to describe current state: apps/game/scripts/m0_actor.gd (FOLLOW_GAP 64 px, FOLLOW_SPEED 220), m0_state.gd (one stable relay_disagreement memory), junction_room.gd (WOLF_SEAM_X, WOLF_BAIT_X: WOLF already chooses to draw the sentry). I edited nothing.

principles.principle: The companion is never a second player. Its separate mind is the point, and the team should say so explicitly.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana: Stjärnljus in the developer commentary says co-op was ruled out 'from the get-go' because 'that magic really disappears as soon as another human being takes control over her'. The dossier marks the commentary quotes UNVERIFIED (YouTube captions returned 429) but not disproved. Little Nightmares II: co-op was 'discarded' at the start of pre-production, and 'By removing players ability to control Six, we're also bringing interesting situation where players are never fully in charge of Six' destiny'. Both quotes are from Lucas Roussel, Lead Producer at publisher Bandai Namco Europe, not Tarsier (dossier correction). Tarsier also cut a direct 'whistling mechanic used to herd enemies' from LN1 (level designer Matthew Compher via Push Square).

principles.principle: Moment-to-moment reliability earns praise. Unreliability belongs in authored story beats, not AI jank. Players punish latency they read as lag.
principles.evidence: LN2 reviews: 'you'll never feel like you're fighting the underlying code' (Push Square, verified); Six is 'an unusually reliable companion' who 'knows what to do anyway' (PlayStation LifeStyle, verified); 'she operates just fine on her own so you don't need to babysit her' (Dread Central). Negatives: calling her 'doesn't always work' (PSLS) and 'would take too long to take a cue/get into position' (Shacknews). The drama lives in the story, where Six refuses Mono's help at first and later lets go of him. In Planet of Lana, no source shows Mui refusing, disagreeing or remembering. Her autonomy is limited to following, idling, reacting and carrying out commands, so the game has no refusal precedent to copy.

principles.principle: Asymmetric bodies make the puzzles and the bond. Each character has things only it can do and at least one hard inability.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana: Mui fits through tunnels, jumps higher, bites rope and cables, holds buttons and hypnotises creatures. Lana moves boxes, swims and gives instructions; 'Mui is afraid of water' (GamesRadar). Commentary: puzzles are 'built around what Lana can do and what Mui can do and what they can do together and separately'. The first joint chapter is a deliberately simple ability tutorial, and difficulty then ramps. LN2: Six boosts Mono to ledges, carries a second item 'if you need more than one' (Dread Central) and takes the complementary half of two-person puzzles (Push Square). Stray: B-12 carries the inventory and translates (why_relevant).

principles.principle: Keep the player-to-companion vocabulary tiny and mostly contextual. Expand it as the relationship grows, not at first meeting.
principles.evidence: LN2: one call verb plus hand-holding. The achievement 'In The Palm Of My Hand' reached a 13.8% Steam unlock. Planet of Lana: one button carries two verbs (B tap = stay, B hold = follow). RT shows a world-space pointer that 'will also smartly snap to particular points of interest', and a Y prompt appears for contextual actions. Pointing ('waypointing') unlocks only after the bond forms. GamesRadar found the cursor 'slightly finicky', with automatic prompts as the save. The sequel let Lana 'point Mui all across the screen' for bigger puzzles.

principles.principle: Attachment comes from constant small idle business and two-way voice, not from emoting only at choice points.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana: a pre-jump 'little butt wiggle' (RPS); 'you can pet Mui at any time' (GamesRadar). Eriksson (Game Developer, verified): the team planned body language only, then 'decided that we needed one more layer of emotional expression' and added a constructed language. In the commentary, 'Mui answers her' is called 'very important gameplay-wise'. Mui's voice was performed by sound designer Ameglio. The dossier's own warning, an inference: a companion who emotes only at choices 'will read as a lock-and-key'.

principles.principle: Build autonomous behaviour as independent intents voting into one body. Layer look-at and breathing on top of locomotion. Let visible contact gate effects, and anticipate before acting.
principles.evidence: INSIDE Huddle (GDC 2017 slides): 'every impulse is just a vote' from independent states (Run, Stumble, Climb, Grab, ArmControl, level scripts), tuned 'by observing the expression of the total system'. The result has 'unmistakable perceived depth... perhaps because it is so difficult to predict'. 'Boxes can not be lifted until a lifting arm actually touches them.' 'At any point we want at least 2-3 arms holding on to a box.' Adding stick arms early showed 'It does not take much to completely change the perception'. The boy's animation stack has additive 'breathe' and 'look around' layers (Danish animation talk). Limbo's boy 'can look forward in time half a second to see what's out there' so he can pre-place his hands (Jensen/Patti).

principles.principle: When a companion or threat is off-camera, carry its state in sound and in a minimal locator. Audit every tell against what the AI actually senses.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana: when separated, 'an animated icon dynamically pops up, showing you which direction Mui is located in and what her status is... if she is sitting or moving towards you' (Wishfully, Xbox Wire). Little Nightmares: the camera hides enemies, so 'the breathing helps to indicate their presence'. Lilja describes using breathing to show enemy state as an experiment that players over-read as scent tracking (corrected framing). Sounds that pass through walls became 'sonic identifiers'. INSIDE: voice intensity can be clamped and 'interpolated in space' ('Useful for indicating proximity to danger') and relaxed over time. Playdead and Tarsier games run with no HUD at all; Lana breaks that rule only for the companion locator.

principles.principle: Putting the companion at risk by the player's choice creates feeling. Remembering it pays that off cheaply.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana stone-crab puzzle: Mui is parked in a safe spot as bait. In playtests 'people have already sort of grown an attachment to Mui and feel a bit bad about using her as bait... that's exactly what we want' (commentary, UNVERIFIED re-pull). Later 'Lana can use herself as bait instead'. Little Nightmares: the Nomes you hugged gather in the ending (12 hugged, the 13th eaten, per correction). INSIDE Huddle: the shader fades in bruises, burns and blood from 9 of 26 rigidbodies as you abuse it. Stray: the 27 collectible memories double as B-12's memory (why_relevant).

principles.principle: The companion should make play richer without becoming a lock the player must turn. If it carries anything essential, its absence must not strand progress.
principles.evidence: LN2 reviewers repeatedly say Six is 'not an escort' and needs no 'babysit[ting]'. Stray puts the whole inventory and the one tool on B-12 (why_relevant). LN2 gives Six only a second carried item. Planet of Lana's Mui is required for almost every puzzle. Steam funnel (corrected): about 21% of players who started stopped before 'A new friend', where Mui is met, and about 40% of starters finished. That is evidence the bond carries the back half, though the companion is introduced late.

targets.metric: Time from a WOLF decision trigger to a visible acknowledgement (head turn, ear, lean or pull-back)
targets.target: Show a tell within roughly 0.5 s, before the action resolves
targets.basis: Derived, not measured in any game. Limbo's boy 'can look forward in time half a second', and Shacknews complained that Six 'would take too long to take a cue'. Treat this as a design target to validate in hands-on play.

targets.metric: Hard abilities per side in each companion room
targets.target: At least 1 thing only WOLF does and at least 1 thing WOLF cannot do that the engineer must (for example water, terminals or the CASE)
targets.basis: Planet of Lana asymmetry (Mui fears water, Lana swims and moves boxes) and LN2's complementary split tasks.

targets.metric: Player-to-WOLF verbs
targets.target: Keep the existing 2 choice buttons plus context. If a 'suggest' verb is added, overload one button by tap vs hold rather than adding inputs
targets.basis: Lana's B tap/hold stay/follow; LN2's call plus hand-hold. Both shipped with one or two companion verbs.

targets.metric: Off-screen WOLF state
targets.target: Whenever WOLF is outside the frame in 1.5-2-screen rooms, show his direction plus one state (waiting / coming / scouting / refusing) by sound or a minimal edge cue
targets.basis: Lana's separated-companion icon shows direction and 'sitting or moving towards you'. Wider rooms will put WOLF off-camera often.

targets.metric: Visible contact before effect
targets.target: No WOLF-caused world change (relay, seam read, sentry draw) fires until his body or light visibly touches or faces the target
targets.basis: INSIDE Huddle: 'Boxes can not be lifted until a lifting arm actually touches them.'

targets.metric: WOLF servo and vocal audio density
targets.target: Stays readable with WOLF plus up to 3 machine sources (for example sentries) playing at once; cut layers rather than add
targets.basis: Planet of Lana's flying-robot sound became unreadable in groups until 'we just got rid of 80% of them' (Ameglio).

targets.metric: Optional WOLF-memory or lore finds (if adopted)
targets.target: Spread discoverability, with some finds easy and some hard, rather than all at one rate
targets.basis: Lana's 10 shrines range from 41.0% to 6.9% of Steam owners; Stray's 27 memories double as companion lore.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Replace m0_actor.gd's single follow rule (64 px gap, 220 speed) with a small typed intent-vote brain: Follow, Scout, Lead, Hold/Refuse and Protect each emit a desired x, facing and weight, and WOLF blends the winner. Keep every authored event deterministic.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: The INSIDE Huddle vote network produced 'perceived depth' from simple parts. It also gives the planned scouting and leading routes one place to live instead of per-room scripts.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Prerequisite for 'WOLF's own routes (scouting, leading)'. Keeps WOLF independent and is not a player command. Typed GDScript with deterministic events, no runtime LLM.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Add additive look-at (head and ears toward the engineer, the next station, a threat or the door) and a breathing or servo idle layer to WOLF. Make every decision show a pre-tell within about 0.5 s, extending the existing lean-toward and pull-back-from-relay reaction to the seam read, mirror check and sentry draw.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Playdead layers 'breathe' and 'look around' on locomotion. Limbo anticipates half a second ahead. Shacknews read Six's slow cueing as lag. The tell makes WOLF's slowness or refusal read as a choice.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: 'Real feel (breathing, look-at)'. AGENT.md: show WOLF's help, disagreement or refusal as authored action, not only text.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Gate each WOLF effect on visible contact: the relay closes only when he reaches it, and the seam reading starts only once he is at WOLF_SEAM_X and facing the seam.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: The INSIDE Huddle rule that a box can't lift until an arm touches it keeps simulation and perception in sync.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: AGENT.md: tie feedback to real state changes, with no fake consequences.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make WOLF's vocal and servo tone a location-clamped intensity (rising near the purge sentry, relaxing over seconds afterwards), and have the engineer audibly answer him at key beats.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: INSIDE clamps voice intensity by space ('proximity to danger') and relaxes it over time. Lana added voice because body language alone was not enough, and 'Mui answers her'.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Procedural audio direction and 'real feel'. Optional WOLF TTS stays subtitled and mutable per PROJECT_CONTEXT.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Design each new 1.5-2-screen room around one WOLF-only capability and one engineer-only necessity. For example, WOLF clears the height change or a vent and scouts ahead; only the engineer works terminals and carries the CASE. The engineer-only fallback is a longer or louder route, not a free bypass.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Planet of Lana and LN2 build puzzles from asymmetry. An explicit hard inability makes the fallback read as story rather than a safety net.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Wider rooms with one walkable height change; WOLF scouting; engineer-only path for essential objectives.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Implement scouting as WOLF going ahead off-camera, with his sound and posture reporting what he finds (sentry hum, freeze, ear-flat), plus a minimal direction-and-state cue when he is out of frame. Prefer a diegetic cue (his cyan light, audio panning) over a HUD icon.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Lana's off-screen companion icon; Lilja's off-camera 'sonic identifiers'. Lilja also warns that players over-read tells, so each cue must match WOLF's real detection.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: WOLF's own routes; wider rooms; no-HUD presentation; touch and controller parity.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Record the Service Junction bait choice (WOLF drawing the sentry at WOLF_BAIT_X: whether he volunteered, was asked or the engineer baited instead) as a second stable memory. Pay it off later with one authored line or a visible mark on his body, never a gate.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: The Lana bait playtest produced guilt and attachment, and Lana later flips the roles. LN's Nomes and INSIDE's Huddle bruises show cheap persistent-memory payoffs.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: 'WOLF remembers how the engineer treated him'. PRIVATE rules: only real observed choices, no automatic moral penalty, never break controls.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Keep the evidence CASE on the engineer. At most, let WOLF optionally carry a second item, and never essential evidence.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Stray puts the inventory and tool on B-12, and LN2 limits Six to a second item. If WOLF carries essentials, his refusal or a death-drop could strand progress.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Evidence CASE plus one tool; death drops unsecured evidence; engineer-only fallback.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Introduce any new WOLF behaviour (leading, scouting, a 'suggest' request) with a simple first room, and unlock it as a relationship beat. Frame it as a request WOLF can decline, never as a pointer command.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Lana unlocks waypointing after the bond forms and teaches abilities in a simpler first chapter. Its pointer still drew 'finicky' complaints, so snap targets must be generous.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Small playable steps. WOLF's agency is never a player command (see conflicts).

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Hands-on playtest WOLF's readability with fresh testers and no questions. Watch only whether they understand what WOLF chose and why. Do not claim validation from headless tests or stills.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Limbo's silent 'tissue testers' and the AGENT.md rule on proving game feel.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: AGENT.md: play the affected route before claiming feel or readability.

conflicts_with_decisions: Command model vs agency: Planet of Lana's stay/follow/pointer makes the companion an executor of commands, and the project forbids turning WOLF's agency into a player command. Copy only the input economy (tap vs hold, snapping, unlocking as the bond grows) and frame it as a request WOLF may decline. Nathanial decides.

Refusal frequency: the strongest reviewer praise (LN2's Six) is for reliability, and Mui never refuses at all. Frequent moment-to-moment refusals risk the 'fighting the underlying code' reading. The research argues refusals should be rare, authored, telegraphed story beats. It does not argue against the refusal decision itself.

Affection timing: Lana lets you 'pet Mui at any time' as idle bonding, but the locked direction makes sunrise petting an earned payoff and not a mechanic. The research supports constant small idle business. Whether that includes player-initiated touch before sunrise is Nathanial's call.

HUD purity vs wider rooms: Playdead and Tarsier ship zero HUD, but Lana breaks that rule only for an off-screen companion locator. 1.5-2-screen rooms plus WOLF scouting will push toward a locator. Keep it diegetic or audio-first if possible.

Companion-dependence vs engineer-only fallback: Lana's bond comes partly from Mui being required, and the bait guilt works because the player had to use her. A fallback that is strictly easier could dilute that. Keep the fallback viable but costlier (time or noise), never punitive. That is a design inference, not a sourced finding.

Leading and scouting are an evidence gap: no dossier I received documents a shipped companion that scouts ahead or leads a route. The Stray dossier, the likeliest source (B-12), was truncated. The decision is unvalidated by this corpus and needs prototyping and hands-on play.

If the CASE or the tool were carried by WOLF (the Stray B-12 precedent), his refusal or the death-drop rule could block essential progress, which conflicts with the engineer-only fallback. The research supports keeping essential evidence on the engineer.

syn.dimension: LEVEL DESIGN AND CAMERA for cinematic side-views: room width and traversal time, height changes without a jump, reveals and landmarks, foreground layers, camera framing and zoom, look-ahead, transitions and doorways. (Corpus note: the Stray dossier reached me truncated after its source list. Its level and camera fields never arrived, so the only Stray item used here is the producer's documented rejection of fail-able jumps, which appears in the dossier's summary. Current-state facts were read from apps/game: ROOM_WIDTH 960 px (scripts/room_depth.gd:15); GAMEPLAY_ZOOM 1.35 on a 960x540 viewport, so the view is 711 px wide (scripts/main.gd:184-185); the camera centres on the engineer's x with smoothing 4.0 and no look-ahead, clamped to a hard-coded 960 (scripts/main.gd:392-401); WALK_SPEED 190 px/s (scripts/m0_actor.gd:11); parallax backdrop 0.9 and near 1.15 (room_depth.gd:17-18); sentry SIGHT_RANGE 180 px, CHASE_SPEED 230 px/s (scripts/sentry_brain.gd).)

principles.principle: The play camera points into the scene and only scrolls. Framing is authored like a stage, not driven by the player.
principles.evidence: INSIDE GDC 2016 rendering talk (Gjøl & Svendsen, slides with notes): the camera "typically points inwards to the screen and only scrolls". The team relied on this enough to zero the x of screen-space reflection rays. Planet of Lana (Stjärnljus, Game Developer art Q&A): they chose a fixed side view because "it's much easier to control the camera framing and stage of each scene." Counter-evidence: for Little Nightmares II, Lucas Roussel (Bandai Namco Europe producer, i.e. the publisher, not Tarsier) said "We also reworked the camera to offer more top views and in-depth character traversals". So authored variety at specific beats is legitimate. Restraint: Playdead's VFX talk is titled "Turn it Down 90%". The only documented ambient camera motion is LN1's ship camera, which "very subtly rocks along with the motion of water" (level designer Matthew Compher via Push Square).

principles.principle: Sell depth with fog, value and silhouettes rather than with many parallax layers. Let bright lights cut through the fog as landmarks.
principles.evidence: INSIDE: "Many of the initial scenes in the game were literally just fog + silhouettes"; "Simple linear fog!" clamped "to a max-value to enable bright objects to 'bleed through'". Depth of field applies only "to things behind the gameplay plane" underwater, and "you hardly notice the parallax or depth after a certain point" (water edge 6-12 m from the near clip). Planet of Lana: black foreground silhouettes give "the feeling of looking into a set-piece or theater stage", and hidden shadow planes let 2D props cast 3D-looking shadows. Limbo is monochrome silhouettes with focused lighting. Phone warning: INSIDE on iPhone was still "so dark that I can't tell whether there is something to interact with" (iMore), even after Playdead fitted a brightness curve to "Get it BRIGHT enough".

principles.principle: Keep the playable space on one readable plane and ground the characters to it. Ambiguous depth kills players.
