principles.evidence: Little Nightmares' shallow-Z dollhouse rooms produced the series' most repeated complaint. Push Square LN1: "you'll inevitably misjudge your position and perish." For LN2, PlayStation LifeStyle (per the fact-check, not Push Square): "The small Z-axis means it's really easy to get slightly the wrong angle when jumping". INSIDE anchors shadow decals "to boy's feet... giving a very OOT blob shadow look" and puts AO and shadow decals under boxes and platforms. Planet of Lana uses shadow planes to ground flat props.

principles.principle: Height changes must never ask for precise positioning. Execution should be easy, and the challenge should sit in the decision.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana (RPS): "When approaching ledges, Lana can't jump up to them if she's too close, meaning I had to move away from the platform to find the sweet spot". Push Square: "animation fidelity over fluidity" causes missed jumps. Limbo (Carlsen, direct quote): "It's very important that the correct solution is fairly easy to execute". Per the Stray dossier's summary, the producer documented trying and rejecting fail-able jumps (details were truncated in my corpus). Wishfully dropped grid movement after about half a year, following publisher feedback during pitching that they found "harsh but ultimately made a lot of sense".

principles.principle: Size a room by its content, not its width. One puzzle or threat per room; walking without a decision reads as filler; vary the pace on purpose.
principles.evidence: INSIDE (Unite 2016): "Each Puzzle span around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay", built as Gameplay, Environment and Backdrop sub-scenes. Planet of Lana: Nintendo Life flagged "quite a bit of uneventful running" and RPS called the middle act "middle of the road", but RPS praised that solving a puzzle meant "the game would quickly move on to the next one". For the sequel Stjärnljus said "varying the pace allows the more intense sequences to land with greater impact" while keeping "space for stillness", and art director Chan changed biome sub-areas "so you don't feel like this repetitiveness". Little Nightmares makes each chapter one antagonist's domain. Mervik: "get in and got out". Limbo cut about 70% of its ideas (Jensen and Patti).

principles.principle: Teach and steer by placement. Show the goal or landmark before the player has to act on it, and use position to stop players fixating on the wrong thing.
principles.evidence: Game Developer's report of Carlsen's GDC Europe 2010 talk (paraphrase, not a direct quote, per the fact-check) says Limbo teaches by forcing the player next to a pullable object with a visual cue, uses positioning to keep players off wrong elements, and threw out puzzles that let wrong approaches feel viable. Planet of Lana's developer commentary points at vistas such as the robot base "far in the distance" as goal-setting (commentary quotes are UNVERIFIED this pass because the captions returned HTTP 429). Little Nightmares reads scale through props at the antagonist's size. INSIDE's fog clamp lets headlights and spotlights read through haze.

principles.principle: Frame less than the room contains, and cover what is off-screen with sound or an edge cue, especially for the companion.
principles.evidence: Lilja (The Sound Architect): "The camera in the game doesn't always allow for you to see the enemy in a room, so the breathing helps to indicate their presence". Sounds that pass through walls became "sonic identifiers". Lilja calls the breathing-as-state idea something "we tried", and players over-read it as smell. Planet of Lana (Wishfully, Xbox Wire): when Lana and Mui are separated, "an animated icon dynamically pops up, showing you which direction Mui is located in and what her status is". The sequel lets Lana "point Mui all across the screen" (The Game Slayer).

principles.principle: Transitions are seamless. No loading screens and no streaming pops; death reloads only the mutable gameplay layer of the current room.
principles.evidence: INSIDE's Unite 2016 goals were "Game can be completed from start to end without loading screens" and "No visual artifacts caused by streaming in content". Its 250 sub-scenes split into immutable Environment and Backdrop scenes and mutable Gameplay scenes, with "Only reload 'dirty' Gameplay scenes at respawn". The audio "scene change" creates "the illusion of no time passing". LN2 (Roussel, publisher): "An efficient streaming system allows quicker loading times when players die". On Xbox Series X|S it gives "a nearly immediate respawn" (corrected platform). Planet of Lana is strictly linear, left to right, with no backtracking.

principles.principle: Checkpoints are dense enough that a death costs seconds, not a room.
principles.evidence: HG101 (reviewer estimate, not a measurement): Limbo's checkpoints stop "even the most irritating of deaths from setting you back more than twenty-ish seconds of progress." Wikipedia supports only unlimited checkpoint restarts. Family Gaming Database rates Planet of Lana 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints' (less than 5 minutes lost). Push Square LN2 says "restarts are rapid", yet scenes still had to be replayed "at least twice" because traps could not be read on the first pass. Planet of Lana's 'Flawless' achievement is 2.4% of Steam owners, about 6.5% of finishers, so nearly everyone dies.

principles.principle: Optional content lives in short spatial detours off the critical path, with deliberately varied difficulty to find.
principles.evidence: Little Nightmares puts collectibles (Nomes, statues, LN2's 18 Glitching Remains) mostly in side spaces reached by dragging boxes, crawling vents or climbing stacked cages. Planet of Lana's 10 shrines run from 41.0% (shrine 2) down to 6.9% (shrine 4) of Steam owners.

principles.principle: Chase and threat spaces end on a hard spatial beat the pursuer physically cannot pass.
principles.evidence: In Little Nightmares, chases are scripted corridor sprints that end at a spatial limit: Six "jumps to another balcony beyond the Guests' reach", and gaps "too small" for adults serve as hiding grammar (Fandom on Nomes). Tarsier cut a whistle mechanic for herding enemies (Compher via Push Square). INSIDE has no published chase tuning (dog speed and catch distance are UNVERIFIED).

targets.metric: Gameplay time per room (entry to exit, including solving)
targets.target: About 1-3 minutes for a room that holds one puzzle or threat. Width follows from the content, not the other way round.
targets.basis: INSIDE Unite 2016: "Each Puzzle span around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay" (verified). Applying it to WOLF rooms is a derived mapping.

targets.metric: Pure walking time across a planned room
targets.target: At the current 1.35 zoom the view is 711 px wide. 1.5 views = 1067 px, about 5.6 s at 190 px/s; 2 views = 1422 px, about 7.5 s. Proposed: no stretch longer than one view (about 3.7 s) without a decision, a WOLF beat, an interactable or a reveal.
targets.basis: Arithmetic from WALK_SPEED 190 and GAMEPLAY_ZOOM 1.35 in apps/game. The one-view rule is DERIVED from Planet of Lana's "uneventful running" criticism (Nintendo Life), not a published number. Validate it by play.

targets.metric: Visible loading screens or fades between rooms
targets.target: 0 on the critical path. Doorways are walk-through, and no streaming pop is visible.
targets.basis: INSIDE Unite 2016 goals: "without loading screens" and "No visual artifacts caused by streaming in content".

targets.metric: Progress replayed after a death
targets.target: At most about 20 s of replay per death (put a safe point inside the same room before each lethal hazard). Hard ceiling under 5 minutes.
targets.basis: HG101 reviewer estimate for Limbo ("twenty-ish seconds"); FGDB's definition of frequent checkpoints (under 5 minutes lost) for Planet of Lana. Both are soft benchmarks, not measured studio targets.

targets.metric: Respawn duration (death to control)
targets.target: Near-immediate, with room tone continuous across it. Exact seconds UNVERIFIED in the corpus, so time it in WOLF builds and compare by play.
targets.basis: INSIDE's scene-change pipeline ("illusion of no time passing"); LN2 "nearly immediate respawn" (Roussel, Xbox Series X|S). The dossier's INSIDE All Deaths speedrun inference was struck as overstated by the fact-check.

targets.metric: Fail-able jumps or positional sweet spots on height changes
targets.target: 0. Every height change is a walkable step or ramp, or a USE climb that accepts the whole approach zone.
targets.basis: Planet of Lana ledge sweet-spot complaint (RPS); Carlsen "correct solution is fairly easy to execute"; Stray producer's rejection of fail-able jumps (from the dossier summary, details truncated).

targets.metric: Play-camera zoom changes during free movement
targets.target: 0 changes during free movement (hold 1.35). Zoom or reframe only on authored beats, such as a room-entry reveal, a choice or a cutscene.
targets.basis: INSIDE "only scrolls"; Planet of Lana fixed side view for staging. The LN2 camera rework is the counter-case for authored variety.

targets.metric: Off-screen companion coverage
targets.target: Every WOLF state while he is outside the view (scouting, leading, refusing, waiting) has a cue. Audio first, plus a direction and status cue at the view edge.
targets.basis: Planet of Lana off-screen Mui icon ("which direction Mui is located in and what her status is"); Little Nightmares off-screen breathing and sonic identifiers.

targets.metric: Rendered-route screenshot QA density
targets.target: One capture per fixed distance along a recorded route, in both desktop and touch layouts. Playdead used 5 m, about 1300 locations for all of INSIDE. A WOLF equivalent of roughly a quarter view (about 180 px) is DERIVED.
targets.basis: INSIDE Shipping on iOS slides: screenshots "every 5 meters from a playthrough", about 1300 locations, diffed against references.

targets.metric: Optional-detour find rates (if optional evidence is placed off-route)
targets.target: A spread from easy (around 40%) to hard (under 10%), not a uniform difficulty.
targets.basis: Planet of Lana shrine unlocks of 41.0% down to 6.9% of Steam owners (verified). These are owner-based percentages, not starter-based.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make room width per room instead of global. ROOM_WIDTH is a 960 const (scripts/room_depth.gd:15), and the camera clamp hard-codes 960.0 (scripts/main.gd:394). Have each room export its width (1067-1422 px for 1.5-2 views at zoom 1.35) and feed it to the clamp, the mid and near plates and the dust bounds.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: The wider-room decision can't ship while the clamp and plates assume one 960 px room (currently 1.35 views wide, about 5 s to walk). INSIDE's model ties a room to a content unit, so per-room width is the right abstraction.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Wider rooms (1.5-2 screens). Keeps the tighter-zoom direction at 1.35.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Plan each new room on paper as beats per view-width before building it: entry reveal (goal or landmark visible), one decision or WOLF beat per view, the height change, the threat or puzzle, and the exit doorway. Cut any view-width that has no beat.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Planet of Lana's main pacing criticism was "uneventful running". INSIDE sizes rooms by 1-3 minutes of puzzle, and Limbo cut about 70% of its ideas. Wider rooms raise pure walking from about 5 s to 5.6-7.5 s, so the extra width has to carry content.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Wider rooms; WOLF's own routes (a scouting or leading beat can fill a view-width).

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Build the one height change per room as a walkable step or ramp, or as a USE climb whose trigger accepts the whole approach. Keep both levels on the same gameplay plane (no Z offset), and add a soft contact shadow under the engineer's and WOLF's feet.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Little Nightmares' shallow Z and Planet of Lana's ledge sweet spot are the most cited deaths and frustrations in the corpus. INSIDE and Lana ground characters with foot shadow decals and shadow planes. WOLF's input has no jump, so execution must be trivial.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: One walkable height change per room; hold-to-move plus one USE; phone touch.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make doorways walk-through. The camera keeps scrolling across the threshold without a fade. Split each room into an immutable environment and backdrop part and a mutable gameplay part, so a death reloads only the gameplay part while room tone keeps playing.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: INSIDE's stated goals (no loading screens, no streaming pops, reload only dirty gameplay scenes, audio "illusion of no time passing").
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Walk-through doorways; death model; procedural room tone.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Place a safe point inside each room before every lethal hazard (purge sentry lane, tank drop) so a death replays about 20 s at most, and never forces a re-walk through a doorway.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Limbo (about 20 s, a reviewer estimate), Planet of Lana (FGDB frequent checkpoints) and LN2 (rapid restarts) all keep deaths cheap. With a resource cost on death, long replays make the penalty compound.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Death drops unsecured evidence; safe points secure it (see conflicts).

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Hold the play zoom at 1.35 during free movement. Allow authored reframes only at room-entry reveals, choices and cutscenes, using the tween pattern the intro already uses (1.8 to 1.95).
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: INSIDE "only scrolls", and Planet of Lana chose a fixed view for staging. LN2's camera rework shows authored variety at beats is fine. Dynamic zoom while moving has no support in the corpus.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Tighter zoom; dimensional or 2.5D presentation.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Add off-screen WOLF cues for the new routes: a positional servo, breath or footstep sound first, then a small direction and status cue at the view edge whenever WOLF is outside the 711 px view (scouting ahead, leading, waiting, refusing).
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: With 1.5-2 view rooms and WOLF routes, WOLF will often be off-camera. Planet of Lana solved separation with an animated direction and status icon, and Little Nightmares covers off-camera actors with distinctive sounds.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: WOLF's own routes (scouting, leading); WOLF independent companion; real feel (room tone). This tensions with Playdead-style zero HUD; see conflicts.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Prototype a small look-ahead offset (camera shifted toward the facing or move direction) against the current centred follow (smoothing 4.0). Accept it only after hands-on play on desktop, controller and phone.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: No dossier publishes camera look-ahead values; this is an evidence gap, not a recommendation from the research. Wider rooms with a threat ahead (sentry sight 180 px against a 356 px half-view) make look-ahead plausible, but it has to be validated by play.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Wider rooms; tighter zoom.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make the goal of each room a fog-cutting light visible from the entry (exit bolt lamp, sentry beam, copy-station glow), and use linear haze clamped so emissives stay bright, instead of adding more parallax layers to the existing 0.9 and 1.15 pair.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: INSIDE builds depth from fog plus silhouettes with a max-clamped fog so bright objects "bleed through", and notes that parallax stops reading past a point. Planet of Lana uses distant vistas as goals (commentary quotes UNVERIFIED).
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Painterly 2.5D layered parallax; wider rooms (a landmark visible across 2 views).

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Keep the near foreground layer as dark, low-detail silhouettes at the frame edges. Never let it cross the engineer, WOLF, interactables or choice and touch buttons at 1.35, and check readability at phone brightness.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Planet of Lana uses black foreground silhouettes as a theater-stage frame. INSIDE's iOS image was called too dark to see interactables (iMore), and reviewers complained that thumbs covered the art (AppUnwrapper).
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Layered parallax rooms; phone touch target.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Design any purge-sentry chase so it ends at a spatial beat the sentry cannot cross (the existing rubble line and alcove are the grammar). In a wider room, keep the distance from detection to safety short enough that the sentry's 230 px/s chase can't catch a 190 px/s engineer who reacts on first sight.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Little Nightmares chases end at a limit the pursuer cannot pass (balcony out of reach, gaps too small). The current RUBBLE_X and cover alcove already follow this; wider rooms must not stretch it.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Wider rooms; Service Junction sentry; death model.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Use the height change to host optional evidence detours off the critical path, with deliberately varied difficulty to find.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Little Nightmares places collectibles in side spaces reached by boxes, vents and cages; Planet of Lana's shrine find rates run 41% to 6.9%.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Evidence CASE inventory; one height change per room.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Add route-replay screenshot QA: a recorded input route through each room, captured at fixed spacing in desktop and touch layouts, diffed against references.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: INSIDE captured every 5 m (about 1300 locations) to keep parity across platforms. WOLF already has rendered framing tests (room_depth_test, sentry_test); a route sweep catches regressions in parallax, foreground and clamp as rooms widen.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Honest test claims (rendered stills versus hands-on play); phone target.

conflicts_with_decisions: Death drops unsecured evidence: every game in the corpus (Limbo, INSIDE, Little Nightmares I and II, Planet of Lana) attaches zero resource cost to death and leans on dense checkpoints. Level layout therefore has to compensate: a safe point inside each room before every hazard, and replay of about 20 s or less. Otherwise the drop compounds with re-walking wider rooms. Nathanial decides whether the penalty stays.

Wider rooms (1.5-2 screens): no source argues for width as such. INSIDE sizes rooms by puzzle content (about 100 m, 1-3 min), and Planet of Lana was criticised for "uneventful running". Width is supported only if every view-width carries a beat; otherwise the research argues for narrower rooms.

WOLF's own routes (scouting, leading) versus no HUD: Playdead and Tarsier ship zero HUD, but Planet of Lana had to add an off-screen direction and status icon once the companion could be separated. Wider rooms plus WOLF routes will likely need that icon or a strong audio substitute. Nathanial decides how diegetic it must be.

Fixed camera versus variety: INSIDE and Planet of Lana argue for a fixed, scroll-only play camera, while the LN2 camera rework (publisher producer's account) added top views and in-depth traversal. The recommendation is fixed in play with authored reframes, but this is a judgement call.
Look-ahead: none of the dossiers documents camera look-ahead, so any look-ahead is untested by this research and must be validated by hands-on play before anyone claims it improves feel.

Height change readability versus dimensional 2.5D: if the walkable height change uses any depth offset to look 2.5D, Little Nightmares' shallow-Z deaths argue against it; keep the gameplay on a single plane and let only the art suggest depth.

syn.dimension: Death, checkpoints and save points: spacing in seconds, presentation of death, what is lost, safe rooms and their rituals, corpse runs and recoverable losses, quitting. Corpus used: Playdead (Limbo, INSIDE), Tarsier (Little Nightmares 1 and 2), Wishfully (Planet of Lana), BlueTwelve (Stray). The Stray dossier was cut off in the input after its why_relevant field, so only that summary is used for Stray. COVERAGE GAP: no game in this corpus has a corpse run, a recoverable loss, a resource cost on death, a manual save, or a safe room with a ritual. All four studios use free, automatic, near-instant retry. For those sub-topics, every recommendation below is a design inference held to the corpus's legibility rules. None is a shipped precedent. Current WOLF//OVERRIDE state was read from apps/game/scripts/main.gd and m0_state.gd, read-only. _fail_beat: hit-stop 0.06 s, red flash, controls off 0.7 s (0.22 s of that is the tilt reaction), fade-out 0.4 s, restore, fade-in 0.35 s, so about 1.45 s from hit to control. Autosave A fires on entering the Junction and autosave B when the door is blown. A manual SAFE POINT station saves and plays WOLF's memory callback. A knockdown 'never touches' Memory or Records flags, so evidence is never lost today. Return to Title shows a warning. When the app goes to the background on mobile, the game pauses but does not save.

principles.principle: Death is a teaching beat, not a punishment. In every game in the corpus, the only thing death costs is a short replay.
principles.evidence: Carlsen, GDC Europe 2010, as reported by Game Developer (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/gdc-europe-i-limbo-i-s-carlsen-on-making-players-your-worst-enemy-and-your-best-friend): "You could call it a learning-by-dying game", "You don't ever really get penalized for dying, it's just how the game plays" and "It's important that you also treat him nicely". The reporter's own paraphrase, not Carlsen's words, is to make the player learn from deaths and make them look entertaining. Wikipedia (Limbo) records unlimited checkpoint restarts, which reviewers found 'plentiful'. LN1/LN2, Planet of Lana and Stray likewise lose nothing on death except replay time. INSIDE's collectibles (orbs) and LN's collectibles persist across death.

principles.principle: Keep checkpoints close: about 20 seconds of lost progress is the reference figure, with at most one 1-3 minute puzzle chunk between restore points.
principles.evidence: Hardcore Gaming 101 (https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/limbo/) says Limbo's checkpoints keep "even the most irritating of deaths from setting you back more than twenty-ish seconds of progress". This is a reviewer's estimate, not a measurement. In INSIDE's Unite 2016 slides (https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1dew0TynVmtQf8OMLEz_YtRxK32a_0SAZU9-vgyMRPlA/edit), "Each Puzzle span around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay", and death reloads only 'dirty' Gameplay sub-scenes. For Planet of Lana, Push Square and Nintendo Life both report 'frequent checkpoints'. The Family Gaming Database tags it 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints', which it defines as losing less than 5 minutes (https://www.familygamingdatabase.com/accessibility/Planet+of+Lana). PlayStation LifeStyle on LN2: checkpointing is 'automatic and very generous'. The Stray dossier summary says 'very short checkpoints' but gives no number. A God is a Geek line that Lana 'saves as soon as one section of a larger puzzle has been completed' is UNVERIFIED.

principles.principle: Make the respawn feel like no time passed. Room tone and music carry on underneath, only the room that changed is reloaded, and the load itself is never shown.
principles.evidence: INSIDE, Wwise Tour 2016 (https://github.com/playdeadgames/publications/blob/master/INSIDE/schmid-Wwise_2016-INSIDE_Audio.pdf): "When main character dies, scenes are reloaded. Audio should retain state and continue during load". The event chain runs death, prepare_spawn_[savepoint], pause Wwise updates, unload, load, post spawn_[savepoint], resume. Audio commands queued during the load all fire at once, which "Creates the illusion of no time passing during scene change". This needed a 2 MB command queue and a 1024-sample buffer, because 512 glitched. Unite 2016 adds: "Only reload 'dirty' Gameplay scenes at respawn". For LN2, Lucas Roussel (Lead Producer, Bandai Namco Europe, i.e. the publisher, not Tarsier) told Xbox Wire (https://news.xbox.com/en-us/2021/03/12/little-nightmares-2-interview/) that "An efficient streaming system allows quicker loading times when players die", and that on Xbox Series X|S there is "a nearly immediate respawn which is a notable improvement over the original Little Nightmares". No source in the corpus gives a measured respawn duration in seconds. The per-death figure that had been inferred from INSIDE speedruns was withdrawn by the fact-check and is UNVERIFIED.

principles.principle: A death has to be readable before it happens. Instant failure is tolerated only when the threat was telegraphed and the correct solution is easy to execute. Unreadable one-shot traps were these games' most-cited complaint.
principles.evidence: Carlsen (Game Developer report): "It's very important that the correct solution is fairly easy to execute". Wikipedia, citing Playdead, says Limbo's gruesome deaths steer players away from solutions that cannot work. PlayStation LifeStyle on LN2 (https://www.playstationlifestyle.net/review/843676-little-nightmares-2-review/): "Instant death is a frequent recurrence and never ceases to be frustrating, especially during chase sequences". Push Square on LN2 (https://www.pushsquare.com/reviews/ps4/little_nightmares_ii): "restarts are rapid" but players had to "replay each scene at least twice" because of unpredictable traps, and in combat "if you miss it's instant death". Push Square on Planet of Lana (https://www.pushsquare.com/reviews/ps5/planet-of-lana): "insta-fail stealth grates". Push Square on LN1 blames depth misjudgement: "you'll inevitably misjudge your position and perish". Lilja (https://thesoundarchitect.co.uk/?p=18494) gave threats audible tells, for example "if an enemy screams, it's because they are alerted". He framed breathing-as-state as an experiment that players over-read.

principles.principle: Nearly every player dies. A no-death run should be an optional mastery tier, not the normal way to play.
principles.evidence: Steam global achievements. Planet of Lana 'Flawless' (finish without dying): 2.4% of owners, about 6.5% of players who finish (https://steamcommunity.com/stats/1608230/achievements). LN1 'Hard to the Core': 1.6%, the rarest achievement, exact condition UNVERIFIED (https://steamcommunity.com/stats/424840/achievements). Limbo has an achievement for finishing "with five or fewer deaths" (Wikipedia). INSIDE has an 'All Deaths' speedrun category, which shows players treat deaths as content. LN1 also had a 'Nine Deaths of Six' trailer (Fandom, secondary).

principles.principle: Present death briefly and in the game's own tone. Haptics and audio carry the threat, and no game in the corpus puts a death screen, death counter or UI in the way.
principles.evidence: There is no HUD in Limbo, INSIDE, LN1/2 or Planet of Lana. Lana shows no lives and no death counter, and its QTEs can be turned off. Planet of Lana's deaths are quick and varied: "chomped by an alien, zapped by a robot, or accidentally yeet yourself off the side of a cliff" (RPS, https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/planet-of-lana-review). On LN1's tone, Mervik told PCGamesN: "We knew we didn't want to go down that well-trodden path of gore and violence and jump scares". In LN1 chases, the controller pulses with the heartbeat (Push Square). The Stray summary describes exactly two kinds of death (Zurk swarm, Sentinel detection), so the death vocabulary is small and learnable.

principles.principle: A chapter or checkpoint select must never strand anything persistent.
principles.evidence: INSIDE's checkpoint Load menu is used for orb hunting. Its exact checkpoint count is UNVERIFIED. LN collectibles are tracked per chapter through Chapter Select, but Fandom notes one Nome area cannot be reached if the chapter is started from Chapter Select. This is the one documented failure where a reload breaks persistent progress.

principles.principle: Many players quit early, so the first shared room should be easy, and losses should not come before the player has learned the threat.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana Steam funnel, corrected: about 21% of players who start never unlock 'A new friend' (meeting the companion), and about 40% of starters finish. 'Point of no return' is at 37.4%. Wishfully says the first chapter with both characters is "on the simpler side. And as we move on in the game, the difficulty ramps up" (developer commentary video, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DcESS2l4RY4; the captions could not be re-checked, so the wording is UNVERIFIED). The corpus never ties quitting to death specifically. That link is UNVERIFIED.

principles.principle: Safe rooms, save rituals and corpse runs have no precedent in this corpus. The nearest material is quiet-state audio and per-savepoint audio states.
principles.evidence: INSIDE names its audio events per savepoint (prepare_spawn_[savepoint], spawn_[savepoint]), so each restore point can have its own sound state. Planet of Lana's 'listening to the world' system adds new ambience layers "if the player stays still", which "meant that we had to design double the amount of ambiences for each biome" (Ameglio, https://www.asoundeffect.com/planet-of-lana-game-audio/). Lilja's 'listening state' pulls "all background sounds and music" down to a minimum. No game in the corpus has a save room, a typewriter-style ritual, dropped resources or a recovery trip. Any WOLF//OVERRIDE design there is original and has not been validated by these sources.

targets.metric: Gameplay progress lost per death (position plus puzzle state)
targets.target: About 20 s or less in normal play. Never more than one puzzle chunk (1-3 min). Hard ceiling under 5 min.
targets.basis: Limbo, HG101 reviewer estimate: 'twenty-ish seconds'. INSIDE: puzzle sub-scenes of 1-3 min, with death reloading only that sub-scene (Unite 2016). FGDB's definition of 'frequent checkpoints' (Planet of Lana): under 5 min lost. The 20 s figure is a reviewer estimate, not measured.

targets.metric: Time from lethal hit to regaining control
targets.target: No longer than the current ~1.45 s (0.7 s controls off including the 0.22 s reaction, 0.4 s fade out, 0.35 s fade in). Do not lengthen it, and add no death screen.
targets.basis: INSIDE aims for 'the illusion of no time passing'. LN2 on Series X|S is described as a 'nearly immediate respawn'. No source in the corpus gives a measured respawn time (UNVERIFIED). This target keeps the current value rather than borrowing one from a shipped game.

targets.metric: Audio continuity across a knockdown
targets.target: Room tone and any active music are never cut or restarted by the restore. State changes are queued and applied at fade-in.
targets.basis: INSIDE Wwise Tour 2016: 'Audio should retain state and continue during load', with commands batched until the scene change completes.

targets.metric: Restore points per wide room (1.5-2 screens)
targets.target: At least one autosave at room entry plus one after each completed beat, so each beat inside the room is its own restore point.
targets.basis: Combines INSIDE's ~100 m / 1-3 min per puzzle with the ~20 s loss target. Derived, not taken from a source.

targets.metric: First-encounter readability of each lethal hazard
targets.target: Every lethal hazard (door blast zone, purge sentry, future traps) has an audio or animation tell before it can kill on first contact. Playtest goal: fresh players never need to 'replay each scene at least twice' just to learn what killed them.
targets.basis: Carlsen: the correct solution must be easy to execute. Push Square's criticism of LN2's 'at least twice'. Playdead's silent 'tissue testers' (about 150 one-time testers) watched only for solvability.

targets.metric: Share of players expected to die at least once
targets.target: Plan for close to 100%. Treat a no-death clear as an opt-in tier reached by a single-digit percentage of players.
targets.basis: Planet of Lana Flawless: 2.4% of owners, about 6.5% of finishers. LN1 rarest achievement: 1.6%.

targets.metric: Evidence at risk per death (planned drop model)
targets.target: No figure is supported by the corpus. Proposed working cap, unvalidated: only evidence copied since the last safe point in the current room, recoverable in the same room.
targets.basis: None of the corpus games attaches any resource cost to death. This is a design inference to be validated by playtest.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Keep the _fail_beat timing (about 1.45 s from hit to control) as a ceiling. Make the knockdown a 'scene change' as INSIDE does: room-tone and junction loops keep playing through the fade, _restore_beat applies only the gameplay-state diff, and any sound changes are queued until fade-in. _return_to_title currently calls _stop_junction_loops. Verify by playing whether _load_game or _sync_scene in the knockdown path also restarts or cuts loops.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: INSIDE engineered respawn audio continuity to create 'the illusion of no time passing'. LN2's publisher sold near-instant respawn as an improvement. A planned evidence penalty makes any added wait feel like a second punishment.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Directly supports the 'real feel: room tone' decision and the planned death model. No new systems needed: AudioStreamPlayers live outside the restored state, and _restore_beat already restores the snapshot in place.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Give each knockdown cause its own readable reaction and line: blast versus sentry, using the existing reason string plus a distinct sound or animation. Before any hazard can kill, check that it has a tell (WOLF's 'Don't stand in front of it' and the hiss already do this for the door). For the purge sentry, add an audible idle or alert state that changes before it fires.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Carlsen and Wikipedia: Limbo's deaths teach which solution is wrong. LN2 and Lana were criticised for unpredictable or insta-fail deaths. Lilja used audible enemy state because the camera hides threats, and WOLF//OVERRIDE's wider rooms will do the same.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Fits the impact kit (one flash, hit-stop, thud and rumble path already exists) and the wider-rooms decision. Keep it to animation and audio, with no alert icons, which matches the no-HUD precedent and AGENT.md's 'tie feedback to real state changes'.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: In the 1.5-2 screen rooms, autosave at room entry and after every completed beat. The Junction already does this with autosave A at entry and B at door down. Extend the pattern so no beat inside a room costs more than about 20 s of replay. Doorways get an autosave, not a load screen.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Limbo's 'twenty-ish seconds', INSIDE's 1-3 min puzzle chunks with only the dirty room reloaded, and the 'frequent checkpoints' praise for Planet of Lana.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Fits the wider rooms, the one height change per room and the walk-through doorways. _save_progress and _mark_beat already provide the beat-snapshot mechanism.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: If evidence drop is kept, use two tiers. Autosaves restore position and puzzle state for free and often. SAFE POINT stations are the only place evidence becomes 'secured'. On a knockdown, only evidence copied since the last safe point is dropped, and it should sit visibly at or near the knockdown spot in the same room so it can be picked up again. It must never be destroyed. Never drop evidence in the first room, and never drop evidence copied less than one beat earlier.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: No corpus game charges anything for death, and their designers treat free death as the basis of 'learning by dying'. If something is lost, the dossiers agree the cost should be the evidence and never the wait (LN dossier), and the Carlsen legibility rules should still apply (Playdead dossier). A drop the player can recover keeps death informative. Planet of Lana's early funnel loss (about 21% of starters) argues against an early penalty.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Puts the decided death model ('dying drops unsecured evidence, safe points secure it') and the evidence CASE inventory into practice. This is a change from today's code, where a knockdown never touches Records flags and copies such as purge_trace_preserved are effectively secured when made. That needs a new 'unsecured' state per CASE item. The recovery-in-room part has no precedent in the corpus and must be playtested.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make the SAFE POINT a quiet audio state, not a menu. When the engineer reaches it, duck the room tone (Lilja's listening-state approach, or Lana's stand-still layers) and play one diegetic 'secured' sound or animation per CASE item banked, then WOLF's existing memory callback. Give each savepoint its own spawn audio state, as INSIDE's spawn_[savepoint] events do.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: The corpus has no safe-room ritual. The closest tools are INSIDE's per-savepoint audio events, Planet of Lana's reward ambience for standing still, and LN's listening-state duck. These give a ritual without adding UI.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Builds on the current _interact_checkpoint, which already saves and plays WOLF's callback. It also serves the WOLF-memory gating and room-tone decisions. This is original design with no precedent in the corpus, so call it unvalidated until the route is played.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Never let WOLF's refusal or his scouting or leading routes cause the engineer's knockdown or evidence loss without an equally readable engineer-only alternative in view. If WOLF leads into danger, he shows the threat (head turn, growl) before it becomes lethal.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Reviewers praised LN2's Six because she was reliable and never an escort mission. Roussel framed her unreliability as story ('never fully in charge of Six' destiny'), not as moment-to-moment risk. Shacknews criticised Six's delayed cues.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Fits 'WOLF's own routes' and 'every essential objective keeps an engineer-only path'. The wolf_will_bait rule already keeps the engineer-only timing path.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Decide what quitting does under the drop model. Return to Title and app backgrounding currently pause or warn but do not save unsecured progress. Proposal: quitting returns the player to the last autosave with unsecured evidence placed where the last knockdown would leave it, so quitting is neither an exploit nor a harsher penalty. Any future chapter or checkpoint select must keep secured evidence and still let the player reach every optional evidence spot.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: LN's Chapter Select made one collectible area unreachable, the only documented reload failure in the corpus. INSIDE's Load menu keeps orb progress per checkpoint. The corpus does not cover quit-scumming. Mobile versions of LN and Lana add cloud save, but the dossiers do not document suspend saves.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Fits the evidence CASE and the phone-touch target. The ReturnWarning and NOTIFICATION_APPLICATION_PAUSED handling are the hook points. Most of this has no direct evidence, so treat it as a rules decision for Nathanial.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Add an optional low-death or no-evidence-lost recognition (an achievement or an end-of-chapter line from WOLF) instead of making flawless play necessary.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Limbo's 'five or fewer deaths' achievement, Lana's Flawless at 2.4% of owners, and LN1's rarest achievement at 1.6% show that this kind of mastery is a small, opt-in tier.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Fits WOLF's memory: he can remember a careful run. Adds no essential gate.

conflicts_with_decisions: Evidence drop on death has no precedent in this corpus. Limbo, INSIDE, LN1, LN2, Planet of Lana and Stray all charge nothing for death except replay time. Playdead's tuning ('You don't ever really get penalized for dying') assumes death is free and frequent. LN2 and Lana drew criticism ('never ceases to be frustrating', 'insta-fail stealth grates') even with nothing lost. With about 94-98% of players dying at least once, nearly everyone will meet the penalty. The Planet of Lana dossier argues the other way: zero consequence is a weakness, and evidence drop is a way to stand out. The research is split, and Nathanial decides.

'Safe points secure evidence' brings back a gap between the restore point and the loss point. The corpus's ~20 s and 1-3 min norms apply to replay time, not to resource loss. If safe points are sparse, a single death could undo several rooms of evidence. No corpus game has measured that. The two-tier proposal (frequent free autosaves plus sparse evidence-banking safe points) is a design inference, not an evidenced pattern.
Wider rooms of 1.5-2 screens with one restore point each could break the ~20 s loss norm. The research supports wider rooms only if there are restore points inside each room (one per beat).

Today's code never touches Records/Memory flags on a knockdown, and the current docs and AGENT.md copy describes secured copies. Moving to the drop model changes player-facing rules and needs the public docs and changelog updated in the same change. This is not a research conflict, but it is a cost to plan for.

Corpse runs, recoverable losses, safe-room rituals and quitting rules are not covered by any game in this corpus. No Souls-like, Hollow Knight, Resident Evil or Alien: Isolation dossier was provided. Recommendations in those areas are unvalidated design proposals, and a dossier on those games would be needed before treating any target there as evidence-based.

syn.dimension: INVENTORY AND EVIDENCE: slots vs no slots, key items vs records, examine text, journals and logbooks, deduction, collected memories, case or attaché UI on controller and touch. Scope note: the corpus handed to this synthesis was truncated partway through the Stray dossier, so Stray evidence is limited to that dossier's header summary (tiny inventory carried by B-12, 27 memories that double as B-12's memory, one time-limited companion tool, two death types, 28 foley surfaces). No dossier in the visible corpus covers deduction boards, journals or logbooks, so nothing below claims evidence for them. WOLF//OVERRIDE's current evidence state was checked read-only: apps/game/scripts/m0_state.gd keeps evidence as booleans (purge_trace_preserved, mirror_trace_preserved), and the Records exit opens "once the first copy is secured". There is no inventory or CASE UI yet.

principles.principle: An inventory is a cost that has to be justified. Every reference shipped with no inventory, or with one that was deliberately tiny, and Limbo's director turned one down on purpose.
principles.evidence: Arnt Jensen ('Hanging in Limbo', Game Developer): "I insisted on having very few elements and no inventory" and "It's great to put mechanisms in, instead of all this inventory crap" (as corrected in the Limbo/INSIDE fact-check). Neither Limbo nor INSIDE has an inventory, a HUD or a tool. Planet of Lana has "no inventory, no held items, no tool, no HUD resource". Little Nightmares 1 and 2 have no inventory: Six carries only a lighter, and Mono gets one flashlight and can hold one long object. The Stray dossier header calls its inventory "deliberately tiny" and says the companion (B-12) carries it. The Lana dossier draws the lesson that every CASE item "must earn its slot by changing a scene or a WOLF reaction, not by being a collectible".

principles.principle: Keep key items and records apart. Key items are physical and contextual: you hold them in your hands, they reset with the room, and you drop them when the body needs its hands. Records and lore are environmental or collected, and they persist.
principles.evidence: In INSIDE, carried state is physical (boxes, the jet crate, raft, lever) and lives only in the current gameplay sub-scene. On respawn, "dirty" Gameplay scenes reload, so dragged objects go back to their checkpoint positions (Unite 2016 slides). In Little Nightmares 1, context items (keys, meat, a sausage bridge) are held in hand and "dropped when you climb or grab". Meanwhile Limbo's eggs and INSIDE's orbs persist across deaths and are tracked by checkpoint or chapter in the Load menu, which the Playdead dossier calls "the closest analogue to a 'secured evidence' state". Little Nightmares collectibles persist and appear per chapter in Chapter Select.

principles.principle: In every reference, records you have already collected survive death. Death resets position and world state, never the archive.
principles.evidence: Little Nightmares: "Nothing is lost on death (no inventory, no collectible loss; collectibles persist and are per-chapter via Chapter Select)". Planet of Lana: "Nothing is lost on death", and the Family Gaming Database lists 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints', defined as losing less than 5 minutes. Limbo/INSIDE: Carlsen says "You don't ever really get penalized for dying, it's just how the game plays", and HG101 estimates a death costs "twenty-ish seconds of progress" (a reviewer estimate). Only 2.4% of Lana's Steam owners hold 'Flawless' (about 6.5% of finishers), so nearly every player dies, and a cost attached to death will hit nearly every player.

principles.principle: Collected records pay off best when they become the companion's or the world's memory, not a percentage counter.
principles.evidence: Stray's 27 collectible memories "double as the companion's memory" (Stray dossier header). In Little Nightmares 1, the Nomes you hugged gather on the staircase in the ending (verified; 12 are hugged, the 13th is eaten, and all 13 count toward 'Little Lost Things', 2.7% on Steam). In Little Nightmares II, all 18 Glitching Remains unlock a secret ending ('No More Remains', 5.3% Steam unlock). INSIDE requires every hidden orb to be deactivated for its secret ending (orb count UNVERIFIED). Limbo's hidden eggs unlock a faster, harder alternate route (egg count platform-dependent, UNVERIFIED). INSIDE's Huddle shader fades in bruises, burns and blood "as the player abuses it", a cheap 'the world remembers what you did'.

principles.principle: Optional evidence works as a spatial detour with a wide spread of find rates. Critical evidence is never hidden.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana has 10 shrines. Steam owner find rates run from 41.0% (shrine 2) down to 6.9% (shrine 4), and a Windows Central reviewer found 3 of 10 blind. Little Nightmares collectibles are "mostly in side rooms reached by dragging boxes, crawling vents or climbing stacked cages - i.e. optional spatial detours, not pickups on the critical path". Lana's 10 shrines support a separate 100% speedrun category (2:02:24 against 1:53:44 Any%).

principles.principle: Examine text and evidence presentation should under-explain. These games let art, audio and placement carry the history, with no subtitles, menus or tutorial text.
principles.evidence: In Game Informer's Afterwords, the interviewer raised the side-by-side toilets and Mervik agreed: "That's such a perfect example of not saying too much." Eriksson (Lana commentary): "a lot of just background detail as well that sort of gives the players clues to as to what's going on". Lana's constructed language has no subtitles, and Eriksson's stated philosophy is "You want to keep building a world that creates more questions than answers." Carlsen (Limbo): "we didn't want to have any in-game menus or anything." Little Nightmares has "no graphical user interface at all" (Lilja).

principles.principle: Let the companion carry or share load without becoming the only holder of anything essential.
principles.evidence: Little Nightmares II: Six is credited with "carrying important items if you need more than one" (Dread Central). Lucas Roussel, the publisher's lead producer, said: "players are never fully in charge of Six' destiny." Stray: the dossier header says B-12 "carries the inventory, translates the world", and the one time-limited tool (the Defluxor) is "bolted onto the companion rather than the player".

principles.principle: The one tool should widen options without empowering the player.
principles.evidence: Mono's flashlight "is just bright enough to stun them [Patients] for brief amounts of time" (PS Blog). Roussel (GamingBolt): "This design choice was mainly to avoid the player feeling too much empowered towards environments and enemies. It was critical to keep this oppressive feeling from the first game." Mervik: the aim was to give "a few more seconds to get away rather than changing the whole complexion of the game". Stray's only tool is time-limited and belongs to the companion (dossier header).

principles.principle: On touch and controller, an evidence interaction has to feel physical and short. Prompts stay contextual and world-space, and hold-heavy inputs get criticised.
principles.evidence: INSIDE on iOS (Gjøl, Digital Dragons 2018) made two separate changes. First, "Swipe _towards_ object to grab", limited to objects that block movement. Second, interaction animations were shortened to match the swipe; this started with the jetcrate and spread to levers, windows, the raft and "pulling secrets". They "Tried auto-complete, ends up waiting for triggered animation to end. loses feeling of interaction" and rejected it. The touch state machine treats all fingers equally and allows "Hold device with a thumb ON-SCREEN". AppUnwrapper: thumbs "Covering up any element of the screen" hurt the art. Lana uses a world-space pointer that "will also smartly snap to particular points of interest", yet GamesRadar still found it "slightly finicky". Lana mobile patch 1.0.5 fixed "button disappearance during environmental interactions". Windows Central called Lana's long holds without toggle exhausting. PlayStation LifeStyle on Little Nightmares II: "Hand cramp is a real issue".

principles.principle: Deduction, journals and logbooks have no evidence base in this corpus.
principles.evidence: None of the visible dossiers (Limbo/INSIDE, Little Nightmares 1-2, Planet of Lana, Stray header) documents a journal, logbook, examine-text system or deduction mechanic. All of them convey story environmentally or through collectibles. Any deduction or journal feature for WOLF//OVERRIDE is therefore UNSUPPORTED by this research and would need its own sources or a prototype.

targets.metric: Essential CASE items carried at once (key items plus unsecured records)
targets.target: 1-2 at most, plus exactly 1 tool. No slot grid.
targets.basis: Derived. The references ship zero (Limbo, INSIDE, Lana, LN) or a 'deliberately tiny' inventory (Stray). LN2 needs a second carried item only for two-person puzzles, and the companion carries it. No reference gives an exact slot count, so the number is a design inference, not a measured value.

targets.metric: Optional records per chapter (about 3 rooms today)
targets.target: About 2-4 per chapter, at most about 1 per room
targets.basis: Derived from shipped counts: Lana 10 shrines over 10 chapters; LN1 13 Nomes + 10 statues over 5 chapters; LN2 18 Remains + 12 hats over 5 chapters; Stray 27 memories over 12 chapters. Limbo's eggs (about 9-10) are platform-dependent and UNVERIFIED.

targets.metric: Find-rate spread for optional records in blind playtests
targets.target: Easiest optional record found by about 40% of testers, hardest by about 7-10%. Essential evidence found by 100%.
targets.basis: Lana Steam owner find rates: 41.0% (shrine 2) to 6.9% (shrine 4). Steam percentages are shares of owners, so rates among people who actually play are somewhat higher.

targets.metric: Most progress lost to one death (time from the last safe point, which bounds what unsecured evidence can be lost)
targets.target: Keep safe points about one room apart: roughly 1-3 minutes of play, and never more than 5 minutes
targets.basis: INSIDE: each puzzle spans "around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay" (Unite 2016). HG101 estimates Limbo deaths cost "twenty-ish seconds" (reviewer estimate). FGDB's 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints' means losing less than 5 minutes (Lana).

targets.metric: Previously secured records lost on death
targets.basis: Every reference persists collected items across death (LN, Lana, Limbo eggs, INSIDE orbs tracked by checkpoint or chapter).

targets.metric: Hold needed to open, examine or secure evidence
targets.target: No sustained hold. Tap to open the CASE from Pause. Any USE-hold on a copy station gets a toggle or a release that keeps progress.
targets.basis: Hold criticism in LN2 ('Hand cramp is a real issue', PSLS) and in Lana (long holds 'exhausting', Windows Central). No reference publishes a hold-duration number, so no seconds figure is given.

targets.metric: Collected optional records reflected in a later payoff
targets.target: 100% of collected optional records, and WOLF's record of how the engineer treated him, are shown or acted on in a late room
targets.basis: LN1: every hugged Nome reappears in the ending. LN2 Remains and INSIDE orbs gate secret endings. Stray memories are the companion's memory.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Formalise two evidence classes in m0_state.gd. (a) RECORDS: copies from stations such as the purge trace and mirror trace, which become permanent once secured. (b) CARRIED items: one physical key item or the tool, which reset with the room. Today's booleans become per-record states: absent, copied (unsecured) or secured. Treat the copy station's existing 'secured' moment as the safe point.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: The references split held, resettable objects (INSIDE dirty-scene reload, LN keys dropped when climbing) from persistent collected records (Limbo eggs, INSIDE orbs, LN collectibles). That split is the natural boundary for 'unsecured' versus 'secured'.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Directly implements the decided death model (death drops unsecured evidence, safe points secure it) and the evidence CASE. It builds on the existing purge_trace_preserved / mirror_trace_preserved flags and the 'first copy is secured' Records exit.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make the CASE pause-only with no slot grid. It is a short list of secured and unsecured records. Each gets a painted thumbnail and at most one or two lines of examine text, written to 'not say too much'. In play, show only a diegetic tell, such as a light on the engineer's case or a contact light at the station, when a copy is unsecured. Open it from Pause by tap or button press, with no hold, and keep it reachable with keyboard, controller focus and touch.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: None of the references shows a HUD or in-game menus (Carlsen, Lilja). Mervik's 'not saying too much' and Lana's background-detail storytelling favour terse examine text. AGENT.md requires visible idle, available and completed states, and those can be diegetic.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Evidence CASE inventory, one USE plus Pause input, and phone touch. It keeps AGENT.md's rule to tie feedback to real state changes (copy confirmation, contact light).

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: On copy stations, make USE a short physical action (a tap, or a short hold with a visible seal or copy motion) using the shortest animation that still reads as an interaction. Do not auto-complete it. On touch, consider swipe or tap toward the station only where the station blocks movement, and keep prompts world-space and anchored to the station so they never vanish mid-interaction.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: INSIDE iOS rejected auto-complete because it "loses feeling of interaction" and shortened interactions instead, including "pulling secrets". Lana's touch port had to patch "button disappearance during environmental interactions". Lana's pointer needed generous snapping.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Hold-to-move plus one USE (tap or hold), phone touch, and the existing Records copy stations.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Keep the unsecured window at about one room, with safe points at most one room apart (1-3 minutes). Make dropped evidence a recoverable physical object left where the engineer died (or at the station it came from) rather than deleting it. Keep respawn continuous, with room tone carried through.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Every reference makes death free. The dossiers warn that a cost on death "will read as punishment" unless the fatal thing is legible, the correct solution is easy to execute and respawn is near-instant. Only 2.4% of Lana owners finish without dying, so the cost lands on nearly everyone.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Death model (drop unsecured evidence, secure at safe points) and wider 1.5-2 screen rooms. It flags the severity of the decided rule; Nathanial decides.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Let WOLF carry or hold a second record only as an option. He might keep a duplicate copy, or refuse to carry one, according to his memory of the engineer. Every essential record must always be securable by the engineer alone. WOLF's choice should change the route or the risk, never whether completion is possible.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: LN2's Six carries the second item when a puzzle needs two, and Stray's B-12 carries the inventory. Both add companion presence through load-sharing. Little Nightmares keeps the companion reliable and saves the withdrawal of help for story beats.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: WOLF as independent companion who can help, disagree or refuse; engineer-only path for essential objectives; WOLF's own routes (scouting, leading); WOLF memory gating.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Place each room's optional record in a detour that uses that room's one walkable height change or a WOLF scouting route, never on the critical path. Tune with fresh, uncoached testers so the easiest is found by about 40% and the hardest by about 10%.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: LN collectibles sit in side rooms and on climbing detours. Lana's shrine find rates run from 41.0% to 6.9%, and Lana's shrines supported a 100% speedrun category.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Wider rooms with one height change each; WOLF scouting and leading routes; evidence CASE.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Design the one tool as non-empowering: it buys seconds or reveals something (stun, jam, light) and never defeats threats. Consider whether WOLF operates it (Stray's companion-mounted Defluxor) or the engineer does. The engineer-only rule implies the engineer should hold any tool essential to progress.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Mono's flashlight only stuns briefly, and the publisher kept melee weak to avoid feeling 'too much empowered'. Stray's only tool is time-limited and sits on the companion.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: The decided 'plus one tool', the purge sentry and door-blast set pieces, and the engineer-only fallback.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make secured records a memory payoff. A late room or WOLF's behaviour should replay what the engineer chose to secure, share or withhold, and how they treated WOLF. That can be a single authored reaction rather than a new system.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: LN1 brings back every hugged Nome in the ending, Stray's memories are the companion's memories, and LN2 and INSIDE tie complete collection to a secret ending. All of these are cheap persistent-memory payoffs.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: WOLF remembers how the engineer treated him; WOLF memory gating; the evidence CASE.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Do not build a deduction board, journal or logbook from this research. If one is wanted, prototype it as a grey-box (Lana's 'without any animation' pipeline) and source it from games that actually use one.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: No dossier in the corpus documents a journal, logbook or deduction mechanic, so any design would be unsupported here.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Neutral. The evidence CASE as decided does not require deduction.

conflicts_with_decisions: Death drops unsecured evidence: every reference in the corpus attaches zero resource cost to death (Limbo, INSIDE, Little Nightmares 1-2, Planet of Lana), and collected items always persist. The Playdead dossier warns that importing a cost without Playdead's legibility rules 'will read as punishment'. The Lana dossier, by contrast, argues an evidence cost could fix 'insta-fail stealth grates'. The research supports the rule only if the unsecured window is short (about one room), dropped evidence stays recoverable, and respawn is near-instant. Nathanial decides.

Evidence CASE inventory: Limbo's director explicitly refused an inventory ('very few elements and no inventory'; 'inventory crap'), and Lana, INSIDE and Little Nightmares shipped none. Only Stray had one, 'deliberately tiny' and carried by the companion. The research argues for a minimal, pause-only CASE with no slot grid. It does not support a full inventory. Nathanial decides.

CASE as UI: Playdead and Tarsier shipped no HUD or in-game menus. A visible CASE departs from that and is defensible only as pause-only or diegetic. AGENT.md's requirement to show idle, available and completed states can be met diegetically.

WOLF's own routes and memory gating combined with evidence: if WOLF can hold or refuse to carry a record, the engineer-only fallback for essential objectives must still hold. The references (LN2 Six, Stray B-12) never let the companion block essential progress through inventory.
Deduction, journals and logbooks are absent from the corpus. Any such feature is unsupported by this research, not contradicted by it.

syn.dimension: ACTION AND IMPACT in narrative games: chases, telegraphs, set pieces, hit-stop and shake, escalation and release, and how much challenge players take before frustration. Evidence comes from the Limbo/INSIDE, Little Nightmares I/II and Planet of Lana dossiers, with their fact-check corrections applied. The Stray dossier was cut off in the corpus I received; only its opening summary (two death types, short checkpoints, one time-limited tool on the companion, fail-able jumps rejected) was readable, and nothing else from it is used. I checked WOLF//OVERRIDE's current numbers read-only in apps/game/scripts (impact.gd, sentry_brain.gd, sentry.gd, drop_arm.gd, m0_actor.gd, main.gd).

principles.principle: Impact is mostly carried by sound and animation state, not by screen effects. None of the reference games has a documented hit-stop, screen-shake or flash value, and the documented habit is cutting back.
principles.evidence: Playdead: no source documents hit-stop, shake or flash. Their VFX talk is titled 'Turn it Down 90%' (Control Conference 2016, from Playdead's publications index). INSIDE's weight comes from a double-buffered 'Effect State' that an Effect Analyzer writes from animation, physics velocity and collider metadata. Sounds fire when that state changes (AES 2016 deck: 'Set land impact parameter to 70, Play land sound', impact 'based on velocity in the direction of surface normal'). Little Nightmares: no fetched source gives hit-stop or shake numbers. Weight is 'purposefully slow and heavy' movement (Push Square LN2) plus a controller that 'pulsates in unison with your pounding heartbeat' during chases (Push Square LN1). Planet of Lana: impact is carried by audio (FMOD landing sounds that depend on jump height, per Ameglio). The flying-robot sound was cut back rather than built up: 'got rid of 80%' of its layers. Family Gaming Database lists 'No Screen Shake', which it defines as absent or able to be turned off.

principles.principle: Every lethal event is readable before it kills, and the correct response is easy to carry out. Players forgive frequent death; they do not forgive deaths they could not have read.
principles.evidence: Carlsen (GDC Europe 2010, verified quote): 'It's very important that the correct solution is fairly easy to execute.' Game Developer's report paraphrases two more rules: wrong solutions should be obviously wrong, and the player should be taught by placement. Limbo's audio brings an approaching hazard forward 'before visual revelation' and silences it once the player has passed (Andersen). Little Nightmares II: Push Square says 'we generally found that we had to replay each scene at least twice, because there was some kind of unpredictable trap waiting.' PlayStation LifeStyle (the corrected attribution): 'Instant death is a frequent recurrence and never ceases to be frustrating, especially during chase sequences.' Planet of Lana: Push Square's only mechanical complaint was 'insta-fail stealth grates.'

principles.principle: A threat announces its change of state on a separate channel, usually sound, before or as it starts to chase. That alert is the telegraph, and its idle sounds tell the player where it is off camera.
principles.evidence: Lilja (Little Nightmares): 'if an enemy screams, it's because they are alerted to your presence and ... most likely chasing you.' Each enemy has its own music track, built from looping stems that crossfade by state with no tempo sync. In pursuit 'the music intensifies', and with several enemies 'the system looks for the currently most aggressive one in the room.' When the player is hidden but still audible (a 'listening' state), background sound and music are 'quickly pulled down to a minimum' so that only the enemy, Six and her heartbeat are heard. Sounds such as the Chef's coughs carry through walls as 'sonic identifiers.' Lilja also reported that breathing used as a state tell was an experiment, and players over-read it as smell-tracking, so a tell will be believed literally. The machines in Planet of Lana are drawn as dense black silhouettes that 'immediately pop off the screen' (RPS).

principles.principle: Chases are short authored sprints that end at a hard spatial line the pursuer cannot cross. Release comes with an audible change, and sometimes chases drop music altogether.
principles.evidence: Little Nightmares: chases are scripted corridor sprints with a hard final beat. Six 'jumps to another balcony beyond the Guests' reach', and the Flesh Wall chase plays out in the Signal Tower. Small gaps that adults cannot fit through are a recurring visual grammar. Planet of Lana: in the beach run past the giant robot 'collector legs', Furukawa 'strongly urged to not have music so that the sound design could take centre-stage' (corrected from 'desert'). Limbo: a 'stinger-like sound, triggered when the boy survives' the rotating rooms marks the release. INSIDE: no primary source on chase tuning (dog speed, catch distance); UNVERIFIED.

principles.principle: Death is fast and frequent, and in every reference it costs nothing except replay. Audio continuity makes the retry feel like no time has passed.
principles.evidence: INSIDE (Wwise Tour 2016): death is a 'scene change'. Audio keeps its state through the reload, commands queued during the load all run at once, and this 'Creates the illusion of no time passing.' Only the 'dirty' Gameplay scenes reload. Limbo: HG101 says checkpoints keep deaths from 'setting you back more than twenty-ish seconds of progress' (a reviewer estimate). Wikipedia supports only unlimited checkpoint restarts. Little Nightmares II: Push Square says 'restarts are rapid'. Roussel (the Bandai Namco producer, speaking about Xbox Series X|S) describes 'a nearly immediate respawn which is a notable improvement over the original Little Nightmares'. Planet of Lana: Family Gaming Database lists 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints', defined as losing less than 5 minutes. Almost every player dies: Planet of Lana 'Flawless' is 2.4% of Steam owners, about 6.5% of finishers; Little Nightmares 'Hard to the Core' is 1.6%, though its exact condition is UNVERIFIED. Stray, from its truncated summary only: two kinds of death, very short checkpoints, and fail-able jumps rejected.

principles.principle: Give the protagonist weak, costly, improvised action rather than mastery. The set-piece 'kill' is a trap built from the room. When an attack misses, the cost should be time, not instant death.
principles.evidence: Roussel (GamingBolt, corrected wording): the Little Nightmares II melee was made hard 'to avoid the player feeling too much empowered towards environments and enemies. It was critical to keep this oppressive feeling from the first game.' Mervik calls it 'improvisation' that gives 'a few more seconds to get away', not Kratos. Shacknews notes 'there's a bit of a wind up.' Critics punished the result: Push Square wrote 'if you miss it's instant death', and PlayStation LifeStyle called it 'clumsy and slow' with 'every hit must be a precisely timed strike'. Planet of Lana has no combat. The scout robot was tuned to be dreaded, and the demo's one kill is a Rube Goldberg trap that uses rope-bite timing plus Lana as bait (developer-commentary quotes are UNVERIFIED pending a caption re-check). Stray (truncated summary): one time-limited tool, the Defluxor, attached to the companion rather than the player.

principles.principle: Escalation needs real release: alternate quiet and threat, start shared mechanics simple and ramp them up, and do not pad the walking between them.
principles.evidence: Planet of Lana: the first joint chapter is 'on the simpler side' and 'the difficulty ramps up' (commentary, UNVERIFIED pending a caption re-check). GamesRadar says some set pieces 'offer a moment away from the dangers.' Nintendo Life criticised 'quite a bit of uneventful running', and RPS called the second act 'middle of the road'. For the sequel, Stjärnljus said 'varying the pace allows the more intense sequences to land with greater impact' while keeping 'space for stillness.' INSIDE: each puzzle spans 'around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay' (Unite 2016). Little Nightmares: Mervik said 'get in and get out', with no padding to reach a target length.

principles.principle: Timing-critical action is the hardest thing to bring to touch. Shorten the interaction instead of auto-completing it, and do not require long holds to survive.
principles.evidence: INSIDE on iOS (Gjøl, Digital Dragons 2018): they 'Tried auto-complete, ends up waiting for triggered animation to end. loses feeling of interaction'. They switched to the 'Short as possible animation while still prioritising the feeling of interaction' and named 'Sentry gun in city, Sentry gun in sewers' as the hardest spots. Limbo on iOS: Game Informer said the invisible d-pad made 'the boy ... just stop moving mid-jog', which made timing puzzles 'notably harder'. Holding inputs: Little Nightmares II drew 'Hand cramp is a real issue' (PlayStation LifeStyle), and Windows Central called Planet of Lana's long holds exhausting. Planet of Lana shipped with QTEs that can be switched off.

principles.principle: If the companion is part of action set pieces, players need it to be reliable and fast to read. Its drama belongs in the story, not in latency.
principles.evidence: Little Nightmares II: Push Square wrote 'you'll never feel like you're fighting the underlying code'. Shacknews found Six 'would take too long to take a cue/get into position'. Roussel (publisher): players are 'never fully in charge of Six' destiny', and that unreliability is reserved for the story. Planet of Lana: GamesRadar found the pointer 'slightly finicky', but a prompt appears automatically when Lana stands in a good spot.

targets.metric: Progress replayed after a death (from the last secure point to where you died)
targets.target: Usually about 20 s or less; never more than 5 minutes
targets.basis: Limbo, HG101 reviewer estimate: 'twenty-ish seconds of progress' (not a measurement). Family Gaming Database's 'frequent checkpoints' threshold is under 5 minutes lost (Planet of Lana). Little Nightmares II reviews accept frequent deaths only because 'restarts are rapid'.

targets.metric: Death-to-control loop (knockdown reaction + fade out + reload + fade in)
targets.target: No longer than WOLF's current ~1.45 s (0.7 s with controls off, including the 0.22 s tilt, then a 0.4 s fade out and a 0.35 s fade in), with room tone continuing through it
targets.basis: WOLF timings come from main.gd (FAIL_CONTROLS_OFF_SECONDS, FAIL_FADE_SECONDS, the 0.35 fade in). INSIDE: the scene change creates 'the illusion of no time passing'. Little Nightmares II: 'nearly immediate respawn' (Roussel, Xbox Series X|S). INSIDE's own respawn duration is UNVERIFIED; the speedrun-gap inference was withdrawn.

targets.metric: Share of players who die at least once
targets.target: Assume nearly all of them: design the evidence-drop rule for about 95% of finishers
targets.basis: Planet of Lana 'Flawless' is 2.4% of Steam owners, about 6.5% of finishers (corrected base). Little Nightmares 'Hard to the Core' is 1.6% of owners (condition UNVERIFIED).

targets.metric: Lethal events with a readable tell before contact (sound and/or animation, matching the real detection model)
targets.target: 100% of lethal events. Fresh testers should be able to say what killed them after their first death, without being asked leading questions
targets.basis: Carlsen: the correct solution should be 'fairly easy to execute'. Little Nightmares II was criticised for unpredictable traps forcing 'at least twice' replays. Lilja: players believe tells literally. Playdead's silent 'tissue tester' method measured solvability only.

targets.metric: Length of an action/puzzle chunk inside a wide room
targets.target: About 1-3 minutes per chunk, with a quiet stretch before or after each threat beat
targets.basis: INSIDE (Unite 2016): each puzzle spans 'around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay'. Planet of Lana II: varying the pace makes intense sequences 'land with greater impact' while keeping 'space for stillness'.

targets.metric: Tank-drop release window on the engineer-only path (derived from current code)
targets.target: Keep it at least as wide as today's patrol case (about 0.63 s; 88 px hit width at 140 px/s, released about 63 px ahead to cover the 0.45 s fall). Treat the chase case (about 0.38 s at 230 px/s) as too tight for touch until it has been played on a phone
targets.basis: drop_arm.gd (HIT_RANGE 44, FALL_SECONDS 0.45) and sentry_brain.gd (PATROL_SPEED 140, CHASE_SPEED 230). INSIDE's iOS port singled out its sentry-gun timing sections as the hardest touch changes.

targets.metric: How many sound layers each threat uses
targets.target: Trim each threat's loop until three of them at once still read separately
targets.basis: Planet of Lana: flying robots were 'way more noisy' until 80% of their layers were removed (Ameglio).

targets.metric: Screen shake / hit-stop magnitudes
targets.target: No evidence-based number exists in this corpus. Use the count of full-strength uses per room as the controlled variable, not the pixel value
targets.basis: No Playdead, Tarsier or Wishfully source documents shake or hit-stop values. Playdead's VFX talk is 'Turn it Down 90%'. WOLF's current caps (10 px max shake, time_scale 0.05 for at most 0.1 s, 0.55 white flash alpha) are neither supported nor contradicted by this research.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Add an alert beat between the sentry seeing the engineer and chasing them. Today sentry_brain.gd goes from patrol to chase in the same tick that _sees() is true, and chase speed (230 px/s) is faster than the engineer's walk (190 px/s). Insert a short 'lock-on' state: the eye turns red (EYE_LOCKED already exists), a distinct alarm stinger plays, and the sentry stops for a beat before it accelerates. Tune the length in hands-on play; the corpus gives no seconds value.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Every reference that players praise announces a state change first (Lilja's scream = chasing; Limbo brings hazards forward 'before visual revelation'). Little Nightmares II's unreadable traps drew the 'replay each scene at least twice' criticism.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Current Service Junction purge sentry. The impact kit's procedural sound can supply the stinger. No new input needed.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Check the sentry's visible beam against its real detection range. sentry.gd draws a 34 px beam that fades to zero alpha, but SentryBrain.SIGHT_RANGE is 180 px, so the visible tell covers about a fifth of the actual sight distance. Either draw a beam or floor glow that reaches the full sight range, or shrink the range to match what is drawn.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Lilja: players over-read tells (they decided enemies could smell Six). A tell shorter than the real sense produces deaths that feel unfair, the exact thing Carlsen's 'obviously wrong' rule (as reported) guards against.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Current sentry. Supports the painterly look if the beam becomes a fog and light shaft (INSIDE clamps fog so bright lights 'bleed through').

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Make the rubble line the chase's readable hard end beat, and give it an audible release. When LOSE_SECONDS (2.5 s) runs out and the sentry gives up, play a survival stinger and bring room tone back up. Draw the rubble as something the sentry visibly cannot cross (treads stopping at debris), not as an invisible x coordinate.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Little Nightmares chases end at a line the pursuer physically cannot pass (the balcony 'beyond the Guests' reach'). Limbo marks survival with a stinger. Release is what makes the escalation land (Planet of Lana II).
recommendations_for_wolf_override.fits_decisions: Current Service Junction. Carries over to the wider rooms with one height change each: a ledge the threat cannot climb is a natural hard line.

recommendations_for_wolf_override.change: Play the Service Junction route hands-on, on desktop and on a phone, to confirm the engineer-only tank drop is reliable. Today a patrolling sentry gives about a 0.63 s release window; after a miss it is chasing, and the window drops to about 0.38 s. Keep USE as short and immediate as possible and never auto-complete the drop. If touch play shows misses, widen HIT_RANGE or slow the sentry while it is near the mark.
recommendations_for_wolf_override.why: Making the timing sections feel good on touch was the hardest part of INSIDE's iOS port ('Sentry gun in city, Sentry gun in sewers'), and auto-complete was rejected because it 'loses feeling of interaction'.
