conflicts_with_decisions: Death drops unsecured evidence: none of the reference games charge a resource on death, and touch players are measurably less precise. Limbo's thumb fell off the invisible d-pad mid-jog, and INSIDE's sentry-gun timing beats were the hardest to port to touch. A precision-timed death that costs evidence will fall hardest on phone players. The research argues for dense safe points and no timing-precision deaths on the evidence path. Nathanial decides.

Real feel / 'weight': Playdead had to cut weighty interaction animations for touch ('Very painful change, since we really liked the weight of the controller input'), and LN's 'purposefully slow and heavy' controls drew cramp and imprecision complaints. Weight that delays response conflicts with touch responsiveness, so keep weight in audio and visuals, not in input latency. Nathanial decides.

Evidence CASE inventory: Limbo's director rejected an inventory on purpose (Jensen: 'very few elements and no inventory'), and none of the reference side-scrollers on mobile has one. On a phone an inventory screen adds UI and covers art. If kept, make it pause-only or diegetic, with no new button.
One tool: a tool used under time pressure means another verb on a small screen. The research supports mapping it to contextual USE rather than adding a button.

Wider rooms (1.5-2 screens): not argued against (INSIDE's ~100 m puzzles support it), but the phone shows a smaller part of each room. Little Nightmares used audio to cover enemies the camera could not show, and touch buttons hide the bottom band. Threats and USE targets need audio tells and must stay out of the thumb zones.

WOLF's own routes, scouting and leading: Planet of Lana's mobile build appears to switch player control to the companion ('switch back to Lana's control', 1.0.4 notes). Copying that would break the engineer-only rule, and its pointer was called finicky.

weak_claims: Planet of Lana developer commentary quotes are used as load-bearing evidence while marked UNVERIFIED (the YouTube captions returned 429). These include 'that magic really disappears as soon as another human being takes control', the bait-guilt playtest quote, 'on the simpler side ... difficulty ramps up' and the robot base 'far in the distance'. They need a transcript re-pull before they support the companion and pacing recommendations.

The '~20 s lost per death' target, used in four syntheses, is one Hardcore Gaming 101 reviewer's estimate for Limbo ('twenty-ish seconds'), not a measurement. Speedrun or footage timing of real checkpoint spacing would be needed to treat it as a benchmark.

The ~1.45 s death-to-control 'target' just restates the current main.gd value (FAIL_CONTROLS_OFF_SECONDS 0.7, FAIL_FADE_SECONDS 0.4, plus a 0.35 fade-in; verified in code). No game in the corpus supplies a respawn duration, so it is not evidence-backed.

The '~0.5 s WOLF tell' target is derived from Limbo's boy looking 'half a second' ahead to pre-place his hands. That is animation anticipation, not companion-response latency, so the mapping is a category stretch. Shacknews's 'take too long to take a cue' gives no number.

Several claims rest on the Stray dossier's truncated header with no fetched source behind them: the producer 'documented trying and rejecting fail-able jumps', '27 memories double as B-12's memory', '28 foley surfaces', 'two death types', 'very short checkpoints', and the Defluxor as the only tool.

'Turn it Down 90%' (Playdead, Control Conference 2016) is cited as evidence of restraint with screen shake and effects, but only the talk's title was seen. Its content was not fetched, so it cannot support claims about shake or hit-stop.

'~95% of players die at least once' and 'about 6.5% of finishers' are derived from Planet of Lana's Flawless achievement at 2.4% of owners. Owner-based Steam percentages are a moving base, and Flawless can be missed for reasons other than dying. LN1's 'Hard to the Core' (1.6%) is used despite its condition being UNVERIFIED.

The Planet of Lana funnel (about 21% stop before 'A new friend', about 40% of starters finish) uses a starter base inferred from achievement percentages, not a measured starter count. The syntheses themselves say tying early quitting to death is UNVERIFIED.

Carlsen's 'teach by placement' and 'wrong solutions should be obviously wrong' are a Game Developer reporter's paraphrase, not direct quotes. Only 'correct solution is fairly easy to execute' and 'learning-by-dying' are verbatim.

Little Nightmares II design-intent quotes (co-op 'discarded', 'never fully in charge of Six' destiny', reworked camera, weak melee) are from Lucas Roussel of publisher Bandai Namco, not Tarsier. Treat them as secondhand on design intent.
FGDB's 'Bank Progress With Frequent Checkpoints' (under 5 minutes lost) is a database category threshold, not a measured Planet of Lana checkpoint interval. It is used as a hard ceiling target.

INSIDE's 'Each Puzzle span around 100 meters or 1-3min' (Unite 2016) is mapped directly to WOLF room length and checkpoint spacing. The mapping is the synthesisers' inference, and 100 m in INSIDE's 3D units has no stated px equivalent.
'Mui never refuses or remembers' is an absence-of-evidence claim drawn from a limited source set, but it is used to argue that refusals should be rare.

The sentry beam claim ('visible tell covers about a fifth of sight distance') compares BEAM_LENGTH 34.0 in sentry.gd draw space with SIGHT_RANGE 180.0 in sentry_brain.gd world px. Both constants are verified, but the ratio assumes the sentry node has no scale, which the synthesis did not check.

The tank-drop windows (0.63 s patrol, 0.38 s chase) are simple 88 px / speed arithmetic. They ignore the 0.45 s fall lead, the sentry's deceleration and the facing turn, so they are rough figures that need measuring in play.

Precise numbers cited without a named fetched source in the synthesis text: Huddle bruises 'from 9 of 26 rigidbodies', Playdead's 'about 150 tissue testers', 'about 256' AO decals, Lana shrine rates 41.0%/6.9%, the LN1 '12 hugged, 13th eaten' (Fandom only) and the speedrun times 2:02:24 / 1:53:44. Each should be re-checked against its URL.

extra.games: Gap-fill dossier for the "no precedent in corpus" conclusions. Covers: Hollow Knight (Shade, benches), Dark Souls (bloodstain, bonfires), Resident Evil 2 remake and the classic RE line (ink ribbons, typewriters, item box, hip pouch), Resident Evil 4 remake (Attaché Case grid), Alien: Isolation (manual save stations, two-brain alien AI), Signalis (six-item inventory, safe rooms), Ico (hand-holding, bench saves, subtracting design), The Last Guardian (Trico's autonomy, wandering), Return of the Obra Dinn (logbook deduction), Outer Wilds (ship log), Her Story (clip database). PIPELINE NOTE, READ FIRST: this agent can only research and return one dossier. It cannot re-run the six syntheses, add the acknowledgement guard, or re-run PRESENTATION or the critic. The workflow script has to do those. The only earlier research output on disk (tasks/wemurfgpn.output) holds 9 dossiers, not 18. Dossiers 10-18, every fact-check, every synthesis, the critic and the reference step all failed there with "You've reached your Fable limit". The 18-dossier corpus the critic describes, with about 445 sources and 168 corrections, is not on disk where this agent can read it, so those counts are UNVERIFIED here. The shared WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out during this pass, so every source below came from direct fetches.
extra.why_relevant: Four planned WOLF//OVERRIDE systems were reported as having "no precedent": a death model where dying drops unsecured evidence and safe points secure it, an evidence CASE inventory plus one tool, WOLF scouting and leading, and journals or deduction. Each has a direct, shipped precedent: Hollow Knight's Shade and Dark Souls' bloodstain (drop on death, one recovery chance), RE and Signalis safe rooms with shared storage, Alien: Isolation's slow manual saves, RE2R and Signalis slot caps, Obra Dinn's batch-validated logbook, the Outer Wilds ship log, and Trico's independent wandering. So the "no precedent" findings came from synthesis input that was cut off, not from a lack of evidence. The precedents also come with limits WOLF needs: a second death erases what was dropped, companion-failure states (Ico), and slow companion obedience (Trico's critics).

extra.companion: SCOUTING AND LEADING HAS SHIPPED PRECEDENT. The Last Guardian: "Though the player initially has little command over Trico, the boy learns to command Trico to leap onto ledges or head in a certain direction". Also, "new areas can be discovered by letting Trico wander independently". So the companion finding the route is part of the design. Ueda framed the trio (boy, Trico, guards) as "a game of rock-paper-scissors that changes throughout the game; at times, the boy needs Trico to protect him, while at others the situation is reversed". For WOLF: the engineer sometimes protects or repairs WOLF and sometimes WOLF covers the engineer. Ueda wanted a creature that "behaved as realistically as possible", and the team used "programmed key frame animations instead of more common motion capture". COST, from critics: the realism "hampered the gameplay causing impatience and frustration due to lack of immediate action by Trico when giving commands". Sony did not run a live E3 demo because Trico's AI "could be sporadic". Lesson for WOLF: a refusal must be legible and fast, an animated "no" with a reason, never a silent delay. Since every essential objective keeps an engineer-only path, a refusal should never stall progress. Ico: "The player can have Ico take Yorda's hand and pull her along at a faster pace". Saves are "stone benches that Ico and Yorda rest on". Ueda left Yorda's speech untranslated because translation "detracted from the 'holding hands' concept". Ico also makes the companion a failure condition: shadows drag Yorda into vortexes and the game ends if she is engulfed. WOLF is independent and not an escort, so do not copy that game-over. Alien: Isolation's two-brain AI (Tommy Thompson, Game Developer) fits WOLF's scouting: "while the director always knows where you are, the alien has to figure it out for itself". A WOLF scouting system can know the room's answer at director level, but WOLF should visibly sniff, listen and look before he leads. The alien's behaviour tree has "over 100 nodes" with parts "locked off" at the start and unlocked over time. That supports WOLF memory gating: unlock WOLF behaviours as trust or memory grows. BioShock Infinite's Elizabeth, Half-Life 2's Dog and Titanfall 2's BT are in the earlier dossier 7, which never reached synthesis. Nothing about them was re-verified here.
extra.level_and_camera: Safe-point placement is a tuning knob, and developers admit getting it wrong. Alistair Hope on Alien: Isolation: "in hindsight that perhaps some of the save point locations could be seen to be a little challenging, but having said that, has saving ever felt so sweet?" Hollow Knight has "50 Benches across Hallownest". Some cost Geo (Greenpath 50; Ancient Basin, City of Tears and Queen's Gardens 150), so a few safe points are paid for and most are free. Resting also "Respawn[s] defeated enemies (excluding enemies in the current room)". Dark Souls bonfires likewise respawn most enemies. Signalis and RE use dedicated safe rooms that pair a save with shared storage. RE7 plays a distinct "Saferoom" music cue on entry (wiki). For WOLF's wider 1.5-2 screen rooms: put a safe point at a room threshold or doorway, never mid-hazard. Keep the walk from the last safe point to a likely death spot short enough that recovering dropped evidence takes seconds, not a repeated gauntlet. Alien: Isolation's Nightmare difficulty makes "the motion tracker ... unreliable and the in game mini-map ... unavailable", which shows difficulty can remove navigation aids. Room-scale numbers (screens per room, camera framing) are not covered by these sources. They are in the Inside/Limbo, Little Nightmares, Somerville and Hollow Knight/Celeste dossiers.
extra.death_and_saves: THE PLANNED DEATH MODEL (drop unsecured evidence, safe points secure it) HAS DIRECT PRECEDENT. Hollow Knight: on death a Shade appears holding "all the Geo that was lost", at "the location where the Knight has most recently died". Until it is beaten the "SOUL meter is broken, limiting it to 66 charge". If you die first, "a new Shade appears at the new death's location and the old one disappears ... all the Geo carried by the previous Shade is lost". There is a paid bypass: Confessor Jiji will "summon the Shade to her room in return for a Rancid Egg". Dark Souls: the player "drops any carried souls and humanity at the place of death", can recover them "by reaching the resulting bloodstain, but loses them permanently after dying again before doing so". Miyazaki called bonfires "recovery and respawn points that also served as rare places of warmth". Benches in Hollow Knight both save and "Replenish all health". MANUAL, RISKY SAVES: in Alien: Isolation "There is a three second pause before the save can be completed, meaning the player can be killed while attempting to save". Hope: "a core component of horror is in 'small victories'" and "Saving becomes part of the fabric of the horror". The team considered other options but kept manual saves (secondary search summary only; the exact quote was not fetched, so UNVERIFIED). SCARCITY AS A DIFFICULTY SETTING: classic RE limited saves through finite ink ribbons ("there was a set amount in the entire game"). The wiki says Capcom found ribbons "too few and far between" for players without long sessions (Unreferenced wiki claim, UNVERIFIED). The RE2 remake keeps ink ribbons only in Hardcore; lower difficulties save freely. Ico: diegetic bench saves with the companion. Outer Wilds: on death or the 22-minute reset, "Nothing is brought back ... with the exception of the data on the spacecraft's computer", so knowledge persists and items do not. Recommendation for WOLF: (1) unsecured evidence drops as a visible, glowing cache at the death spot. (2) There is one recovery chance: reaching it re-secures it. (3) Unlike Hollow Knight, do not destroy the first cache on a second death in a short, story-led game. Either keep the older cache or merge both into the newest one. The double-loss rule is what makes Souls-style corpse runs punishing. (4) Offer a Jiji-like fallback: WOLF can retrieve a dropped cache if trust is high, and an engineer-only terminal does the same at a cost. (5) Securing at a safe point takes a short committed animation (about 1-3 s, like Alien's 3 s) so it reads as a small victory. Keep it cancellable on touch.
extra.inventory_and_evidence: SMALL CAPPED CASE PLUS SHARED STORAGE HAS DIRECT PRECEDENT. Signalis: "Elster is limited to six items on her person, including weapons, ammunition and key items", with safe rooms where players "save progress and store their items". RE2 remake (wiki, Unreferenced): the inventory "initially contains eight slots". Each Hip Pouch adds "two extra inventory slots", up to a maximum of 20. Item Boxes share contents: items in one "can be accessed from any other Item Box". RE0 dropped item boxes and let players drop items anywhere. RE4 remake: the Attaché Case is a grid where "items occupy different shapes and sizes, requiring players to organize and rotate items". Upgrades are bought from the Merchant, and storage at typewriters is mainly for weapons. In classic RE even the save item took a slot: ink ribbons "occupied inventory spaces, so players who were expecting to save had to sacrifice ammunition or weapon space" (Unreferenced wiki). JOURNALS AND DEDUCTION HAVE DIRECT PRECEDENT. Obra Dinn tracks 60 souls. "To deter guesswork, correct fates are validated only in sets of three, with the exception of the last six fates ... validated in sets of two". Pope "created spreadsheets to link all the various characters and their fates ... to ensure that players would be able to logically follow chains of deaths". Pope's first idea, dying repeatedly and going back one minute to recreate deaths, was replaced by frozen moment-of-death scenes; the encyclopedia says it was technically challenging. Outer Wilds: the ship's computer shows found mysteries "organized either by location or in a web of connections". Her Story: 271 clips, keyword search, player-made tags. Barlow first added "more typical game aspects" and the design got more minimalist over development (paraphrase via fetch summary). For WOLF's evidence CASE: a fixed number of evidence slots (around 6, as in Signalis) plus the one tool. Items are unsecured until filed at a safe point, which makes the death drop meaningful. Batch-confirm deductions (Obra Dinn's sets of three) so players cannot brute-force WOLF's memory-gated conclusions. Show evidence links as a connection web, as in Outer Wilds. Keep a design-side spreadsheet proving each conclusion is reachable on the engineer-only path.
extra.action_and_impact: Little of this pass is about impact. Alien: Isolation ties tool use to threat: using tools such as the motion tracker "increases the chance of the Alien finding the player". The director's menace gauge rises with alien proximity, line of sight and motion-tracker proximity. When menace peaks the alien goes "backstage" into vents ("we need to give players a break after a while"). For WOLF: a pressure meter that forces calm beats after peaks, and the one tool should make noise that the purge sentry can hear. Shake, hit-stop and flash evidence is in the Inside/Limbo, Oddworld, Somerville and Hollow Knight/Celeste dossiers, which never reached synthesis and were not re-verified here.
extra.presentation_ui_art: Ico used "subtracting design": interface elements, extra enemy types and gameplay that broke immersion were removed, leaving no HUD. Ueda later "noted that the subtracting design may have taken too much out of the game". He also thought it hurt marketing, because without a HUD the screenshots looked uninteresting to buyers. That is useful for WOLF's trailer and store stills: keep the diegetic UI, but make sure key art shows the CASE, WOLF's state or the choice buttons. Obra Dinn's 1-bit style worked in a window, but "at full screen resolution, players suffered from motion sickness". Pope fixed it by changing the rendering to get a motion-blur equivalent for the dither. Parallax-heavy, high-contrast painterly layers on large screens should be checked for the same discomfort. Signalis deliberately imitates fifth-generation visuals. Alien: Isolation removes the mini-map on Nightmare, so UI aids can scale with difficulty. Diegetic save points with ritual art (Ico's benches, RE typewriters, Alien's phones, Dark Souls bonfires as "places of warmth") show that the safe point should be a lit, warm, recognisable prop in each room. The full PRESENTATION synthesis still has to be re-run by the workflow; this dossier does not replace it.
extra.audio: Only partly covered in this pass. Alien: Isolation: "the Alien is looking and listening for the player" (Hope), and tool noise raises detection, so sound is both feedback and threat. RE7 plays a dedicated "Saferoom" track whenever you enter a safe room (wiki), an audio cue for safety that WOLF's safe points can copy with a room-tone change. Ico kept Yorda's language untranslated so the bond stays non-verbal, which supports WOLF communicating through procedural sound and body language over text. Per-surface footsteps, room tone and breathing evidence is in the Inside/Limbo (Martin Stig Andersen), Little Nightmares (Tobias Lilja) and Stray dossiers. It was not re-verified here.
extra.mobile_and_input: Not substantively covered. Feral's Alien: Isolation support page lists a save-system FAQ, but the answer text was not in the fetched page (UNVERIFIED). RE2R and RE4R inventories rely on extra buttons (move, rotate, auto-sort) that WOLF's input set (hold-to-move, one USE, two choices, Pause) does not have. Avoid grid rotation and use fixed slots. Make "secure at safe point" a single USE hold, and keep inventory actions to USE plus the two choice buttons. Trico's delayed obedience is worse on touch, where players cannot tell a missed tap from a refusal: always acknowledge the input instantly, then show WOLF's decision. Mobile-port evidence is in the earlier mobile-ports dossier, which never reached synthesis.

steal: Hollow Knight/Dark Souls drop-on-death: unsecured evidence becomes a visible cache at the death spot, and reaching it re-secures it
A temporary penalty while the cache is out, like Hollow Knight's 66-SOUL cap. For example, WOLF is uneasy and offers fewer suggestions until the cache is recovered
A paid or alternative recovery, like Confessor Jiji: WOLF fetches the cache if trust is high, and an engineer-only terminal does it at a cost, so recovery never depends on WOLF
Alien: Isolation's committed save: securing evidence takes a short, risky animation, so saving feels like a 'small victory'
Shared storage at every safe point (RE item box): file evidence once and it is available from any safe point
A Signalis-sized CASE (about 6 slots) plus the one tool, so carrying versus securing is a real decision
Obra Dinn batch confirmation: confirm deductions in sets so players cannot brute-force conclusions
Outer Wilds ship-log web: evidence shown as linked nodes by room or by connection
Trico-style wandering: let WOLF find side routes on his own, which counts as scouting
Alien two-brain split: director-level knowledge, but WOLF visibly searches before he leads
Unlock WOLF behaviour nodes as trust and memory grow (Alien's locked behaviour-tree branches)
A diegetic, warm safe-point prop with its own room-tone or music change (Ico benches, bonfires, RE7 Saferoom cue)
avoid: Hollow Knight's double-loss rule (a second death erases the first cache) in a short narrative game: keep or merge caches instead
Companion failure equals game over (Yorda dragged into a vortex): WOLF is independent and essential progress must not depend on him
Silent or slow companion obedience (critics on Trico): acknowledge input instantly and show refusals as clear, quick animated decisions
Finite save items that take inventory space (classic RE ink ribbons) outside an opt-in hard mode
Grid rotation or Tetris inventories (RE4R) that need buttons WOLF's input set does not have
Subtracting the UI so far that key art and screenshots look empty (Ueda's own regret about Ico's marketing)
Full-screen, high-contrast dithered or parallax motion without a comfort check (Obra Dinn's motion-sickness fix)
Safe points placed in 'challenging' spots that Hope admitted were questionable in hindsight
Treating this dossier as the re-run: the six syntheses, the acknowledgement guard, PRESENTATION and the critic still have to be re-run by the workflow script

extra.games: Hollow Knight (Team Cherry, 2017) plus Hollow Knight: Silksong (2025) for comparison; Celeste (Maddy Makes Games, 2018); Alien: Isolation (Creative Assembly, 2014); Resident Evil 2 (Capcom, 2019 remake), with RE1/RE4 typewriter history; Signalis (rose-engine, 2022); Amnesia: The Bunker (Frictional Games, 2023), with The Dark Descent's Hard Mode and Frictional's blog writing on death and saves; Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee (1997), Abe's Exoddus (1998) and New 'n' Tasty (Just Add Water / Oddworld Inhabitants, 2014).
extra.why_relevant: These games are the shipped precedents for the decided death model: dying drops unsecured evidence, and safe points secure it. Three of them map onto it directly. (1) Hollow Knight's Shade: on death you lose everything you carry, it waits where you died, and a second death erases it. Silksong's Cocoon is a later, gentler version of the same idea. (2) Celeste's strawberries are the closest match. A berry follows Madeline and stays "unsecured". It is collected only after she stands on safe ground for 0.15 s. If she dies, it flies back to where it was found. Celeste has no punishment beyond that and a respawn of about 2 s. (3) Alien: Isolation, RE2, Signalis and The Bunker treat the save point as the place that secures progress. Saving is manual, it takes time or a resource, and in Isolation the enemy can still kill you while it runs. The "safe point" is therefore a tension tool, not only a convenience. Frictional's own writing gives the counter-argument that WOLF//OVERRIDE needs to hear: game death is usually "pretty dull", and save hunting can push the story out of the player's head. Oddworld shows the cost of being too sparse. Checkpoint-only saving was the main complaint about Abe's Oddysee and was fixed twice: QuikSave in Exoddus, and denser checkpoints in New 'n' Tasty, capping lost progress at 3 screens. That fits a game made of short, 1.5–2-screen rooms.

extra.companion: No source here describes a companion who changes the death or save rules. Two related facts were found. (1) In New 'n' Tasty co-op, "multiple players on separate controllers [can] take over gameplay when one player dies" (Oddworld Wiki / Wikipedia). Control passes on death, but the companion does not rescue anything. (2) In Silksong, a consumable (the Silkeater) can retrieve the Cocoon "from anywhere on the map", and in Hollow Knight Confessor Jiji will "summon the Shade to her room in return for a Rancid Egg". Both are a paid alternative to the corpse run. Applied to WOLF, this is inference, not precedent: WOLF could offer, or refuse, to fetch dropped evidence, and how he treated the engineer could set whether he does it. The engineer-only rule still needs a guaranteed way back. A Rancid-Egg-style item, or walking back yourself, keeps a path to dropped evidence that never depends on WOLF's mood. Fredrik Olsson's line that the Bunker's beast escalates ("pissing it off will only make it more aggressive the next time", PC Gamer preview paraphrase/quote) shows remembered behaviour carrying across deaths. WOLF's memory could do the same.
extra.level_and_camera: Spacing of safe points, with numbers where sources give them. New 'n' Tasty: checkpoint frequency was raised "so that the most any player would have to redo is a maximum length of three screens" (Wikipedia, citing a Stewart Gilray podcast; that podcast was not fetched). Hollow Knight has 50 benches, including 7 in the Dream Realm. A bench saves the game, is where you "Respawn ... after quitting the game or dying", refills health, and respawns defeated enemies "excluding enemies in the current room". The Bunker: on Easy every sub-area has a save lamp; on Normal and Hard there are only 2 (the Administration room and the entrance to the Roman Tunnels). The safe room has "metal doors that lock, a lantern that serves as a save point, a map, a stash for extra items, and the all-important generator" (PC Gamer preview). The monster cannot pass a locked metal door. Alien: Isolation: Napper does not give spacing. GameSpot criticised "frustrating distances between save points" (Wikipedia summary). Grip says that being "20 minutes from your last save" turns tension into "anger and frustration". RE2: safe rooms "cannot be entered by enemies", and the Tyrant follows the player "except into safe rooms" (Wikipedia, marked citation needed). Hollow Knight boss-death rule: when you die to a boss, the Shade spawns "in a safe location to be recoverable without triggering the boss battle". Copy this. Never put the dropped evidence where picking it up forces the same fatal encounter again. For WOLF//OVERRIDE's 1.5–2-screen rooms, Oddworld's 3-screen cap would mean roughly one secure point every 1–2 rooms. That is derived, not sourced.
extra.death_and_saves: HOLLOW KNIGHT, the Shade. On death you lose all Geo ("All Geo lost on most recent death"). The SOUL meter is capped at "66 charge" until the Shade is beaten. The Shade spawns where you last died and is marked on the map. You respawn at the last bench. Second death: "If the Knight dies before killing the Shade, a new Shade appears at the new death's location and the old one disappears"; the old Geo is gone for good. Shade HP is Nail damage x floor(max HP at death / 2). Dying to a boss puts the Shade outside the arena. Jiji will summon it for a Rancid Egg. Design intent (William Pellen, Game Informer 2018): the idea started from the existing death animation: "his head falling to the ground and cracking", so "you had to travel back to the place you died, find the skull, and crack it open to regain your money". Then "the skull being possessed by an enemy, or suddenly fighting back, which seemed really funny. This evolved into ... a ghost of your previous life that attacks you". Pellen: "a simple mechanical idea ... ending up having a huge impact on the lore". The Kickstarter origin: "we realized we hadn't actually considered that yet." UNVERIFIED: any Team Cherry statement that the Shade exists "to add stakes to exploration". That phrase came only from a search snippet and was not confirmed in a fetched primary source. SILKSONG, the Cocoon. It stores "Rosaries and Silk Spool extensions lost on death" (Silk capped at 9). It breaks in one hit and does not fight back. A second death replaces it and the old Rosaries are lost. A Silkeater retrieves it remotely. CELESTE. From the official Player.cs, Die() increments the death counters, calls Leader.LoseFollowers() (carried berries drop), shakes the screen, plays a light/medium rumble and locks the state machine. The respawn intro tween is ".6f" seconds, after which control returns (StNormal) with a squash scale of (1.5, .5). Unofficial decompile, read for timings only: Freeze 0.05 s; bounce tween 0.5 s cut at 75% (0.375 s) over 24 px; DeathEffect Duration 0.834 s, waited to 65% (~0.54 s); ScreenWipe Duration 0.5 s; then level.Reload. Pressing confirm (Input.MenuConfirm) skips straight to the wipe. DERIVED death-to-control is about 2.0–2.1 s (0.05 + 0.375 + 0.54 + 0.5 wipe + 0.6 respawn, assuming the wipe-in overlaps the respawn tween), or about 1.1 s with the skip. Not measured from footage. UNVERIFIED: any Thorson/Berry quote on instant respawn; the Medium "Celeste & Forgiveness" post returned 403. Golden strawberry: a death with it restarts the whole chapter (GoldenBerryRestart in Player.cs). ALIEN: ISOLATION. To save, the player must "locate a terminal in the world, put in your access card, wait for the systems in the fictional machine to warm up, and then wait for the three simple lights to blink off -- all the while knowing that you could be killed at any moment" (Napper). Wikipedia: "three second pause before the save can be completed, meaning the player can be killed while attempting to save." Simon Adams built it with the scripting tools "to pause the animation for a time whilst three beeps triggered." Why manual: Napper first wanted checkpoints like "Dead Space series, Metroid games and BioShock". Adams asked: "When I get to a soft checkpoint and the alien is about to kill me... What happens when I come back in?" The options were an "infinite loop of dying and respawning" or removing the alien, which would make "sprinting to a checkpoint ... a valid tactic". Neither "supported the core gameplay." Playtesters were "bouncing their knees and talking out loud whilst a save point triggered". They felt "relief" and "excitement at finding a save point", sometimes making them "dash to use it -- even when it wasn't safe". "Players would risk further and further stretches of gameplay between save points". "although some have called it 'punishing,' it fits with the style of the game". Inspired by "Dallas uses a form of key-card to access Mother." Counterpoint, Thomas Grip (Frictional): the stations keep tension up, "But the side-effect is that the save stations become the biggest objective for you as a player. Finding the power station ... is not at all as important as finding the next place to save." Gary Napper also said: "You're going to die a lot, which means restarting a lot, and if the Alien was scripted, you'd see the same behaviour." RESIDENT EVIL. RE1/2/3/CV/0: typewriters need ink ribbons, which are a finite pickup and take inventory slots. RE4 (2005) and the RE2/3/4 remakes use typewriters with unlimited saves. RE2 (2019): the difficulty modes Assisted/Standard/Hardcore set "whether the game autosaves or requires ink ribbons to use typewriters" (Wikipedia, citation needed). The ink ribbon "only appears in Hardcore mode" (RE Wiki, unreferenced). Saves are counted even when unlimited. No Capcom statement on rationale was found: UNVERIFIED. SIGNALIS: "the game can only be saved at safe-rooms where you can stash unused items in a storage chest" (PC Gamer). The Verge calls them "less punishing save points" than the classics. Developer rationale was not fetched (Bloody Disgusting interview, 403): UNVERIFIED. The save device (it is not a typewriter) was not confirmed: UNVERIFIED. AMNESIA. The Bunker: lamps are "an interactive save point. When one is used, it will light up"; "Whenever the player dies, the game will load the last save that was made via interaction with a lamp" (Amnesia Wiki). Frictional patch notes refer to the "save lamp" and its sound when "it goes out". The October 2023 update added "New save systems (saving costs fuel, no saving)" and a "Time Between Saves" stat. Dark Descent Hard Mode: "Autosaves are disabled, and manual saving costs 4 tinderboxes". Frictional's stated rationale for the Bunker's manual saves was not found in any fetched primary source: UNVERIFIED. The nearest is Ian Thomas, 2018: "All it really means is that you go back to a checkpoint, or reload, and all the tension that's built up goes away. The fact is that game death is pretty dull. It becomes much more interesting when it's a part of a mechanic or of the story." Rebirth death rules: not researched or verified. ODDWORLD. In Abe's Oddysee death is instant, lives are unlimited, and you respawn at the last checkpoint. It was criticised for checkpoint-only saving; PC Zone: "Abe is plonked right back at the start of a level when he dies". Per Wikipedia citing Next Generation #41 (not fetched), Oddworld Inhabitants "monitored chat groups and forums and noticed frequent complaints about the difficulty, particularly the save feature". Exoddus added QuikSave, absent from Oddysee "due to programming conflicts" (Wikipedia citing a dead GOG editorial). New 'n' Tasty kept QuikSave and added denser checkpoints (3-screen cap). IGN said this made it easier "even when played on the hardest difficulty".
extra.inventory_and_evidence: The evidence CASE has three precedents. (a) Celeste strawberries: the closest working version of "carried but not yet secured". The berry is a Follower with FollowDelay 0.3 s. It is collected only when "player.OnSafeGround" holds for more than 0.15 s, and the timer resets when you leave the ground. On death (OnLoseLeader) it waits 0.15 s and then flies home along a curve over max(distance/100, 0.4) s. The player loses nothing permanently; they just have to carry it again. (b) Hollow Knight / Silksong: all carried currency drops in one container at the death spot. One retry is allowed; a second death destroys it. (c) Survival-horror item boxes: RE item boxes and the Signalis storage chest have unlimited storage, unlike a 6-slot carry limit (Elster "can only carry six items", PC Gamer). The Bunker's safe room also has a stash. In RE1 the US release planned non-linked item boxes (items retrievable only where stored); this was cut from retail. The decided "safe point secures evidence" rule is a mix of (a) and (c): evidence is held loosely until the engineer reaches a secure point, and that point commits it, the way Celeste commits a berry on safe ground. The open choice is the Shade's second-death rule. Wiping dropped evidence on a second death is the harshest option and the only one in this set that loses permanently. Silksong keeps it, and Celeste avoids it (the item just returns to its origin). For story evidence that gates essential progress, Celeste's "return to origin" or a Jiji-style paid retrieval is safer than permanent loss. That is inference.
extra.action_and_impact: Impact on death in Celeste: from Player.cs, level.Shake() plus a light/medium rumble on Die(). From the decompile: a 0.05 s freeze, the body scaled to 1.5x, a "predeath" sound, then a 0.3 s displacement burst, Shake(0.3), a strong/long rumble and the death sound when the effect bursts. The respawn plays its own sound (char_mad_revive), then a 1.5x by 0.5 squash on regaining control. Alien: Isolation turns the save itself into an action with a cost: card in, warm-up, 3 lights and 3 beeps over about 3 s, with the threat still live. The Bunker turns the save into a visible state change (the lamp lights up) and, in the newer modes, a resource cost (fuel), as Dark Descent Hard Mode did with 4 tinderboxes. Hollow Knight puts a fight on the recovery: Shade HP scales with nail damage, and Joni's Blessing changes it to HP equal to one nail hit.
extra.presentation_ui_art: The Hollow Knight Shade is marked on the map, so the corpse run is never a hunt. A bench's flavour text is "It is warm and safe. Sit and rest." The Alien: Isolation save terminal takes the film's Mother key-card interface as its look ("Dallas uses a form of key-card to access Mother"). Its 3 lights blinking off are the whole progress bar, tied to an in-world device rather than a HUD spinner. This fits AGENT.md's rule of no fake progress, because the lights are the real save interval. The Bunker save lamp lights the room around it when used, so the save state is visible in-world. Celeste shows a death counter (session.Deaths, DeathsInCurrentLevel) as a badge rather than a penalty. RE2 tracks the number of saves even when saving is unlimited.
extra.audio: Safe-room audio rule (RE2 2019): the "Save Room" track "is played at any save room. Unlike most soundtracks of the game, this one doesn't loop" (RE Wiki; the page credits Masami Ueda as a remix of the 1998 save-room theme, unreferenced). Combined with "Safe rooms cannot be entered by enemies" (Wikipedia, citation needed), the rule is: safe room = music plus a guarantee of no threat. A PC Gamer review notes that The Bunker's admin office has its own "take on 'relaxing save room music.'" Alien: Isolation's save stations "give off a faint and distinct beeping noise", which makes players "listen extra carefully when you have gone a long way from a save, making you vulnerable to any other sudden noises" (Grip). The save sequence itself is "three beeps" (Napper). The Bunker's lamp has its own sound when it goes out (patch 1.1 restored "sound effects to the Save lamp in Tunnels when it goes out"). Dark Descent Hard Mode removes danger music. For procedural audio, a single non-looping safe-point cue plus a faint beacon tone audible from the next room is a cheap, sourced pattern.
extra.mobile_and_input: Celeste lets the death animation be skipped with the confirm button (Input.MenuConfirm in PlayerDeadBody.Update calls End() early), which cuts about 1 s from each retry. For WOLF//OVERRIDE, binding the skip to USE makes sense. Alien: Isolation's save is a hold-and-wait interaction, which maps naturally to a USE hold. Hollow Knight benches and RE typewriters are a single interact. None of the fetched sources give touch-specific timings: UNVERIFIED. The Oddworld QuikSave button mapping was not verified.

steal: Celeste's strawberry rule as the core of the evidence CASE: carried evidence follows the engineer visibly and is secured only after a short dwell (Celeste uses 0.15 s) on a secure point. On death it flies back to where it was found instead of being destroyed.
Hollow Knight's map marker for dropped items: always show where unsecured evidence fell, so the walk back is a decision and not a hunt.

Hollow Knight's boss rule: if the engineer dies inside a hazard sequence (sentry, tank drop), place the dropped evidence just outside the trigger so picking it up does not force the same encounter again.
Jiji / Silkeater-style retrieval: a paid or tool-based way to recall dropped evidence. This is a candidate use for the 'one tool', and it gives an engineer-only fallback when WOLF won't fetch it.

Alien: Isolation's in-world save sequence: hold USE at a terminal, 3 lights going out over about 3 s, threat still live. It makes the secure point a tense beat rather than a menu, and the lights are the real progress bar, with no fake loading.
RE2-style safe-room guarantee: the hunter never enters, plus one non-looping safe-room cue. Clear audio tells the player they are safe.
A faint beacon tone from a secure point that can be heard from the neighbouring room (Isolation's beeping stations).
Celeste's skippable death: about 2 s from death to control, with USE skipping the flourish down to about 1 s.
New 'n' Tasty's cap on lost progress: at most about 3 screens repeated after a death, which is about 1-2 WOLF//OVERRIDE rooms.
The Bunker's lamp lights up when used: a visible, in-world state change when evidence is secured.
avoid: Abe's Oddysee's sparse checkpoints with no manual save: the top complaint about the game, fixed in both later releases.
Checkpoints placed near a live hunter: Napper's 'infinite loop of dying and respawning', or despawning the threat so that 'sprinting to a checkpoint' becomes a tactic.

Letting secure points become the only goal: Grip warns the player's story becomes 'a simple hunt for loot and save locations'. Keep evidence and WOLF scenes as the goal and secure points as punctuation.
Long gaps between secure points (Grip's '20 minutes'; GameSpot's 'frustrating distances'). This is out of scale for 3-room content.

Hollow Knight's second-death wipe for essential story evidence. Permanent loss of a progress-critical item breaks the engineer-only guarantee. If anything is wiped, limit it to optional or bonus evidence.
Consumable save tokens (ink ribbons, tinderboxes, fuel) as a default. They fit an optional hard mode, as RE2 Hardcore and Bunker's custom modes do, not the base game.
Death with no consequence beyond a reload. Ian Thomas: game death is 'pretty dull' unless it is part of a mechanic or the story.

extra.games: Half-Life 2: Episode One and Episode Two (Valve, 2006/2007; Alyx Vance and Dog, from the in-game developer commentary transcripts); BioShock Infinite (Irrational Games, 2013; Elizabeth); The Last Guardian (genDESIGN/SIE Japan Studio, 2016; Trico); Fable II (Lionhead, 2008; the dog); Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain (Kojima Productions/Konami, 2015; D-Dog, from guide and community data only); A Plague Tale: Innocence (Asobo, 2019; Hugo); Ico (Team Ico, 2001; Yorda); Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons (Starbreeze, 2013); Titanfall 2 (Respawn, 2016; BT-7274, thin coverage); The Last of Us (Naughty Dog, 2013; Ellie, GDC abstract only). Stray's B-12 was not researched in this pass.
extra.why_relevant: WOLF needs four things that had no evidence behind them: scouting and marking, leading, refusal, and a rule that he never blocks the engineer. All four turn out to be documented, mostly in primary sources. Valve's commentary nodes are the strongest evidence. They are verbatim developer statements based on playtests, they explain why Alyx was changed from leading to following, they give her follow speed, they show that nagging made players hate her within about three minutes, and they list the tricks Valve used to keep her out of the way. Abercrombie's GDC 2014 talk, through GamesBeat's coverage, gives Elizabeth's 'goal-side' positioning, the hidden teleport and the 'icon spotlight' for her callouts. Ueda and the genDESIGN staff explain why Trico disobeys and where the limit sits ('if you can't control it at all it becomes a nuisance, a barrier to progression'). They also describe the play-log-driven hinting and guiding they planned but never shipped. Molyneux describes a dog with no command button whose barks tell the player how important something is, and whose job is to 'lead you off the breadcrumb trail'. D-Dog is the clearest shipped example of automatic marking that grows with the bond (60 m rising to 120 m per a strategy guide), with temporary marks that the player has to make permanent. That maps directly onto 'unsecured vs secured' evidence. One correction to the brief: no fetched source gives a duration for a refusal or intent tell. The companion synthesis's 0.5 s target is still unsupported and should be treated as a number to test in play, not a cited figure.

extra.companion:
SCOUTING AND MARKING (sorted by how strong the evidence is).
(1) Elizabeth: automatic, not requested. Abercrombie (GDC 2014, via GamesBeat): to make her matter in combat 'they would have her call out enemies like snipers. But they soon figured out that players wouldn't always realize where she was pointing. The solution was to employ a spotlight.' His quote: 'We found ourselves needing to provide an icon spotlight on the challenge, much like a dramatic entrance would require a spotlight in the theater.' Levine (GamingBolt, 2011): 'She can toss you ammo, point out enemies, to bring in the tears.' Finding and throwing resources is automatic, and NBC News quotes Levine: 'We wanted to always give you the sense that she's discovering things, that she's finding things.' No detection radius was found. Whether the player must press a button to accept a thrown item is UNVERIFIED.
(2) Fable II dog: automatic, and the player has no command at all. Molyneux (2007): 'We give you no control over the dog... You haven't got a dog button.' and 'You control the dog by playing the game.' In 2008 (PCWorld): 'sniffing out those dig spots, hunting out those chests, warning you of what's going on.' The dog reports finds with a graded bark vocabulary built with dog-behaviour experts: 'There's yaps, there's little trail offs, how fast it trailed off.' The dog's job, from GDC 2008 via Engadget: 'to try lead you off the breadcrumb trail.' Detection radius: UNVERIFIED (Fable wiki is fandom and blocked).
(3) D-Dog: automatic and passive, and it grows with the bond. Gamer Guides (a strategy guide, not Konami): he pinpoints 'enemies, vehicles, weapons, prisoners, and even wild animals, starting at 60m and going up to 120m when his bond meter is full', and also 'plants and mines'. A Steam community guide claims about 150 m at max affinity while standing still, shrinking as the player moves faster, and that 'D-D's temporary tags' should be made 'permanent before closing in'. Temporary tags drop when he is dismissed. Bark and growl as the signal comes only from a search snippet of the fandom wiki, so it is UNVERIFIED. No Konami or Kojima primary source was fetched for any D-Dog number, so every D-Dog figure is UNVERIFIED as a design spec.
(4) Alyx, Episode One: hints by request only. Chet Faliszek (node alyxthekey): 'almost all of Alyx's hint lines were cut... players didn't like having Alyx hand them unsolicited hints, they did want to be able to explicitly request help from her... it's only accessible at the player's request by plus-using Alyx.'
(5) Trico: does not scout. Ueda described an unshipped plan to 'aggregate the play logs of all the players, and if there were stages with low clear rates, we would make Trico give more hints, or hold the boy in its mouth and guide him until he finds the right answer.'

LEADING.
Valve abandoned it as the default. Matt T. Wood (alyxnag): the team 'originally designed Alyx to nag... 'Hurry up!' and 'Keep moving!'... after about three minutes of this, the one thing it definitely did was make the player hate Alyx... led us to switch Alyx from generally leading players to almost always following... players much preferred to set the pace themselves.' alyxconsole: once Alyx followed, a whole lead-and-console scene 'became irrelevant, and we happily cut the whole thing.' Bill Van Buren (alyxcitadeltone): urgency acted out by a leader was 'unsustainable' because 'Alyx eventually ran out of lines or animations'. The fix was that she 'is always content to proceed at whatever pace the player chooses'.
Follow speed, Doug Wood (alyxrunspeed): it 'looks and feels the best when she's moving faster than the player's normal speed, but slower than the player's sprint speed.'
Leading that worked was a designed beat, not a system. Danika Wright (EP2-Comment172): 'Racing Dog to the base was not a preconceived plan. It was born out of testing... repeatedly trying to keep up with Dog... we began to figure out ways to encourage players to do it too.'
Elizabeth was framed as 'leader and follower' (GDC abstract). Her positioning: 'Similar to how soccer defenders try to keep themselves between an attacker and the goal... keep Elizabeth on the screen between the DeWitt and his destination' ('goal-side pathing', credited to Tim Austin, which arrived only in the final year).
How far ahead a companion runs before waiting: no primary source found. This is UNVERIFIED. The only figure is a Steam forum post saying D-Dog runs to catch up if the player gets '40-80 meters away', and his wait command lasts about 10 s. That is community data and unverified.

REFUSAL.
Trico is the only shipped companion in this set that refuses on purpose. Ueda (2010, Game Developer): 'It's not like Trico will not listen to the boy every single time... Maybe it will, maybe it won't. This is an animal.' Ueda to Edge (quoted by Kill Screen, 2015): 'it doesn't always do what you ask it to do. That's one of the themes', and 'another game where you can completely control a creature wouldn't be enjoyable for me.' Ueda (2016, via PSU): 'if you can fully control a character, what's the point? It becomes a pet. But at the opposite end if you can't control it at all it becomes a nuisance, a barrier to progression.' genDESIGN roundtable: cats 'don't always listen to what you say, you probably always end up forgiving them.'
How often Trico refuses: no number exists in any fetched source (UNVERIFIED). PlayStation Blog: 'doesn't always do what you'd like it to do on first asking'. The PSLS guide: 'you may have to tell Trico to do something a couple of times'.
How refusal is telegraphed: Kill Screen, paraphrasing Edge, says Trico's 'eyes also reflect different colors to reflect its current mood, such as pink for anger or wariness'. KeenGamer lists more colours (secondary). Sniffing and other distractions show up in guides. Tanaka animated Trico 'checking several times to make sure the boy was still on its tail'.
The cost: reviewers reported 'impatience and frustration due to lack of immediate action'. Game Revolution called commands sometimes 'ineffective and unnecessary' because Trico acted without input.
Others: Valve cut every impatient line ('lines where Alyx sounded impatient or frustrated... were cut'). Respawn found early BT scripts 'bossy' and reworked them over five months (Wikipedia citing The Verge; Verge not fetched, so UNVERIFIED). Brothers turns one refusal into a mechanic: the younger brother cannot swim, so he clings to the older brother's back.

MEMORY. Fable II's dog 'starts to become a reflection of what you're like... more aggressive to certain sorts of people because you've been aggressive to those sorts of people.' Molyneux also gave a 12 to 14 hour arc to 'cement this relationship'. Elsewhere Fable II colours the dog by the player's alignment. Ueda planned to 'adjust Trico's personality to match the user's play style' through network updates, but it was never shipped.

THE 0.5 S TELL. No fetched source gives a duration for an intent or refusal tell. Treat 0.5 s as a starting value to test in play, not as evidence.
extra.level_and_camera:
Keeping companions from blocking progress came down to level and staging tricks.
Valve:
- Gate scenes with soft blockers, not hard gates. EP2-Comment086 (Doug Lombardi): 'we simply placed a few barrels to block the way while Alyx and the Vortigaunt speak. Even with this slight impediment, every playtester stayed and watched the scene as we intended, so no explicit gate was needed.'
- Let the companion leave by a route the player can't take. justhavetodoit (Matt Scott): 'the final solution was to have Alyx climb out while the player looks for an alternate route... we're not especially happy with this crutch, but it's a trade-off... to get Alyx out of the way of interesting player challenges.'
- Use darkness to slow the player so the companion stays close. benefitsofdarkness: it 'slows the player down, which most of the time keeps Alyx at your side.'
- Take the companion out of boss fights. separatefromalyx: 'Alyx more or less sits out all of our boss encounters' because 'having too much help dilutes the sense of individual accomplishment.'
- Build alternate entry points. EP2-Comment114: Alyx 'needed multiple entries into a vehicle, given that the doorway she wanted to use could be blocked', and Valve refused visible teleporting because it 'would ruin Alyx's believability'.
- Make room for companion behaviour on purpose. EP2-Comment238 (Tom Leonard): 'Normally, Alyx is out of frame during combat'. The inn map pulls the player back from the windows 'to create space for Alyx'.
Irrational:
- Elizabeth is kept 'on the screen between the DeWitt and his destination' (goal-side pathing).
- 'quietly teleporting Elizabeth to the player's side if they happened to get too far ahead — the better to avoid having to deal with obstacles like railings.' Abercrombie: 'players won't know what we're doing... They will only know what they see on the screen.'
- Wikipedia (citing CVG) says Elizabeth's actions depend on 'whether the player is near and looking at Elizabeth', and the game watches the player to keep her out of the line of fire. That claim was not fetched first-hand.
Trico:
- IGN's review faulted the camera in cramped interiors around a large companion (via Wikipedia). For a side view, keep WOLF's body clear of the engineer's next jump.
- R1 call stays available while the boy is grabbed. Colquhoun calls it a 'safety net', and the camera shows Trico's distance and whether something (a glass eye) blocks his path.
For WOLF's 1.5 to 2 screen rooms: put WOLF goal-side (between the engineer and the room's exit or objective, on screen). Teleport him only when he is off-camera. Give every WOLF-only route (a vent or ledge he can reach) an engineer route next to it.
extra.death_and_saves:
- Fable II: the dog 'cannot be killed, but can become injured and ineffective, requiring healing by the player' (Wikipedia). Molyneux: 'The only thing you're really responsible for doing is healing him.' Losing him is story-only (killed in the plot, then a resurrection wish or Knothole Island DLC).
- Elizabeth: requires no protection. Levine (2011): 'You are not obligated to take care of her in the way that you are in an escort mission.' (2013): 'She's not somebody who's along for the ride or somebody that you have to protect.'
- Ico is the counter-example. 'the game is over if Yorda becomes fully engulfed in a vortex', and progress needs doors 'only she can open' (Wikipedia). WOLF's rules forbid this kind of essential dependency.
- Trico: the call button is the protection mechanic. It still works while the boy is grabbed, and mashing it frees him.
- Valve, EP2-Comment090: an injured, slow Alyx was cut because 'playtesters did not enjoy waiting for her to catch up, or going back to retrieve her'. Her recovery was moved to the previous map.
For WOLF's evidence-drop death model: no source here ties a companion to keeping items through a death. That link would be original design, not borrowed.
extra.inventory_and_evidence:
- D-Dog's tags have two tiers: temporary while D-Dog is present, permanent once the player tags them. Source is Steam community guidance, UNVERIFIED by Konami. This maps cleanly onto WOLF: what WOLF sniffs out is 'unsecured' (it shows only while WOLF is near or until the engineer confirms it with USE), and the engineer's confirmation 'secures' it in the CASE.
- Elizabeth hands the player resources (ammo, health, salts, money) and picks locks. Critics also noted the downside. bit-tech (via Wikipedia) complained she 'never mentioned she was picking ammo up' and 'would throw coins during voxaphone listenings and mid-fight'.
- Fable II's dog points out chests and dig spots, but digging needs the player's spade. The companion finds, the player collects.
- Titanfall 2: BT's loadouts come from equipment 'typically found before a sequence which will benefit from the player switching to that loadout' (Wikipedia). The pickup is placed where it is about to matter.
- Trico eats barrels the boy must find and carry. Feeding is the bonding loop ('How does it feel to actually feed Trico?', Ueda, PS Blog 2016).
- Cut idea from genDESIGN: 'feeding Trico jars that were buried in the ground, and having it spit out treasure items.'
extra.action_and_impact:
- Valve, powerboxes (Jake Nicholson): making the player guard Alyx while she worked 'didn't work out. Playtesters were more annoyed than entertained... whenever Alyx commits to some action in a dynamic environment, she needs to finish it quickly and move on.'
- EP2-Comment003 (Marc Laidlaw): Alyx 'is careful not to steal the player's fun by doing it all herself. She doesn't actually solve the puzzle, although she sometimes thinks she has.'
- EP2-Comment150: vehicle Alyx 'constantly targeted and fired her gun at everything. This made her feel a bit like a turret', so she was retuned to fire more slowly while moving.
- EP2-Comment041: the Vortigaunt stuns antlions 'so that the player could finish them off'. The ally sets up, the player lands the blow.
- EP2-Comment167: the Dog vs strider fight began slowly and 'players were uncertain of their role'. It was changed so Dog goes 'straight into action'.
- Irrational 'wanted to avoid giving Elizabeth any of the same tools that the player had, such as a gun' (Wikipedia citing IGN).
- Fable II's dog attacks downed enemies. Molyneux (via search summary, Destructoid not fetched) said a 'Go and attack those enemies' button made it 'a robot dog' (UNVERIFIED wording).
- D-Dog can be ordered to attack, stun or kill depending on gear.
For WOLF: his actions should set up the engineer's beat (stun, distract, brace) rather than finish it, and any WOLF action should resolve within a short, fixed window so he never makes the player wait.
extra.presentation_ui_art:
- Pointing needs a spotlight. Abercrombie's 'icon spotlight on the challenge'. If WOLF reports a find, also highlight the target on screen, not just WOLF's gaze.
- An eye or face that shows mood and gaze. Trico's eye colour shows mood (pink for anger or wariness, per Kill Screen paraphrasing Edge). BT got 'a large emotive eye, so players would know where the titan is looking' (Wikipedia citing The Verge, UNVERIFIED first-hand). A robotic wolf can carry a visor or eye colour plus head direction as the refusal and intent channel.
- Elizabeth was designed with a 'two-tone colour scheme and unique silhouette' and 'hyper-realistic expressions to help players see her from across the battlefield' (Wikipedia).
- D-Dog's targets are 'highlighted in red' (accelerated-ideas guide).
- Fable II's dog changes coat colour with the player's alignment (grey, gold, black), a visible readout of memory.
- Tanaka on Trico's procedural animation: 'it's quite difficult to produce a natural gaze or powerful pose.' Plan to hand-author WOLF's key tells.
extra.audio:
- Fable II: the barks were the reporting UI. 'We really sat down and talked to people who understood dog behavior... dogs do have a language... There's yaps, there's little trail offs, how fast it trailed off' (Molyneux, 2008). This means encoding importance in bark length and decay.
- Valve: urgency and nag lines were cut. Merle Dandridge (EP2-Comment247) was redirected whenever she started 'to sound a little naggy... like somebody's mother'. Her summary: 'You don't want somebody constantly bothering you but you also want a friendly companion, somebody to help you out once in a while.'
- EP2-Comment109: designers made a puzzle's order of states predictable so 'we were able to write a limited number of lines for Alyx, so that she could react each time the puzzle changed state.' Reactions are tied to puzzle state, not timers.
- EP1 youremynewhero: 'Positive feedback from Alyx is one of our primary means of rewarding players.'
- Trico: hints come through the narrator's voiceover. Ueda added a meditate pose (long-press the L stick) so 'players who missed those' could replay the previous hint. Ueda (genDESIGN Part 2): 'We adjusted the number of hints after seeing how the playtests went, but it was still extremely difficult to determine the correct amount.'
extra.mobile_and_input:
- Trico's final scheme (PSLS guide): tap R1 to call; R1 + stick to point; R1 + Triangle to jump; R1 + Square to attack; R1 + Cross or Circle to scold or praise. Commands unlock only after a voiceover establishes the bond.
- Tried and cut for Trico (genDESIGN Part 4): 'at first, pressing a button would change it to first-person view, and then you could choose to give instructions'. Tanaka: 'the most impressive change was the method of giving instructions... once the design of that part was set to how it is now, it determined the direction of the game.'
- Fable II: no dog button at all. Whistling to the dog through the headset microphone was tried and cut as 'too gimmicky' (Engadget, 2009, paraphrase).
- Plague Tale (Dedeine): extended command abilities were cut because 'When you can give more orders it [feels] too much like a robot... "Do this, go here, grab that." It was not natural.' The team 'had to give Hugo back more freedom.'
- Valve flashlightgameplay: directing Alyx's fire with the flashlight was liked because 'you could interact with Alyx in a meaningful way using elements that were already built into the interface.' Help on request comes from +use on Alyx.
- Brothers: one stick plus one trigger per brother.
For WOLF's hold-to-move, one USE and two choice buttons, this evidence supports:
- no dedicated WOLF command menu
- USE on WOLF = ask for a hint or a scouting report (Alyx +use)
- the two choice buttons = praise/scold-style answers that feed his memory (Trico's R1 + Circle/Cross)
- a guaranteed, always-available call that works even when the engineer is grabbed (Trico R1)
On touch, the call and ask actions must be reachable with one thumb. That last point is a conclusion, not sourced.

steal: Make WOLF follow by default and lead only in designed beats. Valve switched Alyx 'from generally leading players to almost always following', and the one leading moment that worked (racing Dog to the base) came out of playtests and was then supported by level design.

Set WOLF's follow speed between the engineer's walk and run, as Valve did for Alyx. Hold-to-move has no sprint, so tune against the engineer's top walking speed and make WOLF's catch-up speed faster than it.
Keep WOLF goal-side, on screen between the engineer and the room's exit or objective (Elizabeth's soccer-defender positioning). In a side-view room this means the exit-side third of the frame.
If WOLF falls behind off-camera, teleport him, but never in view. Irrational did this quietly; Valve refused visible teleports for Alyx's vehicle entry.

Make scouting automatic and passive, with two-tier marks. WOLF finds things on his own; the marks are temporary ('unsecured') and only become permanent ('secured') when the engineer confirms them with USE. This copies D-Dog's temporary tags and fits the evidence-drop death model.
Whenever WOLF calls something out, also spotlight the target on screen. Abercrombie found players could not tell where Elizabeth was pointing and needed an 'icon spotlight'.
Hints only on request: USE on WOLF asks for one. Valve cut almost all of Alyx's unsolicited hints and then restored them behind plus-use.
Give WOLF a graded vocalisation vocabulary in which length and decay encode importance (Fable II's 'yaps... little trail offs, how fast it trailed off').

Make refusal part of the character but never a blocker. Ueda's limit: if the companion 'can't control it at all it becomes a nuisance, a barrier to progression'. Every refusal needs an engineer-only route in the same room.

Telegraph intent and refusal through a mood channel on WOLF's face or visor plus head and gaze direction, as with Trico's eye colours and BT's emotive eye. Hand-author these tells, because Tanaka found procedural gaze hard. Tune the length of the tell in play rather than assuming 0.5 s.
Give the engineer one guaranteed call that always works, even while grabbed, and show WOLF's distance and anything blocking his path (the Trico R1 'safety net').

When WOLF commits to an action, he finishes it fast (Valve powerboxes rule). WOLF sets up the engineer's beat (stun, distract, brace) and the engineer lands it (Vortigaunt stun, Alyx not stealing the puzzle).
Let memory change visible behaviour and appearance. The Fable II dog 'starts to become a reflection of what you're like' and changes coat colour with alignment.
Use the two choice buttons as praise and scold answers that feed WOLF's memory (Trico's R1+Circle/Cross), instead of adding a command menu.
Gate story scenes with soft blockers, not locked doors. A few barrels were enough for every Valve playtester.
Add a 'replay last WOLF hint' action. Trico's meditate pose (long-press the L stick) replays the last voiceover hint.
avoid: Urgency or nag lines ('Hurry up!'). They made players hate Alyx within about three minutes; Valve cut every impatient line.
A bossy companion voice. BT's early scripts were judged 'bossy' (reported five-month rework, UNVERIFIED first-hand), and Alyx's actor was pulled back whenever she sounded 'naggy'.
Making the player wait or guard while the companion works. Valve's powerboxes made playtesters 'more annoyed than entertained' and exposed robotic behaviour.
A slow or injured companion the player has to wait for or go back for. Valve cut injured Alyx's slow run for exactly this reason (EP2-Comment090).

A command menu or order-giving system. Plague Tale's extra orders felt 'too much like a robot'; Fable II found an attack button made a 'robot dog'; Trico's first-person instruction mode was replaced; headset whistling was cut as gimmicky.

Refusal with no fallback or unclear timing. Trico reviews cite 'impatience and frustration due to lack of immediate action', camera fights in cramped interiors, and commands that felt 'ineffective and unnecessary' when Trico acted on its own.
Essential dependency on the companion. Ico's doors only Yorda can open and its game-over when she is taken conflict with WOLF's engineer-only fallback rule.
A companion who solves the puzzle or wins the boss fight. Valve made Alyx sit out bosses ('too much help dilutes the sense of individual accomplishment') and had her not 'steal the player's fun'.
Constant-fire or turret-like help. Vehicle Alyx 'felt a bit like a turret' until her fire rate was cut.
Item hand-offs that interrupt story audio or fights without saying anything. Critics faulted Elizabeth for silently picking up ammo and throwing coins during voxophones and mid-fight.
Gaze-only pointing. Players could not tell where Elizabeth was pointing until a spotlight was added.
Quoting 60/120 m (D-Dog) or 0.5 s (tell length) as established fact. Neither comes from a developer source.

extra.games: Resident Evil 4 (2005) and Resident Evil 4 remake (2023), Resident Evil 2 remake (2019), Resident Evil Village (2021, iPhone port 2023), Signalis (rose-engine, 2022), Return of the Obra Dinn (Lucas Pope, 2018), Outer Wilds (Mobius Digital, 2019), Her Story (Sam Barlow, 2015), Alien: Isolation (Creative Assembly, 2014). PROCESS NOTE: this session's shared WebSearch budget (200 calls) was used up before this agent began, so no web search was run. Sources were found from the reference lists of fetched Wikipedia articles and from URLs already known. YouTube captions for the GDC and Noclip videos were downloaded with yt-dlp and read as auto-generated transcripts. The following were blocked and are NOT cited as fetched: the TIGSource Obra Dinn devlog (Cloudflare challenge), all Fandom wikis (HTTP 402/403), the Bloody Disgusting Signalis interview (403) and the TouchArcade Alien: Isolation mobile review (403). Archive.org copies were deliberately not used.
extra.why_relevant: These games fill the gap the earlier synthesis left open: how a scarce item CASE, a separate evidence log and a "secured" record are designed and laid out. The findings in brief: (1) the slot count is tuned by playtesting toward discomfort. Signalis uses 6 slots, RE2 remake starts at 8 slots and grows to 20, and RE4 uses a grid that starts at 60 cells. (2) Every RE game in this set keeps key items and treasures out of the scarce case. (3) The best logs record only what the player has certainly seen. Outer Wilds entries are "only ever what we're 100% certain the player knows". (4) Correctness is confirmed in batches so players cannot guess. Obra Dinn confirms fates in threes. (5) Controller book layouts separate selecting from page-turning. Obra Dinn's gamepad scheme was built first. (6) Touch ports that put the full controller pad on screen fail; RE Village on iPhone is the example. Designing touch-first with single taps works; Her Story is the example. (7) A save or secure act can carry tension when it takes a short, interruptible moment; Alien: Isolation's card terminal waits through three beeps. Together these map directly onto WOLF//OVERRIDE's evidence CASE, its one tool, its safe points that secure evidence, and its death model in which dying drops unsecured evidence.
