extra.companion: None of these games has an independent companion that touches the inventory or the log, so the research gives no direct precedent for WOLF and the CASE. RE4's Ashley and RE Village's characters were not researched for this question. Indirect lessons follow. (a) Outer Wilds keeps "keeping track of what they've learned" off the player's plate: Kelsey Beachum said it "should not be the challenging part of piecing the story together" (GDC, about 32:30). If WOLF comments on or summarises CASE records, he should add colour on top of the factual log, never replace it, and essential records must exist without him (the engineer-only rule). (b) Obra Dinn keeps the book "passive": Pope said it "can't invoke the watch's power, just allow you to read stuff" and "I didn't want those two beams crossing" (RPS). The equivalent for WOLF//OVERRIDE is to keep the CASE as a record and keep WOLF's actions in the world, so that a refusal by WOLF never locks the player out of reading or securing evidence. This is a design inference, not a sourced finding.
extra.level_and_camera: These sources say little about camera; the relevant points are pacing and placement. Signalis uses a fixed overhead camera and "a map that marks key rooms, and doors as broken, open or locked" (PC Gamer preview). Obra Dinn: until a month before release, a memory scene showed for about "a minute", then the book appeared and the game sent the player back. Pope changed it so players can wander after the book fills in, but admits players are still "waiting for the book to appear", and said "To fix that would have been a lot more work" (RPS). RE4 remake: changes to the environment persist on revisits (Wikipedia RE4 2023). The typewriter is also where storage and case customisation live, which makes safe points the inventory-management locations (IGN wiki). Alien: Isolation save terminals had to be placed throughout the level art. Napper initially refused because "We would have to place terminals everywhere, change the art for the affected areas, and change the code" (Game Developer). Implication for wider rooms: budget one safe point per room cluster as a placed, visible object, not a menu.
extra.death_and_saves: ALIEN: ISOLATION (Gary Napper, design director, Game Developer deep dive, Feb 2015). The game has no soft saves or checkpoints. To save, the player inserts an access card at a terminal, waits for the machine to warm up, then waits "for the three simple lights to blink off -- all the while knowing that you could be killed at any moment". Wikipedia describes this as a "three second pause". Why they rejected checkpoints: with a systemic alien, a soft checkpoint either traps the player in "an infinite loop of dying and respawning" or removes the alien on load, which "would mean sprinting to a checkpoint was a valid tactic". The designer Simon Adams pitched manual saves; Napper "said no many times" until a quick push-button prototype made the team "afraid". Adams then swapped the button for the film-derived card terminal and used scripting "to pause the animation for a time whilst three beeps triggered", which "sold it to the non-believers". Observed effects: knee-bouncing, "Come on! He's nearby!", and "relief" on seeing a save point. Players "would risk further and further stretches of gameplay between save points". A player "only needs to have that sense of loss once". RE2 REMAKE: safe rooms "cannot be entered by enemies" and hold item boxes and typewriters. Ink ribbons are needed only on Hardcore (Wikipedia; that sentence is tagged citation-needed). RE4 REMAKE: the typewriter both saves and opens storage and case customisation (IGN wiki). OUTER WILDS: Kelsey Beachum frames "failure in the game as progression"; the player is "going to learn something from that death" (GDC, about 46:00). That ship-log entries survive each loop's death fits the design but is UNVERIFIED from the fetched text. MAPPING TO WOLF//OVERRIDE: a short, interruptible "secure" interaction at a safe point (Alien's 3 beeps) gives securing evidence its own weight. Dropped unsecured evidence then creates the loss that Napper says players need to feel only once. For accessibility, keep the secure interaction short and fair, and never place it where an unavoidable threat can spawn. That last point is an inference.
extra.inventory_and_evidence: SLOT COUNTS AND WHY. Signalis: a 6-slot inventory that holds everything carried, weapons, ammo and key items included (Wikipedia; PC Gamer). Yuri Stern (Vice): "if you're comfortable in a survival horror game, something isn't quite right"; "We designed much of the game around the number six, but tested the game with various inventory sizes. It turned out testers would still always fill up their inventory to the brim ... even if they didn't need it." The cost, per PC Gamer's preview: one gun plus its ammo is 2 slots, healing makes 3, a defensive item 4, and the flashlight and the camera ("for visual notes of puzzle hints") use the rest before any key item. "Just one extra slot (or letting me permanently equip the torch and camera) would have solved 80% of my inventory woes." RE2 remake: 8 slots, plus 6 hip pouches at +2 each, for 20 at most (Polygon); item boxes in safe rooms (Wikipedia). RE4 (2005): the attaché case is a grid of "60 cells (6x10)" (IGN wiki); the larger original case sizes are UNVERIFIED. RE4 remake: starts at "70 Cells (7x10)", with upgrades of 7x12, 8x12, 8x13 and 9x13 (IGN wiki). Producer Yoshiaki Hirabayashi (IGN 2022): they kept "the briefcase's puzzle-like resource management ... rotating weapons and items to make them fit just right and agonizing over what to keep and what to throw away". The remake adds case colours or charms with passive perks, and 2 quick-slots per D-pad direction ("up from one"). RE Village: an RE4-style briefcase where items can be moved and rotated, plus a separate map and "a diary with sketches recapping the player's progress" (Wikipedia). Producer Morimasa Sato: "This is where we really learned a lot from Resident Evil 4" (IGN First). KEY ITEMS VERSUS FILES. RE4: "Weapons, ammunition, and healing items are kept in the case, while key items and treasures are kept in a separate menu" (Wikipedia RE4; IGN wiki: "All Treasures will be held elsewhere"). Signalis is the counter-example: key items do share the 6 slots, and a utility item (the camera) is needed to make visual notes. Whether Signalis documents use a separate archive tab is UNVERIFIED because the Fandom and wiki.gg pages were blocked. DOES TIME PAUSE IN THE INVENTORY? No fetched source states it for any of these games. The common observation is that RE2R, RE4, RE4R and Signalis inventory screens pause the game, and that Alien: Isolation's crafting happens in real time; all of this is UNVERIFIED and should be checked by play. HOW A DOCUMENT IS FRAMED AS EVIDENCE. Outer Wilds (Kelsey Beachum, GDC, about 32:30 to 33:30): each Nomai text was written to convey "that absolute most basic piece of information", and "entries are only ever what we're 100 certain the player knows from reading that text ... no inferences". They assumed "the player knows any amount and any combination of information at any given time", so the log cannot rely on a funnel. Noclip (about 37:00 to 37:30; the speaker is unclear in the captions, Alex Beachum or Loan Verneau): "we didn't want people to have to take paper notes". The first version was only the solar-system map view; "we added the rumor mode with the lines, the detective board, like a year before launch" because playtesters "just weren't understanding the structure of the game"; "let's just put our design docs into the game". Obra Dinn (RPS): the book began as a "very basic" three-page manifest. After PAX Australia in November 2016 ("60 ... people, four decks, flashbacks that are totally non-chronological") it became a full book. Pope first tried a timeline UI and found it "cluttered". Chapter titles like "The End, Part Three" let the book work as a timeline: "suddenly you could flip through it like a timeline". Chapters "start out blank, magically filling in" when a scene is witnessed. Fates are validated "only in sets of three" (Wikipedia), which stops brute-force guessing. Transcripts mark the dying speaker with a cross because "I don't like reducing somebody to a letter". Her Story: a fake 1990s police terminal, "the computer itself a prop" (Barlow, Guardian), searchable over 271 clips (Wikipedia). Only the first 5 clips matching a word are shown, so "the more revelatory stuff was saved until later" (PocketGamer.biz). Player-made tags become searchable terms. A desktop "database checker" turns each clip's box from red to green once watched (Wikipedia). Barlow tuned word frequency in a spreadsheet so that he was "never at any point scripting a specific path for players" (GamesRadar/Edge). HOW A RECORD SHOWS AS SECURED. Obra Dinn: validation in threes. Her Story: red becomes green. Alien: three lights blink off. No source gives an animation duration for the Obra Dinn confirmation (UNVERIFIED).
extra.action_and_impact: This question had little to do with action. The relevant impact is feedback when something is secured or confirmed. Alien: Isolation proves that a held, short wait with three audible beeps can carry the tension of a whole save system (Napper). Gears of War's active reload was Napper's inspiration for "a simple interaction" that could trigger emotion. RE4 remake frames inventory as a puzzle, "rotating weapons and items to make them fit just right" (Hirabayashi). For WOLF//OVERRIDE, a one-hold USE at a safe point could fill three pips over about 2 to 3 s, using Alien's three-beep pattern, and be cancellable if the engineer moves. That is an inference; the only sourced figure is "a three second pause" (Wikipedia, Alien: Isolation).
extra.presentation_ui_art: Obra Dinn (RPS): Pope wanted the book to "definitely look like a book" and asked "could I print it out, and would it look cool?" The gutter shifts from one side of the spine to the other as pages turn. He promised himself "the most basic UI I could get away with" after the pain of localising Papers, Please (its documents were 50x100 px, laid out by hand pixel by pixel, then put into seven more languages). A looser book layout made localisation easier but cost "a lot of complicated programming". Her Story: the interface is "part Apple II, part Windows 3.1 and part Windows 98" (PocketGamer.biz). A 3D scene with strip lights and an onlooking viewer gives the screen its reflections (GamesRadar/Edge). Footage was run "through two VHS players" for period noise. Signalis: a CRT mode and PS1-era presentation (Wikipedia); low-res 3D over pixel-art backdrops (PC Gamer). RE4 remake: case colours and charms as cosmetic and perk customisation (IGN). Outer Wilds rumor mode: cards linked by lines, a "detective board" (Noclip). Takeaway for the CASE: present it as a diegetic physical object (case or ledger) with a fixed, printable-looking layout. Keep records in a separate ledger or board view with chronology implied by titles, not a timeline widget.
extra.audio: Alien: Isolation: three beeps during the save wait are the core of the save tension (Napper). In Eurogamer's review, the motion tracker's "familiar retro beeps" measure the creature's distance. Signalis: the radio decodes signals; "cryptic messages and noise add another layer of anxiety", and frequencies give codes, sounds or even harm enemies (PC Gamer). Outer Wilds: the ship log has no audio statements in the sources. The signalscope design took inspiration from NASA "sounds from Saturn" recordings (Noclip, about 37:30 to 38:00). For WOLF//OVERRIDE, a short procedural secure tone (3 ticks, then a confirm) fits the existing procedural audio kit. That is an inference.
extra.mobile_and_input: CONTROLLER, Obra Dinn (RPS): Pope designed "a gamepad scheme" for the book first "because he knew it'd be harder to create". He separated "the D-pad selection from page turning to avoid accidental page turns", with shoulder buttons paging in an early mockup. He added bookmarks to "refer back to all the scenes in which a single character appears" ("everyone knows what a bookmark is"). He kept only one shortcut, "which flicks to the table of contents": "Anything else would need a lot of instruction", and "The player will figure out to turn the page." His first mockup's scheme was "bizarre": sticks scrolled the map and sketch windows, the action button edited a fate, and shoulders turned pages. He also dropped a "superfluous" timeline indicator. RE4 remake: 2 quick-slots per D-pad direction (IGN wiki). How Outer Wilds' ship log is navigated on a gamepad is UNVERIFIED (the wiki was blocked). TOUCH, Her Story (PocketGamer.biz, Barlow): "Most of the effort went into working around the differences between the precision of a mouse in a simulated PC desktop vs the way a fingertip works on a touch screen". "I developed first on iOS, so my pretend desktop system has a few Apple-esque features like only using single clicks". The iPhone layout is 640x480 against 800x600 on desktop (Wikipedia). Mobile was 40% of the first 100,000 sales. Barlow called the mobile version a "'sofa' experience" (Wikipedia). RE Village iPhone (Digital Foundry): it "presents a full modern controller layout through an on-screen overlay, which doesn't work well at all", calling it "technically playable, but far from pleasant" and "awful". Bluetooth pads added latency, and a DualSense's stick-clicks were not recognised, "blocking progression". The settings menu is "way too complex for a mobile title". RE4 remake iOS shipped 20 Dec 2023 (Wikipedia); its touch layout for the attaché case is UNVERIFIED. Historical: RE4 Mobile Edition (2008 BREW, 2009 iOS) split the story into sections ("Village", "Ravine", "Fortress", "Subterranean Tunnel") (Wikipedia). Alien: Isolation iOS and Android shipped 16 Dec 2021 (Feral); its touch details are UNVERIFIED (TouchArcade was blocked). MAPPING TO WOLF//OVERRIDE (inference): the CASE should use tap-to-select plus big drag-free targets, with no rotate gestures and no Tetris on touch. Choice buttons can double as page left and page right. Pause or Back closes. Use a single "contents" shortcut.

steal: Split the CASE into two physically distinct parts. (1) A scarce item tray: start small, around 6 cells, following Signalis' 6 and RE2R's 8, and tune by playtest; testers fill whatever you give them, per Stern. (2) A separate evidence ledger that never costs a slot. RE4 keeps key items and treasures in a separate menu.

Do not let utility items consume the scarce slots. PC Gamer says Signalis' flashlight and camera taking 2 of 6 slots caused '80%' of its inventory pain. Make the one tool a permanent equip, not a slot item.

Write each evidence record as only what the source certainly shows, with no inferences. That is Outer Wilds' rule: entries are 'only ever what we're 100 certain the player knows'. This lets records be read in any order.
Name records so they sort themselves into a timeline, the way Obra Dinn's chapter titles do ('The End, Part Three'), instead of building a timeline widget. Pope found a timeline UI 'cluttered'.
Show 'secured' as a visible state change on a fixed grid, such as Her Story's red-to-green database checker boxes. Confirm deductions in batches (Obra Dinn: sets of 3) so they can't be brute-forced.

Make securing at a safe point a short diegetic, interruptible act with a three-beat sound and light pattern, like Alien: Isolation's card terminal ('three simple lights to blink off'). The relief of finding a safe point becomes a highlight in the level.

Controller layout: D-pad or stick selects inside a page, and the two choice buttons (or shoulders) turn pages. Keep selection separate from page-turning to avoid accidental turns. Offer exactly one shortcut, to contents, as Obra Dinn does. Build the gamepad scheme first.
Add bookmarks or filters per subject (Obra Dinn bookmarks per character) instead of many shortcuts.
Touch: design touch-first with single taps (Her Story was 'developed first on iOS ... only using single clicks'). Use large tappable cards and no drag-rotate.
Put item storage and case management at the save point (the RE4R typewriter opens storage), so safe points are where the CASE gets reorganised and secured.
avoid: Do not port a full controller pad as a touch overlay. Digital Foundry on RE Village iPhone: it 'doesn't work well at all' and the touch controls are 'awful'.
Do not use rotate-and-pack Tetris as the touch interaction. RE4's grid puzzle depends on precise rotation, and no fetched source shows it working well by touch (UNVERIFIED either way).
Do not log inferences the player may not have made. The Outer Wilds team assumed players hold 'any amount and any combination of information at any given time'.
Do not force a wait before the record becomes usable. Pope admits Obra Dinn still leaves players 'waiting for the book to appear' and called the fix 'a lot more work'.
Do not add shortcuts that need teaching. Pope: 'Anything else would need a lot of instruction.'
Do not use soft checkpoints that respawn the player near an active threat. Alien: Isolation rejected both the 'infinite loop of dying and respawning' and 'sprinting to a checkpoint' as a tactic.

Do not make the player keep paper notes to progress. Outer Wilds built the ship log because 'we didn't want people to have to take paper notes'. Her Story embraced notebooks only because there was no threat or time pressure.
Do not make evidence readable only through WOLF. This follows the engineer-only rule and Obra Dinn's 'passive' book principle, which keeps record-reading separate from world actions.

Correction to the brief: there is no 2023 Flashback remake. The remake came out in 2013 (VectorCell, directed by Cuisset). The 2023 release is the sequel Flashback 2 (Microids, 16 Nov 2023).
extra.why_relevant: WOLF//OVERRIDE is moving from short single-screen rooms to rooms 1.5 to 2 screens wide, with walk-through doorways, one walkable height change per room, and a 'real feel' layer (per-surface footsteps, room tone, breathing, weight). Of the games here, only New 'n' Tasty made the same flip-screen to scrolling move and wrote down the design consequence: flip screens were secretly the puzzle and AI reset button, and scrolling removed it. Another World and Flashback show rotoscoped weight, cuts between screens, and play with no HUD. Keren's talk is the only primary source found with published look-ahead or lead values, and they are screen-percentage values, not pixels. Stray, Dead Space's ALIVE system and Alien: Isolation give primary or near-primary detail for footsteps per surface, breathing and heart rate driven by state, and dread built through misdirection in ambience. extra.companion: Another World is the root of the independent-companion idea. Lester escapes "along with an alien captive known as 'Buddy'", and at the climax Buddy "assists the wounded Lester" (Wikipedia, citing the game). Chahi's own 2018 assessment (Nintendo Life): "His work on developing a relationship between Ico and Yorda progressed even further than my portrayal of Lester and his alien buddy." He also said Inside held "a lot of common spiritual points with Another World." What carries over to WOLF: the bond is built through shared danger and rescues on screen, with no dialogue. Chahi credits minimalism: "the minimalism of the game gives players the space to build their own world in their mind." Dead Space's ALIVE system offers a pattern for WOLF's body, not his mind: Isaac's lines have "multiple recordings that map to his current state – normal, fatigued, and injured" (TheSixthAxis, recapping the Motive livestream of 11 Mar 2022). Giving WOLF a few variants of the same short bark (normal / strained / damaged) would let his memory of how he was treated surface through delivery as well as through his choices. Somerville (Chris Olsen, Jumpship) also gives a non-human companion, the family dog, no gameplay agency. I could not fetch any Dino Patti or Olsen interview about companion design (UNVERIFIED / not found). Do not cite Somerville for companion mechanics.
extra.level_and_camera:
CAMERA LEAD / LOOK-AHEAD (the admitted gap). Published values from Itay Keren's 'Scroll Back' (GDC 2015 IGS, written version on Game Developer and gamedesignskills.com):
(1) Defender, forward-focus: "Defender always tries to focus the screen on an imaginary point in front of the spaceship, around 25% screen-width forward."
(2) Super Mario Bros, speedup zone: "adding a virtual point, around 25% off-center, where the camera speeds up to catch up with Mario, so when he hits the edge, the camera speed would already be caught up."
(3) Super Mario World, dual-forward-focus with hysteresis: "there are two anchors allowing wide forward view in whatever direction the player chooses to go. However even as the player starts heading back... the camera will keep the target point until Mario hits a predefined threshold, and only then will it lock to the other anchor." The threshold is not given in the article (UNVERIFIED).
(4) Rayman, vertical: the camera-window height is "just over the height of Rayman's jump", and "the camera does not move as Rayman jumps, but rather gently snaps when he lands." This is platform-snapping, defined as "Camera snaps to the player only as it lands on a platform."
(5) Smoothing: "if Lerp is EaseOut, then physics-smoothing is EaseInOut"; use SmoothDamp-style damping "that takes into consideration the distance to the target as well as the current velocity."
(6) Cue focus: in ITSP, "double-ring attractor cues... The outer ring gradually shifts the camera focus towards the cue, using weighted average."
(7) Comfort: "Conflicting sensory signals (Visual vs. Vestibular) may lead to discomfort and nausea... still very much in effect in 2D games."
Keren publishes NO pixel values, lerp factors or seconds; the only numbers are the 25% figures and NES 256x240. GMTK's video: only the page title could be read, so any GMTK pixel or percentage values are UNVERIFIED. Derived (my arithmetic, not a source): 25% of a 1920px-wide viewport is 480px of lead, and 25% of 1280 is 320px. For WOLF's walking pace and its horror tone, a lead well below Defender's would likely read better. Treat 25% as a ceiling, not a target (design opinion).
FLIP-SCREEN TO SCROLLING (New 'n' Tasty). Just Add Water "abandoned the original's flip screen aspect in favor of continuous scrolling, which dramatically changes the gameplay" (Wikipedia, citing the Eurogamer Expo 2012 coverage). The Red Bull feature, quoted by Wikipedia (the live page now returns 404): "In the original, the player could reset a screen's puzzle or AI, by returning to the previous screen and then re-entering the current one. Now, with realtime screen streaming, the developers needed to find a new way to reset enemy AI." Gilray's point (search snippet only, God is a Geek, UNVERIFIED wording): with flip screens you had to decide before going through, but scrolling lets you see farther ahead and change plans without restarting from a checkpoint. He also mentioned discussing an optional original-style flip-screen mode (UNVERIFIED). Look-ahead values for New 'n' Tasty: NOT FOUND in any fetched source.
DOORWAYS / CUTS (Another World): the game has "no HUD or dialog, giving the player only a representation of the surrounding game world during both gameplay elements and the cutscenes" (Wikipedia). Chahi on structure: "the pacing. How events happen, climatic rhythms, moments of surprise while playing." I could not get Chahi's own words on the screen-to-screen cut technique from a fetchable source; the GDC 2011 postmortem video exists (Vault page fetched) but was not transcribed (UNVERIFIED).
SOMERVILLE: reviewers describe the camera as authored and pulled back. TheXboxHub: "pushing the camera far away from the action, making you feel like an observer or spy." Game Informer: "the camera looks out toward the horizon to frame a particularly impressive vista." The cost reviewers name is readability. Game Informer: "jumping up on ledges – a frequent action – is sometimes harder than it should be" and "the protagonist gets stuck in geometry". TheXboxHub: "you'll find yourself stuck, mostly as you miss the slightest opening which you need to get through." I found no Jumpship primary source on camera or doorway handling (UNVERIFIED).
extra.death_and_saves: New 'n' Tasty (Wikipedia, citing a 2014 Gilray podcast): the Exoddus-style quicksave was added "after frustrations from the original Abe's Oddysee", and "a checkpoint save system like the original returned, but the frequency has been increased." A difficulty setting "changes gameplay elements such as Abe's health and enemy reaction times." The key lesson for WOLF's drop-evidence-on-death model is that scrolling removed the free reset that flip screens gave. Once rooms are 1.5 to 2 screens wide, re-entering a room can no longer double as the reset. Safe points and death respawns have to own the job of resetting the sentry, tank and evidence state explicitly. Another World: "numerous checkpoints enabling the player to keep restarting at the last point indefinitely". On machines without saves, "the player can write down an alphanumeric code for these checkpoints" (Wikipedia). Its deaths are quick, frequent and cheap, which supports trial-and-error rooms. Flashback 2013 remake: "The game's difficulty was decreased" (Wikipedia, citing GameSpot).
extra.inventory_and_evidence: Little direct material in these sources. Another World has no inventory and no HUD by design. Chahi: a focus on score "was anti-immersive, so I decided intentionally to break that rule" (Nintendo Life). The Flashback 2013 remake added "a new skill system that trades points for skill improvements and character customization" and 360-degree aiming (Wikipedia, citing Polygon/Eurogamer; neither primary page could be fetched). Takeaway (design inference): keep the evidence CASE diegetic and off-screen except when opened, in line with Chahi's no-HUD stance. Do not bolt RPG progression onto a cinematic platformer; the poorly received remake and sequel are a caution (see avoid).
extra.action_and_impact:
ROTOSCOPED WEIGHT. Chahi defines rotoscoping as "filming real actors, and then copying each step of their movement" (anotherworld.fr). In Another World he used "the Amiga's genlock capabilities to create rotoscoped animations with the polygons, using video recordings of himself performing various actions" (Wikipedia, citing the GDC 2011 postmortem). He calls the polygon tracing work "a time attack race". His tools: "An Amiga 500 with 1 MB ram + 20Mb hard drive", a bytecode VM with "256 variables" and "64 independent execution channels". Flashback has "rotoscoped animation, with unusually fluid movements similar to Prince of Persia", made with "a more complicated method of first tracing video images onto transparencies" (Wikipedia). The 2013 remake switched from "rotoscoped 2D" to "2.5D" (Wikipedia, citing Eurogamer's Cuisset interview, which I could not fetch). I could not reach any Paul Cuisset postmortem in his own words (UNVERIFIED). Practical lesson for the engineer: film yourself doing the turn, start, stop, stumble and crouch, then trace key poses. Rotoscoped starts and stops carry the weight people remember from these games, and that matters more than the smoothness of the walk cycle.
TIMING. Sam Cooper (Alien: Isolation audio lead, MCV): "timing and cohesion is key, a sound that plays a second or two late can mean the difference between abject horror and catastrophic comedy." This applies directly to the impact kit (shake, hit-stop and sound must land on the same frame).
extra.presentation_ui_art: Another World: no HUD except an oxygen bar while swimming, and no on-screen text (Wikipedia, citing a 1UP retrospective). Chahi on score displays: "anti-immersive, so I decided intentionally to break that rule." Chahi's inspirations: "pictorial art, movies and science fiction books, like Dune or Hyperion" (Wikipedia, citing Eurogamer). Flashback: "fully hand-drawn backdrops" with rotoscoped sprites. That pairing of painterly static backgrounds with traced, weighty characters is close to WOLF//OVERRIDE's painterly parallax rooms. Somerville uses letterboxed widescreen and authored, distant framing; reviewers praise the vistas but report missed openings and ledges they could not read. In a painterly 2.5D room, walkable edges and doorway gaps need a readable value or rim-light contrast (design inference). Dead Space remake goal: "an 'uninterrupted sequence shot', absent of loading screens" (Wikipedia, citing GameSpot). This supports walk-through doorways with no fade.
extra.audio:
STRAY, footsteps per surface (A Sound Effect; Raphael Monnin, BlueTwelve sound designer): "we recorded nearly all the foley: footsteps, jumps, and lands on different surfaces (we have 28 in total) such as concrete, dirt, carpet, water, wood, tile, plastic, metal, etc." Scratch sounds were also recorded on wall, tree, carpet and metal. Iteration: "We tried them in the game and if we weren't happy with the results, we restarted the process again until we were satisfied." Yann van der Cruyssen: a custom Unreal physics-audio component that "knows if an object is rolling, sliding, or simply hit, and uses both loops and one-shots, often with multiple round-robin or velocity-mapped alternatives." They used no middleware; it was built on Unreal's native audio. Monnin hit "synchronization problems on different platforms such as PS4 and PS5 with audio artifacts such as crackles" on animation-driven sounds; the fix is not described. Ambience: van der Cruyssen "recorded many ambient soundscapes... in Japan... Korea... and France during the 2020 Covid lockdown" and "manually removed all the human components." Who physically performed the cat foley is not stated in what I read (UNVERIFIED). Note that 28 surfaces covers foot, jump and land per surface. For WOLF, three to five surfaces (metal grate, plate, wet floor, cable/rubber) times walk/land/scuff is the matching scale.
DEAD SPACE remake, ALIVE system (recaps of the EA Motive livestream of 11 Mar 2022; speaker Terry Calico, Senior VO Designer, per MP1st): the system "controls Isaac's heart rate, breathing, and dialogue." It takes "external factors like jump scares, oxygen level, fatigue and more to trigger varying amounts of adrenaline that then impact how he sounds in game." The fix over the original: "In the original game, Isaac's breathing and heart beat would get heavier and faster as he was more damaged, but actually continue to play underneath grunts and cries from physical exertion." In the remake, "Isaac's breathing and physical exertion will be kept separate", and breathing has to recover after vacuum. Scripted lines have "multiple recordings that map to his current state – normal, fatigued, and injured" (TheSixthAxis). The expansion of the A.L.I.V.E. acronym (Adrenaline, Limbic System Response, Intelligent Dialog, Vitals, Exertions) appeared only in a search snippet, not in any fetched page: UNVERIFIED. Also from the A Sound Effect recap: the occlusion/obstruction system gives "more accurate sound positioning and distance attenuation and filtering" (Jean-Francois Tremblay, Lead Sound Designer). No ALIVE numbers (BPM ranges, decay times) were published in what I read.
ALIEN: ISOLATION, room tone and dread. Sam Cooper (audio lead, MCV): they used "psychoacoustic phenomena such as conditioning, misdirection and innate or primal responses to certain sounds and frequencies." Misdirection is "sound that subtly conjures up dark and scary imagery on seemingly mundane objects." Tech: real-time DSP, "convolution reverbs", "HRTF/Binaural processing." Music is dynamic and "changes depending on both what the player and the Alien is doing" (SEGAbits). Talks that exist, but whose content I could not transcribe: Alistair Hope's 'Building Fear in Alien: Isolation' (GDC 2015) and Steve Whetman and Byron Bullock's 'Foley in Alien: Isolation & Gears of War: Ultimate Edition' (GDC 2016). The Sound Architect interview (Cooper, Bullock) could not be fetched because of an expired TLS certificate. From its search snippet only (UNVERIFIED): the soundscape evolves through the game and adds ambiguity so players keep second-guessing what they hear. Bullock reportedly said the alien uses sound as its main hunting sense, so players always weigh their own noise. I found no published layer counts or emitter counts. Accolades (Dynamedion bio): BAFTA 2015 Audio Achievement, GDCA 2015 Best Audio, and others.
extra.mobile_and_input: Nothing in these sources covers touch input. Indirect lessons: Somerville reviewers' complaints ("Grabbing levers and switches is inconsistent", ledges "harder than it should be") are the failures that hold-to-move plus one USE will hit on a phone if interact radii and ledge auto-climb are tight. Generous interact zones and automatic step-up for WOLF's single walkable height change avoid them (design inference). New 'n' Tasty added difficulty settings and more frequent checkpoints. Just Add Water's Unity switch cut per-platform porting from "3–4 months" to "2–4 weeks" (Wikipedia, citing Game Informer); the 14-person team shipped in 16 months.

steal: Dual-forward-focus with hysteresis (Super Mario World, per Keren): two lead anchors, and the camera keeps the current one until the engineer has walked back past a threshold. A brief turn to look at WOLF should not swing the camera.

Cap horizontal lead at about 25% of screen width (Defender, per Keren), and probably use less for a slow horror walk. Ease it in with damping that accounts for both distance and velocity (Keren: 'physics-smoothing is EaseInOut', SmoothDamp).

Platform-snapping for the one walkable height change per room (Rayman, per Keren): keep the vertical camera still within a window about one step-up tall and re-center gently once the engineer lands on the new level.

Cue-focus attractors (ITSP double-ring weighted average, per Keren): let the copy station, sentry or exit bolt pull the framing slightly as the engineer approaches. This works for WOLF's 'look here' scouting too.

Treat losing the flip-screen reset as a design task (New 'n' Tasty): when rooms widen, give each room an explicit reset owner, such as safe points or death respawn resetting the sentry, tank and door state.

Separate breathing from exertion (Dead Space ALIVE): run a breathing/heart layer driven by stress and recovery underneath, and play exertion grunts as one-shots on top, not layered unmanaged under them.
Record 2-3 state variants (normal/strained/hurt) of key engineer and WOLF barks (Dead Space's normal/fatigued/injured), chosen at runtime.
Per-surface foley including jump and land, not just step, with round-robin and velocity-mapped variants (Stray: 28 surfaces; roll/slide/hit-aware physics audio).
Room tone that misdirects: mundane machinery that 'subtly conjures up dark and scary imagery' (Alien: Isolation, Sam Cooper), with convolution reverb per room.
No HUD during play; the world carries the state (Another World). Keep the evidence CASE diegetic.
Rotoscope the engineer's start/stop/turn/stumble from video of a real performer (Chahi filmed himself; Flashback traced video onto transparencies).
Seamless 'sequence shot' doorways with no fades (Dead Space remake goal).
avoid: Authored, distant cinematic framing that makes ledges, levers and narrow openings unreadable. Somerville reviewers report getting stuck in geometry, inconsistent lever grabs, and ledges 'harder than it should be'.
Letting room re-entry silently act as the puzzle or AI reset once rooms scroll (New 'n' Tasty had to replace this mechanic).
Playing breathing/heartbeat loops underneath exertion grunts with no priority. Dead Space's own team called this the original's flaw.
Audio landing even slightly late on scares and impacts. Cooper: 'a second or two late' turns horror into comedy.

Bolting skill-point RPG progression and a 2.5D 3D re-render onto a rotoscoped cinematic platformer. The 2013 Flashback remake swapped rotoscoped 2D for 2.5D and added a skill system; Flashback 2 (2023) was rated 'generally unfavorable' and Metacritic's second worst of 2023 (the specific reasons were not verified).
Citing GMTK or New 'n' Tasty look-ahead pixel values. None were verifiable in this pass.
Over-large camera lead (much beyond 25% of the screen) in a slow walking horror game. Keren warns that visual/vestibular conflict causes nausea even in 2D.

extra.games: Limbo iOS (Playdead, 2013); INSIDE iOS/Apple TV (Playdead, 2017); Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty mobile (Oddworld Inhabitants, 2017); Little Nightmares mobile (Tarsier/Bandai Namco, port by Playdigious, 2023); Alto's Odyssey (Snowman/Team Alto, 2018); Monument Valley (ustwo games, 2014); procedural audio references: No Man's Sky (Hello Games, audio by Paul Weir/Earcom), Nicolas Fournel GDC 2010 (Sony), Andy Farnell's Designing Sound (MIT Press, 2010). Platform rules: Apple HIG (Game controls, Accessibility, Designing for games, Buttons) and Android accessibility (48 dp).
extra.why_relevant: WOLF//OVERRIDE plans to ship phone touch with hold-to-move, one USE (tap or hold), two choice buttons and Pause, in a dark, painterly 2.5D side-view horror game. Four ports in the same genre show which touch schemes worked. All four (Limbo, INSIDE, Oddworld NnT, Little Nightmares) avoid a visible fixed d-pad by default and use relative drag/swipe from wherever the finger lands; none uses tap-to-move. That supports the hold-to-move decision. INSIDE iOS also shows two risks that apply directly here: a hidden press-and-hold interact can confuse players, and dark art on an iPhone screen can hide what is interactable. Oddworld's mobile GameSpeak (tap an icon, then tap a sentence) is the closest shipped precedent for issuing context commands to a companion with few buttons. Apple and Android give hard minimums for target size, padding and text size. No Man's Sky's VocAlien is a shipped precedent for synthesised (not sampled) creature vocals, which suits WOLF's voice and the plan for procedural audio. Gaps: no port team I could fetch published zone sizes in mm/pt, frame-rate targets or thermal targets. My web-search budget ran out mid-task, so a few leads (TouchArcade reviews, the MIT Press page, Little Nightmares developer quotes) are unverified or come only from secondary paraphrase.

extra.companion: No source covers a companion on mobile directly. The closest shipped precedent is Oddworld NnT mobile's GameSpeak, which uses no extra buttons. Pocket Gamer's hands-on: "the voice commands are brought up by tapping an icon and then on the sentence you want Abe to say." Requests to WOLF could work the same way: the two choice buttons appear only when a WOLF request or decision is live, and each shows the words of the line (for example "Scout ahead" / "Stay"). They should not be abstract A/B glyphs. Apple's HIG supports this: "Show and hide virtual controls to reflect gameplay ... hide controls when an action isn't available or relevant." Apple's HIG also says "consider letting players tap objects to select them instead of adding a virtual selection button". For WOLF, a tap on WOLF himself could stand in for a generic "talk to WOLF" command (inference, not tested). A caution from Engadget/TouchArcade: NnT's on-screen controls "can get a little busy" because the console game used most of the pad's buttons. WOLF's design stays within budget only if companion commands share the two choice slots and never add permanent buttons.
extra.level_and_camera: Readability at phone size is the main risk the sources show for a dark side-scroller. iMore on INSIDE iPhone: "it's a little dark on iPhone. I even turned up the brightness ... the right side of the screen is sometimes so dark that I can't tell whether there is something to interact with". On iPad "it's a completely different story. It looks great." In wider 1.5-2 screen rooms, the interactables (copy stations, relays, the bolt) need a lit rim, a silhouette or a WOLF look-at cue that survives a small, dim phone screen. Check the room on the smallest target phone at low brightness. Little Nightmares mobile (Pocket Gamer): seeing tiny Six "in the palm of your hand makes her appear just all the more vulnerable". A small character can add horror on a phone, but only if hazards and interactables stay readable. This fits the decided tighter zoom. Apple HIG: games must work at "16:10, 19.5:9, and 4:3", and in-game menus must stay legible "without obscuring other content". The room framing therefore needs safe margins so the phone's wide 19.5:9 crop does not push the next doorway or the height change off screen. Limbo (Playdead, quoted by Cult of Mac): "we were amazed by how well the game looked on the smaller screens". High-contrast silhouette art carries to phones. Muddy mid-tones are the risk, as INSIDE shows.
extra.death_and_saves: The mobile sources give little on death models. What they show: Monument Valley's store copy says it is "Designed to be easy for everyone to pick up, enjoy and complete". A Kotaku quote in the listing calls it "The most sublime hour my iPad has ever given me", which is a rough length signal of about an hour of total play (press quote, not a developer metric). Alto's team (Pocket Gamer interview) aims for games "that fans may sit with for a short time, but that sits with them for a long time afterward". The Little Nightmares mobile copy (iThinkDiff) stresses cloud saves so players can "pick up and play whenever and wherever". Inference for WOLF (not sourced): phone sessions get interrupted, so app suspend or backgrounding should not cost unsecured evidence unfairly. Either auto-pause on focus loss, or treat a suspend like a soft safe point for position while keeping the drop-on-death rule for actual deaths. I found no developer-stated session-length target for any of these games: UNVERIFIED.
extra.inventory_and_evidence: Apple's HIG rules map directly onto a CASE screen on a phone. Place "secondary controls, like menus, at the top of the screen". Less important controls such as menus need "a minimum size of 28x28 pt". Frequently used controls need "a minimum size of 44x44 pt". Use about 12 pt of padding around bezelled elements and about 24 pt around elements without a bezel. Android: 48x48 dp (about 9 mm) separated by 8 dp or more. Apple: "consider letting players tap objects to select them instead of adding a virtual selection button". In the CASE, evidence items should therefore be tap targets themselves, each at least 44x44 pt, with no separate cursor and Select button. Text rule (HIG Designing for games): iOS default 17 pt, minimum 11 pt. Item names and evidence captions should not drop below 11 pt on a phone, and should aim for 17. None of the ports I studied has an inventory comparable to the CASE, so I have no shipped mobile precedent to give.
extra.action_and_impact: On press feedback, Apple's HIG says: "Always include visible and tactile press states. A virtual control feels unresponsive without a visual and physical press state ... a glow, that they can see even when their finger is covering the control. Combine this press state with sound and haptics". USE (tap or hold) and the choice buttons should glow beyond the thumb's footprint, play a click and fire a light haptic. This also fits the existing impact kit. Hold-to-interact is a known pain point. iMore on INSIDE iOS: "In order to interact with an object, you have to press and hold while near it. It's totally counter-intuitive", and the reviewer got stuck "exiting the submarine or jumping to a rope". WOLF's USE hold needs a visible fill or progress ring and a clear tap-versus-hold threshold. Hold-only actions should be telegraphed in the world before the player needs them. Little Nightmares mobile's swipe scheme "performed very well", but the reviewer's Six still "ate the ground or ended up diving into nothingness more times than I would care to admit". Gesture jumps cost precision. WOLF has no jump, so a hold-to-move plus button scheme avoids the main failure of swipe schemes.
extra.presentation_ui_art: Text legibility (Apple, Designing for games): iOS/iPadOS default 17 pt, minimum 11 pt. Text should contrast well with the background. Do not rely on colour alone ("avoid relying solely on color to convey an important detail"). Let players customise "type size, game control mapping, motion intensity, and sound balance". That supports a screen-shake toggle and a UI-scale option. On a clean screen versus visible controls, Little Nightmares mobile offers two schemes (Pocket Gamer): "an onscreen keypad with permanent buttons ... or an immersive system where swiping decides your movement, jumps, and crouches". The reviewer picked immersive "so you have a cleaner screen". Apple: "consider hiding movement controls until a player touches the screen". On a resting stick, the HIG illustration notes "When the thumbstick is at rest, the virtual control fades". Performance/quality scaling: the Oddworld team let players lower "resolution or turning off post-effects" (Engadget), and NnT lets players "resize or move buttons". For the in-game changelog, none of the sources covered one: no data.
extra.audio: Shipped procedural audio, primary: GDC 2017, Paul Weir (Earcom), "The Sound of 'No Man's Sky'". The talk page says NMS pairs conventional sound design with "an innovative vocal modeling synthesizer plugin and a custom built generative music system". It describes "how we built VocAlien, our physically modeled vocal tract synthesis plugin and the challenges in creating an end-to-end procedural audio pipeline". It also says 65daysofstatic could "both compose a traditional album and create generative soundscapes without compromising their sound". Takeaways: shipped games mix procedural with authored sound, and synthesised creature voices are proven in a released title. That makes VocAlien a direct precedent for a synthesised WOLF voice (growls, servo whines, breath) whose parameters can follow WOLF's trust and memory state. GDC 2010, Nicolas Fournel (SCEE), "Procedural Audio for Video Games: Are we there yet?": he frames procedural audio as the answer to "Explosion of content, non-repetitive sound effects, need for interactive music". The talk covers "design choices to typical game sound models, and from tools and engines requirements to quality assurance". That supports keeping QA in mind, since synth output varies per run. Andy Farnell, Designing Sound (MIT Press, 2010, 688 pp.): verified as a bibliographic record only. I could not fetch the publisher description, so the book's contents and quotes are UNVERIFIED. Mobile audio framing: Monument Valley's listing says "Audio reacts to your manipulation of the world ... Best experienced with headphones"; Alto's Odyssey says "Headphones recommended!". These games treat headphones as the primary mobile listening mode. Room tone and footstep detail should be mixed for earbuds and also checked on the phone speaker.
extra.mobile_and_input: How each port handled movement and visible controls. (1) Limbo iOS (2013): Playdead called it the first touch-only version. They said: "nailing the 'ultimate' touch based controls would be a serious drag and that optimizing the performance all over again would take a while", and earlier "Rethinking the controls and performing extensive optimizations to ensure an amazing touch-based experience" (both via Cult of Mac). The exact gesture mapping (tap and drag left/right to move, drag up to jump, hold and drag to pull) comes from an App Unwrapper guide I could not fetch: UNVERIFIED. (2) INSIDE iOS (2017): "Swipe left or right to move back or forward and swipe up to jump. Move forward while tapping the screen to push objects" (iOS Hacker). Interact is "press and hold while near it" (iMore). There are no on-screen buttons. TouchArcade's reported "swipe and hold anywhere on the screen" is UNVERIFIED (403). (3) Oddworld NnT mobile (2017): "there wasn't a virtual stick in sight. You'll slide your finger left and right to move ..., swipe up to jump, and down to roll". GameSpeak is reached by tapping an icon and then a sentence (Pocket Gamer, GDC 2016 hands-on). At launch: "swipe on the side of the screen to perform actions like 'use,' and 'sneak'", plus "resize or move buttons", plus full controller support (Engadget). (4) Little Nightmares mobile (Playdigious, 2023): the player chooses between a visible keypad with permanent buttons and an immersive swipe scheme for movement, jumps and crouches (Pocket Gamer review). Pocket Gamer reports only a paraphrase that Playdigious "intended to make sure controls came first"; I found no direct developer quote. Hold-to-move versus tap-to-move: none of the four uses tap-to-move or point-and-click. All use relative drag from wherever the finger lands, which is in effect an invisible floating stick. That matches Apple's advice: "opt to show a virtual thumbstick wherever the player lands their thumb instead of a static thumbstick position", "players expect to control movement using the left side of their screen", and "Maximize the amount of space ... by using as large of an input area as possible". Zone sizes: none of the port teams published zone dimensions in pt or mm (gap). The platform floors are Apple 44x44 pt for frequent controls and 28x28 pt for menus, about 12/24 pt padding, and keeping clear of "the Home indicator or Dynamic Island". Android's floor is 48x48 dp, about 9 mm, with 8 dp or more spacing, and it cites an industry 7-10 mm. Placement (Apple): "Place frequently used buttons near a player's thumb, avoiding the circular regions where players expect movement and camera input". Frame-rate and thermal: no port team gave fps or thermal targets in any source I fetched (UNVERIFIED/absent). The only statements are Playdead's "optimizing the performance all over again" and Oddworld's user-facing resolution and post-effects options. iOS exposes four thermal states (nominal, fair, serious, critical; "critical" means "the device needs to cool down"). An adaptive-quality step tied to those states is a reasonable target to investigate in Godot (inference). Proposed WOLF layout, derived from the above and not tested: the left half of the screen is an invisible hold-to-move zone with a fading floating indicator. On the right, one USE button of at least 56-64 pt (the HIG's 44 pt is a minimum) with a hold-fill ring. The two choice buttons sit above USE and appear only when a choice is live, worded, each at least 44 pt with at least 12 pt gap. Pause goes top corner, at least 28 pt, inside the safe area.

steal: Make movement an invisible floating hold-to-move zone on the left half of the screen, anchored where the thumb lands, with no fixed d-pad. All four genre ports avoid a fixed stick by default, and Apple's HIG recommends 'a virtual thumbstick wherever the player lands their thumb' with 'as large of an input area as possible'.
Show a faint indicator while the thumb is down and fade it at rest (HIG). Hide controls that are not relevant right now.
Offer two touch layouts as Little Nightmares mobile does: immersive (minimal, the default) and visible buttons (fixed glyphs for players who want them).

Show the choice buttons only when a choice or WOLF request is live, and label them with words. This follows Oddworld's 'tap an icon and then the sentence' GameSpeak and the HIG's 'hide controls when an action isn't available'.
Let players 'resize or move buttons' (Oddworld NnT mobile) and add a type-size option (HIG personalisation).
Use press states that show past the thumb (a glow), plus a sound and a haptic on USE and the choice buttons (HIG). Add a fill ring for hold-USE so the tap/hold split is never hidden.
Make interactables tappable directly where it makes sense (tap WOLF, tap a CASE item) instead of adding selection buttons (HIG).

Size floors: 44x44 pt for USE and choices (go bigger for USE), 28x28 pt for Pause and menus, about 12 pt padding, 17 pt text by default with an 11 pt minimum, and keep clear of the Home indicator and Dynamic Island.
Ship graphics scaling like Oddworld's (lower resolution, post-effects off). Consider adapting quality to iOS thermal state (inference).
Use VocAlien-style synthesised vocals as the base for WOLF's voice so his timbre can follow trust and memory, layered over authored room tone and footsteps (the hybrid No Man's Sky shipped).
Hold the line on input count as Alto's team did: 'anything that required more than one touch input, didn't really feel right', and they cut the grappling mechanic for adding gestures.
avoid: Hidden press-and-hold interactions with no on-screen cue. iMore found INSIDE's 'press and hold while near it' 'totally counter-intuitive' and got stuck at the submarine exit and the rope jump.
Dark grading that hides interactables on small, dim phone screens. On iPhone, the iMore reviewer could not 'tell whether there is something to interact with'.
Cramming console button counts onto glass. NnT's touch controls 'can get a little busy', and Ryan Cash warns against games that 'cram a lot of inputs into a small space and end up feeling unnatural'.
Gesture-based precision actions. In Little Nightmares, swipe jumps sent Six 'diving into nothingness' too often. Keep WOLF's essential actions on hold-move plus buttons.
Placing buttons inside the movement thumb's circle, or under system UI (HIG).
Claiming port-team fps or thermal targets or touch-zone mm figures: none were found in any fetched source.
Leaning on procedural audio claims attributed to Farnell's book until its text is actually read: only the bibliographic record was verified.

ref.title: WOLF//OVERRIDE Design Reference: what shipped games teach the next slice (2026-10-10)
ref.executive_summary: About 25 shipped games point WOLF//OVERRIDE the same way. Deaths should be quick, easy to read and cheap. Aim for roughly 20 seconds of replay, keep room sound playing through the respawn, and give every hazard a warning before it can kill. The evidence-drop death rule does have precedent: Hollow Knight, Dark Souls and especially Celeste's strawberries all do something like it. The safe version drops unsecured evidence as a visible cache where the engineer fell, outside the hazard. A second death never destroys essential evidence, and evidence is secured by a short in-world action at a safe point. Keep the CASE small, pause-only and carried by the engineer. WOLF feels alive through many small signals: look-at, breathing, idle business and an instant reaction to every input. Frequent refusals do not do that. Refusals stay rare, visible decisions, and every essential task keeps an engineer path. Wider rooms only work if every screen-width holds something to do. Sound should carry off-screen threats and WOLF, and screen effects should be used sparingly. Two code fixes are urgent. The sentry's visible beam covers about a fifth of its real sight range. And it starts chasing on the first frame it sees the engineer, moving faster than the engineer walks. Some research inputs still arrived cut off (see Pipeline status).
top_changes: 1. Make room width per room (NOW). ROOM_WIDTH is a 960 px const (apps/game/scripts/room_depth.gd:15), and the camera clamp hard-codes 960 (main.gd ~394). Each room should export its own width: 1067-1422 px gives 1.5-2 views at the current 1.35 zoom, where the view is 711 px wide. Evidence: INSIDE sizes rooms by content ('Each Puzzle span around 100 meters or 1-3min of gameplay', Unite 2016). Fits: the wider-rooms decision.

2. Plan every wide room as one beat per view-width before building it (NOW). The beats are an entry reveal, a WOLF or decision beat, the height change, the threat or puzzle, and the doorway. Cut any view-width that has no beat. Walking one view takes about 3.7 s at 190 px/s, and a 2-view room about 7.5 s. Evidence: Planet of Lana's 'quite a bit of uneventful running' (Nintendo Life), INSIDE's 1-3 min chunks, Limbo cutting ~70% of its ideas.

3. Build each height change as a walkable step or ramp, or a USE climb that works from anywhere in the approach zone (NOW). Keep both levels on one gameplay plane, and put soft contact shadows under the engineer, WOLF and the sentry. Evidence: Little Nightmares' depth deaths ('you'll inevitably misjudge your position and perish', Push Square), Planet of Lana's ledge sweet spot (RPS), Carlsen's 'correct solution is fairly easy to execute', Stray's prompt-gated jumps that always land, INSIDE's foot shadow decals.

4. Treat respawn as a 'scene change' (NOW). Keep the knockdown at or under today's ~1.45 s (0.7 s controls off, 0.4 s fade out, 0.35 s fade in). Room tone and threat loops keep playing, only the mutable gameplay state reloads, and sound changes are queued until the fade-in. Make doorways walk-through, never a fade. Evidence: INSIDE Wwise Tour 2016 ('Audio should retain state and continue during load', 'the illusion of no time passing'); LN2 'nearly immediate respawn'. Celeste is ~2 s, or ~1.1 s if skipped (derived from code).

5. Give evidence three states: absent, carried (unsecured) and secured (NOW). Today's purge_trace_preserved and mirror_trace_preserved booleans become per-record states. A record is secured only by a deliberate action at a safe point. Evidence: Celeste strawberries follow the player and only count after >0.15 s on safe ground (decompile, derived). Limbo eggs, INSIDE orbs and LN collectibles persist once collected.

6. Use a recoverable drop, not a destructive one (NEXT; needs Nathanial's ruling). On death, unsecured evidence becomes a visible cache at the death spot, placed outside the hazard's trigger. Reaching it re-secures the carry. A second death must never destroy essential evidence: keep or merge the caches, or send them back to where they were found as Celeste does. Evidence: Hollow Knight Shade (a second death erases the old Shade's Geo; the Shade spawns outside boss arenas; it is marked on the map), Dark Souls bloodstain, Silksong Cocoon, Celeste's return to origin.

7. Space restore points tightly (NOW/NEXT). Autosave at each room entry and after each completed beat, so a death replays about 20 s at most. Put evidence-securing safe points at doorways, never inside a hazard, and at most about 1-2 rooms apart. Evidence: Limbo 'twenty-ish seconds' (HG101 reviewer estimate), New 'n' Tasty capped lost progress at 3 screens (Wikipedia citing a podcast; UNVERIFIED), Grip warns that 20 minutes from a save turns tension into 'anger and frustration'.

8. Make the safe point a short, committed in-world action (NEXT). Hold USE for about 1-3 s while the station's own lights count down as the real progress. Use a warm, lit prop, a single non-looping 'secured' cue and a faint beacon tone audible from the next room. Evidence: Alien: Isolation's 3-second save with three lights and three beeps ('Saving becomes part of the fabric of the horror'), the Bunker lamp lighting up, the RE2 (2019) non-looping Save Room track, Ico benches and Dark Souls bonfires as 'places of warmth'.

9. Fix the sentry's tell (NOW). sentry.gd draws a 34 px beam, but SentryBrain.SIGHT_RANGE is 180 px, so the drawn beam covers about 19% of what the sentry can actually see. Draw a light shaft or floor glow out to the full range, or shrink the range. Evidence: Lilja found that players take tells literally (they decided enemies could smell Six); INSIDE clamps its fog so bright lights 'bleed through'.

10. Add an alert beat before the chase (NOW). Today the sentry switches from patrol to chase on the first frame it sees the engineer, then moves at 230 px/s against the engineer's 190 px/s walk. Add a lock-on state: red eye (EYE_LOCKED already exists), an alarm stinger and a brief stop. End chases at the rubble line with a visible barrier and a survival stinger. Evidence: Lilja ('if an enemy screams, it's because they are alerted'), LN chases ending at a line the enemy cannot cross, Limbo's survival stinger, LN2's 'replay each scene at least twice' criticism.

11. Play-test the engineer-only tank drop on a phone (NOW). Today's window is about 0.63 s against a patrolling sentry and about 0.38 s against a chasing one (HIT_RANGE 44, FALL_SECONDS 0.45). Never auto-complete it. If touch play misses, widen it. Evidence: INSIDE iOS named its sentry-gun sections the hardest touch spots and rejected auto-complete because it 'loses feeling of interaction'.

12. Replace WOLF's single follow rule with a small intent-vote brain (NOW). Today it is a 64 px gap at 220 px/s in m0_actor.gd. The new intents are Follow, Scout, Lead, Hold/Refuse and Protect, and each picks an object of interest, moves to it, then acts. Unlock intents as WOLF's memory and trust grow. Evidence: the INSIDE Huddle ('every impulse is just a vote'); Trico's three-step interest model (Famitsu CEDEC 2017); Alien: Isolation's behaviour tree, with branches 'locked off' at the start; Trico finding new areas by wandering.

13. Make WOLF react instantly, then decide visibly (NOW). Every input or trigger gets an immediate acknowledgement (ear, head turn), then a readable decision: lean in, pull back, or paw and look at the reason. Add head-first look-at and a breathing or servo idle layer. Evidence: Trico's critics ('impatience and frustration due to lack of immediate action'), Six 'would take too long to take a cue' (Shacknews), Playdead's additive 'breathe' and 'look around' layers. No source gives a number of seconds, so tune the timing by play.

14. Gate every WOLF effect on visible contact (NOW). The relay closes, the seam read starts and the sentry draws only when WOLF's body or light reaches or faces the target. Evidence: INSIDE Huddle: 'Boxes can not be lifted until a lifting arm actually touches them.'

15. Design each room as two halves, one only WOLF can do and one only the engineer can do, and design every essential objective twice: with WOLF and engineer-only (NEXT). The engineer path costs more (time, noise, risk), but it is never impossible and never punishing. Evidence: Planet of Lana's asymmetry (Mui fears water), LN2's complementary tasks, Asobo redesigning levels by whether rat powers are available, and Ueda's rock-paper-scissors framing of protect and be protected.

16. Cover off-screen WOLF and threats with sound first, plus a minimal edge cue (NEXT). Each threat gets its own idle, alert and pursuit sound stems, a 'listening' duck when the engineer hides, and an off-screen identifying sound. WOLF gets a direction-and-state cue (waiting, coming, scouting, refusing) only when he is out of frame. Evidence: Lilja's stem crossfades and listening duck; Planet of Lana's separated-only Mui icon showing 'which direction Mui is located in and what her status is'.

17. Keep the CASE small, pause-only and with the engineer (NEXT). Use fixed slots, with no grid and no rotation. Carry at most about 6 items (Signalis) plus the one tool. In play, show it only as a diegetic tell, such as a light on the engineer's case when something is unsecured. WOLF may optionally carry a duplicate or second item, never the only copy of an essential one. Evidence: Signalis' 6 items, RE1 6/8 slots, Jensen's 'very few elements and no inventory', Stray's tiny inventory, LN2's Six carrying a second item. RE4R's grid needs buttons WOLF's input set does not have.

18. Build footsteps and breathing as state-driven systems (NEXT). Footsteps are chosen by surface and by speed band, with takeoff and brake sounds and up to ~15 dB of adaptive fatigue attenuation, on their own players. Breathing is a sequencer at 1 breath per 2 steps when running, an exhale on a light landing and a grunt on a hard one, and each breath drives an additive chest pose. Evidence: INSIDE AES 2016 / Wwise Tour 2016; Limbo's ~15 dB attenuation (Andersen); Stray's 28 recorded surfaces; Planet of Lana's landing sounds by jump height.

19. Put the impact kit on a budget (NOW). Save full shake, hit-stop and flash for the door blast, the tank drop and similar climaxes. Carry everyday weight with sound and animation-state changes, and add separate off toggles for shake and flash. Evidence: no reference documents shake or hit-stop values; Playdead's VFX talk is titled 'Turn it Down 90%' (only the title was seen); Planet of Lana cut 80% of its robot sound layers; FGDB 'No Screen Shake'.

20. Build depth from fog, value bands and silhouettes, not more parallax (NOW/NEXT). Use a black foreground frame, the gameplay plane, a fogged midground and a backdrop, with a fog clamp so station lights, the relay and the sentry beam read through. Give every character a contact shadow, a constant ambient floor and a rim light, and reserve a palette accent for the engineer and WOLF. Evidence: INSIDE GDC 2016 rendering ('literally just fog + silhouettes', 'fake ambient color'), Planet of Lana's theatre-stage silhouettes, Mervik on Six's contrast, iMore's 'too dark' iPhone complaint.
